user 3 is nobody
hello, Ada
Grace is registered
require(4) gave none

Figure 7.1. The four ways out of a Maybe. Each names what happens when the value is absent.

  1. else gives a fallback. users.find(3) else "nobody" is the value if present, the fallback otherwise. The fallback is evaluated only when needed, and it may be else throw Error... or else panic "..." when absence is not acceptable at that point.
  2. match handles each case, with the case's payload bound by name. A case that only computes a value fits on one line: match users.find(1) { case Maybe.some(name): "hello, " + name; case Maybe.none: "hello, stranger"; }. A case that needs statements takes a block, and both forms mix in one match. It must cover every case.
  3. Nesting stays readable when each step has a name: a match inside a case is allowed, but a separate variable is usually clearer.
  4. try? converts a typed error into absence: try? users.require(4) is Maybe.some(name) if the call returned and Maybe.none if it threw any error. Its counterpart try! asserts that a call cannot fail and turns a thrown error into a panic.

Notice what is not in the list: a way to take the value out without deciding. There is no .get() that throws, no ! that asserts, no implicit unwrapping at an assignment. Every exit from a Maybe names what happens in the none case, and that name is visible in the code.

No automatic wrapping, no collapsing

Two rules keep Maybe predictable. Results are not wrapped automatically: an action declared is Maybe<string> returns Maybe.some(name), not name, so a reader can see which return statements produce an answer and which produce its absence. And nested Maybe values are never collapsed: Maybe<Maybe<int>> keeps both levels, because "the cache has no entry" and "the cache has an entry saying there is no value" are different facts. Languages that collapse nested optionals — TypeScript's undefined, JavaScript's optional chaining — lose exactly that distinction.

7.4 Where a Maybe comes from

A Maybe is not something a programmer meets only in their own code. The language and the standard library answer with one wherever a question may have no answer, and they never answer with a sentinel — no -1 for "not found", no empty string for "not set".

module app v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Lookup is Error = (unknown(name is string));

object Directory {
    has phones is %string:string;
    Directory(:phones);

    // A lookup that may find nothing answers a Maybe.
    phone(name is string) is Maybe<string> {
        if phones.has(name) { Maybe.some(phones[name]); } else { Maybe<string>.none; }
    }

    // The same question as an error, for callers that cannot go on without it.
    require(name is string) is string {
        self.phone(name) else throw Lookup.unknown(name);
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let names = ["ada", "brian", "grace"];
    // Searches answer Maybe, never -1 or an empty string.
    out.writeln((names.index_of("grace") else -1).string() + " " + (names.index_of("linus") else -1).string());
    out.writeln(names.find() -> n { n.starts_with("b"); } else "nobody");
    out.writeln(("a=1;b=2".find(";") else -1).string() + " " + ("a=1".find(";") else -1).string());
    // An index or a key with a fallback; without one, a miss is a failure.
    out.writeln(names[5] else "past the end");
    let book = Directory(phones: ["ada": "555-0101"]);
    out.writeln(book.phone("ada") else "unlisted");
    // Several sources tried in order: each `else` takes the next.
    let office is Maybe<string> = Maybe<string>.none;
    out.writeln(book.phone("brian") else office else "no number");
    // try? turns an error into absence; a Maybe result is kept whole, never flattened.
    out.writeln(try? book.require("grace") else "unknown");
    let nested is Maybe<Maybe<string>> = try? book.phone("grace");
    out.writeln(if nested == Maybe.some(Maybe<string>.none) { "found the answer: no phone"; } else { "something else"; });
    0;
}

Output:

2 -1
brian
3 -1
past the end
555-0101
no number
unknown
found the answer: no phone
  • Searches. index_of(value) on an array, find(part) and find_last(part) on a string answer a Maybe<int>. The functional find block answers a Maybe of the first element that satisfies it: names.find() -> n { n.starts_with("b"); } else "nobody".
  • Indexes and keys, with a fallback. names[5] else "past the end" and stock["kiwi"] else 0 read an element or an entry that may not exist. Without the else, a miss is a runtime failure: the fallback is part of the expression, not an afterthought. A map answers has(key) without looking the value up, so an action that wants to return absence is one if away from a Maybe (the Directory.phone action above).
  • Actions that say so. Any action may declare is Maybe<T>; the standard library does it for every reader of optional data. The json reader's maybe(name), Environment.maybe(name), the configuration sources and a database row's maybe(column) all answer Maybe per kind: row.maybe("nick").text() is Maybe.none when the column holds SQL NULL.
  • try?. It turns a thrown error into Maybe.none (§7.3).
  • Streams. for await asks a stream for its next element with an async next() is Maybe<T> action, and Maybe.none ends the loop. Absence is how a stream says "no more", exactly as it is how a search says "not here" (Chapter 20).

A value is made with Maybe.some(value) and Maybe<T>.none. The type argument of none may be left out when the context gives it — let m is Maybe<int> = Maybe.none; — and must be written when nothing does, because none alone carries no element type.

7.5 else in detail

else after a Maybe is the most common exit, and it has precise rules.

  • The fallback is lazy. It is evaluated only when the value is absent. Maybe.some(0) else panic "eager" never panics; a fallback that computes, logs or allocates costs nothing on the present path.
  • The fallback has the type of the payload. Maybe<int> else 0 is an int. A fallback of another type is a compile-time error ("Fallback must be int, got string"), not a conversion.
  • Three kinds of fallback. An expression of the payload type; throw with an error, when absence is a failure of the caller's contract (Chapter 10); panic with a message, when absence means the program itself is wrong. These are the only three: return, next and last cannot follow else, because a fallback is a value, and control flow that depends on presence is written as a match or an if, where a reader looks for it.
  • Fallbacks chain. book.phone("brian") else office else "no number" tries each source in order: the right-hand else turns office into a string, the left-hand one takes it when the first lookup misses.
  • The same word in confirm. confirm port > 0 else throw ... uses else for a condition rather than an absence (Chapter 10). The fallback is lazy there too: the error is built only when the condition fails.

7.6 A Maybe is a value

Maybe<T> is an ordinary value, and everything Chapter 16 says about variants applies to it.

  • Equality is structural. Maybe.some(3) == Maybe.some(3) is true, and so is Maybe<int>.none == Maybe<int>.none. An array of Maybe values answers contains and index_of by the same equality.
  • It can be a field. An object may hold has note is Maybe<string>; for data that is genuinely optional, and give it a meaning in one place: shown() is string { note else "(no note)"; }. Callers ask the object, not the field.
  • It is not a map key. Map keys must be scalars or key objects (Chapter 8); a field has index is %Maybe<int>:string; is rejected with "Map key type Maybe is not a scalar key type". A map that needs "no key" as a key is usually two structures: the map and the value for the missing case.
  • It owns what it holds. A Maybe that holds an object with a destroy is that object's owner: the object is destroyed when the Maybe goes out of scope, like any other owner (Chapter 11).

7.7 Presence<T>: three states for updates

Some data needs three states, and the most common example is a partial update. When a client sends a JSON PATCH for a user record, each field can mean one of three things: set the field to a new value, clear the field, or leave it as it is. JSON Merge Patch encodes these as a value, a null, and an absent key [RFC 7396; RFC 8259]. A language with only null cannot represent the third state without an extra flag per field; a language with only Maybe cannot represent it either.

Presence<T> has three cases — some(value), none and missing — for exactly this purpose.

module bible/presence v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

// A PATCH request distinguishes three intents for a field:
// set it (some), clear it (none), or leave it alone (missing).
object NicknamePatch {
    has nickname is Presence<string>;
    NicknamePatch(:nickname);

    applied(current is string) is string {
        match nickname {
            case Presence.some(value): value;
            case Presence.none: "";
            case Presence.missing: current;
        };
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let patches is @NicknamePatch = [
        NicknamePatch(nickname: Presence.some("ace")),
        NicknamePatch(nickname: Presence<string>.none),
        NicknamePatch(nickname: Presence<string>.missing)
    ];
    for patches -> patch {
        out.writeln("[" + patch.applied("old") + "]");
    }
    0;
}

Output:

[ace]
[]
[old]

Figure 7.2. Three states of a partial update: set, clear, leave alone.

The patch object's applied action maps "set" to the new value, "clear" to the empty string and "leave alone" to the current value. The compact choice must name all three cases; forgetting missing is a compile-time error, not a bug report from the first client that sends a partial update.

Because Presence carries more information than Maybe, Okkama does not let it degrade silently. else works only on Maybe; on a Presence it is rejected, and the program must say how to merge the two kinds of absence.

module bible/presence_else v1.0.0;

main() is int {
    let nickname is Presence<string> = Presence<string>.missing;
    let shown = nickname else "anonymous";
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

07-presence-rejected.ok:5:17: semantic error: Optional fallback requires Maybe<T>; fold Presence explicitly

nickname.fold() else "anonymous" is the explicit form: fold() turns missing and none into Maybe.none — on purpose, in writing. (In the other direction, Maybe.as_presence() keeps some and none and never invents missing.)

7.8 Absence at the edges

Inside a program, absence is a type. At its edges — environment variables, configuration files, JSON, databases — absence arrives as data, and the standard library draws the same line everywhere: absent is a value, malformed is an error. Environment.maybe("PORT").int() is Maybe.none when the variable is not set and Maybe.some(8080) when it holds 8080; when it holds 80a0, the read throws InvalidEnvironmentValue naming the variable, because a value that is there but wrong is not the same fact as a value that is not there. The configuration sources throw MalformedSetting by the same rule. The json reader offers both views of a member: maybe(name) answers Maybe and treats an absent key and a null alike, while presence(name) keeps them apart as Presence.missing and Presence.none; in both, a member of the wrong kind is JsonError.wrong_kind. maybe is literally presence followed by fold().

Databases are where null was born a second time. SQL's NULL came from Codd's extension of the relational model [Codd 1979], with a three-valued logic in which NULL = NULL is neither true nor false but unknown. Codd later proposed two kinds of missing value — "missing but applicable" and "missing and inapplicable" — and a four-valued logic to go with them [Codd 1990]; no major system implemented it, and SQL kept one NULL. Okkama maps the database's NULL to Maybe.none in both directions: DbText(Maybe<string>.none) binds a NULL parameter, and row.maybe("nick").text() reads one back as Maybe.none. Equality on the Okkama side stays two-valued: Maybe<int>.none == Maybe<int>.none is simply true. Codd's second mark has a counterpart too, in Presence: none is "there is no value", missing is "nothing was said".

7.9 A worked example: settings

The same absent setting can mean three different things, and only the code that uses the value knows which. A server reads its settings as text and decides, per setting, what absence means.

module app v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "strings/parse" take Number, InvalidInteger;

enum SettingError is Error = (malformed(name is string, text is string));

// Settings as read from a file: a name and its text, nothing more.
object Settings {
    has entries is %string:string;
    Settings(:entries);

    // Absence is an answer: the setting is not there.
    text(name is string) is Maybe<string> {
        if entries.has(name) { Maybe.some(entries[name]); } else { Maybe<string>.none; }
    }

    // Absent gives none; present but not a number is an error that names the setting.
    int(name is string) is Maybe<int> {
        match self.text(name) {
            case Maybe.some(raw): Maybe.some(try {
            Number(raw).int();
        } catch failure is InvalidInteger {
            throw SettingError.malformed(name, raw);
        });
            case Maybe.none: Maybe<int>.none;
        };
    }
}

// What the program does with each setting decides what absence means.
object Server {
    has settings is Settings;
    Server(:settings);

    port() is int { settings.int("port") else 8080; }
    certificate() is string { match settings.text("certificate") { case Maybe.some(path): "TLS with " + path; case Maybe.none: "plain HTTP"; }; }
    workers() is int { settings.int("workers") else throw SettingError.malformed("workers", "(missing)"); }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let full = Server(settings: Settings(entries: ["port": "9000", "certificate": "/etc/tls/site.pem", "workers": "4"]));
    out.writeln(full.port().string() + ", " + full.certificate() + ", " + full.workers().string() + " workers");
    let sparse = Server(settings: Settings(entries: ["workers": "2"]));
    out.writeln(sparse.port().string() + ", " + sparse.certificate() + ", " + sparse.workers().string() + " workers");
    let broken = Server(settings: Settings(entries: ["port": "90o0"]));
    let port = try { broken.port().string(); } catch SettingError.malformed(name, text) { name + " is not a number: " + text; };
    out.writeln(port);
    let lean = Server(settings: Settings(entries: ["port": "80"]));
    let workers = try { lean.workers().string(); } catch SettingError.malformed(name, text) { name + " " + text; };
    out.writeln(workers);
    0;
}

Output:

9000, TLS with /etc/tls/site.pem, 4 workers
8080, plain HTTP, 2 workers
port is not a number: 90o0
workers (missing)
  • port() has a sensible default: absence means 8080.
  • certificate() has no default, and absence is meaningful: no certificate means plain HTTP. The compact choice names both cases, so the meaning of absence is written next to the meaning of presence.
  • workers() has no default and no meaning for absence: the program cannot run without it, so absence is an error, thrown with the setting's name.

The Settings object knows none of this. It answers Maybe for "not there" and throws SettingError.malformed for "there but not a number", and it leaves every decision about absence to its caller. That split — the reader reports, the user decides — is the design the standard library's readers follow.

7.10 Absence in generic code

Maybe<T> is an ordinary generic type, so it composes with generic objects the way any type does. A cache is the textbook case: it knows nothing about its keys and values, and a lookup may miss.

module app v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

// A cache from keys to values of any types. K keys a map, so it must be a key type (Chapter 17).
object Cache<K, V> {
    has entries is %K:V;
    has hits is int;
    has misses is int;
    Cache(:entries) { self.hits = 0; self.misses = 0; }

    // Absence is part of the answer: the caller decides what a miss means.
    find(key is K) is Maybe<V> {
        if entries.has(key) { Maybe.some(entries[key]); } else { Maybe.none; }
    }
    // A lookup that is counted returns the next state of the cache.
    looked_up(key is K) is ^Cache<K, V> {
        if entries.has(key) { ^hits = hits + 1; } else { ^misses = misses + 1; }
    }
    remembered(key is K, value is V) is ^Cache<K, V> {
        ^entries = entries + [key: value];
    }
    report() is string { "hits " + hits.string() + ", misses " + misses.string(); }
}

object Point {
    has x is int;
    has y is int;
    Point(:x, :y);
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let empty is %string:int = [:];
    let prices = Cache(entries: empty).remembered("tea", 300).remembered("cake", 450);
    // Three ways to meet a Maybe: a fallback, a compact choice, a match.
    out.writeln("tea " + (prices.find("tea") else 0).string());
    out.writeln(match prices.find("jam") { case Maybe.some(cents): "jam " + cents.string(); case Maybe.none: "no jam"; });
    let counted = prices.looked_up("tea").looked_up("jam").looked_up("cake");
    out.writeln(counted.report());
    // The same object with a value-object key and a string value.
    let nameless is %Point:string = [:];
    let names = Cache(entries: nameless).remembered(Point(x: 0, y: 0), "origin");
    match names.find(Point(x: 0, y: 0)) {
        case Maybe.some(name) { out.writeln("(0, 0) is the " + name); }
        case Maybe.none { out.writeln("(0, 0) has no name"); }
    }
    out.writeln("(1, 2) is " + (names.find(Point(x: 1, y: 2)) else "unnamed"));
    0;
}

Output:

tea 300
no jam
hits 2, misses 1
(0, 0) is the origin
(1, 2) is unnamed
  • The miss belongs to the answer. find(key) is Maybe<V> returns Maybe.some(value) or Maybe.none, whatever V is. The cache does not invent a default for a type it knows nothing about, and the caller decides what a miss means: a fallback with else or a match (Section 7.3).
  • No sentinel can collide with a value. A cache of prices that returned 0 or -1 for a miss would be wrong for the first item that costs nothing. With Maybe, every value of V, including 0, "" and an empty array, is a hit.
  • The key is a type parameter used as a map key. K keys the map %K:V, so the compiler holds every specialization to the key rules of Section 8.3: Cache<string, int> and Cache<Point, string> compile, and a Cache<@int, string> would not (Chapter 17).
  • Counting is a successor. looked_up(key) returns the next state of the cache with one more hit or miss; the find that answers the question does not change anything.

The design keeps two questions apart that sentinel-based caches merge: "is it there?" and "what is it?". The cost is the same as everywhere in this chapter, one else or one match at each call site, and in generic code it buys more than elsewhere, because a generic object has no value it could safely use as a sentinel for every V.

7.11 Absence with behaviour: the null object

Sometimes absence has behaviour. A service that may or may not have a logger does not want a Maybe<Logger> and a choice at every call; it wants a logger that does nothing. This is Woolf's Null Object pattern [Woolf 1998]: an implementation of the role whose actions are harmless no-ops, passed where the real one would go.

In Okkama the null object is an ordinary implementation of a role (Chapter 14), and the choice between it and Maybe follows one question: does the caller act differently when the thing is absent? If it does — a certificate turns TLS on, a missing phone number changes what the screen shows — absence is data, and it is a Maybe that forces the caller to decide. If it does not — a silent logger, an empty set of listeners, a clock that never ticks in a test — absence is behaviour, and an object that implements the role keeps every call site simple. Elegant Objects arrives at the same place from the other side: never return null, return an object that knows what to do [Bugayenko 2016].

What Okkama rejects is the third option, the sentinel: -1 for "not found", "" for "not set", 0 for "unknown". A sentinel is a null with a disguise — an ordinary value of the type that the reader must remember to treat specially. Okkama's searches answer Maybe precisely so that no int has to mean "nothing".

7.12 How other languages handle absence

Okkama's approach belongs to a family that started with ML's option type and Haskell's Maybe [Pierce 2002; Haskell 2010]. The table compares the mainstream designs.

Language Absence Can a value of type T be absent? Unwrapping without deciding
Java null; Optional<T> in libraries yes, every reference .get() throws; null dereference throws
C# 8+ null; nullable reference types as warnings yes, with warnings ! suppresses the warning
Kotlin T? nullable types no, unless declared T? [Kotlin specification] !! throws
Swift Optional<T>, written T? no, unless declared T? ! traps
Rust Option<T> no [Klabnik 2023] .unwrap() panics
Haskell Maybe a no fromJust errors
Go nil for pointers, maps, slices, interfaces, channels and functions; zero values; v, ok := m[k] yes, for those kinds [Go specification] dereferencing nil panics
Okkama Maybe<T>, Presence<T> no none: every exit names the none case

Kotlin, Swift and Rust made the decisive move — a plain T cannot be absent — and their experience shows that it removes most null-related crashes. Each of them also kept an escape hatch for "I know it is there": !!, !, .unwrap(). Okkama's only equivalent is else panic "reason", which costs a message and therefore a moment's thought. The difference is small in characters and large in culture: the shortest way to get a value out of a Maybe is to say what absence means.

7.13 What it costs

  • Ceremony at the boundaries. Every lookup that may miss needs a fallback, a match or a try?. Code that reads many optional fields — configuration, request parameters, JSON — is longer than in a language with null. The standard library's answer is the json-style reading API: maybe(name).text() else "default" reads an optional field in one line (Chapter 22), and the library audit asks for the same style in every module that reads data.
  • Deciding what absence means. Porting a design built on null forces a decision at every nullable reference: is this a Maybe, an error, a default, or a sign that the object was built wrongly? The decision is work; it is also the work the original design skipped.
  • Two types instead of one. Maybe and Presence are separate types, and converting between them is explicit (fold(), as_presence()). This is the price of keeping the third state; most programs never need Presence.

7.14 Limits

  • Maybe has no library of combinators such as map, and_then or filter in the language today; chained optional computations are written with match, often in its compact form. Whether to add them is an open question: each is convenient, and each is another way to say what match already says.
  • A Maybe cannot be a map key, and a fallback cannot carry control flow: else return and else next do not exist. Both are deliberate, and both occasionally cost a few lines.
  • Standard-library APIs are not yet uniform: some modules return Maybe, some throw a typed error for a missing value, some take an explicit fallback. The json module's style is the reference the library is being aligned with.

Chapter 8Collections

Okkama has three built-in collections — arrays, maps and ranges — and the standard library adds lists, sets, deques, heaps and lazy views on top of them. All of them are immutable. That single fact decides most of this chapter: how collections are built, how they are changed, what they cost and what is still missing.

8.1 Arrays

An array is an immutable, ordered sequence of values of one type, written @T. Literals use brackets, elements are indexed from zero, and every operation that "changes" an array returns a new one.

module bible/collections v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "compare" take Comparing;     // ordering() needs the Comparing role in scope

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();

    // Arrays: immutable, typed, indexed from zero.
    let primes = [2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13];
    out.writeln("size " + primes.size().string()
        + ", first " + primes.first().string()
        + ", last " + primes.last().string());
    out.writeln("slice(1, 4) = " + primes.slice(1, 4).map() -> p { p.string(); }.join(" "));
    out.writeln("index 9, or 0: " + (primes[9] else 0).string());
    out.writeln("contains 7: " + (if primes.contains(7) { "yes"; } else { "no"; })
        + ", reversed " + primes.reversed().map() -> p { p.string(); }.join(" ")
        + ", take(2) " + primes.take(2).map() -> p { p.string(); }.join(" ")
        + ", drop(4) " + primes.drop(4).map() -> p { p.string(); }.join(" "));

    // Ranges expand inside literals; ordering() sorts.
    let mixed = [9, 0, 2..=4, 1];
    out.writeln("expanded " + mixed.map() -> n { n.string(); }.join(" "));
    out.writeln("sorted " + mixed.ordering().map() -> n { n.string(); }.join(" "));

    // Functional operations make new arrays; nothing is changed in place.
    let squares = (1..=5).map() -> n { n * n; };
    let odd = squares.filter() -> n { n % 2 == 1; };
    let total = squares.reduce(0) -> sum, n { sum + n; };
    out.writeln("squares " + squares.map() -> n { n.string(); }.join(" ")
        + "; odd " + odd.map() -> n { n.string(); }.join(" ")
        + "; total " + total.string());

    // Maps: keys are expressions, iteration is in sorted key order.
    let stock is %string:int = ["pear": 3, "apple": 5, "fig": 0];
    out.writeln("keys " + stock.keys().join(", "));
    out.writeln("has kiwi: " + stock.has("kiwi").string() + ", kiwi or 0: " + (stock["kiwi"] else 0).string());
    let available = stock.filter() -> name, count { count > 0; };
    out.writeln("in stock " + available.keys().join(", "));
    let units = stock.reduce(0) -> sum, name, count { sum + count; };
    out.writeln("units " + units.string());
    0;
}

Output:

size 6, first 2, last 13
slice(1, 4) = 3 5 7
index 9, or 0: 0
contains 7: yes, reversed 13 11 7 5 3 2, take(2) 2 3, drop(4) 11 13
expanded 9 0 2 3 4 1
sorted 0 1 2 3 4 9
squares 1 4 9 16 25; odd 1 9 25; total 55
keys apple, fig, pear
has kiwi: false, kiwi or 0: 0
in stock apple, pear
units 8

The first lines of the program show the builtin actions of arrays: size(), first(), last(), slice(start, end), join(separator) for arrays of strings, ordering() to sort, and item(index) — or the indexing operator array[index]. An index outside the array is a runtime failure, unless the expression supplies a fallback: primes[9] else 0 is 0. Like slice on strings, nothing is clamped silently.

Five more builtins search and reshape (issue #211): contains(value) and index_of(value) — a Maybe<int> — compare elements with ==, so a value object is found by its fields; reversed() turns an array around; and take(count) and drop(count) keep, respectively remove, at most count elements from the start. Unlike slice, these two are defined for any count that is not negative — [1, 2].take(5) is [1, 2] — because "at most count" is what their names promise; a negative count fails.

Two more give a copy changed at one index (issues #250, #251).

  • replaced(index, value) is the array with value at index.
  • removed_at(index) is the array without the element at index.

The receiver keeps its elements, as everywhere. An index outside the array fails as indexing does. value meets the element type by the rules of a parameter boundary: an array of a role takes an implementer, and @any boxes. No other conversion applies.

Ranges expand inside array literals: [9, 0, 2..=4, 1] is the array 9 0 2 3 4 1. a..b excludes its end and a..=b includes it; bounds are integers and the start may not exceed the end.

ordering() sorts an array whose elements can be compared. It compares them through the standard role Comparing of the compare module, so the program imports that role even to sort numbers or strings, as the example does. Without the import the compiler names it: "compares elements through the role Comparing, which this program does not load: add import "compare" take Comparing;" (issue #233).

Typed identity

An array remembers its element type. Once it crosses a declared boundary — let names is @string = ..., a parameter, a field — it is tagged with that type, and even an empty result of slice or keys keeps it. An untyped empty literal [] has no evidence of its type, so it may cross any compatible boundary once, and that boundary fixes its type. Inside a larger expression its neighbours count as such evidence, at any depth and in either order: [[1], []] and [[], [1]] are @@int, ["a": [1], "b": []] is %string:@int, and [[1]] == [[]] or if c { [[]]; } else { [[2]]; } type-check. Only never parts are filled in this way. Two concrete types still disagree ([[1], ["s"]]), and an expression that is empty all the way down waits for a boundary. This is why empty collections sometimes need an annotation (Chapter 4).

Equality

Arrays compare deeply: two arrays are equal when they have the same length and equal elements in the same order. Maps compare by keys and values, ranges by their bounds and kind, objects by type and all fields. Comparing values of different categories is an error, not false — the same rule as 1 == 1.0 in Chapter 5.

8.2 Functional operations

Three operations — map, filter and reduce — work on arrays, ranges, maps and any object that performs the Iterating role. They are written with a dedicated block syntax:

let squares = (1..=5).map() -> n { n * n; };
let odd = squares.filter() -> n { n % 2 == 1; };
let total = squares.reduce(0) -> sum, n { sum + n; };

The block after -> names its bindings and computes one value. For a map, map and filter bind key, value, and reduce binds accumulator, key, value. The operations are eager: each produces a complete array (or, for filter on a map, a map). They visit elements in order — maps in sorted key order — exactly once, and the first failure inside a block stops the operation.

map, filter and reduce cover most loops that produce a value. Their blocks are part of the call: they may use surrounding names but cannot be stored or passed on. Lazy views — Taken, Filtered, Chunked and friends — live in collections/views when materialising every step would be wasteful (Chapter 22).

There is no last inside a functional block: reduce always visits every element. Searches therefore have their own operations, which stop at the first decisive item: any (is there one?), all (are they all?) and find (a Maybe of the first match) — xs.any() -> x { x.overdue(); } where one would otherwise write reduce(false) -> found, x { found || x.overdue(); } and walk the whole array (issue #150). A search for an equal element needs no block at all: xs.contains(y).

8.3 Maps

A map %K:V associates keys with values. Map literals use brackets with key: value pairs, and the keys are expressions: ["apple": 5] maps the string "apple"; [apple: 5] would use the value of a variable named apple. There is no implicit string-key shorthand, so a typo cannot quietly turn a variable into a string or the other way round.

Keys are scalar values — integers, strings, booleans and the other scalar categories, except byte and any — or value objects. A rat key is its exact value: rat(1, 2) and 2 / 4 are one key (since 0.4.2). Value objects are objects whose fields are all scalars, enums or such objects, with no destroy. Because objects are immutable, an object key is its fields: two equal cards are one key, exactly as == says. The map keeps its keys in sorted order — objects field by field in declaration order. keys() and values() return arrays in that order, and every functional operation visits entries in it. Iteration order therefore never depends on hashing, insertion history or the memory layout of a run: the same program prints the same output every time. Python made its dictionaries keep insertion order in version 3.7 for the same reason — predictability — and many test suites in languages with unordered maps contain workarounds for nondeterministic output.

A literal names each key once. Two keys the compiler can compute and that are one key — ["a": 1, "a": 2], [rat(1, 2): 1, 2 / 4: 2], [1 + 1: 1, 2: 2] — are a compile-time error that points at the repeat and at the first. Keys known only at run time are checked when the literal is built: every key and value is evaluated once, left to right, and if two keys are equal by the map's own key equality the literal fails with "Duplicate key in map literal" instead of keeping one of them. Many languages let the later entry win; Okkama treats a repeated key in a literal as the mistake it nearly always is (issue #954). Replacing an entry is written as what it is, prices + ["fig": 95].

A lookup of a missing key is a runtime failure unless it has a fallback: stock["kiwi"] else 0. has(key) asks without looking up, and a Maybe is one if away when an action wants to return absence (Chapter 7).

A generic object can key a map by its own type parameter: object Index<T> { has entries is %T:int; … }. Such a T is a key parameter, and the compiler holds every specialization to the key rule above: Index<string> and Index<Card> compile, Index<@int> does not, and neither does a Wrap<U> that passes its U on to an Index<U> and is given an array (issue #242). The standard library's KeyedSet<T> and KeyedFrequencies<T> are built this way — logarithmic membership and counts, traversal in key order — beside OrderedSet and Frequencies, which accept any T with equality, arrays included, and pay for it with a linear search.

8.4 Ranges

A range is a value: 1..5 and 1..=5 can be stored, passed and compared. They are the source of most counted loops (for 0..n -> i), expand inside array literals, and accept the functional operations, producing arrays. Chained ranges such as 1..5..9 are rejected, and a range whose start is greater than its end is an error rather than an empty range — a reversed range is more often a bug than an intention.

8.5 Building and changing collections

Immutability raises the practical question: how do you build a collection element by element, or change one entry of a map?

Figure 8.1. A persistent list: a new version shares every node of the old one and adds one.

The language's answer today has three parts.

  1. Build in one step when possible. map, filter and range expansion build complete arrays in one pass. Most collections in real programs are transformations of other collections, and these are linear.
  2. Accumulate with reduce or a library collection. The standard library has persistent collections — List (a linked list with constant-time prefix), Deque, OrderedSet, KeyedSet, Heap — whose "updates" return new versions that share structure with the old ones.
  3. Rebind a local that holds a successor-capable object. A local may be rebound (counter = counter.increment();) only when its type is an object with successor actions; let n = 1; n = 2; is rejected. Scalar and collection locals cannot be rebound at all, which is why accumulation goes through reduce — or, in synchronous code, through a Cell from the std module cell, the one explicit mutable container, which the compiler keeps out of async actions and object fields (issue #152).

Use + and - to append array elements or set and remove map entries: items + [item], a + b + c, prices + ["fig": 90], prices - ["pear": 0]. A concatenation chain costs the size of its result. Inside reduce, a block that returns only acc or acc + [item] appends in amortized constant time; earlier observable values remain unchanged.

One idiom still copies: it builds a new array with map at each step. Repeating it to grow a collection gives quadratic total work:

let following = (0..old.size() + 1).map() -> index {
    if index < old.size() { old[index]; } else { item; }
};

This is the clearest case in the language of the rule from Chapter 1: removing mutation must not remove efficiency, and the cure is an operation, not a mutable entity.

8.6 Iterating user collections

for walks arrays, ranges, maps' keys through keys(), and any object that performs the standard Iterating<T> role from collections/iteration:

role Cursor<T> {
    available() is bool;
    item() is T;
    successor() is Cursor<T>;
}

role Iterating<T> {
    cursor() is Cursor<T>;
}

A cursor is immutable: successor() returns the next cursor and leaves the current one where it was, so two loops over the same collection never interfere, and a cursor can be kept to resume later. Exhaustion is an ordinary false from available() — no sentinel, no null, no exception. The role is nominal: a collection must declare does Iterating<T>; having the right method names is not enough.

A source that is consumed as it is read — a file, a socket — performs Batching<T> instead, from the same module:

role Batching<T> {
    batch() is @T;      // the next batch; [] ends the source
}

for file.text() -> line { … } asks for a batch, walks it as an array and asks again. next, last and return work as in any loop; map, filter and reduce accept such sources too. Batches amortize the cost of requesting items over several values. A source that does both roles is walked in batches.

8.7 Counts and positions: what happens at the edges

Array actions take two kinds of number, and they behave differently at the edge of the array. A count says how many: asking for more than there is gives what there is. A position names an element: a position outside the array is a failure.

module app v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Show {
    Show();
    of(xs is @int) is string { "[" + xs.map() -> x { x.string(); }.join(",") + "]"; }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let show = Show();
    let xs = [10, 20, 30];
    // take and drop are counts: asking for more than there is gives what there is.
    out.writeln(show.of(xs.take(5)) + " " + show.of(xs.drop(9)));
    // slice, item, replaced and removed_at are positions: a position outside the array fails.
    out.writeln(show.of(xs.slice(1, 3)) + " " + show.of(xs.replaced(1, 99)) + " " + show.of(xs.removed_at(0)));
    out.writeln((xs[7] else -1).string() + " " + show.of(xs.reversed()));
    // `-` removes every element equal to one on the right.
    out.writeln(show.of([1, 2, 2, 3] - [2]));
    // A position outside the array is a runtime failure, not a thrown error: the program stops here.
    out.writeln(show.of(xs.slice(1, 9)));
    0;
}

Output:

[10,20,30] []
[20,30] [10,99,30] [20,30]
-1 [30,20,10]
[1,3]
exit 1
Action Argument Beyond the end Negative
take(n) count the whole array fails
drop(n) count [] fails
slice(start, end) positions fails fails; so does start > end
item(i), xs[i] position fails; xs[i] else v gives v fails; xs[i] else v gives v
replaced(i, v), removed_at(i) position fails fails
first(), last() — fail on an empty array —

Such a failure is not a thrown error a caller can catch; it is a runtime failure that stops the program with its location, like a division by zero (Chapter 10). try? xs.slice(1, 9) does not turn it into Maybe.none. The asymmetry is deliberate. A count is a request — "at most three" — and answering it with fewer is the useful answer. A position is a claim — "the element at five exists" — and a false claim is a bug to surface, not a value to invent. When a position may legitimately be missing, the program says so with else.

8.8 Sorting

ordering() returns the array sorted in ascending order, and it is the only sort the language has. It orders elements through the standard role Comparing<T> from compare, so the program must import that role even to sort integers, and an object sorts when it performs Comparing (Chapter 14). The sort is stable: elements that compare equal keep their original order, so sorting by one key after another composes. Strings sort by code point, as order() compares them (Chapter 6), which puts "B" before "a".

There is no descending variant and no sort by a key function. Descending order is xs.ordering().reversed(), and sorting by a key is an object that performs Comparing on that key — a small object with a name, in place of an anonymous comparator. This is the razor's trade again: one operation and one role instead of a family of sort methods.

The program below sorts runners by time, then by club, then slowest first, and finally by a ranking that does not know every club.

module bible/sorting v1.0.0;

// Sorting by a key is an object that compares by that key. The sort is
// stable, so one key after another composes; descending is a reversal; a
// comparison that throws stops the sort and leaves the array as it was.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "compare" take Comparing, Order;

enum Refused is Error = (unranked(club is string));

object Runner {
    has name is string;
    has club is string;
    has minutes is int;
    Runner(:name, :club, :minutes);
    name() is string { name; }
    club() is string { club; }
    minutes() is int { minutes; }
}

// One key per object: the finishing time.
object ByTime does Comparing<ByTime> {
    has runner is Runner;
    ByTime(:runner);
    runner() is Runner { runner; }
    order(other is ByTime) is Order { runner.minutes().order(other.runner().minutes()); }
}

// The club's name.
object ByClub does Comparing<ByClub> {
    has runner is Runner;
    ByClub(:runner);
    runner() is Runner { runner; }
    order(other is ByClub) is Order { runner.club().order(other.runner().club()); }
}

// A ranking of clubs that knows only some of them.
object ByRank does Comparing<ByRank> {
    has runner is Runner;
    ByRank(:runner);
    runner() is Runner { runner; }
    rank() is int {
        let ranks = ["South": 1, "North": 2];
        confirm ranks.has(runner.club()) else throw Refused.unranked(runner.club());
        ranks[runner.club()];
    }
    order(other is ByRank) is Order { self.rank().order(other.rank()); }
}

object Board {
    has runners is @Runner;
    Board(:runners);
    shown() is string {
        runners.map() -> r { r.name() + " " + r.club() + " " + r.minutes().string(); }.join(", ");
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let runners is @Runner = [
        Runner(name: "Ada", club: "North", minutes: 42),
        Runner(name: "Bo", club: "South", minutes: 39),
        Runner(name: "Cy", club: "North", minutes: 39),
        Runner(name: "Di", club: "East", minutes: 45)
    ];
    let timed = runners.map() -> r { ByTime(runner: r); };
    let byTime = timed.ordering().map() -> k { k.runner(); };
    out.writeln("by time:         " + Board(runners: byTime).shown());
    let clubbed = byTime.map() -> r { ByClub(runner: r); };
    let byClub = clubbed.ordering().map() -> k { k.runner(); };
    out.writeln("by club, time:   " + Board(runners: byClub).shown());
    out.writeln("slowest first:   " + Board(runners: byTime.reversed()).shown());
    let ranked = runners.map() -> r { ByRank(runner: r); };
    let outcome = try {
        Board(runners: ranked.ordering().map() -> k { k.runner(); }).shown();
    }
    catch e is Refused {
        "refused: " + e.text();
    };
    out.writeln("by rank:         " + outcome);
    out.writeln("unchanged:       " + Board(runners: runners).shown());
    0;
}

Output:

by time:         Bo South 39, Cy North 39, Ada North 42, Di East 45
by club, time:   Di East 45, Cy North 39, Ada North 42, Bo South 39
slowest first:   Di East 45, Ada North 42, Cy North 39, Bo South 39
by rank:         refused: Refused.unranked("East")
unchanged:       Ada North 42, Bo South 39, Cy North 39, Di East 45
  • A key is an object. ByTime and ByClub each wrap a runner and compare one field. Sorting by a key is three steps: wrap, ordering(), unwrap. The wrapper has a name, which an anonymous comparator does not, and the name says what the order is.
  • Stability composes. Bo and Cy both ran 39 minutes, and the sort by time keeps them in their input order. Sorting that result by club keeps the time order inside each club: Cy before Ada in North. To sort by several keys, sort by the least significant one first.
  • Reversal is not a stable descending sort. reversed() turns the whole array around, ties included: slowest first puts Cy before Bo. When the order of equal elements matters, the descending key is written as an object of its own, whose order compares the other way.
  • A comparison may fail, and the sort stops. ByRank throws for a club it has no rank for, and the first such comparison ends the sort with that error. There is no half-sorted array to clean up: ordering() returns a new array or fails, and runners is what it was.

8.9 A worked example: counting words

Maps, reduce and ordering() are enough for the classic exercise of counting words, without a mutable counter anywhere.

module app v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "compare" take Comparing;

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let text = "the cat and the hat and the bat";
    // Count with reduce: each step returns the map with one entry set.
    let empty is %string:int = [:];
    let counts = text.split(" ").reduce(empty) -> seen, word {
        seen + [word: (seen[word] else 0) + 1];
    };
    // Keys come back in sorted order, so the report is the same on every run.
    for counts.keys() -> word {
        out.writeln(word + " " + (counts[word] else 0).string());
    }
    // The most frequent words: filter the map, then order the keys.
    let common = counts.filter() -> word, count { count > 1; };
    out.writeln(common.keys().ordering().join(","));
    0;
}

Output:

and 2
bat 1
cat 1
hat 1
the 3
and,the

The reduce threads a map through the words. Each step returns the map with one entry set: seen + [word: n] adds or replaces the entry, and the old map stays as it was. The empty map needs a declared type (let empty is %string:int = [:];), because [:] alone says nothing about its keys and values (Chapter 4). Iterating counts.keys() gives the words in sorted order, and before the, whatever order they arrived in, so the report is identical on every run and every machine. That determinism is a property of the map, not of the program.

8.10 A worked example: grouping and joining

Reports are where collections earn their keep: rows arrive in one order and must be grouped, totalled and joined with other data. Here are five sales, grouped by customer and then by city and month.

module app v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Sale {
    has customer is string;
    has month is int;
    has cents is int;
    Sale(:customer, :month, :cents);
    buyer() is string { customer; }
    period() is int { month; }
    amount() is int { cents; }
}

// A value object: its fields are scalars, so it can key a map.
object Bucket {
    has city is string;
    has month is int;
    Bucket(:city, :month);
    shown() is string { city + "/" + month.string(); }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let sales = [
        Sale(customer: "ada", month: 2, cents: 1200),
        Sale(customer: "bob", month: 1, cents: 300),
        Sale(customer: "ada", month: 1, cents: 450),
        Sale(customer: "cy", month: 2, cents: 990),
        Sale(customer: "bob", month: 2, cents: 700)
    ];
    let cities = ["ada": "Oslo", "bob": "Lima"];

    // Group: each customer's sales, in the order they arrived.
    let nobody is %string:@Sale = [:];
    let by_customer = sales.reduce(nobody) -> groups, sale {
        let earlier = groups[sale.buyer()] else [];
        groups + [sale.buyer(): earlier + [sale]];
    };
    for by_customer.keys() -> name {
        let mine = by_customer[name];
        let total = mine.reduce(0) -> sum, sale { sum + sale.amount(); };
        out.writeln(name + "  sales " + mine.size().string() + "  total " + total.string());
    }

    // Join with the cities and re-key by (city, month); a customer without a city goes to "?".
    let nothing is %Bucket:int = [:];
    let by_bucket = sales.reduce(nothing) -> totals, sale {
        let key = Bucket(city: cities[sale.buyer()] else "?", month: sale.period());
        totals + [key: (totals[key] else 0) + sale.amount()];
    };
    for by_bucket.keys() -> key {
        out.writeln(key.shown() + " " + by_bucket[key].string());
    }
    0;
}

Output:

ada  sales 2  total 1650
bob  sales 2  total 1000
cy  sales 1  total 990
?/2 990
Lima/1 300
Lima/2 700
Oslo/1 450
Oslo/2 1200
  • Grouping is a reduce into a map of arrays. Each step looks up the customer's earlier sales, groups[sale.buyer()] else [], and returns the map with that entry replaced by the longer array. The fallback says what a first sale means, an empty history, at the one place it matters. Nothing is mutated: every step yields a new map, and the arrays inside it keep the sales in the order they arrived.
  • A join is a lookup with a fallback. cities[sale.buyer()] else "?" joins each sale with its customer's city. cy has no city, and the program decides here, in the expression, that such a sale goes to "?". In SQL the same question is the choice between an inner and an outer join; here it is one else, written next to the lookup it qualifies.
  • A composite key is a value object. Bucket has only scalar fields, so it can key a map (Section 8.3), and two buckets with the same city and month are the same key. The map keeps its keys in order field by field: city first, then month. Strings compare by code point (Section 4.7), so "?" comes before "Lima" and "Oslo".
  • The output is the same on every run. Both loops walk keys(), which are sorted, so neither report depends on the order of the input or on hashing. Shuffle sales and the program prints the same eight lines.

In SQL this is GROUP BY and JOIN, and the join itself goes back to Codd's relational model [Codd 1970]. The operations are the same; what the program adds is that each one is a typed expression whose result can be named, tested and passed on.

8.11 Beyond arrays and maps: the library's collections

Arrays, maps and ranges are built in. Everything else is a library object, and the library's collections follow the same rule as the built-in ones: nothing changes, and every operation that adds or removes gives a new collection.

module bible/library_collections v1.0.0;

// The library's persistent collections at work: a Deque as the queue of a
// breadth-first search, an OrderedSet for the towns already reached, and a
// Heap that hands out the most urgent delivery first.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "collections/deque" take Deque;
import "collections/set" take Set, OrderedSet;
import "collections/heap" take Heap;
import "compare" take Comparing, Order;

object Search {
    has roads is %string:@string;
    has queue is Deque<string>;
    has reached is Set<string>;
    has order is @string;

    Search(:roads, :queue, :reached, :order);

    done() is bool { queue.size() == 0; }

    // The front town leaves the queue; its neighbours not reached yet join the back.
    stepped() is ^Search {
        let town = queue.first();
        let fresh = (roads[town] else []).filter() -> n { !reached.membership(n); };
        ^queue = fresh.reduce(queue.tail()) -> q, n { q.suffix(n); };
        ^reached = fresh.reduce(reached) -> s, n { s.addition(n); };
        ^order = order + fresh;
    }

    shown() is string { order.join(" > "); }
}

// A delivery is ordered by the hours left before its deadline.
object Delivery does Comparing<Delivery> {
    has town is string;
    has hours is int;
    Delivery(:town, :hours);
    town() is string { town; }
    hours() is int { hours; }
    order(other is Delivery) is Order { hours.order(other.hours()); }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let roads = [
        "Kostanay": ["Astana", "Aktobe"],
        "Astana": ["Kostanay", "Karaganda", "Pavlodar"],
        "Aktobe": ["Kostanay"],
        "Karaganda": ["Astana", "Almaty"],
        "Pavlodar": ["Astana"],
        "Almaty": ["Karaganda", "Shymkent"],
        "Shymkent": ["Almaty"]
    ];
    let start is Set<string> = OrderedSet(values: ["Kostanay"]);
    let search = Search(roads: roads, queue: Deque(values: ["Kostanay"]), reached: start, order: ["Kostanay"]);
    loop {
        last if search.done();
        search = search.stepped();
    }
    out.writeln("reached: " + search.shown());

    let pending = Heap(values: [
        Delivery(town: "Almaty", hours: 48),
        Delivery(town: "Astana", hours: 12),
        Delivery(town: "Aktobe", hours: 30)
    ]);
    let later = pending.addition(Delivery(town: "Rudny", hours: 3));
    out.writeln("most urgent now: " + pending.top().town() + ", after the new order: " + later.top().town());
    out.writeln("still waiting before: " + pending.size().string() + ", after: " + later.size().string());
    0;
}

Output:

reached: Kostanay > Astana > Aktobe > Karaganda > Pavlodar > Almaty > Shymkent
most urgent now: Astana, after the new order: Rudny
still waiting before: 3, after: 4
  • A Deque is the queue of a breadth-first search. first() reads the front, tail() drops it, and suffix(n) adds at the back. Each returns a new deque, and adding at either end costs O(1) amortized. The search moves forward by rebinding search to its successor (Section 13.5), and nothing else in it changes.
  • An OrderedSet remembers what was reached. membership answers in the time of its kind, and addition gives a new set. The order of insertion is kept, so the traversal of a set never depends on hashing. KeyedSet keeps map keys in key order instead.
  • A Heap hands out the least value by its own order. Delivery does Comparing<Delivery> by the hours left, so top() is the most urgent delivery. addition gives a new heap with one more value, and pending.top() is still Astana after later was made from it.
  • Old versions stay valid and share their parts. pending and later are both usable, and the second shares the tree nodes of the first. This is the persistence of Section 8.5, extended to structures the language does not build in.

The library also has List (a persistent linked list), Frequencies (counts in first-occurrence order), Sorted and its binary-search projections, lazy views (Mapped, Filtered, Chunked and others), and combinatorial cursors. Each is an object that does some of Iterating, Sizing and Sequencing, so for, reduce and the other operations of Section 8.2 accept it as they accept an array.

One wart shows in the example. addition on a set returns the role Set<T>, and the role cannot also promise Iterating<T>, because roles do not compose yet. A set that has gone through addition can answer membership and size, but for cannot walk it without a cast that the language does not have. The example keeps the order in an array of its own. The fix belongs to the language (role composition) or to the library (an addition that returns the concrete set). It is listed with the other gaps in Chapter 27.

8.12 Okkama among other languages

Default collections Map iteration order map, filter
Python mutable list and dict insertion order, guaranteed since 3.7 [Python built-in types] lazy iterators [Python built-in functions]
Java mutable; List.of and List.copyOf give unmodifiable lists [Java SE 21 API] depends on the class: unspecified for HashMap, sorted for TreeMap lazy streams [Java SE 21 API]
Go mutable slices and maps not specified, and not the same from one iteration to the next [Go specification] loops
Rust Vec, HashMap, changed through mut arbitrary for HashMap [Rust standard library], sorted for BTreeMap lazy iterators [Klabnik 2023]
Clojure persistent, immutable, sharing structure [Hickey 2008] unordered hash-map, ordered sorted-map [Clojure Reference] lazy sequences
Okkama immutable arrays and maps always sorted by key eager; lazy views in collections/views

Two columns show the choices.

  • Order. Go goes furthest in the other direction: the specification promises nothing about map order, so a program that depends on it is wrong. Python chose insertion order. Okkama chooses sorted order for every map, so the order follows from the keys alone: two maps with the same entries iterate the same way, however they were built (Section 8.3).
  • Laziness. Python, Java, Rust and Clojure make map and filter lazy: nothing runs until the result is consumed, which saves work on long pipelines and makes the moment of a failure harder to see. Okkama's are eager, so a failure inside a block happens at the call that contains it. When laziness pays, the program asks for it by name with a view (Section 8.2).

Clojure is the closest relative. Its collections are immutable values that share structure between versions, as Okkama's persistent library collections do (Section 8.5); the difference is that in Okkama there is no mutable collection beside them to fall back on.

8.13 Limits

  • What still copies. The map() idiom and a + b of two large arrays cost the full result.
  • A large map’s first update costs a copy. Subsequent updates can be cheaper; do not assume every update has the same cost.
  • ordering() needs import "compare" take Comparing;, even for numbers and strings; the compiler names the missing import (issue #233).

Chapter 9Expressions and Control Flow

Okkama's control flow fits in one sentence. It has two conditionals, if and match, and match has a compact case form for one-line choices. It has two loops: for over a source and an unbounded loop. It has three exits — next, last and return — and a postfix condition. There is no while, no do, no switch with fall-through, no goto, no labels, no += and no ++. Most of what is left are expressions: they produce values.

This chapter covers those constructs, the operators, and the order in which an expression is evaluated. Other chapters cover the rest:

  • failure (throw, try) — Chapter 10;
  • cleanup (defer) — Chapter 11;
  • patterns over enums — Chapter 16;
  • for await — Chapter 20.

The program below uses nearly all of it.

module bible/expressions v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Gradebook {
    has scores is %string:int;
    Gradebook(:scores);

    names() is @string { scores.keys(); }
    score(name is string) is int { scores[name]; }

    // An if chain in tail position is the value of the action.
    letter(score is int) is string {
        if score >= 90 { "A" } else if score >= 75 { "B" } else if score >= 60 { "C" } else { "F" }
    }

    // `return` leaves the action from inside the loop.
    first_below(limit is int) is Maybe<string> {
        for scores.keys() -> name {
            return Maybe.some(name) if scores[name] < limit;
        }
        Maybe.none;
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let book = Gradebook(scores: ["Grace": 58, "Ada": 97, "Edsger": 60, "Alan": 74]);

    for book.names() -> name {
        let score = book.score(name);
        let letter = book.letter(score);
        // `match` compares values; `else` takes the rest.
        let verdict = match letter {
            case "A", "B" { "good"; }
            case "C" { "pass"; }
            else { "retake"; }
        };
        // An `if` expression has two branches of one type.
        let honours = if score >= 95 { ", with honours"; } else { ""; };
        out.writeln(name + ": " + score.string() + " " + letter + ", " + verdict + honours);
    }

    // `next` and `last` take a postfix condition.
    for 1..=20 -> n {
        next if n % 3 != 0;
        last if n > 12;
        out.writeln("multiple of 3: " + n.string());
    }

    out.writeln("first below 60: " + (book.first_below(60) else "nobody"));
    out.writeln("first below 50: " + (book.first_below(50) else "nobody"));
    0;
}

Output:

Ada: 97 A, good, with honours
Alan: 74 C, pass
Edsger: 60 C, pass
Grace: 58 F, retake
multiple of 3: 3
multiple of 3: 6
multiple of 3: 9
multiple of 3: 12
first below 60: Grace
first below 50: nobody

9.1 Blocks have values

The value of a block is the value of its last expression, so an action needs no return to produce its result. letter above is a single if chain: whichever branch runs supplies the string. The semicolon after the last expression is optional. { "A" } and { "A"; } are the same block, and the formatter keeps whichever spelling the author chose.

The idea is older than most languages in use today:

  • McCarthy's LISP introduced the conditional expression [McCarthy 1960].
  • Landin's "The Next 700 Programming Languages" argued for building a language from expressions, with a statement as the special case of an expression whose value nobody uses [Landin 1966].
  • ML, Haskell, Scala, Kotlin and Rust followed that line.

C and Java followed ALGOL 60 instead. In them if is a statement, and since programs still need a conditional value, both languages added a second construct for it, cond ? a : b. Two spellings of one idea are exactly the multiplication Chapter 1 argues against.

if, match, loop and try (Chapter 10) produce values, and so does every call. A bare block { … } does not. It is a statement that opens a scope, and let v = { … }; is a syntax error. A scope that has to produce a value becomes an action, which gives it a name, a type and a test.

9.2 Names are bound once

let binds a name to a value, with an optional declared type:

let limit = 60;                 // inferred: int
let names is @string = [];      // declared: a typed boundary (Chapter 4)

A name cannot be declared twice in the same scope. A nested block may shadow it, and the outer meaning returns when the block ends. A name also cannot be pointed at a new value:

module bible/rebind v1.0.0;

main() is int {
    let total = 0;
    for 1..=3 -> n {
        total = total + n;
    }
    total;
}

The compiler answers:

09-rebind-rejected.ok:6:9: semantic error: Cannot rebind variable "total": type "int" has no successor actions

The rule comes from the manifesto (Chapter 3): a name means what it was bound to, so a reader never has to search forward for the assignment that changed it. Scalars and collections are values, and there is no such thing as "the same total, now bigger". The loop above has three idiomatic replacements:

  • reduce, when the loop computes one value from a collection: (1..=3).reduce(0) -> sum, n { sum + n; } (Chapter 8).
  • A successor object, when the changing state is a thing in the program's domain. A local whose type declares a successor action may be rebound to its successor (section 9.5 and Chapter 13).
  • A Cell, the one explicit mutable container, which is allowed only in synchronous code (Chapter 13).

Without reassignment, compound assignment has nothing to abbreviate. So +=, -= and the rest do not exist, and neither do ++ and --.

9.3 Operators

Operators, loosest first:

Operators Meaning
else fallback for a Maybe, a missing index or key
|| boolean or
&& boolean and
<- write to a stream
== != equality
.. ..= range
< <= > >= ordering
| ^ & bitwise or, exclusive or, and (in this order)
<< >> >>> shifts
+ - addition, concatenation, collection + and - (Chapter 8)
* / % multiplication, division, remainder
! - ~ not, negation, bitwise complement
postfix calls, member access, indexing, unpacking ...

The table departs from C in two places:

  • Bitwise operators bind tighter than comparisons. flags & mask != 0 means (flags & mask) != 0, which is what the programmer meant. In C the same text means flags & (mask != 0). Ritchie traced the C rule to B, where & also served as logical and, and wrote that in hindsight moving & above == would have been better [Ritchie 1993].
  • Writing to a stream has its own operator, <-. As a result << is always a shift.

Every operator requires operands of the right category and converts nothing:

  • &&, ||, ! and every condition take a bool. That includes the conditions of if, next if and confirm. if count { … } is an error, not a test for zero.
  • == and != compare values of one category. 1 == 1.0 is rejected (Chapter 5), and so is comparing an int with a range.
  • < and the other orderings need the same numeric category on both sides. 1 < 2.5 is rejected; write 1.float() < 2.5.
  • + adds numbers, joins strings and concatenates collections, and never mixes them: "n = " + 1 is an error (Chapter 6).
  • / on two integers gives an exact rat. There is no **; powers are written with pow (Chapter 5).
  • An object takes part in arithmetic and ordering only through roles it declares: a + b is a.plus(b) when the type of a does Adding, and a < b asks a.order(b) through Comparing (§14.7). An object without those roles has no operators.

9.4 Choosing

if

The condition of if is a bool, and the braces are mandatory: there is no if (c) statement;. The brace-less form is behind one of the best-known security bugs of the last decade. In 2014 Apple's TLS code had two consecutive goto fail; lines under one unbraced if. The second line always ran, so the signature on the server's key exchange was never verified [Langley 2014]. With mandatory braces, indentation cannot misrepresent which lines a condition guards.

As an expression, if must have an else:

module bible/if_value v1.0.0;

main() is int {
    let ready = true;
    let code = if ready { 0; };
    code;
}

The compiler answers:

09-if-rejected.ok:5:31: syntax error at ";": If expression requires else branch.
  |
5 |     let code = if ready { 0; };
  |                               ^

Kotlin and Rust reject this too. If the arm that is not written were allowed, it would need a value, and Okkama has no such value to supply (Chapter 7).

An else if chain works in every position: as a statement, as the tail of an action (as in letter) and as a value after let x =. Every link has its else, and all branches have one type (issue #257).

Compact if

When each branch is one expression, if can be written with colons:

module bible/if_compact v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Thermostat {
    has target is int;
    Thermostat(:target);
    // A compact if as the action's value.
    mode(reading is int) is string { if reading < target: "heat" else: "idle"; }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let thermostat = Thermostat(target: 20);
    out.writeln(thermostat.mode(17) + " " + thermostat.mode(23));
    let polling = false;
    let timeout = if polling: 30 else: 5;
    // else: goes to the nearest if; a branch's fallback takes parentheses.
    let readings = ["kitchen": 19];
    let shown = if timeout > 10: "slow" else: if timeout > 1: "fast" else: "instant";
    let kitchen = if polling: 0 else: (readings["hall"] else -1);
    out.writeln(timeout.string() + " " + shown + " " + kitchen.string());
    0;
}

Output:

heat idle
5 fast -1

if c: a else: b is not a second conditional. The parser builds the block form from it, each branch a block holding its expression, so the checker and the runtime never learn which form was written (issue #921). Both branches are required, a branch is an expression and never a block, and the two forms do not mix: if c: a else { b; } is a syntax error. This does not reopen the goto fail door. A compact branch cannot hold a statement, and the else is always there, so no line can sit under a condition without its being visible.

An else: belongs to the nearest if, as in shown. A value else fallback inside a branch needs parentheses, as in kitchen: else followed by : is always the conditional's, never a fallback.

match

match compares a subject with each case's values using ==. A case may list several values, and else takes the rest. There is no fall-through and no break: each case is its own block, and cases that share a body list their values in one case, as case "A", "B" does above.

A case value is compared, not tested. case 1..5 compares an int with a range and is rejected as such; a condition on a value belongs in if. A match that produces a value needs an else, unless its cases cover every possibility, which only enums can do (Chapter 16). All its branches must have one type.

Compact cases

A match case can give its value in one line instead of a block: case pattern: value;. The two forms mix in one match, and case _ stands for the remainder, like else:

let greeting = match users.find(1) {
    case Maybe.some(name): "hello, " + name;
    case Maybe.none: "hello, stranger";
};
let size = match count { case 0: "none"; case 1: "one"; case _: "many"; };

It is the same match: the subject is evaluated once, only the chosen case runs, a binding exists only in its case, and all cases have one type. A compact match nests like any other expression, though a nested one usually reads better as a named local.

Until 0.6.0 Okkama also had cond ?? a !! b and x ?? .some(v): v !! _: 0, a separate notation for the same choices. It was removed (issue #893): two spellings of one idea cost more than the brevity they bought, and ?? is now a syntax error that points to the compact case. A two-way choice on a bool is an if expression: if ready { "yes"; } else { "no"; }.

Until 0.4.1 true.string() was "1" and false.string() was "0", a rule inherited from the first implementation, written in Perl, where truth prints as 1 and falsehood as an empty string. It was exact, stable and surprising to every reader of output who expected a word, so programs chose the words themselves, as the order example below still does. Since 0.4.1 string() gives "true" and "false" (issue #262); an if expression remains the way to say "yes" and "no", or "on" and "off".

9.5 Loops

for

for source -> name { … } runs its body once per element. The source can be:

  • an array;
  • a range;
  • an object that performs Iterating<T> or Batching<T> (Chapter 8).

A map is walked through keys() or values(), in sorted key order. A string is not a source by itself, but its characters are: for text.characters() -> letter (Chapter 6). There is exactly one binding. An index comes from a range: for 0..names.size() -> i.

loop

loop { … } repeats until last, return or a failure leaves it. It is an expression: last value leaves the loop with that value. Each iteration runs in a fresh scope, and the tail value of the body is ignored. A bare last gives no value, so a loop whose value is used must end with last value; otherwise the compiler reports "Bare last cannot produce the value of this loop".

module bible/dice v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

// A deterministic die: a linear congruential generator. Rolling does not
// change the die; it returns its successor, with the next seed and one more
// roll counted.
object Die {
    has seed is int;
    has rolls is int;
    Die(:seed, :rolls);
    rolled() is ^Die {
        ^seed = (seed * 1103515245 + 12345) % 2147483648;
        ^rolls = rolls + 1;
    }
    face() is int { seed % 6 + 1; }
    count() is int { rolls; }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let die = Die(seed: 2026, rolls: 0);
    // `loop` is an expression: `last value` leaves it with that value.
    let attempts = loop {
        die = die.rolled();
        out.writeln("rolled " + die.face().string());
        last die.count() if die.face() == 6;
    };
    out.writeln("a six after " + attempts.string() + " rolls");
    0;
}

Output:

rolled 4
rolled 5
rolled 4
rolled 3
rolled 4
rolled 1
rolled 2
rolled 1
rolled 4
rolled 1
rolled 6
a six after 11 rolls

The die is the second replacement from section 9.2. It never changes: rolled() returns its successor, and the local die is rebound to that successor. The rebinding is allowed because Die declares a successor action (is ^Die). The rebinding inside the loop body updates the die declared outside it, and the loop's value is the number of rolls.

There is no while, because loop already covers it:

  • while c { body } is loop { last if !c; body };
  • do { body } while c is loop { body; last if !c; }.

Knuth's survey of structured programming discussed the loop whose exit is in the middle [Knuth 1974]. Neither while nor do can express that loop without duplicating code; loop with last if writes it directly, and the two classic loops become special cases of it. One construct does the work of three.

next, last and the postfix condition

next starts the next iteration and last leaves the loop. Both take a postfix condition, and last can also carry a value. In last value if found; the condition is evaluated first, and the value only if the condition holds. A postfix if also works on an expression statement, out.writeln(line) if verbose;, and on return and throw: return found if done;, throw Empty.list if items.size() == 0; (issue #258). Right after return, if c; is the bare form with a condition, while return if a { 1 } else { 2 }; returns an if expression.

next and last act on the nearest for or loop; there are no labels. To leave two loops at once, move the inner loop into an action and return from it, or make the inner loop a loop whose value tells the outer one what to do.

next and last are also rejected outside a loop and directly inside a functional block. A map visits every element, and searches have their own operations, any, all and find (Chapter 8). These checks happen at compile time, even in code that never runs.

Unbounded loops and budgets

A loop without a last runs until something stops it. The step budget counts function entries and loop iterations. okkama run --max-steps N therefore stops an unbounded loop with a budget report.

9.6 return

return value; leaves the action from any depth. Most actions never need it, because the tail value is the result. return is for early exits: a search that has found its item, like first_below in the first example, or a guard with nothing more to do.

A functional block is part of its call, not a function of its own (Chapter 8). So return inside a map or filter block leaves the enclosing action, just as a return inside a Smalltalk block leaves its home method, or a return inside a Kotlin inline lambda leaves the calling function.

9.7 Order of evaluation

module bible/order v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

// Every call says that it was evaluated.
object Trace {
    has out is Stdout;
    Trace(:out);
    flag(name is string, value is bool) is bool {
        out.writeln("  " + name);
        value;
    }
    number(name is string, value is int) is int {
        out.writeln("  " + name);
        value;
    }
    sum(a is int, b is int, c is int) is int { a + b + c; }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let t = Trace(out: out);

    out.writeln("arguments, left to right:");
    let total = t.sum(t.number("a", 1), t.number("b", 2), t.number("c", 3));

    out.writeln("operands, left to right:");
    let product = t.number("x", 6) * t.number("y", 7);

    out.writeln("&& stops at false:");
    let both = t.flag("left", false) && t.flag("right", true);

    out.writeln("|| stops at true:");
    let either = t.flag("left", true) || t.flag("right", false);

    out.writeln("if evaluates one branch:");
    let chosen = if t.flag("condition", true) { t.number("then", 1); } else { t.number("otherwise", 2); };

    out.writeln(total.string() + " " + product.string() + " "
        + (if both { "true"; } else { "false"; }) + " " + (if either { "true"; } else { "false"; }) + " " + chosen.string());
    0;
}

Output:

arguments, left to right:
  a
  b
  c
operands, left to right:
  x
  y
&& stops at false:
  left
|| stops at true:
  left
if evaluates one branch:
  condition
  then
6 42 false true 1

An expression is evaluated by these rules:

  • the receiver first, then the arguments left to right, each exactly once, all before the call;
  • the left operand, then the right one, for every binary operator. Only && and || may skip their right operand, as soon as the answer is known;
  • for if and match, the condition or subject once, then one branch;
  • for else, the fallback only when the value is missing;
  • for last value if c, c first, and value only if c holds.

C leaves the order of operands and arguments unspecified. f() + g() may call either function first, and a program whose output depends on the order is legal and unpredictable. Java fixed the order as left to right [Gosling 2023], and Okkama does the same.

9.8 A worked example: a small calculator

The constructs of this chapter combine into programs without loops that mutate a variable. A reverse Polish calculator reads tokens left to right: a number is pushed, an operator replaces the top two numbers with their result.

module app v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "strings/parse" take Number, InvalidInteger;

enum Bad is Error = (token(text is string), underflow(op is string), leftover(count is int));

// A reverse Polish calculator: each token either pushes a number or combines the top two.
object Calculator {
    Calculator();

    value(text is string) is int {
        let start is @int = [];
        let stack = text.split(" ").filter() -> t { !t.empty(); }.reduce(start) -> items, t {
            if t == "+" || t == "-" || t == "*" {
                confirm items.size() >= 2 else throw Bad.underflow(t);
                let right = items.last();
                let left = items[items.size() - 2] else 0;
                let rest = items.take(items.size() - 2);
                rest + [if t == "+" { left + right; } else { if t == "-" { left - right; } else { left * right; } }];
            } else {
                items + [try { Number(t).int(); } catch failure is InvalidInteger { throw Bad.token(t); }];
            }
        };
        confirm stack.size() == 1 else throw Bad.leftover(stack.size());
        stack.first();
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let calc = Calculator();
    for ["3 4 +", "5 1 2 + 4 * + 3 -", "2 3", "1 +", "7 x *"] -> line {
        let shown = try {
            calc.value(line).string();
        } catch Bad.token(text) {
            "not a number: " + text;
        } catch Bad.underflow(op) {
            op + " needs two numbers";
        } catch Bad.leftover(count) {
            count.string() + " numbers left";
        };
        out.writeln(line + " => " + shown);
    }
    0;
}

Output:

3 4 + => 7
5 1 2 + 4 * + 3 - => 14
2 3 => 2 numbers left
1 + => + needs two numbers
7 x * => not a number: x
  • The loop is a reduce. The stack is the accumulator: each step returns a new array, items + [number] or rest + [result], so no variable is ever reassigned (§9.2). The empty starting stack needs a declared type, let start is @int = [];, because [] alone has no element type.
  • Every branch is a value. The operator case ends with an array built from a nested if expression; the number case ends with an array built from a try expression. Neither branch "assigns the result somewhere".
  • Failures carry their reason. A missing operand is confirm … else throw Bad.underflow(t); a token that is not a number turns the parser's InvalidInteger into Bad.token(t) inside the try; leftovers at the end are a third case. The caller's try matches each case of the error enum and prints its own message, so the calculator never decides how an error is shown.

The program is short not because it is clever but because there is nothing to keep in sync: no index variable, no stack pointer, no flag for "an error happened". Each token's effect is the value of one block.

9.9 A worked example: binary search

Binary search is short, classic and famously easy to get wrong. Bentley reports that most professional programmers he asked to write it handed in a program with a bug [Bentley 2000], and Bloch later found that the midpoint computation (low + high) / 2 in the Java library's binary search, and in the version Bentley had published, overflows on very large arrays, a bug that went unnoticed for years [Bloch 2006]. Here it is in Okkama, twice.
