module app v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

// The part of a sorted array still to search: positions low..high-1.
object Window {
    has low is int;
    has high is int;
    Window(:low, :high);

    empty() is bool { low >= high; }
    middle() is int { int((low + high) / 2); }
    above(position is int) is ^Window { ^low = position + 1; }
    below(position is int) is ^Window { ^high = position; }
}

object Sorted {
    has items is @int;
    Sorted(:items);

    // The position of `wanted`, if it is there.
    find(wanted is int) is Maybe<int> {
        let window = Window(low: 0, high: items.size());
        loop {
            last Maybe.none if window.empty();
            let middle = window.middle();
            last Maybe.some(middle) if items[middle] == wanted;
            if items[middle] < wanted {
                window = window.above(middle);
            } else {
                window = window.below(middle);
            }
        }
    }
}

// Two bounds around an answer: `yes` passes the test, `no` fails it.
object Bracket {
    has yes is int;
    has no is int;
    Bracket(:yes, :no);

    settled() is bool { no - yes == 1; }
    middle() is int { int((yes + no) / 2); }
    passed(at is int) is ^Bracket { ^yes = at; }
    failed(at is int) is ^Bracket { ^no = at; }
    answer() is int { yes; }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let evens = Sorted(items: (0..100000).map() -> n { n * 2; });
    out.writeln("131072 at " + (evens.find(131072) else -1).string());
    out.writeln("131071 at " + (evens.find(131071) else -1).string());

    // The integer square root of 10^40 by bisection. yes + no exceeds 2^64 here.
    let n = (10).pow(40);
    let bracket = Bracket(yes: 0, no: n + 1);
    let root = loop {
        last bracket.answer() if bracket.settled();
        let middle = bracket.middle();
        if middle * middle <= n {
            bracket = bracket.passed(middle);
        } else {
            bracket = bracket.failed(middle);
        }
    };
    out.writeln("isqrt(10^40) = " + root.string());
    0;
}

Output:

131072 at 65536
131071 at -1
isqrt(10^40) = 100000000000000000000

Figure 9.1. One loop with its exits where the decision is made: the binary search of Section 9.9.

  • The loop exits in the middle. find is one loop with two exits: last Maybe.none if window.empty() when nothing is left to search, and last Maybe.some(middle) if … when the probe hits. The loop's value is the action's result, so there is no flag, no found variable and no code after the loop. This is the loop Knuth described, with its exit where the decision is made (Section 9.5).
  • The bounds are one value. Window holds both bounds and knows the two facts the algorithm needs: whether it is empty and where its middle is. Narrowing is a successor, above(middle) or below(middle), and window = window.above(middle) rebinds the local to it, which is allowed because Window declares successor actions (Section 13.7). The invariant "the answer, if any, is in low..high-1" lives in one object, not in two integers that must be updated together.
  • The midpoint cannot overflow. (low + high) / 2 divides two integers, which gives an exact rational, and int(...) truncates it (Chapter 5). The sum is an int, and Okkama integers grow instead of wrapping, so Bloch's bug has nothing to stand on. The second search makes the point with numbers: it finds the integer square root of 10^40, where yes + no is far beyond 2^64, with the same textbook midpoint.
  • A bracket states the invariant. Bracket keeps a value known to pass the test (yes) and one known to fail it (no); the search is over when they are adjacent. The loop produces the answer as its value, and root is bound once.

The program is longer than the same search in C, by the two small objects. In return each state of the search is a value with a name, the invariant has a home, and the overflow that broke the library version cannot happen.

9.10 Expressions in other languages

Whether if is a statement or an expression looks like a matter of syntax, but it decides how often a program declares a name before it knows the value.

  • Statement languages add an expression form later. C has the conditional operator ?: beside if. Go has neither, so a value that depends on a condition is declared first and assigned in both branches [Go specification]. Python added a conditional expression, a if c else b, in 2.5 [PEP 308], and an assignment expression, :=, in 3.8 [PEP 572]. Java made switch usable as an expression in Java 14 [Bierman 2020].
  • Expression languages start from values. In Rust a block's last expression is its value, and if, match and loop produce values; break value leaves a loop with one [Klabnik 2023]. In Kotlin, if, when and try are expressions [Kotlin specification].

Okkama is in the second group. A block has a value (Section 9.1), if, match and try produce one, and a loop gives one through last value (Section 9.5), much as Rust's break value does. What Okkama adds is the other half of Section 9.2: the name a value is bound to is bound once, so the pattern "declare, then assign in each branch" has nothing to assign to, and the expression form is the only one.

9.11 What is not there

Elsewhere In Okkama
while (c) { … } loop { last if !c; … }
do { … } while (c) loop { …; last if !c; }
break, continue last, next
break outer (labels) an action and return, or a loop value
x = x + 1, x += 1, x++ a new name, reduce, a successor or a Cell
c ? a : b if c { a; } else { b; }
switch with fall-through match, several values per case
goto none [Dijkstra 1968]
if (c) statement; braces always

The compiler knows this table. while, do, += and its kin, ++, --, break and continue are rejected with a message that names the Okkama form (issue #256):

syntax error at "while": Okkama has no `while`: write `loop { last if !(condition); ... }`.
syntax error at "=": Okkama has no compound assignment: a name is bound once; bind a new name, or use `reduce` or a successor.
semantic error: Undefined variable "break"; Okkama leaves a loop with `last`

9.12 Limits

  • One binding per for. An index comes from a range, not from a second binding.

Writing this chapter turned up three more: messages for while, += and break that did not name the Okkama form, else if that worked only where if was a statement, and return and throw without a postfix condition. All three were fixed in 0.4.1 (issues #256, #257, #258).

Chapter 10Failure: throw, panic, try/catch, causes, confirm

Every program meets two kinds of trouble, and they have little in common.

  • The world says no. A file is missing, a server refuses the connection, a user types sixty where a number belongs, an account would go below zero. Nothing is wrong with the program: this is an outcome it must expect, and someone — the caller, or the caller's caller — knows what to do about it.
  • The program is wrong. An index runs past the end of an array, an invariant the author was sure of turns out false, a divisor is zero where the code assumed it never would be. No caller can repair this, because the caller cannot know which assumption broke. The useful response is to stop, clean up, and report precisely where.

Okkama gives the two kinds two channels and does not let them mix. Expected failures are values: cases of an error enum, thrown with throw and caught with a typed catch. Bugs are not values: a panic, a failed bare confirm or a runtime error ends the run after cleanup, and no catch clause can see it. Everything in this chapter follows from that split.

The program below imports a tiny ledger. Each line is account,amount. The import can fail in four ways the caller cares about: a blank line, a line of the wrong shape, an amount that is not a number, and an overdraft. Each is a case of an error enum with the context in its payload. report turns each failure into a sentence, and try? turns one into a fallback value.

module bible/failure v1.0.0;

// A ledger import: every failure the import can report is a case of one
// error enum, and the context travels in the payload.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "strings/parse" take Number, InvalidInteger;

enum LineError is Error = (blank(line is int), shape(line is int, text is string), amount(line is int, cause is InvalidInteger));
enum LedgerError is Error = (line(cause is LineError), overdraft(account is string, short is int));

object Entry {
    has account is string;
    has amount is int;
    Entry(:account, :amount);
    name() is string { account; }
    value() is int { amount; }
}

object Lines {
    Lines();
    entry(number is int, text is string) is Entry {
        confirm text.length() > 0 else throw LineError.blank(number);
        let parts = text.split(",");
        confirm parts.size() == 2 else throw LineError.shape(number, text);
        let amount = try { Number(parts[1]).int(); } catch e is InvalidInteger { throw LineError.amount(number, e); };
        Entry(account: parts[0], amount: amount);
    }
}

object Ledger {
    has balance is int;
    Ledger(:balance);
    after(entry is Entry) is Ledger {
        let after = balance + entry.value();
        confirm after >= 0 else throw LedgerError.overdraft(entry.name(), 0 - after);
        Ledger(balance: after);
    }
    total() is int { balance; }
}

object Import {
    has lines is @string;
    Import(:lines);
    run(start is int) is int {
        let parser = Lines();
        let ledger = (0..lines.size()).reduce(Ledger(balance: start)) -> book, i {
            let entry = try { parser.entry(i + 1, lines[i]); } catch e is LineError { throw LedgerError.line(e); };
            book.after(entry);
        };
        ledger.total();
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let report = (lines is @string, start is int) is string {
        try {
            "balance " + Import(lines: lines).run(start).string();
        }
        catch LedgerError.overdraft(account, short) {
            "overdraft on " + account + " by " + short.string();
        }
        catch LedgerError.line(cause) {
            match cause {
                case LineError.shape(line, text) { "line " + line.string() + " is not account,amount: " + text; }
                else { "rejected: " + cause.text(); }
            }
        }
        catch e is LedgerError {
            "rejected: " + e.text();
        }
    };
    out.writeln(report(["cash,100", "rent,-60", "food,-25"], 0));
    out.writeln(report(["cash,100", "rent,-160"], 0));
    out.writeln(report(["cash,100", "rent -60"], 0));
    out.writeln(report(["cash,100", "rent,sixty"], 0));
    out.writeln(report(["cash,100", ""], 0));
    let quick = try? Import(lines: ["cash,ten"]).run(0) else -1;
    out.writeln("quick " + quick.string());
    0;
}

Output:

balance 15
overdraft on rent by 60
line 2 is not account,amount: rent -60
rejected: LineError.amount(2, InvalidInteger.source("sixty"))
rejected: LineError.blank(2)
quick -1

The rest of the chapter takes the pieces apart:

  • the two channels, and why the history of error handling points at them;
  • error enums and throw;
  • try/catch and its deliberate omissions;
  • causes, confirm, try? and try!;
  • failures from the host;
  • what reaches the top of the program.

Cleanup — defer and destroy — runs on these failure paths; Chapter 11 describes it. Budget stops have a separate rule (§10.13).

10.1 Who should hear about a failure

Before choosing a mechanism, it helps to sort failures by who can act on them.

Figure 10.1. Two channels. An expected failure is a value a caller catches; a bug ends the run after cleanup; a budget stop ends it at once.

Kind Example Who can act Okkama
Expected failure file not found, bad input, refused connection the caller error enum, throw, typed catch
Bug index out of bounds, broken invariant the developer, after reading the report panic, confirm, runtime error: uncatchable
Exhaustion step, memory or time budget spent whoever started the run budget stop: uncatchable, not a failure of the program
Cancellation the task that awaited this work went away the scheduler Cancelled (Chapter 20)

The first row is the only one where code inside the program can do better than stop. A mechanism that treats all four rows alike — a single catch (Exception e) that sees an out-of-bounds index and a missing file in the same variable — invites code that "handles" a bug by logging it and carrying on with corrupted state. Okkama's split is the table above turned into syntax.

10.2 A short history: codes, exceptions, values

Error handling has been reinvented roughly once a decade, and each reinvention fixed a real problem of the previous one.

Return codes. C reports failure through the return value and a global errno. It costs nothing at run time, and nothing forces the caller to look. Unix's close returns an error that almost no program ever checks, and a full disk discovered on close is silently lost. The failure and the normal result also share one channel: -1 is both "error" and, for some functions, a legitimate value.

Exceptions. John Goodenough's 1975 paper laid out the design space still in use: how a failure is raised, how a handler is found, and whether control resumes after the handler or terminates the failed operation [Goodenough 1975]. CLU, in 1979, chose termination and made each procedure declare the exceptions it can signal; an undeclared one becomes a failure [Liskov 1979]. That pair of choices — termination, and a distinction between declared exceptions and everything else — is the ancestor of nearly every modern design, Okkama's included.

Exception hierarchies. C++ and Java made exceptions objects of a class hierarchy, caught by type [Stroustrup 1994]. Java went further with checked exceptions: a method must declare in its signature the checked exceptions it may throw, and the compiler verifies that each one is caught or passed on [Gosling 2023]. Checked exceptions have been argued over ever since. The usual complaint is that signatures fill with exception types that change with the implementation, and callers wrap or swallow them to make the compiler quiet. Java also kept a second, unchecked family, RuntimeException and Error. That is CLU's distinction again, though a handler catching Exception sees both.

Errors as values. Go returned to return values, but as a convention rather than an accident: a function returns (result, error), and the caller checks err != nil. Rob Pike's "Errors are values" argues that an error is data the program can compute with, not a special control path [Pike 2015]. The cost is repetition, and the old weakness of return codes: nothing forces the check. Rust keeps the value approach but makes it impossible to ignore: a fallible function returns Result<T, E>, which must be unwrapped or propagated with ?, and a separate mechanism, panic!, is for bugs [Klabnik 2023]. Two channels again.

Let it crash. Erlang drew the line most sharply. A process that meets a condition it was not written for does not try to recover. It crashes, and a supervisor that knows the larger picture restarts it in a known state [Armstrong 2003]. Defensive code that tries to handle every imaginable failure locally is, in Armstrong's account, where reliability goes to die.

Abandonment. The design closest to Okkama's is the one Joe Duffy describes for Midori, Microsoft's research operating system. Bugs — contract violations, out-of-bounds indexing, arithmetic overflow — abandon the whole process, with no chance for local code to intercept them. Recoverable errors are declared in signatures and handled with a lightweight try [Duffy 2016]. Duffy's argument is that the two need different mechanisms. Code that treats a bug as recoverable continues in a state nobody designed for, and a model without that option is both simpler and more reliable.

The empirical record outside research systems agrees. Yuan and colleagues studied 198 user-reported failures of five widely used distributed systems (Cassandra, HBase, HDFS, Hadoop MapReduce and Redis). In 92% of the catastrophic ones, the last step was the incorrect handling of a non-fatal error the code had explicitly signalled. Many of the faulty handlers were empty, or did nothing but log, or contained a TODO [Yuan 2014]. The lesson is uncomfortable. Error handlers are code that rarely runs, so they are rarely tested, so they are where the bugs live. A language cannot make handlers correct, but it can make them fewer, typed and impossible to write by accident.

Okkama takes from each step:

  • From CLU and Midori: termination, and a hard line between declared failures and bugs.
  • From Go and Rust: the declared failures are plain values.
  • From Erlang: bugs are not handled locally at all.
  • From Yuan et al.: no construct catches "anything".

10.3 Resumption: the road not taken

Goodenough's paper allowed two outcomes after a handler runs. Termination abandons the failed operation; resumption lets the handler repair the situation and the operation continues where it stopped [Goodenough 1975]. PL/I's ON-conditions resumed, and so do the conditions of Common Lisp, the most expressive error system in wide use. In Lisp, signalling a condition does not unwind the stack: handlers run on top of the code that signalled, and that code offers named restarts — use another value, retry, skip this record — among which a handler higher up chooses [Pitman 1996]. The policy is decided by the code that knows the larger picture, the mechanism by the code that knows the details, and nothing is unwound until the choice is made.

C++ considered resumption and left it out. Stroustrup recounts that the committee heard from people who had used resumption in large systems: it was seldom used, and where it was used, a termination with a retry written around it served as well [Stroustrup 1994]. Every widely used language since has chosen termination.

Okkama terminates too, for two reasons of its own.

  • A resumed handler runs inside the failed scope. Its resources are still owned and live, half-built objects included. Termination closes that scope first, and its resources are destroyed before any handler runs.
  • Restarts would be a second control-flow vocabulary. What a restart offers can be said with what Okkama already has: a role the caller passes in. The low-level code asks the policy what to do, and the caller's policy decides.
module bible/policy v1.0.0;

// What a Lisp restart offers, as a role: the code that meets a bad amount
// asks a policy the caller passed in, and the caller's policy decides.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "strings/parse" take Number;

enum AmountError is Error = (invalid(text is string));

role BadAmount {
    replacement(text is string) is Maybe<int>;
}

object Strict does BadAmount {
    Strict();
    replacement(text is string) is Maybe<int> { Maybe<int>.none; }
}

object Zero does BadAmount {
    Zero();
    replacement(text is string) is Maybe<int> { Maybe.some(0); }
}

object Amounts {
    has policy is BadAmount;
    Amounts(:policy);
    total(texts is @string) is int {
        texts.reduce(0) -> sum, text {
            let parsed = try? Number(text).int() else -1;
            let amount = if parsed >= 0 { parsed; } else {
                match policy.replacement(text) { case Maybe.some(n): n; case Maybe.none: throw AmountError.invalid(text); };
            };
            sum + amount;
        };
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let texts = ["10", "x", "5"];
    out.writeln(Amounts(policy: Zero()).total(texts).string());
    out.writeln(try { Amounts(policy: Strict()).total(texts).string(); } catch e is AmountError { e.text(); });
    0;
}

Output:

15
AmountError.invalid("x")

Amounts does not know whether a bad amount should count as zero or stop the import. It asks its BadAmount, and only a .none answer becomes an error. The decision stays with the caller, as with a restart. It is visible in the type, travels as an ordinary value and can be faked in a test, and no stack is held open while it is made.

10.4 Bugs are not values: panic and runtime errors

These end the run, whatever catch clauses surround them:

  • panic "message" — the program's own declaration that something impossible happened. The message is any string, usually a literal sentence that names the assumption that broke.
  • A bare confirm condition; whose condition is false (§10.9).
  • Runtime errors. An index or slice out of bounds, division or modulo by zero, a failed narrowing of a role or any value. Each is detected during execution and reported as RuntimeError: ….

The run does not simply stop. It unwinds: every scope between the failure and the top runs its defer blocks and destroys the resources it owns, in reverse order (Chapter 11). The report then goes to standard error and the process exits with status 1. Here is a withdrawal in which the program throws an expected error for a zero amount, and panics on a case it believes cannot happen:

module bible/panic v1.0.0;

// A panic is not an error value: no catch clause sees it, and the run ends
// with exit status 1 after cleanup.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Rejected is Error = (rejected);

object Account {
    has balance is int;
    Account(:balance);
    withdraw(amount is int) is Account {
        confirm amount > 0 else throw Rejected.rejected;
        confirm amount <= balance else panic "Withdrawal checked above, still overdrawn";
        Account(balance: balance - amount);
    }
    left() is int { balance; }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let account = Account(balance: 50);
    out.writeln(try { account.withdraw(0).left().string(); } catch e is Rejected { "rejected: " + e.text(); });
    out.writeln(try { account.withdraw(80).left().string(); } catch e is Error { "never printed"; });
    0;
}

Output:

rejected: Rejected.rejected
exit 1

The second try has a catch e is Error, the widest typed clause there is, and it still does not run. The report names the panic, its location and the call stack:

Panic: Withdrawal checked above, still overdrawn
  --> 10-panic.ok:14:9
   |
14 |         confirm amount <= balance else panic "Withdrawal checked above, still overdrawn";
   |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
Stack trace (most recent call first):
  at Account.withdraw (10-panic.ok:14:9)
  at main (10-panic.ok:24:23)

A runtime error looks the same, with RuntimeError: in place of Panic:. An index past the end prints RuntimeError: Array index out of bounds, and 7 % d with d zero prints RuntimeError: Modulo by zero, each with the offending expression underlined.

Why not let the program catch these? Because a caught bug is a hidden bug. A handler that catches an out-of-bounds index has no way to know which assumption failed or what state the half-finished operation left behind. In practice such a handler logs the error and lets the program carry on with that state. That is the pattern Yuan et al. found at the root of catastrophic failures. Stopping preserves the evidence. A long-running service that must survive its own bugs does what Erlang does: it runs the risky work in a separate unit (a task or a worker process) and lets the supervising code react to the unit's death, not to the bug inside it.

10.5 Error enums

An expected failure is a value, and its type is an error enum: an enum declared is Error. Its cases are the ways the component can fail, and their payloads carry the context.

enum LineError is Error = (
    blank(line is int),
    shape(line is int, text is string),
    amount(line is int, cause is InvalidInteger)
);
enum LedgerError is Error = (line(cause is LineError), overdraft(account is string, short is int));

The rules are short.

  • is Error is the only role an enum may declare. An error enum is not generic, and it is always a variant enum. A match over it must cover every case or have else, even when no case has a payload.
  • Payloads are values. A payload field may hold string, int, byte, float, rat, bool and enums whose payloads follow the same rule. That includes other error enums, which is how one failure carries another (LedgerError.line(cause)). Objects, roles, collections, char, actions and any are rejected. An error must survive the scope that raised it, and its owner's resources must not, so an error cannot hold a resource.
  • text() is generated. It spells the case the way the source would: LineError.blank(2), LineError.amount(2, InvalidInteger.source("sixty")). Strings are written as Okkama string literals, escapes included: a payload with a quote and a line break prints back as Ferr.text("a \"q\"\n"), exactly as the source wrote it, so one payload never reads as two arguments and the report stays on one line (#306). Numbers use string(), booleans are true/false, and nested enums are written out recursively. The report of an uncaught error starts with it.

The role Error is built in and requires a public text() is string. Three kinds of value do it:

  • error enums;
  • NativeFailure, a host failure (§10.11);
  • Cancelled, a cancelled task (Chapter 20).

An object cannot. object Fault does Error is a compile error, and the message names the fix: Object "Fault" cannot do Error: errors are enums, declare `enum Fault is Error = (...)` .

That rule is the most visible difference from Java or C#, and it is deliberate. In those languages an exception is an object of a class hierarchy. Callers catch a superclass to mean "any of these", the hierarchy grows with the implementation, and fields are added to carry whatever someone needed once. An error enum is a closed list, visible in one declaration. Adding a case is a change every exhaustive match notices. Grouping is explicit, because a component that wraps another component's failures says so with a payload, not with a superclass. And since the value is data, two errors compare by value and print the same.

One enum per component is the intended granularity. LineError is everything the line parser can report, and LedgerError everything the import can report, including "a line was bad" as a case that carries the LineError.

10.6 throw

throw raises an expected failure. It takes an error enum value, an Error reference — usually a caught error being passed on — or a NativeFailure:

throw LineError.blank(number);
throw LedgerError.line(e);        // a new error carrying the caught one
throw e;                          // pass on a caught error
throw;                            // rethrow the error being handled

Bare throw; exists only inside a catch body, and the compiler checks that lexically. An action called from a catch body cannot rethrow implicitly, because it cannot know what is being handled. Bare throw; preserves the thrown value's identity and origin: the report still points at the place where the error was first raised, not at the rethrow.

throw never produces a value, like return, so a catch body that throws needs no value of its own. The parser in the opening example relies on that:

let amount = try { Number(parts[1]).int(); }
             catch e is InvalidInteger { throw LineError.amount(number, e); };

The try yields an int. The catch body never yields, because it throws.

confirm condition else throw value; (§10.9) is the guarded form, and it is how most errors are raised in practice: a check, and the failure if the check does not hold.

10.7 try and catch

try evaluates a block and, if the block throws, selects a catch clause by the type of what was thrown:

let message = try {
    "balance " + Import(lines: lines).run(start).string();
}
catch LedgerError.overdraft(account, short) {
    "overdraft on " + account + " by " + short.string();
}
catch e is LedgerError {
    "rejected: " + e.text();
};

The rules:

  • try is an expression and a statement. Like if, it yields the value of the block that ran, the try body or the selected catch body. It can also stand alone as a statement.
  • At least one typed clause. Each clause names its types, and the types must guarantee Error: Error itself, an error enum, NativeFailure or Cancelled. A clause can name several types, catch e is DbError, NetError { … }, and the binding then has the type Error.
  • Patterns instead of a binding. A clause may list error enum cases with their payloads bound positionally, _ for an ignored field: catch LedgerError.overdraft(account, short) { … }. A case of the right enum that does not match the pattern goes on to the next clause of the same try. Patterns are one level deep. catch LedgerError.line(LineError.shape(line, text)) is rejected with Expected a binding or _ in variant pattern, so a nested cause is taken apart with a match in the clause body, as report does in the opening example.
  • Source order. Clauses are tried top to bottom, and the first that fits wins. A failure no clause fits leaves the try unchanged, with its type, value and origin.
  • Separate scopes. The try body and each catch body are separate child scopes. Names bound in the body are not visible in a clause, and the binding of a clause exists only in that clause.
  • Cleanup comes first. Before a clause is selected, the try body's scope is closed: its defer blocks run and the resources it owns are destroyed, newest first. Only the thrown error's own payload survives into the clause. A failure during that cleanup does not replace the body's failure; it is attached to it (§10.8).

What try does not have is as important as what it has.

No catch-all. There is no catch e { } and no catch (...). The narrowest way to catch everything expected is catch e is Error. Even that clause sees only thrown errors, never a panic, a runtime error or a budget stop, and a reader sees in the source that it is the widest net. A lowercase name alone does not compile:

module bible/catch_all v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

main() is int {
    let text = try { "ok"; } catch e { "anything"; };
    Stdout().writeln(text);
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

10-catchall-rejected.ok:6:38: syntax error at "{": Expect "is" after catch error name.
  |
6 |     let text = try { "ok"; } catch e { "anything"; };
  |                                      ^

No finally. Work that must happen whether the block succeeds or fails is a defer in that block (Chapter 11). A finally clause would be a second spelling of the same idea, and it would run in a different scope from the code it cleans up after.

No guards. A clause cannot add a condition (catch e is DbError if e.retryable()). The condition belongs in a case of the error enum, where the thrower decides it once, not in each handler.

10.8 Causes

A failure often has a reason that is itself a failure. A storage error makes an order fail, and a parse error makes a line fail. Okkama keeps the reason in two ways.

As a payload. When the cause is part of what the caller needs to decide, put it in the error: enum OrderError is Error = (storage(cause is StoreError), …). The cause is then an ordinary value. The caller can match on it, text() prints it, and it means the same.

module bible/cause v1.0.0;

// Two ways to keep the cause of a failure: as a payload (a value the
// program can match), and as the runtime link a new error gets when it
// leaves a catch (for the report).
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum StoreError is Error = (closed, full(limit is int));
enum OrderError is Error = (storage(cause is StoreError), rejected(reason is string));

object Store {
    Store();
    save(id is int) is int {
        if id > 2 { throw StoreError.full(2); }
        id;
    }
}

object Orders {
    has store is Store;
    Orders(:store);
    place(id is int) is int {
        try { store.save(id); } catch e is StoreError { throw OrderError.storage(e); }
    }
    explain(id is int) is string {
        try {
            self.place(id).string();
        }
        catch OrderError.storage(cause) {
            match cause {
                case StoreError.full(limit) { "store holds " + limit.string(); }
                case StoreError.closed { "store closed"; }
            }
        }
        catch e is OrderError { e.text(); }
    }
}

main() is int {
    let orders = Orders(store: Store());
    let out = Stdout();
    out.writeln(orders.explain(1));
    out.writeln(orders.explain(3));
    out.writeln(OrderError.storage(StoreError.full(2)).text());
    0;
}

Output:

1
store holds 2
OrderError.storage(StoreError.full(2))

Figure 10.2. A cause as a payload the program reads, and as a link the report prints.

As a runtime link. Every new error raised while a catch body is handling another one keeps the handled error as its cause, with its value, origin and stack. This happens whether or not the new error mentions the old one, so a catch that throws a less detailed error does not lose the evidence. It also holds after an await. The link is diagnostic: the program cannot read it, but the report of an uncaught failure prints it:

OrderError: OrderError.failed(7)
Caused by:
  StoreError: StoreError.closed
  --> uncaught.ok:10:56

A catch body that completes normally leaves no link behind, so a later, unrelated throw is not blamed on an old failure. Bare throw; keeps the original carrier instead of creating a new one.

The third kind of extra failure is a secondary. When cleanup itself fails while a scope unwinds from a failure, the cleanup failure does not replace the original; it is attached to it as a secondary and reported after it. The first failure is usually the one worth reading, and cleanup code should not be able to hide it. Section 11.14 works through an example.

10.9 confirm: the contract inside the code

confirm states a condition the code relies on. It is Okkama's form of the assertions of Design by Contract, in which preconditions, postconditions and invariants are part of the program's text, not of its comments [Meyer 1992]. There are three forms, one per failure channel:

confirm items.size() == 3;                            // a bug if false
confirm amount > 0 else throw Rejected.rejected;      // an expected failure
confirm amount <= balance else panic "Overdrawn";     // a bug, with a sentence
  • Bare confirm is an internal invariant. If it fails, the run stops with RuntimeError: confirm failed and the location of the confirm.
  • confirm … else throw is a precondition of a public action, checked against input the caller supplied. A false condition throws the given error, and the caller may catch it. Most errors in the standard library are raised this way. Number(text).int() starts with confirm source.length() > 0 && source != "-" … else throw InvalidInteger.source(source);.
  • confirm … else panic is an invariant that deserves a sentence in the report.

The else at the top level of the condition belongs to confirm, even when the condition ends in an index. confirm size >= pair[1] else panic "short"; runs the panic; before 0.5.6 the index took that else as its own fallback, the sentence was lost and a false condition stopped with the bare confirm failed (issue #521). An index or Maybe fallback inside a condition is written in parentheses: confirm size >= (pair[5] else 0) else throw …;.

The condition must be a bool, and there is no way to switch confirm off. A contract that disappears in production is a contract nobody tests, and a confirm costs one evaluation of its condition.

10.10 try? and try!

Two prefix forms adapt a fallible expression to code that wants to treat failure as a value, or as impossible:

module bible/marks v1.0.0;

// try? turns a thrown error into Maybe.none; try! turns it into a panic.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "strings/parse" take Number;

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let port = try? Number("8080").int() else 80;
    let fallback = try? Number("http").int() else 80;
    out.writeln(port.string() + " " + fallback.string());
    let parsed = try? Number("12").int();
    out.writeln(match parsed { case Maybe.some(n): "some " + n.string(); case Maybe.none: "none"; });
    let sure = try! Number("42").int();
    out.writeln(sure.string());
    let broken = try! Number("forty-two").int();
    out.writeln(broken.string());
    0;
}

Output:

8080 80
some 12
42
exit 1
  • try? value has the type Maybe<T>. It is Maybe.some(value), or .none if evaluating it throws any error. It combines with else, which supplies a fallback, and with match (Chapter 7). A void call cannot be wrapped, since there is no value to put in the Maybe, and neither can a successor result, since its must-use obligation would be lost.
  • try! value keeps the type of the value and turns a thrown error into a panic, Unexpected error: <text()>, located at the try!. It says "this cannot fail here". When the author is wrong, the run stops with the original error in the report, not with a silently wrong value.

T is the type of the operand's successful paths. A branch that throws does not erase it, even when a literal condition selects that branch: try? (if true { throw E.a; } else { 2; }) else 7 is 7. When no path succeeds, T comes from the Maybe<T> boundary or from the fallback after else, and without either the compiler asks for one. A caught error leaves none, so code after a try? is reachable even when its operand never returns normally. A throw ends its own path, not the expression that handles it (#307).

Both forms see thrown errors only. Panics and runtime errors pass through them, and cleanup runs as for try. try? discards the error, so it is for the cases where why something failed does not matter, such as a fallback port or an optional setting. Where the reason matters, the error stays an error.

10.11 Failures from the host

Code that reaches outside the program — files, sockets, processes, databases, cryptography — gets the host's failures as values too. A native provider reports a failure as a NativeFailure with a stable domain (core.fs, core.crypto, …), a stable code (not_found, already_closed, invalid_input, permission_denied, …), the canonical operation that failed and a diagnostic message:

try { open(path, 1, 0); }
catch failure is NativeFailure {
    failure.domain();     // "core.fs"
    failure.code();       // "not_found"
    failure.message();    // for people, never for branching
}

Code should branch on domain and code only. Raw errno values, host exception classes and localized OS messages never become language values, so a program behaves the same on macOS and Linux.

Most programs never see a NativeFailure directly. The standard library catches it at the boundary and rethrows a typed error that belongs to the module's own vocabulary. crypto/error turns a NativeFailure with invalid_input into InvalidCryptoInput.because(message), permission_denied into AuthenticationFailed.failed, and anything else into CryptoUnavailable. A program that uses crypto/kdf catches the crypto errors, not the host's codes.

An unexpected host error, one the provider has no stable code for, is not a NativeFailure. It is a runtime error and ends the run.

Cancelled is the failure a task sees when the work it awaited was cancelled. Chapter 20 explains it with structured concurrency.

10.12 A boundary in practice

The pieces meet at module boundaries. Below is a settings loader. Reading the file can fail in the file system's terms, and parsing can fail in the loader's own terms. The caller should see only the loader's terms.

module bible/config v1.0.0;

// A settings loader at a module boundary: the file system's failures arrive
// as FileError (std turned the host's NativeFailure into it), and the loader
// answers in its own vocabulary, ConfigError.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "fs/path" take Path;
import "fs/file" take File;
import "fs/error" take FileError;

enum ConfigError is Error = (missing(path is string), unreadable(path is string), syntax(line is int, text is string));

object Settings {
    has pairs is %string:string;
    Settings(:pairs);
    value(key is string, fallback is string) is string { pairs[key] else fallback; }
    size() is int { pairs.size(); }
}

object SettingsText {
    has text is string;
    SettingsText(:text);
    settings() is Settings {
        let lines = text.split("\n").filter() -> line { line.length() > 0; };
        let pairs is %string:string = (0..lines.size()).reduce([:]) -> found, i {
            let parts = lines[i].split("=");
            confirm parts.size() == 2 else throw ConfigError.syntax(i + 1, lines[i]);
            found + [parts[0]: parts[1]];
        };
        Settings(pairs: pairs);
    }
}

object SettingsFile {
    has path is string;
    SettingsFile(:path);
    settings() is Settings {
        let text = try {
            File(path: Path(path)).text().content();
        }
        catch FileError.not_found(_) {
            throw ConfigError.missing(path);
        }
        catch failure is FileError {
            throw ConfigError.unreadable(path);
        };
        SettingsText(text: text).settings();
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let parsed = SettingsText(text: "port=8080\nhost=example.org\n").settings();
    out.writeln(parsed.value("host", "localhost") + ":" + parsed.value("port", "80"));
    let describe = (load is () is Settings) is string {
        try { "loaded " + load().size().string(); }
        catch ConfigError.missing(path) { "no file " + path + ", using defaults"; }
        catch ConfigError.syntax(line, text) { "line " + line.string() + " is not key=value: " + text; }
        catch e is ConfigError { e.text(); }
    };
    out.writeln(describe(() is Settings { SettingsFile(path: "no-such-settings.conf").settings(); }));
    out.writeln(describe(() is Settings { SettingsText(text: "port=8080\nverbose\n").settings(); }));
    0;
}

Output:

example.org:8080
no file no-such-settings.conf, using defaults
line 2 is not key=value: verbose

Three things happen at the boundary.

  1. fs/file already caught the host's NativeFailure and rethrew it as a case of FileError, here FileError.not_found(path). The loader never touches a host code directly.
  2. The loader translates once, in one place. A missing file becomes ConfigError.missing(path), the case a caller is likely to handle, by falling back to defaults. Any other file-system failure becomes ConfigError.unreadable(path).
  3. The caller's describe names the cases it handles and lets catch e is ConfigError print the rest. Nothing outside the loader mentions FileError. If the loader one day reads settings from a database, its callers do not change.

The two catch clauses read in order: the one case the loader turns into its own meaning first, then the rest of the enum. A clause binds what it needs from the case and drops the rest with _.

10.13 Budgets are not failures

A run can be given budgets: --max-steps, --max-memory, --max-output and --timeout. Running out of one is neither an expected failure nor a bug in the program. It is the environment withdrawing permission to continue. The run ends with Execution budget exhausted: steps (memory, output) or Execution interrupted and exit status 1. No catch sees it, not even catch e is Error, and destroy does not run, because the budget would be spent again by the cleanup.

Budget stops are observed at these points:

  • every step, function entry and loop iteration;
  • inside a long sort;
  • between the rounds of a PBKDF2 derivation.

A native that cannot look, such as an Argon2 hash or a blocking read, ends when it ends. With --timeout, the command line then stops the run at most a second after the deadline.

10.14 Failures across tasks

await passes a task's failure to the awaiting code unchanged: same type, same value, same origin. The awaiting code catches it like any other:

module bible/tasks v1.0.0;

// A failure crosses await unchanged: the awaiting task catches it by type.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum FetchError is Error = (timeout(host is string), refused(host is string));

object Fetcher {
    has host is string;
    Fetcher(:host);
    async body() is string {
        if host == "slow.example" { throw FetchError.timeout(host); }
        "page from " + host;
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let fast = spawn Fetcher(host: "fast.example").body();
    let slow = spawn Fetcher(host: "slow.example").body();
    out.writeln(await fast);
    let text = try { await slow; } catch FetchError.timeout(host) { "gave up on " + host; };
    out.writeln(text);
    0;
}

Output:

page from fast.example
gave up on slow.example

Two rules make concurrent failure as strict as sequential failure.

  • A failure is never lost. If a spawned task fails and no one awaits it, the run itself fails: the report is printed and the process exits with status 1, even when main returned 0. A forgotten task cannot hide an error. This is a deliberate choice, and the conformance suite pins it (L08.shutdown.unobserved-failure).
  • Cancellation is a failure value of its own. When the work a task awaited is cancelled, the task sees Cancelled, which does Error and can be caught. Structured await (Chapter 20) guarantees that the task resumes only after the cancelled work has finished its cleanup.

Within one run, a bug in any task ends the run, as it does in sequential code. A program that must outlive its own bugs needs a boundary a bug cannot cross, which is Erlang's lesson again. In Okkama that boundary is a separate process, supervised from outside (Chapter 21).

10.15 What reaches the top

An error that no catch handles unwinds the whole run like a panic: cleanup runs scope by scope, and the process exits with status 1. The report starts with the error's type and text(), then gives the location of the throw, the cause chain and the call stack:

OrderError: OrderError.failed(7)
Caused by:
  StoreError: StoreError.closed
  --> uncaught.ok:10:56
   |
10 |         try { self.save(id); } catch e is StoreError { throw OrderError.failed(id); }
   |                                                        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
Stack trace (most recent call first):
  at Orders.place (uncaught.ok:10:56)
  at main (uncaught.ok:14:17)

main returns the exit status of a successful run, and it must be in 0–255. A larger value is reported as RuntimeError: main() must return an int in 0..255, got N, so the success channel and the failure channel stay apart here too.

10.16 Designing an error vocabulary

A module's error enums are part of its public API, as much as its actions. The standard library follows a handful of rules, and they work outside it too.

  • One enum per kind of failure the caller tells apart. strings/parse has InvalidInteger. crypto/error has InvalidCryptoInput, AuthenticationFailed and CryptoUnavailable, because a caller reacts differently to bad input, a forged message and a missing algorithm.
  • Name the case after what happened, not after who noticed. ConfigError.missing(path), not ConfigError.file_system_error. The caller decides from what happened. Who noticed is in the stack trace.
  • Put in the payload what the caller needs to act, and nothing else. A line number for a syntax error, the missing amount for an overdraft. The host's message goes into a diagnostic payload at most. It is not stable across platforms, and code must never branch on it.
  • Translate at the boundary, once. A module catches the failures of the modules it uses and rethrows them in its own terms, as the settings loader does. Failures that pass through many layers unchanged tie every caller to the bottom layer.
  • Wrap when the caller needs the cause, pass on when it does not. LedgerError.line(cause) wraps because the caller may want to know which line failed and how. throw e; passes on when the module has nothing to add.
  • Do not use errors for control flow. A lookup that may find nothing returns Maybe (Chapter 7), not an error. An error says the operation could not do what it promised. A missing optional value is not that.

10.17 Testing failures

A failure is part of an action's contract, so it gets tests like the successful path. The test runner (okkama run -t) provides test.throws(Type) { … }, which passes when the block throws a value of that type and fails otherwise. When the payload matters, a try with a pattern says exactly which case is expected:

test "an overdraft is refused with the missing amount" {
    test.throws(LedgerError) { Account(balance: 50).withdraw(80); };
    let short = try { Account(balance: 50).withdraw(80).left(); }
                catch LedgerError.overdraft(missing) { missing; };
    test.is(short, 30);
}

A panic or a runtime error inside a test fails that test, not the whole run: the runner isolates each test, reports --- FAIL with the message, and goes on to the next one.

Error handlers are rarely exercised in production, and that is where Yuan et al. found the catastrophic bugs. A failure path that a test has never run is a guess. Chapter 15 returns to tests, fakes and properties.

10.18 Okkama among other languages

Language Expected failure Bug Forced to handle? Catch everything Cleanup
Java checked exception (declared) RuntimeException, Error checked ones, by the compiler catch (Throwable t) finally, try-with-resources
Kotlin exception (all unchecked); Result in the library exception no catch (e: Throwable) finally, use { }
Go error value panic no, by convention recover() in a deferred call defer
Rust Result<T, E> panic! warned if ignored (#[must_use]) catch_unwind, discouraged Drop
Haskell Either, Maybe; exceptions in IO error, exceptions by the type, for Either catch on SomeException bracket
Okkama error enum value, thrown panic, confirm, runtime error no none (catch e is Error sees thrown errors only) defer, destroy

Two columns set Okkama apart. In the bug column it is the only language in the table where a bug cannot be caught at all; Rust comes closest. In the catch-everything column it is the only one where no construct catches everything. Okkama is weaker in the "forced to handle" column: nothing makes a caller deal with an error, and the compiler does not know which errors an action can throw.

10.19 What this design costs

The two channels are a strong opinion, and opinions cost something.

  • More declarations. Every component that can fail declares an error enum. A Java programmer reaches for IllegalArgumentException. An Okkama programmer writes a case.
  • No catch-all. Code that really means "any expected failure" writes catch e is Error, and code that wants to survive bugs has to put the risky work in a separate task or process. That is more structure than a catch (Throwable t). Okkama counts it as a feature; a programmer who needs a quick script may not.
  • Signatures do not say what an action throws. CLU and Java's checked exceptions put the failures in the signature, and Midori did too. Okkama does not: the caller learns from the documentation and the source which error enums an action may throw, and the compiler does not check that a caller handles them. Declaring them would bring back the churn checked exceptions are known for; not declaring them leaves a gap a reader must fill.
  • Errors cannot carry objects. An error that would naturally hold the request that failed must hold the request's identifying values instead.
  • Patterns are one level deep. A nested cause is taken apart with a match in the clause body.
  • The runtime cause chain is for reports only. A program cannot walk it. A cause the program must inspect has to be a payload.
  • No named handlers yet. A handler shared by several try blocks has to be an action called from each clause. Named catch handlers were proposed and declined as too magical (#148).

Against these costs stands what the design removes:

  • handlers that swallow bugs;
  • exception hierarchies that grow with the implementation;
  • finally blocks that clean up in the wrong scope;
  • error messages that differ between platforms;
  • the guess, at every catch, about what might arrive there.

The next chapter takes up the other half of the story: what runs when a scope ends, on success or failure.

Chapter 11defer and destroy: deterministic resources

Memory is not the only thing a program borrows. Files, sockets, transactions, locks, temporary directories and child processes need timely release. Okkama manages memory automatically and guarantees resource release at scope exit.

Two constructs give resources back:

  • defer registers work to run when the current block ends.
  • destroy declares, in an object, what releasing that object means. The scope that owns the object runs it when the scope ends.

Both run on every exit from a scope: normal completion, return, last, next, a thrown error, a panic, and the cancellation of an async task. The program below opens handles in a block, in a called action and in a loop, and prints every open and close:

module bible/resources v1.0.0;

// A resource is an object with destroy. The scope that owns it destroys it
// when the scope ends, newest first, after the scope's defer blocks.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Log {
    Log();
    line(text is string) is void { Stdout().writeln(text); }
}

object Handle {
    has name is string;
    has log is Log;
    Handle(:name, :log) { log.line("open " + name); }
    label() is string { name; }
    destroy { log.line("close " + name); }
}

object Opener {
    has log is Log;
    Opener(:log);
    kept(name is string) is Handle {
        let temp = Handle(name: name + ".tmp", log: log);
        Handle(name: name, log: log);
    }
}

main() is int {
    let log = Log();
    {
        let a = Handle(name: "a", log: log);
        let b = Handle(name: "b", log: log);
        defer log.line("defer 1, sees " + a.label());
        defer log.line("defer 2");
        let alias = a;
        log.line("body uses " + alias.label() + " and " + b.label());
    }
    log.line("after the block");
    let kept = Opener(log: log).kept("report");
    log.line("caller holds " + kept.label());
    for [1, 2] -> i {
        let step = Handle(name: "step" + i.string(), log: log);
    }
    log.line("end of main");
    0;
}

Output:

open a
open b
body uses a and b
defer 2
defer 1, sees a
close b
close a
after the block
open report.tmp
open report
close report.tmp
caller holds report
open step1
close step1
open step2
close step2
end of main
close report

The output reads like a contract.

  • The block's defers run first, newest first. Then its resources are destroyed, newest first: b before a.
  • alias names the same object as a, and a is closed once.
  • The action kept closes its temporary handle when it returns, and the handle it returns lives on in main until main ends.
  • Each loop iteration closes its own handle before the next begins.

This chapter explains those rules, their origins and their costs.

11.1 Memory and resources are different problems

Automatic memory management alone does not promise timely resource release. A program can exhaust file descriptors or database connections while still having plenty of memory; these resources need an explicit lifetime tied to scopes.

Finalizers, code the collector runs when it reclaims an object, were the first answer, and they failed. Hans Boehm showed that a finalizer runs at an unpredictable moment, on an unpredictable thread, possibly after other objects it needs have been finalized, and that making finalizers correct requires synchronization most programmers never write [Boehm 2003]. Java deprecated Object.finalize and then marked finalization for removal [Christian 2021]. Its replacement is explicit: try-with-resources, which closes an AutoCloseable at the end of a block.

When a destroy runs is determined by the program’s scopes and ownership, independently of memory pressure.

11.2 The lineage

Deterministic cleanup has three ancestors, and Okkama takes from each.

  • Destructors. C++ ties a resource to the lifetime of a scoped object: the constructor acquires it and the destructor releases it when the scope ends, whatever the exit. Stroustrup calls the idiom "resource acquisition is initialization" [Stroustrup 1994]. Rust keeps the idea, as Drop, and adds ownership checked at compile time, so a value is dropped exactly once by its single owner [Klabnik 2023].
  • Block-scoped release. Python's with statement [Rossum 2005], Java's try-with-resources and C#'s using release a resource at the end of a block. The call site must remember to use the construct; forgetting it compiles.
  • defer. Go and Swift register a call that runs when the function (Go) or the block (Swift) exits. It handles work that is not about one object, such as an audit line, restoring a setting or removing a file.

Okkama's destroy is a destructor: the object says how it is released, and callers do not have to remember. Its defer is Swift's: block-scoped, not function-scoped. Ownership, the question "who runs the destructor", follows object identity at run time, not a static borrow checker (§11.5).

11.3 defer

defer log.line("defer 1, sees " + a.label());

Figure 11.1. What runs when a block ends: defers first, then the objects the block owns, newest first.

A reached defer registers its expression and runs it exactly once when the block that contains it ends.

  • The expression is evaluated at exit, not at registration. The receiver and the arguments are read when the block ends. In the opening example the first defer sees a, which is still alive, because defers run before the block's resources are destroyed.
  • Only reached defers count. A defer in a branch that did not run registers nothing.
  • Newest first. The defers of a block run in reverse order of registration, and then the block's owned resources are destroyed, also newest first.
  • The current block, not the function. A defer inside a loop body runs at the end of that iteration, and one inside an inner block runs when the inner block ends. This is Swift's rule, not Go's.
  • Every defer is attempted. If one fails, the remaining ones still run. An existing failure of the body has priority. The failure of a defer cancels a pending return, and otherwise the first defer failure wins.
  • A defer may await. In an async action, defer await audit.flush(); suspends the scope's exit until the work is done, cancellation included.
  • The discard rules still apply. A defer cannot silently drop a value that must be used, such as the result of a successor action.

defer is for work that belongs to a block. Releasing a resource belongs to the resource, and that is destroy.

11.4 destroy

object Handle {
    has name is string;
    Handle(:name) { Stdout().writeln("open " + name); }
    destroy { Stdout().writeln("close " + name); }
}

An object has at most one destroy block. It is not an action: nothing can call it. It runs once, when the scope that owns the object ends. It may read self and the fields, and call actions. It cannot assign fields through a successor: the object is being released, not updated.

The order of destruction is fixed:

  1. Inside one scope, objects are destroyed in reverse order of construction, so a resource opened later, which may depend on an earlier one, is released first.
  2. An owner is destroyed before the objects held in its fields. Its destroy still sees intact fields, and the fields are destroyed after it, newest first. The session in §11.7 shows the order: end session, close s2.out, close s2.in.
  3. Every identity enters destruction at most once. That holds even when its destroy fails, and even when the destroy makes an alias of self.

A destroy that fails does not stop the others. Every remaining resource is still destroyed, and the failure is reported. If the scope was already unwinding from a failure, the cleanup failure is attached to that failure as a secondary (Chapter 10), not put in its place.

The standard library's resources combine destroy with an explicit close(). A File or a TlsConnection does Closing, whose close() is idempotent, and its destroy closes it too. Code that wants to release early calls close(), and code that forgets gets the same release at scope exit.

11.5 Who owns what

"The scope that owns the object" needs a definition, and Okkama's is about identities, not names.

Figure 11.2. Who owns what: a binding owns, an alias and a parameter borrow, a fresh argument is adopted, a result moves to the caller.

  • A binding owns a fresh object. let a = Handle(...) makes the block of the let the owner of the new handle.
  • An alias borrows. let alias = a; creates a second name for an object the scope already owns. No second owner appears, so there is no double destroy.
  • Parameters and receivers borrow. An action that receives an existing object does not own it. A fresh argument nobody owns yet, such as use(Handle(...)), is adopted by the called action and destroyed when it returns, unless the action returns it.
  • A returned object moves to the caller. When an action ends, the resources reachable from its result are released from its ownership and taken over by the caller. In the opening example, kept closes report.tmp and hands report to main.
  • Aggregates carry identities. An array, a map, the fields of an object and an any box hold the identities they contain. A fresh resource put into a fresh array is owned by whoever owns the array, and repeated references never duplicate ownership.
  • A cap is its owner. A cap (Section 12.8) carries the object it was taken from. Returned from an action, it moves the object and its resources to the caller; taken from an object a scope owns, it borrows.
  • Successors are independent. A successor action returns a new object with a new identity and its own lifetime (Chapter 13).
  • Loop iterations are scopes. What an iteration owns is destroyed when the iteration ends. A value the loop produces, through last value or the result of map, reduce and the other functional operations, moves to the enclosing scope.
  • Branches are scopes. An if, match, try or catch branch destroys what it owns when it ends, its last let included, in reverse order. Only a value the branch produces and the program uses moves out: let log = if verbose { File.create(a); } else { File.create(b); }; (#308; before 0.4.2 the last let of a branch lived until the enclosing scope ended).

One program walks through the rules in order. Every Tag says when it is destroyed, so the output shows which scope owned it:

module bible/owners v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Tag {
    has name is string;

    Tag(:name);

    label() is string { name; }

    destroy { Stdout().writeln("  destroy " + name); }
}

object Desk {
    Desk();

    // A parameter borrows: the caller's tag outlives this action.
    look(tag is Tag) is int { tag.label().length(); }

    // A fresh argument is adopted, and destroyed when the action returns.
    adopt(tag is Tag) is int { tag.label().length(); }

    // A returned object moves to the caller.
    make(name is string) is Tag { Tag(name: name); }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let desk = Desk();
    out.writeln("alias");
    {
        let a = Tag(name: "a");
        let alias = a;
        out.writeln("  " + alias.label() + " has one owner");
    }
    out.writeln("parameter");
    let kept = Tag(name: "kept");
    desk.look(kept);
    out.writeln("  still here: " + kept.label());
    out.writeln("fresh argument");
    desk.adopt(Tag(name: "adopted"));
    out.writeln("returned");
    {
        let made = desk.make("made");
        out.writeln("  main owns " + made.label());
    }
    out.writeln("aggregate");
    {
        let tags = [Tag(name: "first"), Tag(name: "second")];
        out.writeln("  " + tags.size().string() + " in the array");
    }
    out.writeln("loop");
    for ["x", "y"] -> name {
        let t = Tag(name: name);
        out.writeln("  iteration " + t.label());
    }
    out.writeln("branch");
    if kept.label().length() > 0 {
        let b = Tag(name: "branch");
        out.writeln("  inside " + b.label());
    }
    out.writeln("end");
    0;
}

Output:

alias
  a has one owner
  destroy a
parameter
  still here: kept
fresh argument
  destroy adopted
returned
  main owns made
  destroy made
aggregate
  2 in the array
  destroy second
  destroy first
loop
  iteration x
  destroy x
  iteration y
  destroy y
branch
  inside branch
  destroy branch
end
  destroy kept
  • alias names a a second time; a is destroyed once, when its block ends.
  • look borrows kept, which is still there after the call and lives until main ends.
  • adopt receives a tag nobody owned yet and destroys it when it returns.
  • make returns its tag, so main's block owns made and destroys it there.
  • The array owns both tags and destroys them in reverse order of creation.
  • Each loop iteration and the if branch destroy what they own when they end.

The conformance suite pins the same rules: alias borrowing, returned resources, independent successors, branch scopes and resources gathered by reduce.

A role can hide a resource

A field typed by a role holds whichever implementation it was given, and ownership follows that value, not the type. Ledger is done by Account, which has nothing to close, and by Vault, which has a destroy. A Record built with an account owns nothing to release; one built with a vault owns the vault. Every tenth record below holds a vault, and the array of records that records returns moves to the caller with the three vaults in it:

module bible/role_resource v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

// Any ledger answers its balance; only a vault holds something to close.
role Ledger {
    balance() is int;
}

object Account does Ledger {
    has amount is int;

    Account(:amount);

    balance() is int { amount; }
}

object Vault does Ledger {
    has amount is int;

    Vault(:amount);

    balance() is int { amount * 2; }

    destroy { Stdout().writeln("  vault " + amount.string() + " closed"); }
}

object Record {
    has id is int;
    has ledger is Ledger;

    Record(:id, :ledger);

    total() is int { ledger.balance(); }
}

object Bank {
    Bank();

    // Every tenth record holds a vault; the array of records is returned.
    records(count is int) is @Record {
        (0..count).map() -> i {
            let ledger is Ledger = if i % 10 == 0 { Vault(amount: i); } else { Account(amount: i); };
            Record(id: i, ledger: ledger);
        };
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    {
        let records = Bank().records(25);
        let sum = records.reduce(0) -> total, record { total + record.total(); };
        out.writeln("main owns 25 records, total " + sum.string());
    }
    out.writeln("the block ended");
    0;
}

Output:

main owns 25 records, total 330
  vault 20 closed
  vault 10 closed
  vault 0 closed
the block ended
  • The vaults are made inside a map in Bank.records. The array they end up in is that action's result, so they move to the block in main with it.
  • Nothing closes while the block reads them: reduce borrows every record.
  • When the block ends, the three vaults close, newest first. The other twenty-two records hold accounts, and nothing happens to them.

A role does not make its values resources; each value decides for itself. Code that holds a Ledger reads the same whether the ledger behind it has something to close or not, and nothing is closed where nothing is held.

An Atomic names, it does not own

Atomic is the mutable cell tasks share (Section 13.11), and it borrows. Putting an object into it does not move the object, and the cell does not keep it alive: the object is destroyed when its owner's scope ends, whatever the cell still names.

module bible/atomic_borrows v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "async/atomic" take Atomic;

object Lamp {
    has name is string;

    Lamp(:name);

    label() is string { name; }

    destroy { Stdout().writeln("  " + name + " off"); }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let hall = Lamp(name: "hall");
    // The cell names a lamp; it does not own one.
    let current = Atomic(hall);
    {
        let desk = Lamp(name: "desk");
        current.replace(desk);
        out.writeln("the cell names " + current.value().label());
    }
    // desk's block has ended, and so has desk: the cell still names it.
    out.writeln("after the block the cell names " + current.value().label());
    current.replace(hall);
    out.writeln("the cell names " + current.value().label() + " again");
    0;
}

Output:

the cell names desk
  desk off
after the block the cell names desk
the cell names hall again
  hall off
  • hall is owned by main, and the cell starts by naming it.
  • desk is owned by the inner block. The cell names it from the inside of the block, and the block still destroys it when it ends.
  • After the block the cell names a lamp that is already off. Its fields can still be read, but whatever it held has been closed, and a call that needs the resource fails as a closed one does (Section 11.10).

The rule is the price of a cell that many tasks may read: if writing to it moved ownership, the cell would become an owner that no scope closes. Put into an Atomic what outlives it, an object its own scope owns, or keep the owner in a task that lives as long as the cell (Section 20.6).

11.6 Resources in collections and closures

Containers do not own; they carry. A map of handles, an array of connections and a closure that captured a socket all hold identities, and whoever owns the container owns what it holds.

module bible/containers v1.0.0;

// Resources inside a map, and inside a closure: the container carries their
// identities, so whoever owns the container owns them.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Handle {
    has name is string;
    Handle(:name) { Stdout().writeln("open " + name); }
    label() is string { name; }
    destroy { Stdout().writeln("close " + name); }
}

object Pool {
    Pool();
    named(names is @string) is %string:Handle {
        let first is %string:Handle = [names[0]: Handle(name: names[0])];
        (1..names.size()).reduce(first) -> found, i { found + [names[i]: Handle(name: names[i])]; };
    }
    greeter(name is string) is () is string {
        let handle = Handle(name: name);
        () is string { "hello from " + handle.label(); };
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    {
        let handles = Pool().named(["db", "cache"]);
        out.writeln("using " + handles["cache"].label());
    }
    out.writeln("map released");
    {
        let greet = Pool().greeter("socket");
        out.writeln(greet());
    }
    out.writeln("closure released");
    0;
}

Output:

open db
open cache
using cache
close cache
close db
map released
open socket
hello from socket
close socket
closure released

The map built in named leaves the action as its result, so main's inner block owns both handles and closes them when it ends, newest first. The closure returned by greeter captured handle. The handle therefore moves with the closure, the closure keeps it usable, and it closes when the block that holds the closure ends, not when greeter returns.

Two consequences are worth stating.

  • Removing an element does not release it. Maps and arrays are values: removing a key with - builds a new map, while the old map, still owned, keeps the handle. A resource is released when its owner's scope ends, not when the last collection that mentions it is computed.
  • A closure is as much an owner's tool as a field. A callback that keeps a connection alive keeps it alive exactly as long as the callback is reachable from an owning scope. That is usually what the author meant, and when it is not, the remedy is to pass the connection as an argument instead of capturing it.

11.7 Cleanup on the failure path

Cleanup does not depend on how a scope ends. A thrown error unwinds through the same defers and destroys as a normal exit, and so do a panic and a runtime error. A try closes its body's scope before it chooses a catch clause, so a clause never runs while the failed body still holds resources.

module bible/unwind v1.0.0;

// On a failure the same cleanup runs: the try body's resources are closed
// before a catch clause is chosen. A constructor that fails cleans what it
// opened, and its unfinished object is never destroyed.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Refused is Error = (refused(name is string));

object Handle {
    has name is string;
    Handle(:name) { Stdout().writeln("open " + name); }
    destroy { Stdout().writeln("close " + name); }
}

object Session {
    has input is Handle;
    has output is Handle;
    Session(name is string, allowed is bool) {
        input = Handle(name: name + ".in");
        confirm allowed else throw Refused.refused(name);
        output = Handle(name: name + ".out");
    }
    destroy { Stdout().writeln("end session"); }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let result = try {
        let first = Handle(name: "first");
        defer out.writeln("defer in try");
        throw Refused.refused("body");
        "unreachable";
    }
    catch Refused.refused(name) {
        "caught " + name;
    };
    out.writeln(result);
    out.writeln(try { Session("s1", false); "made"; } catch e is Refused { "session refused: " + e.text(); });
    {
        let ok = Session("s2", true);
        out.writeln("session open");
    }
    0;
}

Output:

open first
defer in try
close first
caught body
open s1.in
close s1.in
session refused: Refused.refused("s1")
open s2.in
open s2.out
session open
end session
close s2.out
close s2.in

Three rules are visible.

  • In the first try, defer in try and close first print before caught body. The catch clause runs after the body's cleanup.
  • Session("s1", false) opens s1.in and then fails its confirm. The handle it opened is closed. The session itself was never finished, so its destroy does not run: an object that did not finish construction is never released as if it had.
  • A finished session is destroyed owner first: end session, then its fields, newest first.

The thrown error's own payload survives the cleanup: it moves into the matching catch clause. It cannot hold a resource in any case (Chapter 10), so the move releases nothing early.

11.8 async destroy

Some resources cannot be released instantly. A connection must flush what it buffered, and a server must let its requests drain. Their destroy has to wait, and Okkama lets it: async destroy (#154).

module bible/async_destroy v1.0.0;

// A destroy that must wait is async: it is awaited where the owning scope
// of an async action ends, before the action's result is delivered.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Channel {
    has name is string;
    Channel(:name);
    async flush() is int { Stdout().writeln("flush " + name); 1; }
}

object Connection {
    has channel is Channel;
    Connection(:channel);
    send(text is string) is void { Stdout().writeln("send " + text); }
    async destroy {
        let flushed = await channel.flush();
        Stdout().writeln("closed after " + flushed.string() + " flush");
    }
}

object Client {
    Client();
    async talk() is string {
        let connection = Connection(channel: Channel(name: "c1"));
        connection.send("hello");
        "talked";
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let said = await Client().talk();
    Stdout().writeln(said);
    0;
}

Output:

send hello
flush c1
closed after 1 flush
talked
  • It is awaited where the owner's scope ends, in the same reverse order as other destroys, on every exit, a failure included. talk delivers its result only after the connection has flushed and closed.
  • A cancellation does not interrupt it. A task cancelled while an async destroy runs gets Cancelled at its next await, after the scope has closed. Cleanup that can be interrupted halfway is worse than no cleanup.
  • Only async code may own such an object. A synchronous scope has nothing to suspend, so owning one there is a compile error:
module bible/async_owner v1.0.0;

object Connection {
    Connection();
    async destroy { 0; }
}

object Client {
    Client();
    talk() is int {
        let connection = Connection();
        1;
    }
}

main() is int { Client().talk(); }

The compiler answers:

11-async-owner-rejected.ok:11:26: semantic error: Connection has an async destroy; own it in an async action

The rule is transitive. An object that holds an async-destroy resource in a field, an array or a map has to be owned in async code too. Borrowing one, by passing it to a synchronous action that does not keep it, is fine.

An async destroy replaces a pattern that needed two defers, a close and an awaited settled(). In 0.4.2 the standard library dropped 33 helper objects that existed only to await one child in cleanup, because a structured await already waits for it (#264). In 0.6.2 nine of its remaining cleanup guards, in the HTTP client and server and in TCP, moved from defer await onto async destroy, which costs no more than the deferred close it replaces (#329).

11.9 Resources and tasks

A task is a scope too. What an async action makes and keeps is released when the action's task ends. What it returns moves to the scope that awaits it, exactly as a synchronous result moves to its caller:

module bible/task_resources v1.0.0;

// Tasks own what they make: a resource a task keeps to itself is released
// when the task ends; one it returns moves to the scope that awaits it.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Handle {
    has name is string;
    Handle(:name) { Stdout().writeln("open " + name); }
    label() is string { name; }
    destroy { Stdout().writeln("close " + name); }
}

object Worker {
    has name is string;
    Worker(:name);
    async count() is int {
        let scratch = Handle(name: name + ".scratch");
        scratch.label().length();
    }
    async opened() is Handle {
        let temp = Handle(name: name + ".tmp");
        Handle(name: name);
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let length = await Worker(name: "w1").count();
    out.writeln("counted " + length.string());
    {
        let handle = await Worker(name: "w2").opened();
        out.writeln("awaited " + handle.label());
    }
    out.writeln("end");
    0;
}

Output:

open w1.scratch
close w1.scratch
counted 10
open w2.tmp
open w2
close w2.tmp
awaited w2
close w2
end

w1.scratch closes before counted is printed: the task that made it has ended. w2.tmp closes inside opened, and w2 lives in the block that awaited it, until that block ends.

A task that is never awaited still releases what it owns when it finishes, and a cancelled task unwinds through its scopes like a failure, async destroys included (Chapter 20). A resource cannot outlive its owner unnoticed by escaping into a forgotten future.

11.10 Close early, destroy anyway

Scope exit is the latest moment a resource is released, not the only one. The resources of the standard library follow one pattern:

  • an idempotent close(), part of the Closing role;
  • closed(), to ask whether it already happened;
  • a destroy that calls close().

Code that knows it is done releases early. Code that forgets, or fails halfway, still gets the release when the scope ends.

module bible/closing v1.0.0;

// The standard library's resources pair an idempotent close() with a destroy
// that calls it: release early when you can, and the scope still releases
// whatever you forgot.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "fs/directory" take Directory;
import "fs/path" take Path;
import "fs/entry" take FileEntry;
import "fs/temp" take TemporaryDirectory;

object Workspace {
    Workspace();
    used(parent is Directory) is bool {
        let scratch = TemporaryDirectory(parent, "bible-");
        let where = scratch.path();
