        let before = FileEntry(where).existence();
        scratch.close();
        scratch.close();
        before && !FileEntry(where).existence() && scratch.closed();
    }
    forgotten(parent is Directory) is Path {
        let scratch = TemporaryDirectory(parent, "bible-");
        scratch.path();
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let parent = Directory(Path("."));
    out.writeln("closed early, twice: " + Workspace().used(parent).string());
    let left = Workspace().forgotten(parent);
    out.writeln("closed by destroy: " + (!FileEntry(left).existence()).string());
    0;
}

Output:

closed early, twice: true
closed by destroy: true

used closes its temporary directory twice. The second call does nothing, and the directory is gone before the action returns. forgotten never calls close(): the directory is removed when forgotten ends, because the action owned it and returned only its path, a plain value.

The pattern costs one rule for authors of resource objects: close() must be idempotent, and every other action of a closed resource should fail with a catchable already_closed, not misbehave.

11.11 Replacing a resource: rebinding keeps, folding releases

A log that rotates its file is a resource that is replaced over and over. In Okkama the replacement is a successor, rotated(), which builds a new Log around a new Segment. Where the old Log goes then depends on how the program holds it, and the two usual ways give different lifetimes.

module bible/rotation v1.0.0;

// A successor that replaces a resource: rebinding keeps every old segment
// open until the scope ends; a fold releases each one as the next is made.

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Segment {
    has name is string;
    Segment(:name) { Stdout().writeln("open " + name); }
    destroy { Stdout().writeln("close " + name); }
    name() is string { name; }
}

object Log {
    has current is Segment;
    has index is int;
    Log(:index) { current = Segment(name: "log." + index.string()); }
    rotated() is ^Log {
        ^current = Segment(name: "log." + (index + 1).string());
        ^index = index + 1;
    }
    name() is string { current.name(); }
}

object Runs {
    Runs() {}
    rebound() is void {
        let log = Log(index: 0);
        for 1..=3 -> n {
            log = log.rotated();
            Stdout().writeln("writing to " + log.name());
        }
        Stdout().writeln("done rebound");
    }
    folded() is void {
        let final = (1..=3).reduce(Log(index: 0)) -> log, n { log.rotated(); };
        Stdout().writeln("writing to " + final.name());
        Stdout().writeln("done folded");
    }
}

main() is int {
    Runs().rebound();
    Stdout().writeln("--");
    Runs().folded();
    0;
}

Output:

open log.0
open log.1
writing to log.1
open log.2
writing to log.2
open log.3
writing to log.3
done rebound
close log.3
close log.2
close log.1
close log.0
--
open log.0
open log.1
close log.0
open log.2
close log.1
open log.3
close log.2
writing to log.3
done folded
close log.3
  • Rebinding keeps every old value. In rebound, log = log.rotated() gives the name a new value, but it does not destroy the old one early: the old Log belongs to the scope that declared log, and its destroy runs when that scope ends (Section 13.7). All four segments stay open until done rebound, and then close newest first. For three rotations this is harmless; for a server that rotates every hour and runs for a month, it is a file per hour held open until the action returns.
  • A fold releases each value. In folded, reduce passes each Log to the next step and keeps only what the step returns. Each step is an iteration, and an iteration's scope ends with it (Section 11.5), so the old segment closes as soon as its successor exists: open log.1, then close log.0. Only the last Log leaves the loop.

The rule behind both is the one this chapter has used throughout: a resource lives as long as the scope that owns it, not as long as a name refers to it. A long-running program that replaces a resource should therefore replace it inside a scope that ends: a fold, a loop iteration that produces the next value, or a state owner whose request handler is such a scope (Section 20.6). Rebinding a name in a scope that lives for the whole program is the one shape to avoid.

11.12 A worked example: a connection pool

A pool is the textbook case where resources outlive the code that uses them. In Okkama a pool is an ordinary object whose field holds its connections; lending one out is a borrow, and nothing else is needed.

module app v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Connection {
    has id is int;
    Connection(:id) { Stdout().writeln("open " + id.string()); }
    query(text is string) is string { "#" + id.string() + " " + text; }
    destroy { Stdout().writeln("close " + id.string()); }
}

// The pool owns its connections through its field; lending one only borrows it.
object Pool {
    has connections is @Connection;
    Pool(size is int) {
        self.connections = (1..=size).map() -> id { Connection(id: id); };
    }
    lend(turn is int) is Connection { connections[turn % connections.size()]; }
    destroy { Stdout().writeln("drain pool of " + connections.size().string()); }
}

object Worker {
    has pool is Pool;
    Worker(:pool);
    run(jobs is @string) is int {
        for 0..jobs.size() -> turn {
            Stdout().writeln(pool.lend(turn).query(jobs[turn] else ""));
        }
        jobs.size();
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    {
        let pool = Pool(size: 2);
        let done = Worker(pool: pool).run(["select 1", "select 2", "select 3"]);
        out.writeln(done.string() + " jobs");
    }
    out.writeln("after the block");
    0;
}

Output:

open 1
open 2
#1 select 1
#2 select 2
#1 select 3
3 jobs
drain pool of 2
close 2
close 1
after the block
  • The pool owns, through its field. The constructor builds an array of fresh connections with map, and the array becomes the pool's field, so the pool's owner owns every connection in it (§11.5).
  • Lending borrows. lend returns a connection that the pool still owns. The worker queries it and never closes it: a borrower cannot destroy what it does not own, and no "return to pool" call exists to be forgotten.
  • One end, in a fixed order. When the block that holds the pool ends, the pool's own destroy runs first and sees intact connections, then the connections close, newest first: drain pool of 2, close 2, close 1. The worker's three jobs used the connections in turn and released nothing.

What the example does not do is as telling. There is no reference counting on the connections and no release in a finally. The worker holds the pool it borrowed and lives inside the same block, so every connection it used is still owned when it uses it, and released once, by the pool's owner. A pool that must hand a connection to code that outlives it moves the connection out instead, and that is a different, visible operation.

11.13 A worked example: commit or roll back

A transaction is the classic resource whose release depends on how the work ended: if the work finished, commit; if anything went wrong, roll back. In Okkama the rollback is the transaction's destroy, and the commit is an explicit call.

module app v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "async/atomic" take Atomic;

enum Rejected is Error = (amount(cents is int));

// A transaction rolls back unless it was committed before its scope ended.
object Transaction {
    has label is string;
    has committed is Atomic<bool>;
    Transaction(:label) {
        self.committed = Atomic(false);
        Stdout().writeln(label + ": begin");
    }
    commit() is void {
        committed.replace(true);
        Stdout().writeln(label + ": commit");
    }
    destroy {
        if !committed.value() {
            Stdout().writeln(label + ": rollback");
        }
    }
}

object Shop {
    Shop();
    order(label is string, cents is int) is string {
        let tx = Transaction(label: label);
        confirm cents > 0 else throw Rejected.amount(cents);
        Stdout().writeln(label + ": charge " + cents.string());
        tx.commit();
        label + " done";
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let shop = Shop();
    out.writeln(shop.order("first", 250));
    let second = try { shop.order("second", -5); }
        catch Rejected.amount(cents) { "second refused: " + cents.string(); };
    out.writeln(second);
    0;
}

Output:

first: begin
first: charge 250
first: commit
first done
second: begin
second: rollback
second refused: -5
  • The rollback cannot be skipped. Whatever path leaves order — the confirm that refuses a non-positive amount, a failure further down, a bug — the transaction's scope ends and its destroy runs (§11.7). The second order shows it: begin, then rollback, then the caller's catch.
  • The commit is the one decision. Without tx.commit() the transaction rolls back, so forgetting the commit loses the work instead of half-doing it. The commit is the last step of order that can change the outcome.
  • What destroy must see is a field it can read. The flag is an Atomic<bool>, declared in the object, where a reader sees it. A successor would be the wrong tool here: committed() returning ^Transaction would make a new identity with its own lifetime (§11.5), and the original, never committed, would still be destroyed and roll back.

Other languages put the same decision in different places. Python's sqlite3 connection, used as a context manager, commits or rolls back when the with block ends [Python sqlite3]; D's scope(failure) runs a block only when the scope is left by an exception [D specification]. Both depend on the caller writing the construct at every use. In Okkama the transaction carries the rule itself: there is no way to hold one that its scope will not settle.

11.14 When cleanup itself fails

Releasing can fail as well. A journal that flushes its buffer when it is released may find the disk full, and a connection may fail to send its goodbye. Section 11.4 stated the rule in one sentence; this example shows what it means:

module bible/cleanupfails v1.0.0;

// A destroy that fails does not stop the others. On a normal exit the first
// cleanup failure becomes the failure; on a failing exit the original stays,
// and cleanup failures ride along as secondaries.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Unflushed is Error = (full(name is string));
enum Rejected is Error = (empty);

// A journal flushes its buffer when it is released; a full disk refuses.
object Journal {
    has name is string;
    has disk_full is bool;

    Journal(:name, :disk_full);

    destroy {
        Stdout().writeln("flush " + name);
        confirm !disk_full else throw Unflushed.full(name);
    }
}

object Export {
    has rows is int;

    Export(:rows);

    run() is string {
        let orders = Journal(name: "orders", disk_full: true);
        let audit = Journal(name: "audit", disk_full: false);
        let metrics = Journal(name: "metrics", disk_full: true);
        confirm rows > 0 else throw Rejected.empty;
        rows.string() + " rows";
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let quiet = try {
        Export(rows: 3).run();
    }
    catch e is Unflushed {
        "export failed: " + e.text();
    };
    out.writeln(quiet);
    out.writeln("--");
    let refused = try {
        Export(rows: 0).run();
    }
    catch e is Rejected {
        "export refused: " + e.text();
    }
    catch e is Unflushed {
        "export failed: " + e.text();
    };
    out.writeln(refused);
    0;
}

Output:

flush metrics
flush audit
flush orders
export failed: Unflushed.full("metrics")
--
flush metrics
flush audit
flush orders
export refused: Rejected.empty
  • Every destroy runs. Two of the three journals fail to flush, and audit and orders are still flushed after metrics fails. A failed release does not stop the others, so one full disk cannot leak a file handle.
  • On a normal exit, the first cleanup failure becomes the failure. run would have returned "3 rows". It throws Unflushed.full("metrics") instead: metrics was released first, newest first, so its failure came first. The other failure, from orders, is attached to it as a secondary.
  • On a failing exit, the original failure stays. With no rows, run throws Rejected.empty, and that is what the caller catches. Both flush failures happened while unwinding from it, and they ride along as secondaries instead of replacing it. A failure in cleanup cannot hide the failure that caused the cleanup.
  • Secondaries are for the reader, not the program. A catch receives only the primary failure. A program cannot list secondaries and decide by them. The report of an uncaught failure prints them:
Rejected: Rejected.empty
Secondary cleanup failure:
  Unflushed: Unflushed.full("metrics")
Secondary cleanup failure:
  Unflushed: Unflushed.full("orders")
  --> cleanup.ok:33:9

The question is old, and languages have answered it in four ways.

  • C++ forbids the failure. A destructor that throws while the stack unwinds from another exception ends the program with std::terminate. Since C++11, destructors are noexcept unless they say otherwise. Stroustrup's guarantees of exception safety assume destructors that do not throw [Stroustrup 2001]. A release that can fail must therefore report it some other way, or not at all.
  • Python keeps both by chaining. An exception raised while another is being handled keeps the first as its __context__, and the traceback shows both [PEP 3134]. But the new exception is the one that propagates. A failing __exit__ or finally replaces the original as the thing the caller catches.
  • Go leaves it to the programmer. defer f.Close() discards the error unless the code captures it. Since Go 1.20, errors.Join combines several errors into one value, so the deferred close and the original error can travel together, if the programmer writes it [Go 1.20 Release Notes].
  • Java suppresses. try-with-resources closes resources in reverse order, and a close does not stop the others. An exception from the body propagates, and close failures are added to its suppressed list. When only closes fail, the failure of the resource closed first propagates, and the rest are suppressed on it (JLS §14.20.3 [Gosling 2023]).

Okkama's rule is Java's, with two differences. It applies to every owned resource at every scope end, not only inside a try that names the resource. And the suppressed list is not a value a program can read. Java's getSuppressed() lets a handler branch on a cleanup failure that was not the reason the code failed. Okkama keeps the handler on the reason, and it leaves the secondaries to the person reading the report.

11.15 What is not promised

Deterministic cleanup has limits, and they are worth knowing.

  • A scope that never ends never cleans up. A loop without an exit keeps its resources until the process ends.
  • A killed process runs nothing. kill -9, a power failure or an out-of-memory kill from the operating system skip every destroy. Durable state needs a transaction or a write-ahead design, not a destructor.
  • A budget stop runs no destroy. When --timeout or another budget ends the run, cleanup does not run, since it would spend the budget again (Chapter 10). The process exits, and the operating system closes what the process held.
  • A destroy cannot be retried. It runs at most once. If it fails, the failure is reported and the identity is considered released.

11.16 What this design costs

  • Ownership is checked at run time, not at compile time. Rust rejects a program that would release a value twice or use it after release. Okkama prevents the double release by construction (at most once per identity), but a program can still use a closed resource. The Closing objects of the standard library answer that with a catchable already_closed failure, not with undefined behaviour.
  • Async destroy constrains the owner. A synchronous library cannot own a resource whose release must wait. It has to borrow one or become async.
  • Cleanup order is fixed. Newest first, owner before fields. A program that needs another order must express it with defer, or by nesting scopes.

Against that stands what the design removes:

  • finally blocks;
  • forgotten close() calls;
  • finalizers and their surprises;
  • resource leaks that show up only under load.

All of it comes from two constructs and one rule: the scope that owns a resource releases it.

Chapter 12Objects, fields and constructors

Part IV is about objects, and Okkama has nothing else to put behaviour in. There are no free functions, no static methods, no classes with class-level state and no inheritance. A program is objects calling objects, and a main that creates the first of them. Chapter 2 told the history that led here, and Chapter 3 the rules. This chapter shows what an object is in the language: its fields, its constructors, its actions and the few things it may not do.

module bible/objects v1.0.0;

// An object: private fields, explicit constructors that check their input,
// public behaviour, hidden helpers. Its state never changes.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum InvalidCash is Error = (negative(cents is int));

object Cash {
    has digit is int;
    has cents is int = 0;
    has currency is string = "USD";

    Cash(digit is int, cents is int) {
        self.digit = digit;
        self.cents = cents;
        confirm digit * 100 + cents >= 0 else throw InvalidCash.negative(digit * 100 + cents);
    }
    Cash(:digit, :currency);

    total() is int { self.in_cents(digit) + cents; }
    label() is string { currency + " " + self.total().string(); }

    hidden in_cents(units is int) is int { units * 100; }
}

object Bag {
    has items is @int;
    Bag() { items = []; }
    Bag(items is ...int) { self.items = items...; }
    size() is int { items.size(); }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    out.writeln(Cash(3, 25).label());
    out.writeln(Cash(digit: 2, currency: "EUR").label());
    out.writeln(Bag().size().string() + " " + Bag(1, 2, 3).size().string());
    out.writeln((Cash(1, 0) == Cash(1, 0)).string());
    out.writeln(try { Cash(-1, 50).label(); } catch e is InvalidCash { e.text(); });
    0;
}

Output:

USD 325
EUR 200
0 3
true
InvalidCash.negative(-50)

The rest of the chapter takes that program apart:

  • Cash holds three fields and never changes them;
  • it has two constructors, one of which checks its input;
  • it exposes behaviour (total, label), never its fields;
  • a helper marked hidden is callable only by Cash itself;
  • two Cash values with the same fields are equal;
  • Bag shows an empty and a variadic constructor side by side.

12.1 Declaring an object

object Cash {
    has digit is int;
    has cents is int = 0;
    has currency is string = "USD";
    Cash(digit is int, cents is int) { … }
    total() is int { … }
    hidden in_cents(units is int) is int { … }
}

An object declaration has a name and a body, and nothing else: the header takes no parameters, because state is declared only by has. The name is a type name and starts with an upper-case letter. Two objects of one module cannot share a name. The body may hold:

  • has fields;
  • constructors, at least one;
  • actions, public or marked hidden;
  • at most one destroy (Chapter 11);
  • cap contracts (§12.8);
  • test blocks.

The order of these parts does not matter to the compiler. The style used in the standard library and in this book puts fields first, then constructors, then the public actions, then the hidden ones.

An object is not a class in the Java sense. There is no extends, no super, no protected, no abstract or virtual method, no static member. Sharing behaviour between objects is done by composition: an object holds another and calls it. Sharing a contract between objects is done with roles (Chapter 14). The rationale is Chapter 2's: implementation inheritance couples a subclass to every detail of its superclass, and the fragile base class problem is the result [Mikhajlov 1998]. Composition couples it only to a contract.

12.2 Fields are private and permanent

has is the only way to declare state.

has digit is int;                 // required: a constructor must bind it
has cents is int = 0;             // optional: a default
has given, family is string;      // several names, one type
has currency = "USD";             // the type comes from the initializer: string

A field's type may come from its initializer. has currency = "USD"; declares a string field exactly as has currency is string = "USD"; does. This is inference at compile time, not dynamic typing: the compiler takes the initializer's static type once, every object keeps that one type, and constructors and successors are checked against it as against a written type. Only the initializer gives the type, never a constructor's assignment, so has digit; is an error that asks for the type. An initializer that settles no type, such as an empty [] or [:], needs the type written (has items is @string = [];), and nothing widens to any.

Two rules make fields different from fields in most languages.

A field is private to its object. Code outside the object cannot read it, not even with the same type in the same module:

module bible/private_field v1.0.0;

object Cash {
    has cents is int;
    Cash(:cents);
}

main() is int {
    Cash(cents: 1).cents;
}

The compiler answers:

12-field-rejected.ok:9:20: semantic error: Field "cents" of object "Cash" is private; call an action instead

The message says what to do instead: call an action. That is the Elegant Objects rule "no getters" turned into a compile error [Bugayenko 2016]. A caller who needs something derived from the state asks the object for the behaviour (total(), label()), and the object decides how to compute it. The idea is Parnas's information hiding: a module's data representation is the decision most likely to change, so it is the one to hide [Parnas 1972].

A field never changes. Outside a constructor there is no assignment to a field at all:

module bible/assign v1.0.0;

object Counter {
    has count is int;
    Counter(:count);
    bump() is int {
        count = count + 1;
        count;
    }
}

main() is int { 0; }

The compiler answers:

12-assign-rejected.ok:7:9: semantic error: Field "count" cannot be assigned after construction: objects are immutable; return a successor instead (`is ^Counter` and `^count = …`)

The fix the message suggests is the subject of Chapter 13: an action that returns a successor, a new object with updated fields. A value is the same value for as long as anyone holds it. Concurrent tasks can share it without a lock, and a caller cannot be surprised by a change made behind its back.

Inside the object, a field is read by its bare name (cents) or as self.cents. A parameter or a local may shadow the bare name, and self.cents then still means the field. Field defaults are evaluated for each construction, before the constructor body, in the scope of the declaration: a default may use literals, other declarations and imports, but not the caller's locals and not other fields of the object being built.

12.3 Constructors are explicit

Every object declares at least one constructor, even an object without fields. None is generated from the fields:

object Marker {
    Marker();
}

An object with fields and no constructor is an error, Object "Marker" must declare a constructor, even if nothing ever constructs it. The rule is deliberate. A generated constructor would make the field list part of every caller's code, and adding a field would silently change how the object is made.

A full constructor has parameters and a body. The body binds fields, with field = value; or self.field = value;, and may run any other statement:

Cash(digit is int, cents is int) {
    self.digit = digit;
    self.cents = cents;
    confirm digit * 100 + cents >= 0 else throw InvalidCash.negative(digit * 100 + cents);
}
  • A field bind is legal only inside a constructor body and its nested blocks, while the object is being built. A later bind of the same field replaces an earlier one, and once the constructor returns the field never changes. Outside constructors the only name = value; is the rebinding of a local to its successor (Section 13.7).
  • Every field must be bound or defaulted by the end of the constructor. Otherwise the compiler reports Object "Cash" field "cents" was not initialized.
  • Parameters may have defaults, as an action's may (Section 13.2): Cash(digit is int, cents is int = 0) is called as Cash(3).
  • The call uses positional or named arguments, never a mix: Cash(3, 25) or Cash(digit: 3, cents: 25). Positional arguments bind to the constructor's parameters, not to the order of the fields.

12.4 Shorthand constructors

Most constructors only copy their arguments into fields. The shorthand says so in one line:

Cash(:digit, :currency);

:digit names a field, and the constructor takes an argument of the field's name and type and binds it. The list is a closed allow-list:

  • Named arguments only. Cash(digit: 2, currency: "EUR") works, and Member(7) is rejected with Constructor of "Member" takes named arguments only: write Member(id: …, name: …) before any argument is evaluated. A listed field that has a default may be left out of the call.
  • Unlisted fields cannot be supplied. They take their defaults, or the constructor's body must bind them.
  • A bodyless shorthand must complete the object. If an unlisted field has no default, the declaration is an error: Constructor shorthand for "Member" cannot initialize required field "name".
  • A shorthand may have a body. The listed fields are bound first, and then the body runs. It may bind the remaining fields and check the input: Score(:value) { confirm value >= 0 else throw InvalidScore.negative(value); }.

Marker(); is the shorthand with no fields, the usual constructor of a stateless object.

12.5 Several constructors

An object may have several constructors, and they overload like actions: by the number of arguments, their types, and, for shorthands, by the names supplied. Cash has a full constructor taking (int, int) and a shorthand taking digit and currency by name, and each call picks the one that fits. Two candidates that fit equally well are an ambiguity error. Declaration order never breaks a tie.

A full constructor may end with a variadic parameter, as Bag(items is ...int) does. Its calls are positional; inside the body the parameter is unpacked with items.... A fixed constructor that fits a call wins over the variadic one, so Bag() takes the empty constructor and Bag(1, 2, 3) the variadic one.

There is no constructor chaining, no this(...) call from one constructor to another. Each constructor binds and checks on its own, and checks are not inherited between overloads. When two constructors share logic, the shared part is an object of its own, or a hidden action both call.

12.6 Validation belongs in the constructor

An object should not exist in an invalid state. The constructor is the only place that can guarantee it, so validation goes there:

confirm digit * 100 + cents >= 0 else throw InvalidCash.negative(digit * 100 + cents);

The last line of the opening example shows the result: Cash(-1, 50) throws InvalidCash.negative(-50) and no Cash is ever made. Everything after the constructor can rely on the invariant without checking it again. This is the Elegant Objects advice "fail fast in constructors" and Meyer's class invariant from Design by Contract, the condition every instance satisfies between public calls [Meyer 1997]. Since Okkama objects never change after construction, the invariant only has to be established once.

When a constructor fails, its defers run and the resources it already owned are released. The unfinished object is never destroyed as if it were complete (Chapter 11, §11.7).

How much work belongs in a constructor? The standard library keeps constructors cheap: bind, normalise, check. Expensive or effectful work — reading a file, parsing a document, opening a connection — happens in an action, often the first one called. ParsedIni(text) stores the text, and the variant that takes explicit limits checks them. Parsing happens in document(), so constructing a ParsedIni never fails for a syntax error in the document. This keeps construction predictable: it validates what it was given and does nothing else.

12.7 Actions and hidden actions

Public actions are the object's interface: total() is int { … }. Their full treatment, with overloading, default arguments and successors, is Chapter 13. Two points belong here.

  • Calls to the object's own actions go through self. Inside Cash, self.in_cents(digit) calls the helper. A bare in_cents(digit) is Undefined action "in_cents". Okkama has no free functions, so a bare call would have nothing to refer to.
  • hidden keeps an action out of the contract. hidden in_cents(...) is callable only by the object itself, through self. Each action is marked on its own; constructors cannot be hidden, since they are how the object is made. A hidden action is an implementation detail, free to change; a public one is a promise. The word means the same as before a hidden object or enum (Chapter 19): not part of the public contract.

12.8 Caps: a read-only view of an object

Sometimes a caller should see a few derived facts about an object and nothing else. Passing the whole object hands over all its behaviour. A cap is a named contract of computed fields that the object grants explicitly:

module bible/caps v1.0.0;

// A cap is a named, read-only view of an object: a few computed fields,
// acquired explicitly with `::`, and nothing else of the owner.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Customer {
    has given, family is string;
    has card_number is string;
    Customer(:given, :family, :card_number);
    cap BusinessCard {
        full_name is string { given + " " + family; }
        initials is string { given.slice(0, 1) + family.slice(0, 1); }
    }
    charge(amount is int) is string { "charged " + amount.string() + " to " + card_number.slice(card_number.length() - 4, card_number.length()); }
}

object Printer {
    Printer();
    print(card is Customer::BusinessCard) is string { card::full_name + " (" + card::initials + ")"; }
}

main() is int {
    let customer = Customer(given: "Ada", family: "Lovelace", card_number: "4000123412341234");
    Stdout().writeln(Printer().print(customer::BusinessCard));
    Stdout().writeln(customer.charge(10));
    0;
}

Output:

Ada Lovelace (AL)
charged 10 to 1234

Figure 12.1. A cap grants a named, read-only view; nothing else of the object is reachable through it.

  • cap BusinessCard { full_name is string { … } } declares the computed fields. Their bodies read the owner's fields by name, but have no self and cannot call the owner's actions.
  • customer::BusinessCard acquires the view, and its type is Customer::BusinessCard. A function that takes that type, like Printer.print, can read card::full_name and card::initials. It cannot call charge, read card_number, or turn the view back into a Customer.

Caps are the object-oriented answer to "I need a getter for this one caller". The answer is not to open the field to everyone, but to grant a named, typed view to whoever is handed it.

Inside the object or beside it

A cap is usually declared inside its object, as above. It can also be declared at module scope, beside an object of the same module. Its body then names the owner's fields through the owner type, Box::label:

module bible/cap_outside v1.0.0;

// A cap declared beside its object, in the object's module: the body names
// the owner's fields through the owner type. A generic owner's cap takes the
// owner's type arguments.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Box<T> {
    has item is T;
    has label is string;
    Box(:item, :label);
}

cap Box::Tag {
    text is string { "[" + Box::label + "]"; }
}

object Shelf {
    Shelf();
    show(tag is Box<int>::Tag) is string { tag::text; }
}

main() is int {
    let box = Box(item: 42, label: "answer");
    Stdout().writeln(Shelf().show(box::Tag));
    0;
}

Output:

[answer]

Both forms share one namespace, so an object cannot have two caps of the same name. An imported object cannot be given a cap: only the module that owns an object decides what it shows. A cap of a generic object takes the object's type parameters. It is written Box::Tag where it is declared and Box<int>::Tag where it is used.

What a cap field may do

A cap field's body is an ordinary Okkama block, with local bindings, if, match, confirm and errors. It reads the owner's private fields by name. Three things are missing on purpose.

  • There is no self, not even inside a nested anonymous action, so the body cannot call the owner's actions. Writing self.norm() in a cap is an error:

    module bible/cap_self v1.0.0;

// A cap body has no self and cannot call the owner's actions. object Point { has x, y is int; Point(:x, :y); norm() is int { x * x + y * y; } cap Shown { norm is int { self.norm(); } } }

main() is int { Point(x: 1, y: 2)::Shown::norm; }

The compiler answers:

12-cap-self-rejected.ok:8:31: semantic error: self is not available inside a cap field
  • A field cannot name the cap's other fields. Each field stands on the owner alone.
  • A field is synchronous: there is no await. It may still return a Future it makes explicitly.

A cap cannot write fields or stage a successor. It may call actions of the objects its owner holds, as Report below calls hits.value().

Every read computes

Acquiring a cap evaluates the owner expression once. Every read of a field runs its body again, and nothing is cached, neither a value nor an error:

module bible/cap_reads v1.0.0;

// A cap computes on every read: nothing is cached, neither a value nor an
// error.
import "async/atomic" take Atomic;
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum NoHits is Error = (none);

object Counter {
    has hits is Atomic<int>;
    Counter() { hits = Atomic(0); }

    hit() is void { hits.replace(hits.value() + 1); }

    cap Report {
        seen is string { hits.value().string() + " hits"; }
        share is rat {
            confirm hits.value() > 0 else throw NoHits.none;
            100 / hits.value();
        }
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let counter = Counter();
    let report = counter::Report;
    out.writeln(report::seen);
    out.writeln(try { report::share.string(); } catch e is NoHits { "no share yet"; });
    counter.hit();
    counter.hit();
    out.writeln(report::seen);
    out.writeln(report::share.string());
    0;
}

Output:

0 hits
no share yet
2 hits
50

The first read of share throws NoHits.none, and the read after two hits returns 50. A cap is a view, not a copy. A field whose answer is expensive belongs in an action, where once let (Section 13.13) can keep it.

A cap keeps its owner whole

A cap holds its owner, the whole object with everything it owns, including resources in its fields. For ownership (Section 11.5) a cap is its owner. A cap of a fresh object that an action returns moves the object to the caller. A cap of an object that a scope already owns borrows it, like an alias:

module bible/cap_owner v1.0.0;

// For ownership a cap is its owner: a cap of a fresh object moves the
// object, resources and all, to whoever receives it; a cap of an object a
// scope already owns borrows it.

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Log {
    has name is string;
    Log(:name);
    destroy { Stdout().writeln("close " + name); }
}

object Account {
    has log is Log;
    has owner is string;
    Account(:owner) { log = Log(name: owner); }
    cap Label { text is string { "account of " + owner; } }
}

object Bank {
    Bank();
    label(owner is string) is Account::Label {
        Account(owner: owner)::Label;
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let label = Bank().label("ada");
    out.writeln("got " + label::text);
    {
        let account = Account(owner: "bob");
        let view = account::Label;
        out.writeln("inner " + view::text);
    }
    out.writeln("after inner");
    0;
}

Output:

got account of ada
inner account of bob
close bob
after inner
close ada

ada's log is closed when main ends, because her account came to main inside the cap. bob's log is closed when the inner block that owns his account ends.

A cap is also bound to the version it was taken from. A successor (Chapter 13) is a new version, with caps of its own:

module bible/cap_snapshot v1.0.0;

// A cap stays bound to the version of the object it was taken from; a
// successor has caps of its own.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Order {
    has number is int;
    has paid is bool = false;
    Order(:number);

    settled() is ^Order { ^paid = true; }

    cap Status {
        line is string { "#" + number.string() + (if paid { " paid"; } else { " open"; }); }
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let order = Order(number: 7);
    let before = order::Status;
    let after = order.settled();
    out.writeln(before::line);
    out.writeln(after::Status::line);
    0;
}

Output:

#7 open
#7 paid

before still reads the open order after settled() made the paid one.

What a cap is not

A cap's type is exact. Locals, parameters, results, fields, collections, generics, closures and Futures keep Customer::BusinessCard as it is. Inside any it is opaque. Nothing turns a cap back into its owner: there is no conversion, and no pattern or reflection reaches the owner through it.

A cap has no equality, no ordering and no hashing, so it cannot be a map key. It is not formatted or serialized automatically:

module bible/cap_compare v1.0.0;

// A cap has no equality: two views are not values to compare.
object Point {
    has x, y is int;
    Point(:x, :y);
    cap Shown { text is string { x.string() + "," + y.string(); } }
}

main() is int {
    let p = Point(x: 1, y: 2);
    if p::Shown == p::Shown { 1; } else { 0; }
}

The compiler answers:

12-cap-compare-rejected.ok:12:8: semantic error: Cannot compare Point::Shown and Point::Shown

A cap cannot become a role, have constructors, actions, has fields or nested caps, or be constructed by hand. It is an interface boundary and nothing more. It promises no secrecy against code that holds the full object, no purity, since a field may call actions of objects the owner holds, and no revocation: a cap handed out stays readable as long as it lives.

Cap, role or hidden action

Three tools look alike.

Tool Question it answers Who decides
hidden action what the object does inside the object, for itself
role (Chapter 14) what any object of the role can do the role, for every implementation
cap what this object shows to whoever it hands it the object, for one view

A role is behaviour that many objects provide; a caller holding a role does not know which object it holds. A cap belongs to one object and shows its state; the caller knows exactly whose view it reads. A hidden action is not seen at all.

The standard library follows one rule (Chapter 22): an object reveals itself through a cap. It declares about 130 caps, named for the part they show: page::Head::status, date::Calendar::year, range::Bounds::start, duration::Span::seconds. A cap holds facts that are already computed, or that are trivial to compute, such as a parsed part of a URL or a date's year. Anything that is work stays an action: file.text() reads a file and response.body() reads a body, so neither is a cap.

Caps elsewhere

Most languages answer "show this caller a few facts" with accessors that everyone can call. A Java record gives every component a public accessor [Bierman 2021]. A Kotlin data class and a C# record do the same with properties [Kotlin documentation; C# language reference]. Narrowing the view takes an interface. Then the caller can cast it back to the full class, unless the designer hides the class.

TypeScript's Pick<T, K> and Readonly<T> name a narrower shape. They are structural and erased, so any object of that shape fits, and a cast gets the rest [TypeScript Handbook].

Object-capability languages take another view of what a reference means: holding one is the authority to use it, and a narrower facet is a separate object that forwards only some requests [Miller 2006]. An Okkama cap is closer to such a facet than to a getter. It is a separate, nominal type, the holder cannot widen it, and the owner chooses what it shows. It is not an authority boundary, though: a cap shows state and grants no actions.

12.9 Objects are values

Two Cash objects with the same fields are equal: Cash(1, 0) == Cash(1, 0) is true in the opening example. Okkama compares objects structurally, field by field, without calling any of their actions. An object has an identity too: it decides who owns a resource (Chapter 11), and a successor gets a new one (Chapter 13). But identity is not what == compares. There is no equals to override and no hashCode to keep consistent with it.

That matches how immutable objects are used. A value that cannot change is characterised by what it holds. Two copies of the same amount of money are the same amount, wherever they were made. It also makes value objects usable as map keys: a %Card:int keys on the card's fields, ordered by them, so more[Card(10, Suit.hearts)] finds an entry made with another Card of the same rank and suit. A key object must be a value through and through: every field a scalar, an enum or another such object, and no destroy and no caps. %Tagged:int for an object with a tags is @string field is rejected: Map key type Tagged cannot be a key: field "tags" is @string. Objects that should compare by something else, such as a business key, expose an action for it, and the map keys on that action's result instead.

12.10 Handing self out of a constructor

A constructor cannot call its own actions. self.initials() inside the constructor is rejected, even after the fields that initials reads are bound:

module bible/self_call v1.0.0;

object Account {
    has owner is string;
    has code is string;

    Account(owner is string) {
        self.owner = owner;
        code = self.initials() + "-1";
    }

    initials() is string { owner.slice(0, 2); }
}

main() is int { 0; }

The compiler answers:

12-self-call-rejected.ok:9:16: semantic error: Cannot call actions on self before construction completes

An action may rely on everything the constructor establishes, including the checks that have not run yet. The compiler cannot see which fields an action reads through the actions it calls, so it forbids the call outright.

The constructor may pass self itself to a collaborator. This is the only way two immutable objects can refer to each other: the second one is made while the first is still being built.

module bible/escape v1.0.0;

// A constructor may hand its unfinished `self` to a collaborator. This is the
// only way two immutable objects can refer to each other.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Leaf {
    has up is Tree;
    Leaf(:up);
    describe() is string { "leaf of " + up.name(); }
}

object Tree {
    has name is string;
    has leaf is Maybe<Leaf>;

    Tree(name is string) {
        self.name = name;
        leaf = Maybe.some(Leaf(up: self));
    }

    name() is string { name; }
    describe() is string {
        match leaf {
            case Maybe.some(l) { name + " has a " + l.describe(); }
            case Maybe.none { name; }
        }
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    out.writeln(Tree("oak").describe());
    0;
}

Output:

oak has a leaf of oak

The collaborator holds an unfinished object, and the rule from the start of this section follows it there. The specification forbids calling any action on a receiver whose construction is pending, "through aliases, role references, bound actions and collaborators", and requires the run time to reject such a call before evaluating its arguments. Leaf above only stores up; calling up.describe() in Leaf's constructor would break the rule. The compiler catches the direct self. call, and indirect calls are rejected at run time:

module bible/escape_call v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Echo {
    Echo();
    said(text is string) is string {
        Stdout().writeln(text);
        text;
    }
}

object Leaf {
    has up is Tree;
    has seen is string = "";
    Leaf(up is Tree) {
        self.up = up;
        seen = up.greeted(Echo().said("argument"));
    }
}

object Tree {
    has name is string;
    has leaf is Maybe<Leaf>;
    Tree(name is string) {
        self.name = name;
        leaf = Maybe.some(Leaf(self));
    }
    greeted(text is string) is string { text + " " + name; }
}

main() is int {
    Tree("oak");
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

RuntimeError: Action "greeted" on object "Tree" was called before its construction completed

The call fails before Echo().said("argument") is evaluated, also through a role or bound action. If a constructor fails after self escaped, the object never completes and every later call on it is rejected.

The first use of self may occur inside a functional block, a nested block or a conditional branch. Every collaborator receives the same object identity, including collaborators created in a loop.

The problem is old. Java lets this escape from a constructor and leaves the consequences to the programmer. A non-null field of an object under construction can still read as null. Fähndrich and Leino gave such objects their own "raw" types [Fähndrich 2003]. Summers and Müller's "Freedom Before Commitment" tracks which objects are fully initialised and which may still be "free", with few annotations [Summers 2011]. Okkama takes the cheaper road: one static rule for self, and a run-time check for the indirect cases.

12.11 When construction fails

Section 12.6 made the constructor the gate: an object that exists is valid. This section covers the other side of the gate, the work a constructor did before it refused, and the fields it never got to. Three rules decide both.

Every field is bound when construction ends. Defaults are filled before the body runs, and then the arguments and the body bind the rest. A field that no path of the constructor binds is a compile-time error:

module bible/unbound_rejected v1.0.0;

// A field that no path of the constructor binds is rejected at compile time.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Ticket {
    has route is string;
    has seat is int;

    Ticket(route is string) {
        self.route = route;
    }

    shown() is string { route + ", seat " + seat.string(); }
}

main() is int {
    Stdout().writeln(Ticket("Kostanay - Astana").shown());
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

12-unbound-rejected.ok:10:5: semantic error: Object "Ticket" field "seat" was not initialized

A field bound on some paths and not on others is checked when construction ends, on the path the call actually took:

module bible/unbound v1.0.0;

// A field bound on some paths of the constructor and not on others. The
// check runs when construction ends, on the path actually taken.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Transfer {
    has from is string;
    has via is string;

    Transfer(from is string, direct is bool) {
        self.from = from;
        if direct {
            via = "-";
        } else if from == "Kostanay" {
            via = "Astana";
        }
    }

    shown() is string { from + " via " + via; }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    out.writeln(Transfer("Almaty", true).shown());
    out.writeln(Transfer("Kostanay", false).shown());
    // Not an error value: a catch of the Error role does not take it.
    let shown = try {
        Transfer("Aktau", false).shown();
    }
    catch e is Error {
        "caught: " + e.text();
    };
    out.writeln(shown);
    0;
}

Output:

Almaty via -
Kostanay via Astana
exit 1
  • Transfer("Almaty", true) and Transfer("Kostanay", false) take paths that bind via, so they build complete objects.
  • Transfer("Aktau", false) takes the missing else. Construction fails with Object "Transfer" field "via" was not initialized and points at the constructor.
  • This is not an error value. It reports a defect in the program, as an index out of range does (Chapter 10). catch e is Error does not take it, and the run ends with the report.

The split between the two checks is the language owner's decision, recorded as D-035 in the conformance suite's ledger:

  • The compiler rejects what is certain, a field no path binds.
  • The rest is checked where it happens.

The price is visible in Transfer: the missing branch is a mistake the compiler could have pointed at, and it surfaces only when an input takes that branch. A test that covers the branches (Chapter 15) finds it before a user does.

What was bound is released, newest first. Section 11.7 showed the rule on a session: a constructor that fails closes what it opened, and the object's own destroy does not run. The details matter when the constructor binds fields inside blocks:

module bible/partial v1.0.0;

// A constructor that fails halfway. Whatever it already bound to fields is
// released, newest first, after the temporaries of its body; the object never
// existed, so its own destroy does not run.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Refused is Error = (tooLarge(size is int));

object Area {
    has name is string;
    Area(:name) { Stdout().writeln("open " + name); }
    destroy { Stdout().writeln("close " + name); }
}

object Upload {
    has staging is Area;
    has lock is Area;
    has size is int;

    Upload(size is int) {
        staging = Area(name: "staging");
        if size > 0 {
            lock = Area(name: "lock");
        } else {
            lock = Area(name: "empty lock");
        }
        let scratch = Area(name: "scratch");
        confirm size <= 1000 else throw Refused.tooLarge(size);
        self.size = size;
    }

    size() is int { size; }

    destroy { Stdout().writeln("upload of " + size.string() + " done"); }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let outcome = try {
        let upload = Upload(5000);
        "built " + upload.size().string();
    }
    catch e is Refused {
        "refused: " + e.text();
    };
    out.writeln(outcome);
    out.writeln("--");
    {
        let upload = Upload(300);
        out.writeln("built " + upload.size().string());
    }
    0;
}

Output:

open staging
open lock
open scratch
close scratch
close lock
close staging
refused: Refused.tooLarge(5000)
--
open staging
open lock
open scratch
close scratch
built 300
upload of 300 done
close lock
close staging
  • A temporary of the body dies first. scratch belongs to the constructor's block and closes when the block unwinds, before any field.
  • A field bound inside a block belongs to the construction. lock is bound in a branch of the if, and it outlives the branch. That is what makes it a field. When the confirm fails, lock is released with the construction, not with the branch.
  • Fields go in reverse order of binding. lock closes before staging, as locals do in a scope (Section 11.4).
  • The error reaches the caller unchanged. The catch sees Refused.tooLarge(5000) after all the cleanup, so it runs with nothing half-open.
  • The object never existed, so its destroy does not run. upload of ... done prints only for the second upload. A destroy may rely on everything the constructor establishes, the same argument Section 12.10 made for actions, and running it on a half-built object would break that. The fields' own destroys do run, because each field is a complete object.

Nobody observes the half-built object. No reference to an unfinished Upload exists outside its constructor. The one exception is self handed to a collaborator (Section 12.10), and every call through such a reference is refused until construction completes, and forever if it fails.

Other languages split the same three questions differently:

  • C++ has the release rule. When a constructor throws, the destructors of the members and bases already constructed run in reverse order, and the object's own destructor does not. Stroustrup builds the basic exception-safety guarantee of the standard library on exactly this rule [Stroustrup 2001]. The gap is the raw resource: a pointer or file handle acquired in the body and not yet held by a member leaks, unless it is wrapped in an object first. In Okkama every resource is an object with an owner, so there is no raw handle to wrap.
  • Java has no unbound fields, and no release rule. Every field starts as null, 0 or false, so "not initialized" cannot be told apart from a value. Only a final field must be definitely assigned by every constructor (JLS Chapter 16, [Gosling 2023]). A constructor that throws leaves a partly initialized object behind, and a subclass's finalizer can catch and use it. SEI CERT rule OBJ11-J, "Be wary of letting constructors throw exceptions", describes the attack [SEI CERT Oracle Coding Standard for Java]. Nothing is closed.
  • Kotlin moves the check to the first read. A lateinit property may stay unset after construction, and reading it before it is set throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException [Kotlin documentation]. The failure appears far from the constructor that caused it.
  • Swift checks statically. Every stored property must have a value before the initializer finishes, and self cannot be used before then. A failable init? returns nil instead of an object [The Swift Programming Language].
  • Rust has no constructors. A struct literal must name every field, so a half-built struct cannot be written. Values made before a failure are ordinary locals and are dropped as the function unwinds.

Okkama's position is between Swift's and C++'s. It is static where that is certain and checks the path otherwise, as no other language here does, and it releases what was bound as C++ does, without raw handles.

12.12 A worked domain model: money and an order

Small objects are easiest to judge in a domain everyone knows. An order has lines; a line has an item, a quantity and a unit price; prices are money in one currency.

module app v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Mismatch is Error = (currency(left is string, right is string));
enum Invalid is Error = (quantity(given is int), price(given is string));

// An amount of money in one currency, exact: a rat, never a float.
object Money {
    has amount is rat;
    has currency is string;
    Money(:amount, :currency) {
        confirm amount >= 0.rat() else throw Invalid.price(amount.string());
    }
    plus(other is Money) is Money {
        confirm currency == other.code() else throw Mismatch.currency(currency, other.code());
        Money(amount: amount + other.value(), currency: currency);
    }
    times(count is int) is Money { Money(amount: amount * count.rat(), currency: currency); }
    code() is string { currency; }
    value() is rat { amount; }
    string() is string { amount.string() + " " + currency; }
}

// One line of an order: what, how many, at what unit price.
object Line {
    has item is string;
    has quantity is int;
    has price is Money;
    Line(:item, :quantity, :price) {
        confirm quantity > 0 else throw Invalid.quantity(quantity);
    }
    total() is Money { price.times(quantity); }
}

// An order knows its lines and nothing else; its total is computed, never stored.
object Order {
    has lines is @Line;
    Order(:lines);
    total(currency is string) is Money {
        lines.reduce(Money(amount: 0.rat(), currency: currency)) -> sum, line { sum.plus(line.total()); };
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let tea = Money(amount: 7.rat() / 2.rat(), currency: "EUR");
    let order = Order(lines: [
        Line(item: "tea", quantity: 3, price: tea),
        Line(item: "cup", quantity: 2, price: Money(amount: 12.rat(), currency: "EUR")),
    ]);
    out.writeln(order.total("EUR").string());
    let mixed = Order(lines: [Line(item: "tea", quantity: 1, price: Money(amount: 4.rat(), currency: "USD"))]);
    let shown = try { mixed.total("EUR").string(); } catch Mismatch.currency(left, right) { left + " cannot meet " + right; };
    out.writeln(shown);
    let refused = try { Line(item: "air", quantity: 0, price: tea).total().string(); } catch Invalid.quantity(given) {
        "quantity " + given.string() + " refused";
    };
    out.writeln(refused);
    0;
}

Output:

69/2 EUR
EUR cannot meet USD
quantity 0 refused
  • One noun per idea. Money is an amount and a currency, nothing else; Line is one row; Order is its lines. Each object answers questions about itself (total()), and none exposes its fields: Money offers code() and value() for the one comparison plus needs, and string() for display.
  • The constructor is the gate. A negative amount and a zero quantity are refused where the object would be born, with a typed error that names the bad value (§12.6). An object that exists is valid, so total() never checks its own fields again.
  • Exact arithmetic is the default. The amounts are rat, so three teas at 7/2 and two cups at 12 make exactly 69/2, with no rounding to explain later. A currency mismatch is an error, not an implicit conversion.
  • Derived values are computed. Order.total folds its lines with reduce; nothing stores a running total that could drift from the lines. Changing an order means building a new one with other lines (Chapter 13).

The model is three short objects and two error enums. A design with getters and setters would have more code and fewer guarantees: every reader would have to trust that nobody set a quantity to zero after construction.

12.13 Objects elsewhere

Most languages that took immutability seriously added a shorthand for "an object that is its fields". Comparing them shows what Okkama chose to leave out.

Okkama object Java record Kotlin data class Rust struct
Fields readable from outside never via generated accessors yes (properties) within the module, or if pub
Constructor written by hand; shorthand (:x) generated canonical, may be compact primary constructor none; a new function by convention
Validation confirm in each constructor in the compact constructor init block in the new function
Equality structural, always generated from components generated from the primary constructor #[derive(PartialEq)]
Mutation none none (fields final) var allowed mut binding
Copy with changes successor actions (Chapter 13) none built in copy(x = …) struct update ..old

Java records (JEP 395) are the closest: final fields, a canonical constructor, generated equals, hashCode and toString [Bierman 2021]. The difference is the accessors. A record publishes every component, so its representation is its API. Kotlin's data classes do the same, and only properties of the primary constructor take part in the generated equals [Kotlin documentation]. Rust hides fields behind module privacy, which is coarser than an object: any code in the same module can read them [Klabnik 2023].

Okkama keeps the generated equality and drops the generated access. A record is a tuple with names. An Okkama object is a value with behaviour, and its fields are nobody else's business. Bloch's advice for Java, "minimize mutability" and "favor composition over inheritance", needs no discipline here: the language allows nothing else [Bloch 2018].

12.14 What this design costs

  • More objects. Without free functions, a small computation that would be a function elsewhere becomes an object with one action, or an action on an existing object. The standard library is full of small objects: Number, Utf8Decoded, HexEncoded. Each is a noun for one computation. It reads well once one is used to it, and it is verbose until then.
  • No inheritance. A family of similar objects shares code by composition and contracts by roles. The flexibility is greater, and so is the amount of forwarding code (Chapter 14).
  • Constructors are written by hand. No record syntax generates them. Shorthands make the common case one line, and every other case is explicit.
  • No mutation. An object that would naturally change — a counter, a buffer — becomes a chain of successors, or holds its changing part in a dedicated mutable cell from the library (Atomic in async/atomic). Chapter 13 shows the first, Chapter 20 the second.

In return:

  • every object is valid from the moment it exists;
  • it can be shared freely and compared by value;
  • its fields can change their representation without touching a single caller.

Chapter 13Actions, successors and immutability

Chapter 12 built objects that never change. This chapter is about what they do: actions, which answer questions about an object, and successors, which answer the question "what would this object be after …?" with a new object. Between them they cover everything other languages do with methods, setters and mutable fields.

module bible/successors v1.0.0;

// State changes are successors: `is ^Type` actions that stage new field
// values with `^field = …` and return a new object. The original stays.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum TabError is Error = (closed, over_limit(total is int));

object Tab {
    has items is int = 0;
    has total is int = 0;
    has limit is int;
    has open is bool = true;

    Tab(:limit);

    ordered(price is int) is ^Tab {
        confirm open else throw TabError.closed;
        confirm total + price <= limit else throw TabError.over_limit(total + price);
        ^items = items + 1;
        ^total = total + price;
    }

    closed() is ^Tab {
        ^open = false;
    }

    summary() is string {
        items.string() + " items, " + total.string() + (if open { " (open)"; } else { " (closed)"; });
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let empty = Tab(limit: 100);
    let two = empty.ordered(30).ordered(25);
    out.writeln(empty.summary());
    out.writeln(two.summary());

    let tab = Tab(limit: 100);
    for [10, 20, 30] -> price {
        tab = tab.ordered(price);
    }
    out.writeln(tab.summary());

    let refused = try { tab.ordered(50).summary(); } catch e is TabError { e.text(); };
    out.writeln(refused);
    out.writeln(tab.summary());

    let done = tab.closed();
    out.writeln(done.summary());
    out.writeln(try { done.ordered(1).summary(); } catch e is TabError { e.text(); });
    0;
}

Output:

0 items, 0 (open)
2 items, 55 (open)
3 items, 60 (open)
TabError.over_limit(110)
3 items, 60 (open)
3 items, 60 (closed)
TabError.closed

The program keeps a bar tab:

  • ordered and closed are successors. Each returns a new Tab and leaves the one it was called on as it was;
  • empty still has no items after two was made from it;
  • the loop moves the name tab from one successor to the next;
  • a refused order throws, and tab is unchanged after the failure;
  • a closed tab refuses every order.

13.1 An action is a typed request

summary() is string {
    items.string() + " items, " + total.string() + …;
}

An action has a name, a parameter list and a declared result. The result declaration is mandatory: is <type>, or is void for an action called for its effect. Leaving it out is a syntax error. There is no inference of results across a declaration. A reader of the signature knows what comes back without reading the body.

The value of an action is its final expression. return value; leaves earlier:

first_negative(values is @int) is int {
    for values -> value {
        if value < 0 { return value; }
    }
    return 0;
}
  • return leaves the action, not the block it is in. Blocks, loops, if, match and try are not return boundaries. An anonymous action is.
  • A functional iteration block (map, reduce and the like, with ->) is not a boundary either. A return inside it returns from the enclosing action, not from the block.
  • return takes exactly one expression. To return two values, return an array or an object.
  • The value is computed before cleanup. Then the defers that were reached run, and the owned objects are destroyed (Chapter 11). The returned object itself stays alive for the caller.
  • return is not allowed directly in a constructor, a destroy or a test body.

void is a result marker, not a type. There is no void value, no Unit and no null behind it. A field, a parameter, a variable or a collection element cannot have it as a type. Using the absent result of a void call as a value is a compile error. The final expression of a void body is evaluated and discarded.

An action that returns its own receiver says so: touch() is Cash { self; }. That is the only way to return self, and it needs both the explicit result and the explicit self.

Recursion

An action may call itself, or another action of its object, through self.. Okkama has no special form for it and no limit on its depth other than the memory of the run (--max-memory bounds it, Section 10.13).

module bible/recursion v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Numbers {
    Numbers() { }

    // Direct recursion: the depth is the size of the input.
    factorial(n is int) is int {
        if n <= 1 { 1; } else { n * self.factorial(n - 1); }
    }

    // Mutual recursion through self.
    even(n is int) is bool { if n == 0 { true; } else { self.odd(n - 1); } }
    odd(n is int) is bool { if n == 0 { false; } else { self.even(n - 1); } }

    // A self tail call: nothing is left to do after it, so it runs in
    // constant stack, a million levels deep.
    counted(n is int, total is int) is int {
        if n == 0 { total; } else { self.counted(n - 1, total + n); }
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let numbers = Numbers();
    out.writeln("30! = " + numbers.factorial(30).string());
    out.writeln("7 is odd: " + numbers.odd(7).string());
    out.writeln("1 + ... + 1000000 = " + numbers.counted(1000000, 0).string());
    0;
}

Output:

30! = 265252859812191058636308480000000
7 is odd: true
1 + ... + 1000000 = 500000500000
  • Direct and mutual recursion are ordinary calls. factorial calls itself, and even and odd call each other.
  • A self tail call runs in constant stack. When the call is the last thing an action does, as in counted, nothing is kept for the return, and a million levels need no more stack than one.
  • Recursion that cannot end is a compile error. An action whose every path calls itself before it can finish never returns, and the compiler says so before the program runs:
module bible/recursion_rejected v1.0.0;

object Clock {
    Clock() { }
    ticks() is int { self.ticks() + 1; }
}

main() is int {
    Clock().ticks();
}

The compiler answers:

13-recursion-rejected.ok:5:5: semantic error: Infinite recursion: "Clock.ticks" cannot complete without calling itself

The check looks for an action with no way out; it does not try to prove that a recursion with a base case reaches it. Anonymous actions cannot call themselves by name at all (Section 18.11): recursion is a property of a named action of an object, where the reader can find both the call and the exit.

13.2 Parameters and calls

module bible/actions v1.0.0;

// Actions: typed results, defaults, named arguments, overloads by type,
// a variadic tail and an early return.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Greeter {
    has greeting is string;
    Greeter(:greeting);

    greet(name is string, mark is string = "!") is string {
        greeting + ", " + name + mark;
    }

    describe(value is int) is string { "int " + value.string(); }
    describe(value is string) is string { "string " + value; }
    describe(value is any) is string { "something else"; }

    total(values is ...int) is int {
        let all is @int = values...;
        all.reduce(0) -> sum, value { sum + value; };
    }

    first_negative(values is @int) is int {
        for values -> value {
            if value < 0 { return value; }
        }
        return 0;
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let hello = Greeter(greeting: "Hello");
    out.writeln(hello.greet("Ada"));
    out.writeln(hello.greet("Ada", "?"));
    out.writeln(hello.greet(mark: ".", name: "Alan"));
    out.writeln(hello.describe(7) + " / " + hello.describe("x") + " / " + hello.describe(1.5));
    out.writeln(hello.total().string() + " " + hello.total(1, 2, 3).string());
    out.writeln(hello.first_negative([3, -2, -5]).string());
    0;
}

Output:

Hello, Ada!
Hello, Ada?
Hello, Alan.
int 7 / string x / something else
0 6
-2
  • Grouped names. Names before one type share it: full(separator, suffix is string). The grouping works in every parameter list except for a variadic parameter, which takes its own type.
  • Positional or named, never both. hello.greet("Ada", "?") and hello.greet(mark: ".", name: "Alan") are calls; a mix of the two is an error. Named arguments may come in any order.
  • Defaults. Trailing parameters may declare a default: greet(name is string, mark is string = "!"). A call leaves them out from the end positionally, or in any combination by name. A parameter after a defaulted one needs a default too.
  • Where a default is computed. The default is evaluated at each call, in the declaring module. It sees module names, not the caller's locals and not self. Moving a call to another module never changes what a default means.
  • Evaluation order. The receiver and the arguments are evaluated once, left to right, in the caller's scope.

Variadic actions, role signatures, natives and enum payloads have no defaults.

13.3 Overloads

An object may declare several actions with one name. They differ by the number of parameters, by their types, and, for named calls, by parameter names. describe(int), describe(string) and describe(any) in the example are three actions. The call with 1.5 takes the any one, because neither of the others accepts a float.

The rules are short, and they never guess:

  1. Candidates with the wrong arity or the wrong names drop out. Then argument types are checked against declared types.
  2. If a fixed candidate fits, variadic candidates are not considered.
  3. Exact concrete types beat role-compatible types, and both beat any.
  4. A candidate wins only if it is no less specific in every position and more specific in at least one.
  5. Declaration order never breaks a tie. A tie is an error.
  6. Overloads of one name and arity may declare different results when their parameter types differ. A call gets the result of the overload it selects: minus(duration is Duration) is Instant and minus(other is Instant) is Duration sit side by side (§14.7).

Rule 4 makes (int, any) and (any, int) ambiguous for a call with two integers. Each is better in one position and worse in the other:

module bible/ambiguous v1.0.0;

object Pairing {
    Pairing();
    joined(left is int, right is any) is string { "left"; }
    joined(left is any, right is int) is string { "right"; }
}

main() is int {
    Pairing().joined(1, 2);
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

13-ambiguous-rejected.ok:10:5: semantic error: Ambiguous call of action "joined" on object "Pairing" with (int, int): joined(int, any) and joined(any, int) fit equally well

The message names the argument types and the candidates that tie, so the fix is visible: convert one argument, or narrow one overload. Until 0.4.2 it named neither (#273). The no-match message lists the types too: No action "joined" on object "Pairing" accepts (string, string).

Overloading is resolved before execution from static types. A value typed any is not narrowed to its contents to choose an overload. Okkama has no dispatch on argument types at run time; dispatch on the receiver happens through roles (Chapter 14).

13.4 Variadic actions

total(values is ...int) takes zero or more integers after its fixed prefix:

  • The variadic parameter is the last one, unique, explicitly typed and has no default.
  • Calls to it are positional. Each value in the tail is checked against the element type.
  • Inside the body, values is not an array. It is an opaque binding that can only be unpacked with values...: as the whole value of a let, as the whole value of a constructor field bind, as a for source, or as the last argument of another variadic call.
  • A fixed candidate that fits wins over a variadic one. total(1) picks total(a is int) if both exist, and total() or total(1, 2) picks the tail.

hello.total() in the example is 0: the tail is empty, and reduce(0) over an empty array returns its seed.

A ...string tail turns the values it is given into text. A value that is not a string reaches it through its own string(): int, float, rat, byte, bool, char, and any object or role value whose type answers string() is string. So out.writeln("count: ", 5, ", ready: ", true) prints count: 5, ready: true, and Formatted("{} version {}", id, id.version()) fills its slots. The conversion is chosen at compile time and only as a last resort: a signature that fits the call as written wins, so kind(1, "a") still picks kind(values is ...any) over kind(values is ...string). A value without string() is a compile error, and a spread values... is not converted.

13.5 Successors

Fields never change (Chapter 12). A state change is therefore a new object, and the language has a construct for making it: an action whose result type is ^Type.

Figure 13.1. A successor is a new object. The original stays as it was, and both can be used.

ordered(price is int) is ^Tab {
    confirm open else throw TabError.closed;
    confirm total + price <= limit else throw TabError.over_limit(total + price);
    ^items = items + 1;
    ^total = total + price;
}

  • ^field = value; stages a new value for a field. It is allowed only in a successor action. Anywhere else it is an error:

    module bible/staged v1.0.0;

object Counter { has count is int = 0; Counter(); bump() is int { ^count = count + 1; count; } }

main() is int { 0; }

The compiler answers:

13-staged-rejected.ok:7:9: semantic error: `^field = value` is allowed only in successor actions

  • When the action finishes, the result is a new object. Every field is copied from the receiver, and the staged fields are replaced. The receiver is untouched: empty stays at 0 items after two is made from it.

  • The successor is a new identity with its own lifetime (Chapter 11).

  • On an object, a successor returns the object's own type. is ^Tab on Tab is legal; is ^Package is not, and a ^Role result belongs in a role signature (Chapter 14).

  • The body's final expression is discarded, as in a void action. Ending a successor with a value of its own type is an error, because it would read as a replacement result that is then thrown away:

    module bible/replacement v1.0.0;

object Counter { has count is int = 0; Counter(); reset() is ^Counter { Counter(); } }

main() is int { 0; }

The compiler answers:

13-replacement-rejected.ok:7:9: semantic error: A successor action cannot return a replacement value; its final expression would be discarded

Two details matter when a body stages several fields.

Reads see the receiver, not the staged values. After ^items = items + 1;, the name items still means the receiver’s original field.

A successor that stages ^count = count + 1; ^twice = count * 2; sets twice from the old count. The order of the staging statements does not change what the reads see.

The last stage wins. ^count = 10; ^count = 20; makes a successor with count 20. Each staging statement replaces the value staged before it; there is no error.

13.6 The result must be used

A successor that is called and then dropped is almost always a bug: the caller meant to change the tab and kept the old one. Okkama makes the common form of that bug a compile error:

module bible/unused v1.0.0;

object Bottle {
    has opened is bool = false;
    Bottle();
    open() is ^Bottle { ^opened = true; }
}

main() is int {
    let bottle = Bottle();
    bottle.open();
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

13-unused-rejected.ok:11:5: semantic error: Successor action result must be used

The compiler tracks every successor result from where it is made to where it is consumed. A result is consumed when it is:

  • returned, explicitly or as the final expression;
  • used as the receiver of another call, as in empty.ordered(30).ordered(25);
  • passed as an argument;
  • bound to a field in a constructor or staged in a successor;
  • stored in an array, a map or another aggregate;
  • used in an eligible rebind (§13.7).

let unused = bottle.open(); is not enough if unused then leaves its scope without a use. Every normal path has to consume the value. A use only inside a try does not count for the path through its catch, which starts from what was pending when the try began. That is why the example calls done.summary() once before the try. Without that line, the compiler reports that done "can leave scope without consumption", at the binding (before 0.5.0 it pointed at the first line of main, #272).

The check is not linear typing. A consumed successor can be used again. Aliases share one obligation, and consuming any of them is enough. The rule is about the result being looked at, not about it being used once.

13.7 Rebinding a name

A loop that advances a value needs a name that moves with it. A bare name = expr; without let rebinds an existing local:

let tab = Tab(limit: 100);
for [10, 20, 30] -> price {
    tab = tab.ordered(price);
}

The rule for rebinding is deliberately narrow. The local must already exist, and its declared type must be an object with at least one real ^-marked successor action. A plain action that happens to return the same type does not qualify. Neither do scalars, arrays, maps or enums:

module bible/rebind v1.0.0;

main() is int {
    let n = 1;
    n = 2;
    n;
}

The compiler answers:

13-rebind-rejected.ok:5:5: semantic error: Cannot rebind variable "n": type "int" has no successor actions

The narrowness is the point. A rebind is allowed exactly where the type's author declared that the type has successors, so a name can only be moved along a path of states the author designed. n = n + 1 has no such path: int is a value, not a state machine.

  • The new value must satisfy the declared type of the binding.
  • A rebind in a nested scope updates the scope that declared the name. That is what makes the loop above work: each iteration is its own scope.
  • The previous value is not destroyed early. If it owns resources, its destroy runs at the normal end of its owner's scope (Chapter 11).

13.8 Successors and failure

A successor that fails produces nothing. If confirm throws in the middle of ordered, no partial Tab exists. The staged values are dropped, the resources the successor itself owned are destroyed, and the receiver remains what it was:

TabError.over_limit(110)
3 items, 60 (open)

This is what makes successors safe to call in a try. Nothing needs to be rolled back, because nothing was changed. In a language with mutable fields, a method that fails after updating two of three fields leaves the object half-changed. The usual remedy is copying the state first and swapping at the end. A successor does that copy-and-swap by construction.

13.9 Naming a transition

A successor describes a domain transition: opened(), ordered(price), closed(), enqueued(item). It is not a setter in disguise. The parser rejects the most common disguise outright:

module bible/setter v1.0.0;

object Tab {
    has limit is int;
    Tab(:limit);
    with_limit(limit is int) is ^Tab { ^limit = limit; }
}

main() is int { 0; }

The compiler answers:

13-with-rejected.ok:6:5: syntax error at "with_limit": Action names "with" and "with_*" are forbidden; use domain composition or an explicitly named result.
  |
