6 |     with_limit(limit is int) is ^Tab { ^limit = limit; }
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^

Other names will compile, so the rest of the rule is a matter of design. One successor per field, or a chain of successors that configure an object step by step, is a public setter API with extra copies. Elegant Objects argues that getters and setters turn an object into a data structure with methods attached [Bugayenko 2016]. A Tab with with_limit, with_items and with_total would let any caller build any combination, including the ones ordered refuses.

The alternatives:

  • complete state in a constructor, when the values are known together;
  • a successor named after the event that changes them, which checks the transition (ordered checks the limit);
  • a new composed object, when a part of the state changes independently.

Meyer's command–query separation distinguishes queries, which return a value and change nothing, from commands, which change state and return nothing [Meyer 1997]. Okkama keeps the separation and changes what a command is. A query is an ordinary action. A command is a successor: it returns the changed object instead of changing this one.

13.10 Composition

An object whose part changes stages a successor of that part:

module bible/composition v1.0.0;

// A successor of an outer object stages a successor of its part. Where a
// value must change in synchronous code, a Cell holds it.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "cell" take Cell;

object Lamp {
    has on is bool = false;
    Lamp();
    switched() is ^Lamp {
        if on { ^on = false; } else { ^on = true; }
    }
    lit() is bool { on; }
    state() is string { if on { "on"; } else { "off"; } }
}

object Room {
    has name is string;
    has lamp is Lamp = Lamp();
    has visits is int = 0;
    Room(:name);

    entered() is ^Room {
        ^visits = visits + 1;
        if !lamp.lit() { ^lamp = lamp.switched(); }
    }
    left() is ^Room {
        if lamp.lit() { ^lamp = lamp.switched(); }
    }
    report() is string { name + ": lamp " + lamp.state() + ", " + visits.string() + " visits"; }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let hall = Room(name: "hall");
    let busy = hall.entered().left().entered();
    out.writeln(hall.report());
    out.writeln(busy.report());

    let lengths = Cell(0);
    for ["ab", "cde", "f"] -> word {
        lengths.replace(lengths.value() + word.length());
    }
    out.writeln(lengths.value().string());
    0;
}

Output:

hall: lamp off, 0 visits
hall: lamp on, 2 visits
6

entered stages two fields: visits, and lamp replaced by lamp.switched(). The successor of a Room holds a successor of its Lamp. The original hall still has its old lamp, which is off. The change travels up the chain of owners. Each level makes a new object, and everything the change does not touch is shared.

A successor can be hidden. Then it is a transition only the object's own actions take through self:

object Door {
    has open is bool = false;
    Door();
    toggled() is Door { if open { self.shut(); } else { self.opened(); } }

    hidden opened() is ^Door { ^open = true; }
    hidden shut() is ^Door { ^open = false; }
}

toggled is a plain action that returns a Door. It is not a successor, so it cannot stage anything itself. It picks the transition and returns its result. A hidden successor keeps the must-use rule and cannot implement a role's action.

13.11 When a value must change: Cell

Some state really is a variable: a running total, a parser's position, headers gathered while reading. reduce covers most accumulations. Where it reads badly, the standard library has one explicit mutable container, Cell from the module cell:

let lengths = Cell(0);
for ["ab", "cde", "f"] -> word {
    lengths.replace(lengths.value() + word.length());
}
lengths.value();    // 6

A cell is a fenced exception to immutability:

  • It has three operations: Cell(value: initial), value() and replace(value). The values it holds are ordinary immutable values. Cells compare by identity, not by content: two cells are equal only when they are the same cell (issue #956).

  • It stays in synchronous code. An async action cannot create, receive or use one. A synchronous action that uses a cell may still be called from async code. Synchronous code has no suspension point, so no task can see a cell between a read and a write.

  • An object cannot hold one:

    module bible/cell_field v1.0.0;

import "cell" take Cell;

object Meter { has reading is Cell<int>; Meter() { reading = Cell(0); } }

main() is int { 0; }

The compiler answers:

13-cell-field-rejected.ok:6:9: semantic error: Field "reading" cannot hold a Cell: a cell stays in synchronous code; state an object shares with tasks is an Atomic

The message points to the other exception: state shared between tasks is async/atomic's Atomic, with compare-and-replace and an explicit close() (Chapter 20). An object's fields stay immutable even then. The object holds the same Atomic for its whole life, and only what is inside the Atomic changes.

13.12 What a successor costs

A successor keeps unchanged fields and replaces the fields named by the transition. Objects held in unchanged fields retain their identities; a transition does not duplicate everything the receiver reaches.

So the cost of a transition is proportional to the number of fields of the object being copied, not to the size of everything it reaches. A change deep inside a composition copies the path from the changed part up to the outer object. Persistent data structures use the same path copying: the new version shares every untouched branch with the old one [Okasaki 1998]. Clojure built its whole model of state on that sharing [Hickey 2008].

Two consequences for design:

  • Wide objects make transitions more expensive. Group fields that change together into a part to keep transitions small.
  • A long successor loop creates a value per step. For a hot loop over a large count, consider reduce over a range or a scalar Cell.

13.13 A value computed once: once let

Immutability makes one kind of cache safe without any discipline. An answer that depends only on an object's fields cannot change while the object lives, so the object can keep it. once let says so in the action that computes it:

hidden values() is @int {
    once let kept = source.items();   // read once per object
    kept;
}

The first successful evaluation is remembered for that object; later calls reuse it (#491). Several actions can share a result by calling one hidden action. The following restrictions apply:

  • A once let stands only in an object's action, as a statement of the action's body itself, not inside a nested block or branch: there is one remembered value per action and object, and a branch would make it depend on which way the first call went.
  • A once let reads fields, self, constants and earlier once lets, never a call parameter.
  • It must be free of effects: no clock, file, network, process, randomness, Cell, async object, await or spawn. Calls through roles rely on their contracts.
  • Its value must not retain a resource. A closure or role value is allowed only when it cannot retain a resource in this program (issue #520).

The remembered result does not participate in ==, map keys or Dumper. A successor computes its own result on first use. If evaluation throws, the next call tries again.

once let is the reason a constructor in the standard library never does work: an object binds its input when it is made, and computes from it on the first question.

13.14 Async successors

A successor that has to wait before it can build the new state is declared async, and its caller awaits the new object.

module bible/asyncsuccessor v1.0.0;

// A successor may be async: it waits before it builds the new state, and the
// caller awaits the new object. The receiver stays what it was.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Refused is Error = (unapproved(amount is int));

object Ledger {
    Ledger() {}
    async approved(amount is int) is bool { amount <= 500; }
}

object Account {
    has balance is int;
    has ledger is Ledger;
    Account(:balance, :ledger);

    async deposited(amount is int) is ^Account {
        let ok = await ledger.approved(amount);
        confirm ok else throw Refused.unapproved(amount);
        ^balance = balance + amount;
    }

    balance() is int { balance; }
}

async main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let opened = Account(balance: 100, ledger: Ledger());
    let first = await opened.deposited(200);
    let second = await first.deposited(50);
    out.writeln(opened.balance().string() + " " + first.balance().string() + " " + second.balance().string());
    let refused = try {
        (await second.deposited(900)).balance().string();
    }
    catch e is Refused {
        "refused: " + e.text();
    };
    out.writeln(refused);
    out.writeln("still " + second.balance().string());
    0;
}

Output:

100 300 350
refused: Refused.unapproved(900)
still 350
  • It is still a successor. The awaits yield first and second, and the receiver opened still has its 100. Waiting changes when the new object exists, not what happens to the old one.
  • A failure produces nothing. The refused deposit throws inside the successor, so no new account is made and second stays at 350, as for a synchronous successor (Section 13.8).
  • The obligation follows the Future. await opened.deposited(200); with its result thrown away is rejected, exactly like the synchronous call. Until it is awaited, the obligation belongs to the Future, which must be awaited or handed on: passed, returned, stored or spawned. A Future bound to a name and then dropped is rejected at the binding, and so is one that is only asked done() or cancelled().
  • Cancelling is a decision. f.cancel() discharges the obligation. The program says in its text that the transition will not happen, so there is nothing left to lose, and no await is needed just to observe Cancelled. Forgetting the Future silently is still an error. This was the language owner's choice when the check was made complete (#754).

13.15 A worked example: an order's life

Successors are how an object goes through stages without a mutable field. An order is drafted, paid, shipped and delivered; each transition is a successor action that checks the stage it starts from.

module app v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Stage = (draft, paid, shipped, delivered);
enum Refused is Error = (step(from is Stage, action is string));

// An order's life as successors: each transition returns the order in its next stage.
object Order {
    has id is int;
    has stage is Stage;
    has paid_cents is int;
    Order(:id) { self.stage = Stage.draft; self.paid_cents = 0; }

    pay(cents is int) is ^Order {
        confirm stage == Stage.draft else throw Refused.step(stage, "pay");
        ^stage = Stage.paid;
        ^paid_cents = cents;
    }
    ship() is ^Order {
        confirm stage == Stage.paid else throw Refused.step(stage, "ship");
        ^stage = Stage.shipped;
    }
    deliver() is ^Order {
        confirm stage == Stage.shipped else throw Refused.step(stage, "deliver");
        ^stage = Stage.delivered;
    }
    shown() is string {
        let name = match stage {
            case Stage.draft { "draft"; }
            case Stage.paid { "paid"; }
            case Stage.shipped { "shipped"; }
            case Stage.delivered { "delivered"; }
        };
        "#" + id.string() + " " + name + " (" + paid_cents.string() + ")";
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let order = Order(id: 7);
    let done = order.pay(1250).ship().deliver();
    out.writeln(order.shown());
    out.writeln(done.shown());
    let early = try { order.ship().shown(); } catch Refused.step(from, action) { "cannot " + action + " a draft"; };
    out.writeln(early);
    0;
}

Output:

#7 draft (0)
#7 delivered (1250)
cannot ship a draft
  • Each step returns the next order. order.pay(1250).ship().deliver() is a chain of three successors. The original order is still a draft afterwards, printed as such: nothing was updated in place, and both values can be used side by side.
  • A transition guards its own precondition. ship() on a draft is refused with a typed error that names the stage and the action; the caller decides what to do with it. There is no "status" field that some code path forgot to check.
  • A transition cannot be ignored. Calling order.pay(1250); as a statement is rejected: "Successor action result must be used". A step whose result is dropped is almost always a bug — the programmer believed the order changed — so the language refuses it (§13.6).
  • Only the changed fields are written. pay sets ^stage and ^paid_cents; ship sets only ^stage, and the successor keeps every other field of its receiver.

The same life could be an enum of stages with a match per transition (Chapter 16). Successors fit when the stages share most of their data and the transitions are actions of one object; variants fit when each stage carries different data.

13.16 Immutability elsewhere

Okkama Java Kotlin Rust Clojure
Fields can change after construction never unless final var yes, val no through mut no (values)
Copy with changes successor (^field) by hand copy(x = …) Struct { x, ..old } assoc
Mutable escape hatch Cell (sync), Atomic (tasks) any field var Cell, RefCell, Mutex atom, ref

Two things set Okkama apart. The copy is a named transition that can check its input, rather than a generic copy of selected fields. And dropping the new value is a compile error. Most languages say nothing about a discarded result; Rust warns, but only for functions and types marked #[must_use]. Kotlin's copy and Rust's struct update syntax make any combination of fields reachable from any caller [Kotlin documentation; Klabnik 2023]. A successor makes reachable only what its author named.

13.17 What this design costs

  • More allocation. Every state change is an object. Most are small and short-lived, but a design that ignores the cost of wide objects (§13.12) pays it on every step.
  • Ceremony for simple counters. ^count = count + 1 in an action with is ^Counter, plus a rebind at the call site, where another language writes count++. Cell exists for the cases where that ceremony buys nothing.
  • The must-use check is conservative. A use only inside a try does not count for the catch path, and loops cannot prove a use by mentioning the value in a body that may not run. Sometimes the fix is an extra use that a human can see is unnecessary.
  • No setters, by rule. A team used to builders and withX methods has to find the domain transitions instead. That is the intent, and it is also work.

In return:

  • an object never changes under the code that holds it;
  • a failed transition leaves nothing to roll back;
  • a forgotten state change is a compile error;
  • every legal state change has a name the author chose.

Chapter 14Roles: nominal contracts and composition

Without inheritance, two things that other languages get from a base class have to come from somewhere else. The first is a contract: "anything that can be opened and labelled". The second is shared behaviour. Okkama answers the first with roles and the second with composition. This chapter is about both, and about the third thing a role does that most interfaces do not: it limits what its holder may do.

module bible/roles v1.0.0;

// A role is a named contract. Objects declare that they do it; code that
// holds a role sees only the role's actions, and successors stay successors.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

role Package {
    label() is string;
    opened() is ^Package;
}

object Bottle does Package {
    has open is bool = false;
    has volume is int;
    Bottle(:volume);

    label() is string { "bottle " + volume.string() + (if open { " open"; } else { " sealed"; }); }
    opened() is ^Bottle { ^open = true; }
    poured() is int { volume; }
}

object Crate does Package {
    has count is int;
    has open is bool = false;
    Crate(:count);

    label() is string { "crate of " + count.string() + (if open { " open"; } else { " sealed"; }); }
    opened() is ^Crate { ^open = true; }
}

object Shelf {
    has packages is @Package;
    Shelf(packages is ...Package) { self.packages = packages...; }

    labels() is string {
        packages.map() -> p { p.label(); }.join(", ");
    }
    unpacked() is @Package {
        packages.map() -> p { p.opened(); };
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let shelf = Shelf(Bottle(volume: 500), Crate(count: 12));
    out.writeln(shelf.labels());
    out.writeln(Shelf(shelf.unpacked()...).labels());
    let one is Package = Bottle(volume: 330);
    let unsealed = one.opened();
    out.writeln(unsealed.label());
    0;
}

Output:

bottle 500 sealed, crate of 12 sealed
bottle 500 open, crate of 12 open
bottle 330 open
  • Package is a role: two signatures and no bodies.
  • Bottle and Crate each declare does Package and implement both actions.
  • Shelf holds @Package. It never knows which objects it holds.
  • opened() is a successor on the role. Each object implements it with its own ^Bottle or ^Crate, and the caller gets a ^Package back.
  • poured() exists on Bottle, but nothing holding a Package can call it.

14.1 Declaring a role

role Package {
    label() is string;
    opened() is ^Package;
}

Figure 14.1. Roles are nominal: an object performs a role only when it says does.

A role is a list of action signatures: names, parameters and results. It has no fields, no constructors and no bodies. (The one exception is a fake block for tests, the subject of Chapter 15.) A role may declare several signatures with one name, as long as their parameter types differ; like the overloads of an object (Section 13.3), they may declare different results.

An object implements a role by saying so:

object Bottle does Package { … }
object Wallet does Account, Labelled { … }

The compiler checks the claim:

  • every action of the role exists on the object;
  • parameter types, and the fixed or variadic shape, match exactly;
  • result types are compatible: ^Bottle satisfies ^Package because Bottle does Package.

"Exactly" means exactly. A role action that takes int is not implemented by one that takes float, even though the float version could accept every integer:

module bible/mismatch v1.0.0;

role Meter { reading(scale is int) is int; }

object Thermometer does Meter {
    has degrees is int;
    Thermometer(:degrees);
    reading(scale is float) is int { degrees; }
}

main() is int { 0; }

The compiler answers:

14-mismatch-rejected.ok:5:8: semantic error: Action "reading" parameter 1 on object "Thermometer" must be int for role "Meter", got float

Function subtyping in type theory would allow it, since parameters are contravariant [Pierce 2002]. Okkama keeps parameters invariant for the same reason it keeps overloads strict (Chapter 13): a call through the role and a direct call must select the same code, with no conversion in between.

14.2 Nominal, not structural

An object that has the right actions but does not declare the role does not satisfy it:

module bible/nominal v1.0.0;

role Presentation { label() is string; }

object Invoice {
    has number is int;
    Invoice(:number);
    label() is string { "invoice " + number.string(); }
}

main() is int {
    let shown is Presentation = Invoice(number: 7);
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

14-nominal-rejected.ok:12:33: semantic error: Cannot initialize variable "shown" of type Presentation with Invoice

Invoice has label() is string, exactly what Presentation asks for. It still cannot be used as one, because nobody said it was. Go makes the opposite choice: a type satisfies an interface whenever its method set contains the interface's methods, with no declaration at all [Go specification]. TypeScript does the same. Java, C# and Rust are nominal: a class implements an interface, a type has an impl Trait [Klabnik 2023]. Pierce sets out the trade-off: structural typing is more flexible, while nominal typing makes the type names carry intent and gives the checker something to report against [Pierce 2002].

Okkama's reason is the one behind Liskov and Wing's behavioural subtyping. A contract is more than a set of signatures. It includes what the actions mean: their preconditions, their results, the states they lead to [Liskov 1994]. Two label() actions with the same signature may promise different things. does Presentation is the author's statement that this object keeps the role's promises, and the compiler holds them to the parts of it that it can check.

The cost is ceremony at the boundary between modules. An object written before a role existed cannot satisfy it after the fact. A role can only be implemented in the module that declares the object. To use a foreign object as a role, wrap it in a small object that does the role and forwards to it (§14.6).

14.3 A role reference limits what its holder can do

In Java, a variable of an interface type can be cast back to the class, and instanceof tells which class it is. In Okkama a role-typed value is a restricted reference. It points to the same object, nothing is copied, and only the role's actions are reachable through it:

module bible/restricted v1.0.0;

role Presentation { label() is string; }

object Customer does Presentation {
    has number is int;
    Customer(:number);
    label() is string { "customer " + number.string(); }
    id() is int { number; }
}

main() is int {
    let shown is Presentation = Customer(number: 7);
    shown.id();
}

The compiler answers:

14-restricted-rejected.ok:14:11: semantic error: Role "Presentation" has no action "id"

An object becomes such a reference only where the role is already the expected type: a typed let, a field, a parameter of an action or of a builtin (shapes.contains(Square(side: 2)) on a @Shape), a result, the fallback of a Maybe<Shape> or of find(), and the branches of an if, match or choice whose value has a declared role type. Okkama never looks for a role two values happen to share. shape == Square(side: 2) is rejected: the operands keep their exact types, and the comparison goes through a role-typed binding. if c { Rect(w: 1, h: 2); } else { Square(side: 2); } with no declared type is rejected too, even though both objects do Shape. The conversion happens where the program states the contract, and nowhere else.

There is no way back to the concrete type:

module bible/downcast v1.0.0;

role Presentation { label() is string; }

object Customer does Presentation {
    has number is int;
    Customer(:number);
    label() is string { "customer " + number.string(); }
    id() is int { number; }
}

main() is int {
    let shown is Presentation = Customer(number: 7);
    let customer is Customer = shown;
    customer.id();
}

The compiler answers:

14-downcast-rejected.ok:14:32: semantic error: Cannot initialize variable "customer" of type Customer with Presentation

The restriction holds through everything a reference can pass through:

  • aliases, parameters, fields, results and collections;
  • bound actions, Maybe and Presence, enum payloads;
  • generic inference: a T inferred from a role reference is the role, not the hidden class;
  • boxing into any. any never narrows, so the box keeps the restriction.

The implementation still runs with its full self. Bottle.label reads volume and open as usual. The restriction is on the holder, not on the object.

The restriction is shallow. A result of an allowed action is accessible according to its own declared type. If Package had an action returning Bottle, the holder could use that Bottle fully. A role restricts exactly what its signatures expose.

This makes a role reference a capability in the sense of object-capability security. Holding a reference is the permission to use it, and handing out a narrower reference hands out fewer rights. That is attenuation, Mark Miller's term for building least authority into a program [Miller 2006; Saltzer 1975]. A function that receives a Labelled can print a label. It cannot learn the balance, even with a cast, because the language has no cast to try.

A role limits what a holder may do. To let a holder only see part of an object's state, the object grants a cap instead (Section 12.8): a named view of computed fields, with no actions at all.

Exceptions do not reopen the restriction either. Objects cannot do Error:

module bible/object_error v1.0.0;

object Failure does Error {
    Failure();
    text() is string { "failed"; }
}

main() is int { 0; }

The compiler answers:

14-error-rejected.ok:3:21: semantic error: Object "Failure" cannot do Error: errors are enums, declare `enum Failure is Error = (...)`

Errors are enums (Chapter 10), so a catch never names an object type and can never recover a concrete object from a role.

14.4 Moving between roles

A role reference may cross into another role on two conditions:

  • the underlying object nominally does the target role;
  • every action of the target role is already reachable through the current role.

That is narrowing: going from more rights to fewer.

module bible/narrowing v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

role Account { label() is string; balance() is int; }
role Labelled { label() is string; }

object Wallet does Account, Labelled {
    has owner is string;
    has cents is int;
    Wallet(:owner, :cents);
    label() is string { owner; }
    balance() is int { cents; }
}

object Printer {
    Printer();
    print(item is Labelled) is string { "[" + item.label() + "]"; }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let account is Account = Wallet(owner: "Ada", cents: 250);
    out.writeln(Printer().print(account));
    let tag is Labelled = account;
    out.writeln(tag.label());
    0;
}

Output:

[Ada]
Ada

Account has label and balance; Labelled has only label. A Wallet does both, so an Account reference passes as Labelled to Printer.print, and binds to a Labelled local. The reverse is widening, and it is rejected even though the object behind the reference does Account:

module bible/widen v1.0.0;

role Account { label() is string; balance() is int; }
role Labelled { label() is string; }

object Wallet does Account, Labelled {
    has owner is string;
    has cents is int;
    Wallet(:owner, :cents);
    label() is string { owner; }
    balance() is int { cents; }
}

main() is int {
    let tag is Labelled = Wallet(owner: "Ada", cents: 250);
    let account is Account = tag;
    account.balance();
}

The compiler answers:

14-widen-rejected.ok:16:30: semantic error: Cannot initialize variable "account" of type Account with Labelled

If Wallet did only Account, the narrowing would be rejected too, with the same message for Labelled. A role is a nominal contract, and a subset of signatures is not a contract the object signed.

14.5 Successors through a role

A role may declare successor actions. opened() is ^Package says: calling this gives the next state, and it is still a Package. Each implementation returns its own type, ^Bottle or ^Crate. The caller holding a Package receives a restricted ^Package. The must-use rule of Chapter 13 still applies through the role.

On an object, a successor always returns the object's own type. is ^Package on Bottle is an error. The role decides what a caller sees; the object decides what it builds.

Successors on roles make roles into state views. Give each state of a protocol its own role, exposing only what is valid in that state, and let each transition return the role of the next state:

module bible/states v1.0.0;

// Typestate with roles: each state is a role that exposes only what is valid
// in it, and a successor declared on a role returns the next state.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

role Created    { id() is string; authorize(approve is bool) is Authorization; }
role Authorized { id() is string; capture() is ^Captured; }
role Captured   { id() is string; refund() is ^Refunded; }
role Refunded   { id() is string; }
role Declined   { id() is string; reason() is string; }

enum Authorization = (approved(payment is Authorized), declined(payment is Declined));

enum Stage = (created, authorized, captured, refunded, declined(reason is string));
enum PaymentError is Error = (invalid_transition(action is string));

object Payment does Created, Authorized, Captured, Refunded, Declined {
    has key is string;
    has stage is Stage = Stage.created;
    Payment(:key);

    id() is string { key; }
    authorize(approve is bool) is Authorization {
        confirm stage == Stage.created else throw PaymentError.invalid_transition("authorize");
        if approve {
            Authorization.approved(self.approved());
        } else {
            Authorization.declined(self.rejected("card declined"));
        }
    }
    capture() is ^Payment {
        confirm stage == Stage.authorized else throw PaymentError.invalid_transition("capture");
        ^stage = Stage.captured;
    }
    refund() is ^Payment {
        confirm stage == Stage.captured else throw PaymentError.invalid_transition("refund");
        ^stage = Stage.refunded;
    }
    reason() is string {
        match stage {
            case Stage.declined(text) { text; }
            else { ""; }
        }
    }

    hidden approved() is ^Payment { ^stage = Stage.authorized; }
    hidden rejected(reason is string) is ^Payment { ^stage = Stage.declined(reason); }
}

object Payments {
    Payments();
    open(id is string) is Created { Payment(key: id); }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    for [true, false] -> approve {
        let result = match Payments().open("p-" + approve.string()).authorize(approve) {
            case Authorization.approved(payment) { payment.capture().refund().id() + " refunded"; }
            case Authorization.declined(payment) { payment.id() + " declined: " + payment.reason(); }
        };
        out.writeln(result);
    }
    0;
}

Output:

p-true refunded
p-false declined: card declined
  • Payments.open returns a Created. The only things a caller can do with it are id() and authorize(...).
  • authorize returns an enum whose two cases carry different views: an Authorized or a Declined. The match must handle both.
  • capture() exists only on Authorized, and returns ^Captured. refund() exists only on Captured.
  • One immutable object, Payment, implements all five roles. A private stage field records the real state, and each transition checks it with confirm.

Skipping a state does not compile:

module bible/skip_state v1.0.0;


role Created    { id() is string; authorize(approve is bool) is Authorization; }
role Authorized { id() is string; capture() is ^Captured; }
role Captured   { id() is string; refund() is ^Refunded; }
role Refunded   { id() is string; }
role Declined   { id() is string; reason() is string; }

enum Authorization = (approved(payment is Authorized), declined(payment is Declined));

enum Stage = (created, authorized, captured, refunded, declined(reason is string));
enum PaymentError is Error = (invalid_transition(action is string));

object Payment does Created, Authorized, Captured, Refunded, Declined {
    has key is string;
    has stage is Stage = Stage.created;
    Payment(:key);

    id() is string { key; }
    authorize(approve is bool) is Authorization {
        confirm stage == Stage.created else throw PaymentError.invalid_transition("authorize");
        if approve {
            Authorization.approved(self.approved());
        } else {
            Authorization.declined(self.rejected("card declined"));
        }
    }
    capture() is ^Payment {
        confirm stage == Stage.authorized else throw PaymentError.invalid_transition("capture");
        ^stage = Stage.captured;
    }
    refund() is ^Payment {
        confirm stage == Stage.captured else throw PaymentError.invalid_transition("refund");
        ^stage = Stage.refunded;
    }
    reason() is string {
        match stage {
            case Stage.declined(text) { text; }
            else { ""; }
        }
    }

    hidden approved() is ^Payment { ^stage = Stage.authorized; }
    hidden rejected(reason is string) is ^Payment { ^stage = Stage.declined(reason); }
}

object Payments {
    Payments();
    open(id is string) is Created { Payment(key: id); }
}

main() is int {
    let payment = Payments().open("p-1");
    payment.capture().id();
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

14-state-rejected.ok:55:13: semantic error: Role "Created" has no action "capture"

Strom and Yemini named this idea typestate in 1986: the operations allowed on a value depend on its state, and the compiler tracks the state [Strom 1986]. Typestate in Rust and similar languages relies on move semantics, so that an old state cannot be used after the transition. Okkama does without them. The old state is an immutable object and remains valid: authorized.capture() can be called twice on the same Authorized, and each call returns a Captured. Whether the second capture should succeed is a question about the outside world (has the money moved?), and it belongs in durable state with idempotency keys, not in the type system. The confirm in each transition is the second line of defence inside the module.

In a real program, Payment and Stage are declared hidden, so that other modules cannot name the class at all. They only ever hold one of the five views.

14.6 Composition instead of inheritance

A role is a contract; it carries no code. Shared behaviour comes from objects that hold other objects. The decorator is the basic form: an object that does a role, holds another implementation of the same role, and adds one behaviour around it [Gamma 1994].

module bible/decorators v1.0.0;

// Composition through a role: each decorator does the role it wraps, holds
// another implementation of it, and adds one behaviour.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

role Pricing {
    price(item is string) is int;
}

object Catalog does Pricing {
    has prices is %string:int;
    Catalog(:prices);
    price(item is string) is int { prices[item] else 0; }
}

object Discounted does Pricing {
    has origin is Pricing;
    has percent is int;
    Discounted(:origin, :percent);
    price(item is string) is int {
        let full = origin.price(item);
        full - (full * percent / 100).int();
    }
}

object Rounded does Pricing {
    has origin is Pricing;
    Rounded(:origin);
    price(item is string) is int {
        let exact = origin.price(item);
        exact - exact % 10;
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let base = Catalog(prices: ["tea": 345, "cake": 520]);
    let sale is Pricing = Rounded(origin: Discounted(origin: base, percent: 15));
    for ["tea", "cake", "soup"] -> item {
        out.writeln(item + ": " + base.price(item).string() + " -> " + sale.price(item).string());
    }
    0;
}

Output:

tea: 345 -> 290
cake: 520 -> 440
soup: 0 -> 0

Catalog knows prices. Discounted takes 15 percent off whatever its origin says. Rounded rounds down to ten. Each is a few lines, each can be tested alone, and they combine in any order. The caller holds a Pricing and cannot tell how many layers it has. sale.price("tea") goes through three objects: 345, then 294, then 290.

Compare a class hierarchy for the same job: Catalog, DiscountedCatalog, RoundedDiscountedCatalog. Every new behaviour multiplies the classes, and every subclass depends on the details of its parent, which is the fragile base class problem of Chapter 12. "Favor object composition over class inheritance" is the Gang of Four's own advice [Gamma 1994]. Okkama makes it the only option. Elegant Objects leans on such decorators throughout: small objects, each wrapping another behind a shared interface [Bugayenko 2016].

The cost is forwarding. A role with ten actions needs ten forwarding actions in every decorator, even when the decorator changes one of them. Okkama has no delegation shorthand ("implement Pricing by forwarding to origin"). The forwarding code is plain to read and tedious to write. Keeping roles small keeps it short: a role with one or two actions is the common case in the standard library.

14.7 Operators are roles

Arithmetic on objects goes through roles as well. The standard module operators declares one role per operator (#215). The first type parameter is the right operand, the second the result:

Role Action Operator
Adding<T, R> plus(other is T) is R a + b
Subtracting<T, R> minus(other is T) is R a - b
Multiplying<T, R> times(other is T) is R a * b
Dividing<T, R> divided(other is T) is R a / b
Remaindering<T, R> remainder(other is T) is R a % b
Negating<R> negated() is R -a 
module bible/operators v1.0.0;

// Arithmetic on an object is a call to a role action: a + b is a.plus(b)
// when the type does Adding<…>, and a < b asks Comparing for an Order.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "operators" take Adding, Subtracting, Multiplying, Negating;
import "compare" take Comparing, Order;

object Money does Adding<Money, Money>, Subtracting<Money, Money>, Multiplying<int, Money>,
        Negating<Money>, Comparing<Money> {
    has cents is int;
    Money(:cents);

    cents() is int { cents; }
    plus(other is Money) is Money { Money(cents: cents + other.cents()); }
    minus(other is Money) is Money { Money(cents: cents - other.cents()); }
    times(count is int) is Money { Money(cents: cents * count); }
    negated() is Money { Money(cents: -cents); }
    order(other is Money) is Order { cents.order(other.cents()); }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let price = Money(cents: 1250);
    let total = price * 3 + Money(cents: 499);      // price.times(3).plus(…)
    let refund = -Money(cents: 300);                // Money(cents: 300).negated()
    out.writeln(total.cents().string() + " " + (total + refund).cents().string());
    out.writeln(if total > price && price <= price { "ordered"; } else { "not ordered"; });
    0;
}

Output:

4249 3949
ordered

With an object on the left, a + b means a.plus(b) through its declared role. The right operand gets no implicit conversion. Ordering uses compare.Comparing<T>: a < b means a.order(b) == Order.less. == stays structural (Chapter 12).

The roles are nominal, like every role (§14.2). An action named plus does not give an object +:

module bible/undeclared v1.0.0;

object Weight {
    has grams is int;
    Weight(:grams);
    grams() is int { grams; }
    plus(other is Weight) is Weight { Weight(grams: grams + other.grams()); }
}

main() is int {
    let both = Weight(grams: 300) + Weight(grams: 200);
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

14-operator-undeclared-rejected.ok:11:16: semantic error: Operator + cannot be applied to Weight and Weight: Weight does not do Adding

One role may be declared several times with different arguments. Instant does Subtracting<Duration, Instant> and Subtracting<Instant, Duration>: an instant minus a duration is an instant, an instant minus an instant is a duration. Its two minus actions are overloads with different results, which §13.3 allows because their parameter types differ. In the standard library BigInt does all six roles and Comparing; Duration, Instant and MonotonicInstant do the ones time arithmetic needs.

Other languages find operators in one of three ways. C++ and Python look them up by name: a function operator+ [Stroustrup 1994], or a method __add__. Haskell puts them in a class, and Num bundles +, -, *, negate, abs, signum and fromInteger together [Haskell 2010]. A type that can be added but not multiplied, such as a duration, cannot be a Num honestly. Rust has one trait per operator, Add, Sub, Mul, each with the right operand as a parameter and the result as an associated type [Klabnik 2023]. Okkama is closest to Rust: a role per operator, the result spelled out, conformance declared. Lookup by name was ruled out because nothing in a name says that plus means addition, which is the argument of §14.2. One class for all arithmetic was ruled out because a contract should not ask for actions the object cannot keep.

14.8 A collection of your own: Iterating and Cursor

Generic roles are where roles meet the rest of the language. A collection becomes usable by for, map, filter and reduce by doing one standard role, Iterating<T> from collections/iteration, whose only action hands out a Cursor<T>.

module app v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "collections/iteration" take Cursor, Iterating, IterationEnded;

// A collection of your own: the days of a month that fall on a weekday.
object Weekdays does Iterating<int> {
    has days is int;
    has first is int;    // 0 = Monday, ... 6 = Sunday, for day 1
    Weekdays(:days, :first);
    cursor() is Cursor<int> { WeekdayCursor(days: days, first: first, day: 1).settled(); }
}

// A cursor is a value: successor() returns the next position and leaves this one as it was.
object WeekdayCursor does Cursor<int> {
    has days is int;
    has first is int;
    has day is int;
    WeekdayCursor(:days, :first, :day);

    // Skip forward to the first weekday at or after this day.
    settled() is WeekdayCursor {
        if day <= days && (first + day - 1) % 7 >= 5 {
            WeekdayCursor(days: days, first: first, day: day + 1).settled();
        } else {
            self;
        }
    }
    available() is bool { day <= days; }
    item() is int {
        confirm day <= days else throw IterationEnded.ended;
        day;
    }
    successor() is Cursor<int> { WeekdayCursor(days: days, first: first, day: day + 1).settled(); }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    // A month of 30 days whose first day is a Saturday.
    let month = Weekdays(days: 30, first: 5);
    // for, map, filter and reduce accept it like an array.
    let first_week = month.filter() -> d { d <= 7; };
    out.writeln(first_week.map() -> d { d.string(); }.join(" "));
    out.writeln(month.reduce(0) -> count, d { count + 1; }.string() + " working days");
    for month -> d {
        last if d > 4;
        out.writeln("day " + d.string());
    }
    // Two walks over one collection never interfere: each starts its own cursor.
    let start = month.cursor();
    out.writeln(start.item().string() + " " + start.successor().item().string() + " " + start.item().string());
    0;
}

Output:

3 4 5 6 7
20 working days
day 3
day 4
3 4 3

The contract is small and every part of it is a value:

  • cursor() returns the position of the first item. Each call starts a new walk, which is why the last line can read the first item, step to the second, and read the first again: nothing moved.
  • available() answers whether there is an item here. The end is an ordinary false, not a sentinel and not an exception.
  • item() returns the item, and throws IterationEnded if asked at the end; a well-behaved loop never asks.
  • successor() returns the next position as a new cursor. The cursor is immutable, so a walk can be resumed from any position kept in a variable.

Weekdays holds two numbers and computes its items on demand, yet filter, reduce and for with last if treat it exactly like an array. The role is nominal (§14.2): a collection must say does Iterating<int>; having actions with the right names is not enough, and the type argument says what the loop's binding will be. A source that is consumed as it is read — a file, a socket — does the other standard role, Batching<T> (Chapter 8).

14.9 Async actions in a role

A role may promise an action that waits. Exchange rates come from a slow source in production and from a table in a test, and the code that converts money should not know which:

module bible/asyncrole v1.0.0;

// A role may promise an async action. Every implementation keeps the promise
// with an async action of its own, and the caller awaits through the role
// without knowing which one it holds.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Unknown is Error = (currency(code is string));

role Rates {
    async rate(code is string) is rat;
}

// Asks a slower source, here another async object.
object Desk {
    Desk() {}
    async quote(code is string) is rat {
        confirm code == "EUR" else throw Unknown.currency(code);
        117 / 100;
    }
}

object Remote does Rates {
    has desk is Desk;
    Remote(:desk);
    async rate(code is string) is rat { await desk.quote(code); }
}

// A fixed table, for tests and for currencies the desk does not quote.
object Table does Rates {
    has known is %string:rat;
    Table(:known);
    async rate(code is string) is rat {
        confirm known.has(code) else throw Unknown.currency(code);
        known[code];
    }
}

// A decorator: the first source, and the second when the first does not know.
object Fallback does Rates {
    has first is Rates;
    has second is Rates;
    Fallback(:first, :second);
    async rate(code is string) is rat {
        try {
            await first.rate(code);
        }
        catch e is Unknown {
            await second.rate(code);
        };
    }
}

object Converter {
    has rates is Rates;
    Converter(:rates);
    async converted(amount is rat, code is string) is rat { amount * await rates.rate(code); }
}

async main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let table = Table(known: ["EUR": 6 / 5, "KZT": 1 / 500]);
    let rates = Fallback(first: Remote(desk: Desk()), second: table);
    let converter = Converter(rates: rates);
    out.writeln("100 EUR = " + (await converter.converted(100.rat(), "EUR")).string());
    out.writeln("5000 KZT = " + (await converter.converted(5000.rat(), "KZT")).string());
    let missing = try {
        (await converter.converted(1.rat(), "XAU")).string();
    }
    catch e is Unknown {
        "unknown: " + e.text();
    };
    out.writeln(missing);
    out.writeln("test double: " + (await Converter(rates: table).converted(10.rat(), "EUR")).string());
    0;
}

Output:

100 EUR = 117
5000 KZT = 10
unknown: Unknown.currency("XAU")
test double: 12
  • The caller awaits through the role. Converter holds a Rates and writes await rates.rate(code). It does not know whether a desk, a table or a decorator answers.
  • A decorator is an implementation like any other. Fallback holds two Rates. It asks the first and, when that one throws Unknown, the second. The euro comes from the desk at 1.17. The tenge is not quoted by the desk, so it comes from the table. Gold is known to neither, and the error from the table reaches the caller.
  • The test double is a role implementation too. Converter(rates: table) converts at the table's 1.2, and no desk is involved. Chapter 15 builds whole suites this way.

Async is part of the action's shape. An implementation that answers at once still writes async, as Table does. A synchronous rate does not conform:

module bible/async_shape_rejected v1.0.0;

// A role's async action is kept only by an async action.

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

role Rates {
    async rate(code is string) is rat;
}

object Fixed does Rates {
    Fixed() {}
    rate(code is string) is rat { 1 / 1; }
}

async main() is int {
    Stdout().writeln((await Fixed().rate("EUR")).string());
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

14-async-shape-rejected.ok:11:8: semantic error: Action "rate" on object "Fixed" must match async shape for role "Rates"

The rule is the same as for parameters (§14.1): the implementation repeats the role's signature exactly. The colour follows the role to its callers (Chapter 20). An action that holds a Rates and wants a rate must itself be async:

module bible/async_caller_rejected v1.0.0;

// An async action of a role is awaited only inside an async action.

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

role Rates {
    async rate(code is string) is rat;
}

object Fixed does Rates {
    Fixed() {}
    async rate(code is string) is rat { 1 / 1; }
}

object Report {
    has rates is Rates;
    Report(:rates);
    line() is string { "EUR " + (await rates.rate("EUR")).string(); }
}

async main() is int {
    Stdout().writeln(Report(rates: Fixed()).line());
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

14-async-caller-rejected.ok:19:34: semantic error: await is available only inside an async action

The languages that have both interfaces and async disagree about the direction of conformance:

  • Swift. An async protocol requirement may be satisfied by a synchronous function, but a synchronous requirement may not be satisfied by an async one [Swift Evolution]. A synchronous answer is a special case of an asynchronous one.
  • Kotlin. An override must repeat suspend exactly, in both directions, because a suspending function takes a hidden continuation parameter and the two are different signatures on the JVM.
  • Rust. async fn in traits arrived only in Rust 1.75, at the end of 2023 [Rust Blog]. An implementation may also write the desugared form, a function that returns impl Future, and do synchronous work before it builds the future.
  • C#, TypeScript and Java's CompletableFuture. The interface returns a task or a promise, and async is an implementation detail. A method that returns Task.FromResult(x) conforms like any other.

Okkama takes Kotlin's side, and it costs Table one word, async. In return, one rule covers parameters, results and waiting alike: an implementation repeats the role's signature exactly. A reader who sees one implementation knows how every call through the role looks. Section 20.11 gives the scheduler's side of the rule: an implementation cannot answer synchronously where the role promised to wait.

14.10 Where roles came from

The idea of a contract separate from its implementations has a short and traceable history.

  • CLU (1977). Liskov's clusters gave a type a set of operations and hid its representation behind them [Liskov 1977]. A cluster was one implementation; there was not yet a way to say that two clusters offered the same contract.
  • Type classes (1989). Wadler and Blott proposed type classes for Haskell: a class names operations, and an instance declares that a type provides them [Wadler 1989]. Conformance is declared, as in Okkama, but an instance may be written in any module, so a type can join a class after the fact. Okkama does not allow that (§14.2): the object's module is the only place that can say what the object does.
  • Interfaces (1995). Java made a contract a type of its own: an interface lists method signatures, and a class implements any number of them while inheriting implementation from one superclass [Gosling 2023]. Java 8 later let interfaces carry default methods, and with them part of what interfaces had been introduced to avoid.
  • Traits (2003). Schärli, Ducasse, Nierstrasz and Black proposed traits as units of reusable behaviour: a trait supplies method bodies, a class composes several traits, and conflicts between them must be resolved explicitly [Schärli 2003]. Scala, PHP and Rust use the name; what they mean by it ranges from Schärli's composable behaviour to something close to Haskell's type classes.

Okkama's role takes the contract from this line and leaves the code. A role has signatures, successor results and an optional fake for tests, and never a method body. With no bodies there is nothing to compose and nothing to resolve: the question traits answer, which of two inherited methods wins, does not arise. Shared behaviour lives in an object that others hold (§14.6), which is where Chapter 2 argued it belongs.

14.11 Roles elsewhere

Okkama role Java interface Go interface Rust trait
Conformance declared (does) declared (implements) implicit, by method set declared (impl)
Default method bodies no yes no yes
Downcast from the contract impossible cast, instanceof type assertion, type switch only through Any
Parameter matching exact exact (overriding) exact exact
Successor (next-state) results yes (^Role) no no a method that consumes self and returns a new type
Conformance of a foreign type no; wrap it no automatic, if the methods match if the trait or the type is local
Operators on user types through roles (Adding, …) no no through traits (Add, …)

Two rows matter most. Default bodies: Java and Rust let an interface carry code, which brings back part of inheritance, including the question of which default wins when two interfaces supply one. A role carries none; shared code lives in an object. Downcasting: every other language in the table has a way back from the contract to the concrete type. Okkama has none, and that is what makes a role reference a capability rather than a type annotation.

14.12 What this design costs

  • Forwarding code. Decorators repeat every action of the role. No delegation syntax shortens it (§14.6).
  • No retroactive conformance. A role cannot be added to an object from outside its module. The usual fix, an adapter object, is one more object.
  • No downcast, ever. Code that "just needs to check what this really is" has to be redesigned: an action on the role that answers the question, or an enum that carries the alternatives.
  • Invariant parameters. An implementation cannot accept more than the role asks for. Usually it does not need to.
  • Operators look only to the left. price * 3 works; 3 * price does not, because int cannot be given a role. Python asks the right operand through __rmul__, and Rust allows impl Mul<Money> for i64 in Money's crate. Okkama has neither (no retroactive conformance, above).

In return:

  • a contract states intent, not an accident of shape;
  • a reference can be narrowed, and narrowed is final;
  • behaviour composes from small objects instead of growing down a hierarchy;
  • protocols can be typed by state, with no linear types.

Chapter 15Fakes, tests and properties

A language that forbids mutation, setters, downcasts and inheritance also forbids most of the tricks that testing frameworks are built on. There is no monkey-patching, no mocking library that rewrites a class at run time, and no way to reach into an object and set a field. Okkama's answer is not a framework. It is three pieces of the language and a small library:

  • tests are declared next to the code they test;
  • every role can carry its own fake, a working implementation for tests;
  • assertions are a binding that exists only while a test runs;
  • testing/property checks a claim against generated inputs and shrinks the first counterexample.
module bible/library v1.0.0;

import "async/atomic" take Atomic;

// A role ships its own fake. Tests use the fake; production code only ever
// sees the role.
enum Refused is Error = (because(reason is string));

role Books {
    remember(id is int, title is string) is void;
    title(id is int) is string;
    has(id is int) is bool;

    fake {
        has shelf is Atomic<%int:string> = Atomic([:]);
        remember(id is int, title is string) is void { shelf.replace(shelf.value() + [id: title]); }
        title(id is int) is string { shelf.value()[id]; }
        has(id is int) is bool { shelf.value().has(id); }
    }
}

role Door {
    opened() is ^Door;
    open() is bool;

    fake {
        has times is int = 0;
        opened() is ^Door { ^times = times + 1; }
        open() is bool { times > 0; }
    }
}

object Library {
    has books is Books;
    Library(:books);

    shelve(id is int, title is string) is string {
        confirm id > 0 else throw Refused.because("non-positive id");
        confirm !books.has(id) else throw Refused.because("id " + id.string() + " is taken");
        books.remember(id, title);
        books.title(id);
    }

    test "a shelved title can be read back" {
        let books = Books.fake();
        test.is(Library(books: books).shelve(7, "Dune"), "Dune");
        test.ok(books.has(7));
    }
}

test "a bad id is refused" {
    let refused = test.throws(Refused) { Library(books: Books.fake()).shelve(0, "x"); };
    test.is(refused, Refused.because("non-positive id"));
}

test "an id cannot be shelved twice" {
    let library = Library(books: Books.fake());
    library.shelve(3, "Emma");
    let refused = test.throws(Refused) { library.shelve(3, "Persuasion"); };
    test.is(refused, Refused.because("id 3 is taken"));
}

test "a fake keeps its state through successors" {
    let door is Door = Door.fake();
    test.ok(!door.open());
    test.ok(door.opened().open());
}

main() is int { 0; }

Output:

=== RUN   Library :: a shelved title can be read back
--- PASS: Library :: a shelved title can be read back
=== RUN   a bad id is refused
--- PASS: a bad id is refused
=== RUN   an id cannot be shelved twice
--- PASS: an id cannot be shelved twice
=== RUN   a fake keeps its state through successors
--- PASS: a fake keeps its state through successors
PASS

15.1 Tests live next to the code

test "a bad id is refused" {
    let refused = test.throws(Refused) { Library(books: Books.fake()).shelve(0, "x"); };
    test.is(refused, Refused.because("non-positive id"));
}

A test block has a name and a body. It may stand at module level, inside an object or inside a role. okkama run -t runs the tests of the file it is given, in declaration order, and does not call main:

=== RUN   Library :: a shelved title can be read back
--- PASS: Library :: a shelved title can be read back
=== RUN   a bad id is refused
--- PASS: a bad id is refused
…
PASS
  • A test inside an object or a role is shown as Owner :: name. That is only a namespace. The test gets no self and no access to the owner's hidden actions or fields; it uses the object like any other caller.
  • Names are unique within a module, and per owner for object and role tests. A duplicate is a compile error before any test runs.
  • Each test uses the imports of the file that declares it.
  • In a normal run, the parser skips test and fake blocks without building them. Test-only code cannot affect a production program, and it costs nothing there.

Without --workers, tests run in the runner's own process (Section 15.9). okkama run -t --filter TEXT runs only the tests whose names contain TEXT; with several --filters, those that contain any of them. A test may stand anywhere among an object's members, between hidden actions too; it is still a test of the object. The standard library can render a test report as human text, TAP, JSON or JUnit (testing/report), and the command line writes human text, JSON or JUnit with --report (Section 15.9).

15.2 The test binding

Inside a running test, the name test is bound to the current case. It is not imported and does not exist outside a test:

  • test.ok(condition) requires an exact bool;
  • test.is(actual, expected) and test.isnt(actual, expected) use the language's structural equality, deep through collections and objects;
  • test.close(actual, expected, tolerance) compares two floats: they pass when equal or no further apart than the tolerance, and a NaN is never close;
  • test.text(actual, expected) compares two strings and names where they part: the scalar, its line and column in the expected text, and the text around it;
  • test.bytes(actual, expected) compares two @byte arrays and names the first offset where they differ, or their sizes;
  • test.fail("explanation") records a failure;
  • test.skip("reason") ends the test and reports it as skipped;
  • test.throws(Type) { … } requires the block to throw a Type, and returns the caught error for further checks.

test.skip is for a test that cannot run here: a missing volume, a service that is not configured. The code after it does not run, and no catch takes it, so a helper that skips cannot be overruled by its caller. Cleanup runs as for any failure. A skipped test does not fail the run, unless an assertion had already failed; a skip does not erase a failure. The example also puts a test among the hidden actions:

module skip_tests;

object Ledger {
    has entries is int;

    Ledger(entries is int) {
        self.entries = entries;
    }

    count() is int {
        self.checked();
    }

    hidden checked() is int {
        entries;
    }

    test "a test among the hidden actions" {
        test.is(Ledger(3).count(), 3);
    }
}

test "the archive is not mounted" {
    test.skip("needs the archive volume");
    test.ok(false);
}

Output:

=== RUN   Ledger :: a test among the hidden actions
--- PASS: Ledger :: a test among the hidden actions
=== RUN   the archive is not mounted
--- SKIP: the archive is not mounted
    needs the archive volume
PASS

A failed assertion does not stop the test. The remaining assertions still run, and every failure is reported:

=== RUN   a failing one
--- FAIL: a failing one
    expected 3, got 2
FAIL

An uncaught throw, a panic or a failure in cleanup ends only the current case. Its defers and destroys run, and the next case starts. The process exits with 0 when no case failed; a skipped case does not fail.

test.throws(Refused) { … } means exactly try { …; panic …; } catch e is Refused { e; }. The error it returns is an ordinary enum value, so test.is(refused, Refused.because("non-positive id")) compares the case and the payload. There is no test.panics. A panic is a broken invariant, not an outcome to assert (Chapter 10), and nothing catches it.

The binding follows the whole dynamic extent of the test, so a helper object in another module can call test.is on behalf of the test that called it. The checks of testing/check build on that (Section 15.9).

15.3 Why a fake and not a mock

Meszaros sorts test doubles into five kinds: dummy, stub, spy, mock and fake [Meszaros 2007]. A mock is programmed with expectations: "expect remember(7, "Dune") to be called once". The test then verifies that the calls happened. A fake is a working implementation that takes a shortcut, such as keeping data in memory instead of a database. Fowler's essay draws the consequence. Mocks make a test check how the code under test talks to its collaborators, and such tests break when the conversation changes even if the result does not [Fowler 2007].

Elegant Objects goes further: every interface should ship its own fake, so that tests never build ad-hoc mocks [Bugayenko 2016]. Okkama makes that a language feature. A role may contain one fake block:

role Books {
    remember(id is int, title is string) is void;
    title(id is int) is string;
    has(id is int) is bool;

    fake {
        has shelf is Atomic<%int:string> = Atomic([:]);
        remember(id is int, title is string) is void { shelf.replace(shelf.value() + [id: title]); }
        title(id is int) is string { shelf.value()[id]; }
        has(id is int) is bool { shelf.value().has(id); }
    }
}

Books.fake() makes one. The fake is a Books. Code that takes a Books, like Library, cannot tell it from the real thing, and it has no reason to. The test then checks results: the title comes back, the second shelving of an id is refused. It does not check which calls were made in which order.

The fake lives with the role, written once by the role's author, and every test of every user of the role shares it. When the role changes, the compiler checks the fake against the new contract like any other implementation.

15.4 Writing a fake

  • A role has at most one fake block.
  • Its actions must implement the role exactly, as an object would: names, parameter types, fixed or variadic shape, results.
  • It may declare fields with has, and every field needs a default. A fake takes no constructor arguments, so nothing else could set them. Defaults are evaluated for each Role.fake().
  • It may stage successors with ^field, like an object's successor (§15.5).

Role.fake() works only in test mode. Anywhere else the compiler rejects it:

module bible/fake_production v1.0.0;

role Clock {
    now() is int;
    fake {
        now() is int { 1700000000; }
    }
}

main() is int {
    Clock.fake().now();
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

15-fake-production-rejected.ok:11:5: semantic error: Clock.fake() is available only in test mode

A production program therefore cannot reach a fake, not even by accident in a code path that tests happen to cover. Mistakes inside the fake block are reported when the tests are compiled, in terms of the role and at the fake's own code: Fake field "value" of role "Counter" needs a default: a fake takes no constructor arguments, Action "count" of the fake of role "Counter" must return int, got string. Before 0.5.0 they named the generated object Counter$fake (#276).

15.5 State in a fake

A fake that only returns constants is a stub. A useful fake often has to remember something: what was stored, how many times a door was opened. It has two places to keep it.

Fields and successors. A fake's fields are ordinary immutable fields, and its successors make new fakes, exactly as for objects:

role Door {
    opened() is ^Door;
    open() is bool;

    fake {
        has times is int = 0;
        opened() is ^Door { ^times = times + 1; }
        open() is bool { times > 0; }
    }
}

Door.fake().opened().open() is true; the original fake still says false. This suits state that the role's own successors carry.

A field that holds an Atomic. A fake that emulates a repository needs state that changes while the test runs, and a fake keeps it the way production code does: in a field that holds an Atomic (async/atomic), as Books above does with shelf. value() reads it and replace(…) puts a new value; the map inside is an ordinary immutable value, replaced whole.

  • Each Role.fake() gets its own Atomic, because a field's default is evaluated for each fake. Two fakes in one test never see each other's data.
  • A successor copies the fields, and with them the reference to the same Atomic, so a fake and all its successors share one state, and data survives a transition without being copied.
  • The field cannot be a Cell. A cell stays inside one piece of synchronous code and cannot be a field of anything (Section 25.3); a fake is an object like any other, and the rule is the same.
  • A missing key reads as it does anywhere else: shelf.value()[id] on an absent id is a runtime error, and has asks first.

Until 0.6.0 the language had a separate key–value store for fakes, fake.storage. It was removed (#583): it was the one place with hidden mutable state, and a fake that keeps its state in a typed field needs no special rules and reads like the production code it stands in for.

15.6 Properties

An example-based test checks the cases its author thought of. A property states a claim about every input and lets the machine look for a counterexample. Claessen and Hughes's QuickCheck made the idea practical: generate random inputs, run the claim, and when it fails, shrink the input to a minimal one before reporting it [Claessen 2000].

testing/property follows that design:

module bible/properties v1.0.0;

// A property states a claim about every input; the library generates
// inputs from a seed and shrinks the first counterexample.

import "testing/generation" take IntegerGeneration;
import "testing/property" take Property;

object Cents {
    has total is int;
    Cents(:total);
    digit() is int { (total / 100).int(); }
    rest() is int { total - self.digit() * 100; }
}

test "digit and rest rebuild the amount" {
    let property is Property<int> = Property(
        IntegerGeneration(-100000, 100001), 42, 200, 1000, 64,
        (value is int) is bool {
            let cents = Cents(total: value);
            cents.digit() * 100 + cents.rest() == value;
        },
    );
    property.check();
}

test "rest is never negative" {
    let property is Property<int> = Property(
        IntegerGeneration(-100000, 100001), 42, 200, 1000, 64,
        (value is int) is bool { Cents(total: value).rest() >= 0; },
    );
    property.check();
}

main() is int { 0; }

Output:

=== RUN   digit and rest rebuild the amount
--- PASS: digit and rest rebuild the amount
=== RUN   rest is never negative
--- FAIL: rest is never negative
    property failed: seed=42 case=1 size=5 value=-1 false condition
FAIL
exit 1

Property(origin, seed, cases, maximum_size, shrink_limit, condition):

  • IntegerGeneration(-100000, 100001) produces integers from −100000 up to, but not including, 100001.
  • 42 is the seed of the property's own PCG random stream. The same seed produces the same inputs and every run.
  • 200 cases, with a size that grows from 0 to 1000 across them, so the early cases are small.
  • When a case fails, up to 64 reductions are tried, and the smallest input that still fails is reported.

The second property is false. Cents(total: -1).rest() is -1, because int(...) truncates toward zero (Chapter 5): the digit of −1 cents is 0, and the rest is −1. The report gives everything needed to reproduce it: the seed, the case index, the size and the shrunk value. The value is -1, the simplest counterexample there is.

A condition that throws a typed error counts as a failure and is reported with the error's text. A property is a Checking like the other checks of testing/check, and AsyncProperty takes an async condition.

15.7 A worked suite: a service with a clock and a store

A service that depends on time and on storage is the classic case for test doubles, and the one where mocks do the most damage. Here the service Reminders sees a Clock and a Store only through their roles, and each role ships the fake its tests need.

module bible/reminders v1.0.0;

import "async/atomic" take Atomic;

enum Unsaved is Error = (full(limit is int));

// The clock and the store are roles; each ships the fake its tests need.
role Clock {
    // Minutes since midnight.
    minute() is int;

    fake {
        minute() is int { 600; }
    }
}

role Store {
    save(at is int, text is string) is void;
    texts(until is int) is @string;

    fake {
        has items is Atomic<%int:string> = Atomic([:]);
        save(at is int, text is string) is void {
            confirm items.value().size() < 3 else throw Unsaved.full(3);
            items.replace(items.value() + [at: text]);
        }
        texts(until is int) is @string {
            let saved = items.value();
            saved.keys().filter() -> at { at <= until; }.map() -> at { saved[at] else ""; };
        }
    }
}

object Reminders {
    has clock is Clock;
    has store is Store;
    Reminders(:clock, :store);

    remind(after is int, text is string) is int {
        let at = clock.minute() + after;
        store.save(at, text);
        at;
    }

    due() is @string {
        store.texts(clock.minute());
    }
}

test "a reminder for later is not due yet" {
    let reminders = Reminders(clock: Clock.fake(), store: Store.fake());
    test.is(reminders.remind(30, "call the plumber"), 630);
    test.is(reminders.due(), []);
}

test "past and present reminders are due, in time order" {
    let store = Store.fake();
    store.save(590, "water the plants");
    store.save(540, "take the pills");
    let reminders = Reminders(clock: Clock.fake(), store: store);
    reminders.remind(0, "leave for work");
    test.is(reminders.due(), ["take the pills", "water the plants", "leave for work"]);
}

test "a full store refuses the fourth reminder and keeps the first three" {
    let store = Store.fake();
    let reminders = Reminders(clock: Clock.fake(), store: store);
    for 1..=3 -> n {
        reminders.remind(-n, "task " + n.string());
    }
    let refused = test.throws(Unsaved) { reminders.remind(-9, "one too many"); };
    test.is(refused, Unsaved.full(3));
    test.is(reminders.due().size(), 3);
}

main() is int { 0; }

Output:

=== RUN   a reminder for later is not due yet
--- PASS: a reminder for later is not due yet
=== RUN   past and present reminders are due, in time order
--- PASS: past and present reminders are due, in time order
=== RUN   a full store refuses the fourth reminder and keeps the first three
--- PASS: a full store refuses the fourth reminder and keeps the first three
PASS

Three things carry the suite.

  • The clock is a constant. Clock.fake() answers 10:00 every time. A test that needs another moment does not wind a mock; it computes its inputs relative to the one moment the fake defines (remind(30, …) is due at 630). Time-dependent code becomes arithmetic.
  • The store is a working store. The fake keeps reminders in an Atomic map, answers texts(until:) by real filtering, and enforces a real limit. The second test saves two reminders directly through the fake before the service adds a third, and the order of the answer, by minute, comes from the map, not from the test's script.
  • Failures are part of the contract. The third test fills the store, catches the fourth save with test.throws(Unsaved), compares the error value structurally, and then checks that nothing was half-saved. A mock would have been told to throw; the fake throws because it is full.

No test names a call count or an argument list. If Reminders later caches due(), or saves in a different order, the suite still passes as long as the behaviour is the same: what the tests pin is the service's contract, not its conversation with its collaborators.

15.8 Waiting without waiting: a retry policy

Some code exists to wait. A retry policy tries, waits, and tries again with a longer wait. Section 20.11 builds a retry over a bound async action; this one adds the waits, and this section tests them. A suite that really waits for it would take seconds per test, and a flaky one at that. The policy below takes its clock as a Timing role, so the suite replaces the clock:

module bible/backoff v1.0.0;

// A retry policy with doubling waits, tested without waiting: the clock is a
// fake that records each wait and returns at once, and the source is a stub
// that answers from a script.
import "time/clock" take Timing, Instant, MonotonicInstant;
import "time/duration" take Duration;
import "testing/double" take RecordedCalls, Stub;

enum Down is Error = (unavailable(attempt is int));

role Source {
    async read(attempt is int) is string;
}

object Backoff {
    has timing is Timing;
    has attempts is int;

    Backoff(:timing, :attempts);

    async fetched(source is Source) is string {
        await self.attempt(source, 1, Duration(seconds: 1));
    }

    async attempt(source is Source, number is int, delay is Duration) is string {
        try {
            await source.read(number);
        }
        catch e is Down {
            confirm number < attempts else throw e;
            await timing.wait(delay);
            await self.attempt(source, number + 1, delay.plus(delay));
        };
    }
}

// The clock never waits: it writes each wait down and returns.
object Recording does Timing {
    has waits is RecordedCalls<Duration>;

    Recording(:waits);

    instant() is Instant { Instant(Duration(seconds: 0)); }
    monotonic_instant() is MonotonicInstant { MonotonicInstant(origin: Duration(seconds: 0)); }
    async wait(duration is Duration) is void { waits.record(duration); }
}

// The source answers from a script: "down" fails that attempt.
object Scripted does Source {
    has answers is Stub<string>;

    Scripted(:answers);

    async read(attempt is int) is string {
        let answer = answers.next();
        confirm answer != "down" else throw Down.unavailable(attempt);
        answer;
    }
}

async test "two failures cost one and then two seconds" {
    let waits is RecordedCalls<Duration> = RecordedCalls();
    let backoff = Backoff(timing: Recording(waits: waits), attempts: 4);
    let source = Scripted(answers: Stub(["down", "down", "ready"]));
    test.is(await backoff.fetched(source), "ready");
    test.is(waits.size(), 2);
    test.is(waits.records().item(0).value(), Duration(seconds: 1));
    test.is(waits.records().item(1).value(), Duration(seconds: 2));
}

async test "the first answer needs no wait" {
    let waits is RecordedCalls<Duration> = RecordedCalls();
    let backoff = Backoff(timing: Recording(waits: waits), attempts: 4);
    test.is(await backoff.fetched(Scripted(answers: Stub(["ready"]))), "ready");
    test.is(waits.size(), 0);
}

async test "after the last attempt the failure reaches the caller" {
    let waits is RecordedCalls<Duration> = RecordedCalls();
    let backoff = Backoff(timing: Recording(waits: waits), attempts: 3);
    let outcome = try {
        await backoff.fetched(Scripted(answers: Stub(["down", "down", "down", "ready"])));
    }
    catch e is Down {
        e.text();
    };
    test.is(outcome, "Down.unavailable(3)");
    test.is(waits.size(), 2);
}

Output:

=== RUN   two failures cost one and then two seconds
--- PASS: two failures cost one and then two seconds
=== RUN   the first answer needs no wait
--- PASS: the first answer needs no wait
=== RUN   after the last attempt the failure reaches the caller
--- PASS: after the last attempt the failure reaches the caller
PASS
  • The clock writes waits down. Recording does Timing, and its wait records the duration in a RecordedCalls and returns at once. The three tests run in milliseconds, and the second test proves that a first answer costs no wait at all.
  • The source follows a script. Stub(["down", "down", "ready"]) hands out its answers in order, and Scripted turns "down" into the typed failure the policy catches. A stub that runs out throws StubExhausted, so a policy that tried once too often would fail loudly instead of reading a stale answer.
  • The last failure is the caller's. With three attempts the policy waits twice and then rethrows Down.unavailable(3). The fourth answer in the script is never read.

This suite counts calls, which Section 15.7 avoided, and here that is correct. A retry policy is its schedule: one second, then two. The waits are what it promises, not a conversation with a collaborator, so recording them is the specification and not a mock in disguise. The test still does not say how the policy is built. It could be a loop, recursion or a table of delays, and the suite would not change.

Recording returns at once, which is right for code that waits in sequence. Code that waits while other tasks run, a timeout racing an answer for example, needs a clock that holds its waiters until the test moves it. That is ManualClock from testing/time, and Section 20.11 uses it to time out a courier after thirty seconds that never pass.

A failed comparison of two Durations reports both values by their fields, expected Duration(origin: 2), got Duration(origin: 1). Before 0.6.0 it printed heap identities (#756).

15.9 The rest of the toolbox

The standard library adds a few more pieces, all usable only inside a running test:

  • testing/check: checks with readable failure output. TextEquals shows a diff of two texts, SequenceEquals compares sequences item by item, CloseTo compares floats within a tolerance, MatchingRegex matches text, and Eventually polls an async condition against an explicit clock.
  • testing/time: ManualClock, a clock a test advances by hand. It does the Timing role, so code that takes a Timing instead of reading the host's clock can be tested without sleeping.
  • testing/double: RecordedCalls<T> records values in order, and Stub<T> hands out configured values one by one. They are building blocks for fakes that need them. There are deliberately no generated mocks, no reset and no implicit expectations.
  • testing/generation: generators for booleans, integers, finite floats, choices from a list, filtered values and sequences, each with its own shrinking.
  • testing/snapshot: compares text with a stored file. Checking and updating snapshots are separate commands, so a test run never rewrites its own expectations.

Async code is tested with async test "…" { … }. The runner waits for the body and its cleanup before it records the result. Tasks still pending at the end are cancelled and drained. There is no implicit timeout, so a test that may hang should bound itself with a budget or a deadline.
