A table of cases is one test with named sub-cases. test.case(name) { … } runs one row as a case of its own, in the same block shape as test.throws: a failed check or a thrown error fails that sub-case, and the rows after it still run. A panic or a runtime error cannot be caught (Chapter 10): it fails the sub-case it happened in and ends the test, so the rows after it do not run and are not in the report.

test "postage at every boundary" {
    for cases -> row {
        test.case(row.name()) { test.is(row.got(tariff), row.wanted()); };
    }
}

The report shows each sub-case as Test/name, and --filter "postage/50 g" runs only the matching rows.

The runner itself has three more switches:

  • --report json or --report junit writes one report of the run for a machine, the tests in declaration order. What the tests print then goes to standard error, so the report owns standard output.
  • --seed N runs the tests in a reproducible shuffled order. A property's generator keeps its own seed.
  • --workers N runs every test in a process of its own and captures what it prints. --test-timeout SECONDS then stops a test that passes its deadline and reports it as timed out.

Examples in documentation are tests too

A doc comment (Section 22.12) may show code in fenced examples, and okkama run -t checks them with the tests:

module bible/doc_examples v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

// A price in whole cents.
//
// ```okkama
// let price = Price(250);
// ```
//
// Run, and its output checked:
//
// ```okkama,run
// import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
// Stdout().writeln(Price(250).shown());
// ```
// ```output
// 2.50
// ```
//
// Shown, never compiled:
//
// ```okkama,ignore
// let price = Price("2.50");   // a sketch: Price takes cents, not text
// ```
object Price {
    has cents is int;
    Price(cents is int) { self.cents = cents; }
    shown() is string {
        let rest = cents % 100;
        (cents / 100).int().string() + "." + (if rest < 10 { "0"; } else { ""; }) + rest.string();
    }
    test "shown" { test.is(Price(305).shown(), "3.05"); }
}

main() is int {
    Stdout().writeln(Price(1999).shown());
    0;
}

Output:

=== RUN   Price :: shown
--- PASS: Price :: shown
PASS
ok - doctest 15-doc-examples-tests.ok:7 (compile)
ok - doctest 15-doc-examples-tests.ok:13 (run)
  • A fence marked okkama must compile, with the module's own declarations in scope, so an example cannot quietly rot when an action is renamed.
  • A fence marked okkama,run runs in a process of its own, and the output fence right after it is its exact standard output. Change 2.50 to 2.51 and the run fails with expected stdout "2.51\n", got "2.50\n".
  • A fence marked okkama,ignore, and an indented or other-language block, only illustrates: it is shown, never compiled.

15.10 Okkama among other languages

Every language with a test culture answers the same four questions: where a test lives, how the runner finds it, what stands in for a collaborator, and whether the machine can invent inputs.

Language Where tests live How they are found Test doubles Generated inputs
Java, JUnit 5 [JUnit User Guide] separate test classes, by build-tool convention in a separate source tree the @Test annotation libraries outside the language libraries
Go [Go package testing] _test.go files in the package functions named TestXxx hand-written implementations of interfaces coverage-guided fuzzing, FuzzXxx
Rust [Klabnik 2023] a #[cfg(test)] module in the same file; integration tests in tests/ the #[test] attribute crates outside the standard library crates outside the standard library
Python [Python doctest; Python unittest.mock] separate modules; examples inside docstrings (doctest) the runner's naming rules unittest.mock, which patches objects at run time libraries
D [D specification] unittest blocks in the module compiled in with -unittest hand-written —
Okkama test blocks in a module, an object or a role okkama run -t one fake per role, checked against the role testing/property, with shrinking

Okkama's nearest relatives are D and Rust. All three keep tests in the module they test and leave them out of a production build: D compiles unittest blocks only when asked, Rust compiles the cfg(test) module only for cargo test, and Okkama's parser skips test and fake blocks in a normal run (Section 15.1).

Two things in the last row have no counterpart above. The fake belongs to the role: it is written once, next to the contract, and the compiler checks it against that contract whenever the role changes. Elsewhere this is a convention a team may follow [Bugayenko 2016]. And there is no run-time patching: what Python's unittest.mock.patch does, replacing an attribute of a module while a test runs, has nothing to act on in a language whose objects never change. A collaborator is replaced the way it is in production, by passing a different object that does the role.

15.11 What does not work yet

  • TAP is not a report format, and a per-test deadline needs --workers: a test running in the runner's own process cannot be stopped from outside (#339, #938).

Until 0.4.1, a successor passed to test.is crashed the compiler and did not count as used (#275). It is now an ordinary argument: test.is(bottle.open().close(), bottle) compares the two bottles.

15.12 What this design costs

  • A fake must be written. A mocking library generates a double from an interface in one line. A fake is code, and for a large role it is a lot of code. The author of the role writes it once; every user saves the work.
  • No interaction testing. "Was flush called before close?" has no direct answer. A fake can record calls with RecordedCalls, and a test can check the record, but nothing is generated for it. Most such questions are better asked of the result.
  • No access to private state. A test sees an object as its callers do. If something cannot be tested through the public actions, the object is doing too much, or the role is missing an action. That is the intended pressure, and sometimes it is just inconvenient.
  • Properties need thought. A good property is harder to write than an example. The library makes running one cheap; it cannot invent the claim.

In return:

  • tests sit beside the code and vanish from production;
  • every role has a double, maintained with the role and checked by the compiler;
  • a failed property comes back as a seed and a minimal input that reproduce it.

Chapter 16Enums and pattern matching

Some values come from a short list that is known in advance: a priority is low, normal or urgent; an order is a draft, paid, shipped or cancelled. Some of those alternatives carry data of their own. A paid order has an amount, a shipped one has a carrier and a tracking number, and a draft has nothing. Okkama covers both with one declaration, enum, and takes them apart with match, in blocks or in compact one-line cases. The compiler knows every case, so it can tell when code forgets one.

module bible/enums v1.0.0;

// A payload-free enum names a closed set; a variant carries data in some of
// its cases. match takes either apart, and the compiler checks the cases.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Priority = (low, normal, urgent);

enum Stage = (draft, paid(amount is int), shipped(carrier is string, tracking is string),
    cancelled(reason is string));

object Order {
    has number is int;
    has priority is Priority;
    has stage is Stage;
    Order(:number, :priority, :stage);

    line() is string {
        let flag = match priority { case Priority.urgent: "!"; case _: " "; };
        let state = match stage {
            case Stage.draft { "draft"; }
            case Stage.paid(amount) { "paid " + amount.string(); }
            case Stage.shipped(carrier, tracking) { "shipped by " + carrier + ", " + tracking; }
            case Stage.cancelled(reason) { "cancelled: " + reason; }
        };
        flag + " #" + number.string() + " " + state;
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let orders is @Order = [
        Order(number: 1, priority: Priority.normal, stage: Stage.draft),
        Order(number: 2, priority: Priority.urgent, stage: Stage.paid(4250)),
        Order(number: 3, priority: Priority.low, stage: Stage.shipped("DHL", "JD0142")),
        Order(number: 4, priority: Priority.normal, stage: Stage.cancelled("out of stock"))
    ];
    for orders -> order { out.writeln(order.line()); }
    0;
}

Output:

  #1 draft
! #2 paid 4250
  #3 shipped by DHL, JD0142
  #4 cancelled: out of stock
  • Priority is a payload-free enum: three names and nothing else.
  • Stage is a variant enum: some of its cases carry typed fields.
  • match stage has one branch per case and binds each case's fields to names. Drop the cancelled branch and the program no longer compiles.
  • match priority { case Priority.urgent: "!"; case _: " "; } is the one-line form: compact cases, and _ for everything else.

This chapter covers enums of both kinds and the rules of matching, and then asks the design question that enums share with roles: when should a set of alternatives be closed, and when open?

16.1 A closed set of names

enum Priority = (low, normal, urgent);

An enum declaration names a type and lists its cases. The type name is capitalised, like every type; the cases are lower-case identifiers (enum Status = (Ready, failed) is a syntax error: Expect enum case name). A case is always written with its type, Priority.urgent. There is no bare urgent in scope, so two enums can share a case name without conflict. A duplicate case is an error: Enum "Status" already has case "ready". A long enum is written one case per line, and, as in any list of parameters, arguments or literals, a trailing comma after the last case is allowed.

What an Okkama enum value does not have is as important as what it has:

  • No number. A case has no ordinal you can read, and there is no conversion to or from int.
  • No order. Priority.low < Priority.urgent is rejected:
module bible/order v1.0.0;

enum Priority = (low, normal, urgent);

main() is int {
    let first = Priority.low < Priority.urgent;
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

16-order-rejected.ok:6:17: semantic error: Operator < cannot be applied to Priority and Priority
  • No actions. An enum value is not an object. Priority.low.string() is an error, Can only call actions on objects, and there is no values() that lists the cases. The one exception is an error enum, whose values answer text() (Chapter 10).
  • No mixing. Two cases are equal only if they belong to the same enum and are the same case. Status.ready == Other.ready is not false, it is a compile error, Cannot compare Status and Other, like any comparison across categories (Chapter 4).

What it does have is equality, and the right to be a map key and an array element. [Unit.celsius: 2, Unit.kelvin: 1] is a %Unit:int, and @Status is an array of statuses.

Each refusal has a history. In C an enumerator is an int constant. It can be added, compared, stored in any integer variable and printed as a number [Kernighan 1988], so an enum gives a name to a number without giving it a type. Pascal made the enumerated type a type of its own, but an ordinal one: its values are ordered, succ and pred step through them, and they index arrays and drive for loops [Wirth 1971]. Java turned each case into an object with methods, fields, an ordinal() and a generated values() [Gosling 2023]. Bloch's advice in Effective Java is to use enums instead of int constants and never derive anything from ordinal() [Bloch 2018]. Go has no enum declaration at all: a block of constants with iota numbers them [Go specification].

Okkama takes the type from Pascal and leaves out the arithmetic. An ordinal invites code that depends on the order of a declaration: if level > Priority.normal silently changes meaning when someone inserts high between normal and urgent. If a domain does have an order, the order is a fact about the domain, and the program states it: a match that maps each case to a weight, or an object that does Comparing (Chapter 14). The same goes for text. The word printed for a case is a presentation decision. It depends on the audience and the language. A string() on the enum would pick one silently. A match makes the choice where it is used.

Declaration order is visible in maps: enum keys sort by their position in the declaration:

enum Unit = (celsius, kelvin, fahrenheit);
let units = [Unit.fahrenheit: 3, Unit.kelvin: 2, Unit.celsius: 1];
// units.keys(): celsius, kelvin, fahrenheit

That gives iteration a stable order without making the order an operator.

16.2 Cases that carry data

enum Stage = (draft, paid(amount is int), shipped(carrier is string, tracking is string),
    cancelled(reason is string));

A case may declare fields. The enum is then a variant, a tagged union, or what the ML family calls an algebraic data type. A value of Stage is exactly one of four things, and the case decides which fields exist:

  • Stage.paid(4250) builds a value. Payload fields are given positionally, in declaration order. Stage.paid(amount: 4250) is rejected: Variant Stage.paid expects 1 positional payload field(s).
  • Payload fields are immutable and have no accessors. stage.amount does not exist, because on a draft there would be nothing to return. The only way to read a field is a pattern that has first established the case.
  • Equality compares the enum, the case and the payload, field by field.

A variant may be generic:

module bible/variants v1.0.0;

// A variant may be generic. Equality compares the enum, the case and the
// payload; a payload-free enum is also a map key.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Reading<T> = (missing, single(value is T), range(low is T, high is T));
enum Unit = (celsius, kelvin);

object Sensor {
    has name is string;
    has unit is Unit;
    has reading is Reading<int>;
    Sensor(:name, :unit, :reading);

    text() is string {
        let suffix = match unit { case Unit.celsius: " C"; case Unit.kelvin: " K"; };
        let shown = match reading {
            case Reading.missing { "no data"; }
            case Reading.single(value) { value.string() + suffix; }
            case Reading.range(low, high) { low.string() + ".." + high.string() + suffix; }
        };
        name + ": " + shown;
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let sensors is @Sensor = [
        Sensor(name: "hall", unit: Unit.celsius, reading: Reading.single(21)),
        Sensor(name: "cellar", unit: Unit.celsius, reading: Reading.range(8, 11)),
        Sensor(name: "probe", unit: Unit.kelvin, reading: Reading<int>.missing)
    ];
    for sensors -> sensor { out.writeln(sensor.text()); }
    let same = Reading.single(21) == Reading.single(21);
    let other = Reading.single(21) == Reading.range(21, 21);
    out.writeln(same.string() + " " + other.string());
    let units = [Unit.celsius: 2, Unit.kelvin: 1];
    out.writeln(units.has(Unit.kelvin).string());
    0;
}

Output:

hall: 21 C
cellar: 8..11 C
probe: no data
true false
true

Reading.single(21) infers Reading<int> from its argument. A case without fields has nothing to infer from, so without an expected type it needs explicit arguments: Reading<int>.missing. Writing Reading.missing alone is rejected: Cannot infer type arguments for Reading.missing; provide an expected type or explicit type arguments. In the Sensor constructor the field type supplies the context.

Two enums of the standard prelude are variants of exactly this kind: Maybe<T> = (some(value), none) and Presence<T>, which adds missing (Chapter 7). Error enums declared is Error are variants too, even when no case has a payload, and a catch takes them apart with the same patterns (Chapter 10).

Pascal's variant records gave the idea wide use in an unsafe form [Wirth 1971]. The tag was an ordinary field, and the language did not check that a program read the fields of the variant the tag named. HOPE combined data types defined by cases with functions defined by patterns over them [Burstall 1980], and ML made the pair standard, with the compiler checking the patterns [Milner 1997]. Haskell kept it [Haskell 2010], and Rust brought it to systems programming as enum with match [Klabnik 2023]. Java reached it in steps: records, then sealed interfaces that close a hierarchy, then switch with patterns that checks the hierarchy is covered [Bierman 2021; Bierman 2021; Bierman 2023].

Okkama's variant is the ML one with the field names of a record. Its fields are named in the declaration and positional at use, and the compiler checks both arity and types.

16.3 match

let state = match stage {
    case Stage.draft { "draft"; }
    case Stage.paid(amount) { "paid " + amount.string(); }
    case Stage.shipped(carrier, tracking) { "shipped by " + carrier + ", " + tracking; }
    case Stage.cancelled(reason) { "cancelled: " + reason; }
};

Figure 16.1. A match used as a value covers every case of its enum, or ends with else.

The subject is evaluated once. Each case lists one or more patterns, and the first case with a matching pattern runs. There is no fall-through and no break; a branch is a block, and its last value is the value of the match. else takes whatever no case matched.

Patterns are of two kinds:

  • A value. case Priority.low, Priority.normal, case 404, case "GET". The subject is compared with ==, so the rules of equality apply: the value must be of the subject's category, and case 1..5 against an int is rejected rather than read as a range test (Chapter 9).
  • A variant pattern. case Stage.shipped(carrier, tracking) tests the case and binds each field to a name, or ignores it with _. The number of bindings must equal the number of fields: Wrong number of variant pattern bindings. A binding exists only inside its branch.

All branches of a match that produces a value must produce one type:

semantic error: Branches produce different types: int and string

A branch that returns, throws or panics produces no value and does not take part in the check.

Exhaustiveness

The compiler knows every case of an enum, so it checks that a match covers them:

module bible/missing v1.0.0;

enum Stage = (draft, paid(amount is int), cancelled(reason is string));

object Report {
    Report();
    text(stage is Stage) is string {
        match stage {
            case Stage.draft { "draft"; }
            case Stage.paid(amount) { "paid " + amount.string(); }
        }
    }
}

main() is int { 0; }

The compiler answers:

16-missing-rejected.ok:8:9: semantic error: Non-exhaustive match: missing cancelled

The rule depends on the kind of enum:

  • A match over a variant enum — one with a payload anywhere, an error enum, Maybe, Presence — must cover every case or have else. That holds for a statement match as well as for one that produces a value.
  • A match over a payload-free enum that produces a value must cover every case or have else. Otherwise there would be no value to produce:
module bible/value v1.0.0;

enum Priority = (low, normal, urgent);

object Queue {
    Queue();
    weight(priority is Priority) is int {
        let weight = match priority {
            case Priority.low { 1; }
            case Priority.normal { 2; }
        };
        weight;
    }
}

main() is int { 0; }

The compiler answers:

16-value-rejected.ok:8:22: semantic error: match over enum `Priority` does not cover urgent, so it has no value here; add the cases or an `else` branch

The same message names the cases when the match is the last value of an action. Until 0.5.0 that error named only the action ("must produce a return value", issue #291):

module bible/tail v1.0.0;

enum Priority = (low, normal, urgent);

object Queue {
    Queue();

    weight(priority is Priority) is int {
        match priority {
            case Priority.low { 1; }
            case Priority.normal { 2; }
        }
    }
}

main() is int { 0; }

The compiler answers:

16-tail-rejected.ok:9:9: semantic error: match over enum `Priority` does not cover urgent, so it has no value here; add the cases or an `else` branch
  • A statement match over a payload-free enum may leave cases out; it then does nothing for them. okkama lint reports it:
warning[non-exhaustive-match]: match over enum `Status` does not handle failed, done; add the cases or an `else` branch

The second and third rules differ because a payload-free enum used to be treated as a set of constants, and a statement over constants may legitimately act on some of them only. The lint keeps the old freedom visible. Variants never had it. A missing case of a variant is a missing piece of data handling, and the compiler treats it as such.

Exhaustiveness pays off most when the enum changes. Add refunded(amount is int) to Stage, and every match over a stage that lists cases becomes an error that names refunded. The list of places to update comes from the compiler, not from a search. This is the reason to prefer listing cases over else. An else covers today's remaining cases and every future one, and so it hides exactly the places that a new case should reach. Maranget describes the two checks a compiler can make on a match: exhaustiveness, whether some value is matched by no case, and usefulness, whether a case can never be reached [Maranget 2007]. Okkama implements both for the cases it can compare: a repeated case is an error (Duplicate variant pattern), so is a repeated literal (Duplicate case pattern), and so is an else after cases that already cover every value (Unreachable else). Until 0.6.0 only the first of those was reported (issue #286).

16.4 Compact cases

A case that only computes a value fits on one line: case pattern: value;. With it, a whole match is one expression:

let suffix = match unit { case Unit.celsius: " C"; case Unit.kelvin: " K"; };
let flag = match priority { case Priority.urgent: "!"; case _: " "; };
let label = match reading { case Reading.single(value): value.string(); case _: "no single value"; };
  • A compact case is a pattern, a colon, the value and a semicolon. The value may also be a throw: case Reading.none: throw Missing.reading;. Block cases and compact cases mix in one match.
  • case _ covers the cases not named; it is another spelling of else, and it takes either form, while else always takes a block.
  • Patterns are written in full (Priority.urgent), as in any match, and the rules are the same: coverage, repeated cases, one result type.

A match that produces a value and misses a case names it: match over enum `Priority` does not cover normal, so it has no value here; add the cases or an `else` branch. Until 0.6.0 the same choices had a notation of their own, priority ?? .urgent: "!" !! _: " "; it was removed in favour of compact cases (issue #893), so that one construct does one job.

16.5 Closed or open: enums and roles

An enum and a role are two answers to one question: how to describe a value that can be one of several kinds.

  • An enum lists the kinds in one place. Code that uses it switches on the kind. Adding a new operation over stages is easy: write one more function with a match, and nothing else changes. Adding a new kind is harder: every match must learn it, and the compiler lists them.
  • A role leaves the kinds open. Each kind is an object that does the role and carries its own behaviour. Adding a new kind is easy: write one more object, and nothing else changes. Adding a new operation is harder: the role gains an action, and every object must implement it.

Reynolds described this duality in 1975, and Cook revisits it as the difference between abstract data types and objects [Cook 2009]. Wadler named it the expression problem: define a data type by cases so that both new cases and new functions can be added without recompiling existing code and without losing static type safety [Wadler 1998]. Okkama does not solve the expression problem; very few languages do without extra machinery. It offers both sides and asks the programmer to choose by what is expected to change:

The set of kinds is… …and the operations are… Use
closed, part of the domain's definition (order states, token kinds, protocol messages) many, added over time (rendering, pricing, persistence) an enum, with match
open, extended by other modules or by tests (storage backends, transports, clocks) few and stable a role, with objects

The test is whether a newcomer must be written into one list or may be added from outside. A stage of an order belongs to the order's definition. A new stage is a change to the business, and every place that handles stages should be reviewed. A storage backend does not belong to the service that uses it, and a fake in a test is one more backend (Chapter 15). A role cannot be matched on, because there is no downcast (Chapter 14). An enum cannot be extended, because its declaration is the complete list. Each property is what makes the other choice worse.

Java's sealed interfaces sit in between: a closed list of classes, each with its own methods, which a switch can also take apart [Bierman 2021; Bierman 2023]. Okkama has no single construct for this, but the effect is reachable: a variant enum whose payloads are objects.

16.6 A worked example: a protocol and a state machine

Enums with payloads are the natural shape of a protocol. A vending machine receives commands, has a state, and answers with replies; each of the three is a closed set of cases, and each case carries exactly the data it needs.

module app v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

// What a customer can do, what the machine can be, and what it answers.
enum Command = (insert(cents is int), choose(item is string, price is int), refund);
enum State = (idle, credit(cents is int));
enum Reply = (accepted(total is int), vended(item is string, change is int), refunded(cents is int),
    refused(why is string));

// One transition: the next state and the reply. Every pair is handled; a new case breaks the build here.
object Machine {
    has state is State;
    Machine(:state);

    step(command is Command) is Machine { Machine(state: self.next(command)); }

    next(command is Command) is State {
        match command {
            case Command.insert(cents) { State.credit(self.balance() + cents); }
            case Command.choose(item, price) { if self.balance() >= price { State.idle; } else { state; } }
            case Command.refund { State.idle; }
        }
    }

    reply(command is Command) is Reply {
        match command {
            case Command.insert(cents) { Reply.accepted(self.balance() + cents); }
            case Command.choose(item, price) {
                if self.balance() >= price {
                    Reply.vended(item, self.balance() - price);
                } else {
                    Reply.refused("insert " + (price - self.balance()).string() + " more");
                }
            }
            case Command.refund {
                if self.balance() > 0 { Reply.refunded(self.balance()); } else { Reply.refused("nothing to refund"); }
            }
        }
    }

    balance() is int {
        match state {
            case State.idle { 0; }
            case State.credit(cents) { cents; }
        }
    }
}

object Show {
    Show();
    of(reply is Reply) is string {
        match reply {
            case Reply.accepted(total) { "credit " + total.string(); }
            case Reply.vended(item, change) { item + ", change " + change.string(); }
            case Reply.refunded(cents) { "refund " + cents.string(); }
            case Reply.refused(why) { "refused: " + why; }
        }
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let show = Show();
    let commands = [Command.insert(50), Command.choose("tea", 120), Command.insert(100), Command.choose("tea", 120),
        Command.refund];
    let final = commands.reduce(Machine(state: State.idle)) -> machine, command {
        out.writeln(show.of(machine.reply(command)));
        machine.step(command);
    };
    out.writeln("ends with " + final.balance().string() + " cents");
    0;
}

Output:

credit 50
refused: insert 70 more
credit 150
tea, change 30
refused: nothing to refund
ends with 0 cents
  • Messages are variants. Command.choose(item, price) carries what a choice needs and nothing else; Command.refund carries nothing. There is no "command type" string to dispatch on and no optional fields that only some commands fill.
  • The state is a variant too. State.idle and State.credit(cents) make an impossible state unrepresentable: there is no credit field to forget to reset when the machine goes idle.
  • Transitions are a match over the command. next and reply each handle every case, and the compiler checks it: adding a case Command.service stops the build with "Non-exhaustive match: missing service" at every match that must learn about it.
  • The machine is a value. step returns a new machine; the run is a reduce over the commands, so the whole history is a fold and any intermediate machine could be kept and replayed.

This is the shape that object-oriented designs reach with the State pattern and that functional languages write as algebraic data types. The trade-off of §16.5 applies: a new kind of message touches every match, which is exactly the list of places that must decide what the message means.

16.7 Where enums came from

Okkama's enum joins two lines of descent.

  • Named values. Pascal gave programmers enumerated types: a closed set of names such as (red, green, blue), with an order and the operations succ and pred [Wirth 1971]. Its variant records attached data to a tag, but the compiler did not check that the tag matched the data read. C's enumerations went the other way and are names for integers.
  • Cases that carry data. HOPE, designed by Burstall, MacQueen and Sannella, declared a type by its constructors, each with its own fields, and defined functions by pattern matching on them [Burstall 1980]. ML adopted these datatypes [Milner 1997], and through ML they reached Haskell, Rust and Swift as algebraic data types.
  • Checked coverage. With a closed set of constructors, a compiler can tell whether a match covers every case and name the one it misses. Maranget describes how compilers do it and how to report the missing pattern usefully [Maranget 2007].

Okkama takes the closed set from Pascal without the order: cases have no ordinal and no < (§16.1). It takes payloads from HOPE and ML, and checked coverage for every match that produces a value. It does not yet take recursive datatypes (#287) or nested patterns (#288), the two features that make algebraic data types the natural way to write trees and interpreters in ML and Haskell.

16.8 Enums elsewhere

Okkama C Pascal Java Rust Haskell Go
Case is a number no yes (int) ordinal ordinal() as cast for payload-free enums Enum class, if derived yes (iota)
Ordering operators no yes yes compareTo if derived if derived yes
Data per case variants no (unions are separate and untagged) variant records, unchecked tag sealed classes and records yes yes no
Exhaustiveness checked yes; lint only for statement matches over payload-free enums no no switch expressions and pattern switch yes warning (-Wincomplete-patterns) no
Recursive data no (#287) through pointers through pointers yes through Box yes —
Nested patterns no (#288) — — yes yes yes —
Actions on cases no — — yes impl blocks type classes methods on the type

Okkama's enum keeps the type safety of the Haskell and Rust column. It leaves out what those languages build on top of it: nested patterns, recursion, derived orderings and methods. The first two are missing for now. The last two are left out on purpose, for the reasons in §16.1.

16.9 Limits

  • No recursive variants. A case cannot carry its own enum, directly or indirectly:
module bible/recursive v1.0.0;

enum Tree = (leaf, node(left is Tree, value is int, right is Tree));

main() is int { 0; }

The compiler answers:

16-recursive-rejected.ok:3:1: semantic error: Recursive variant payload types are not supported

Trees, lists and expression syntax trees, the classic uses of algebraic data types since HOPE, have to be built from objects for now (issue #287).

  • No nested patterns. case Pair.both(Maybe.some(x), y) is rejected: Expected a binding or _ in variant pattern. A second match on the bound field does the same job in more lines (issue #288).
  • Variants are not map keys. A payload-free enum is a key; a variant is not: Map key type Reading is not a scalar key type (issue #289).

16.10 What this design costs

  • Text and order are written out. Printing a case or sorting by priority takes a match. A language with toString and ordinal would do it implicitly. The cost is a few lines per enum, paid once and kept in one place.
  • No list of cases. There is no values(). Code that needs every case, for example to fill a menu, writes the array, and nothing checks that the array is complete.
  • Positional payloads. Fields are named in the declaration, but a construction like Stage.shipped("DHL", "JD0142") does not show which string is the carrier. A case with more than two or three fields is often better as an object carried by a one-field case.
  • The closed world. An enum cannot be extended from another module. That is what makes exhaustiveness possible, and it is why an open family of kinds should be a role.

In return:

  • a forgotten case is a compile error, not a run-time surprise;
  • a value cannot be read through the wrong case;
  • equality is exact, and two enums can never be compared by accident;

Chapter 17Generics

A box that holds an int and a box that holds a string do the same work. So do a sorted list of prices and a sorted list of names, a channel of jobs and a channel of results. Without type parameters a language makes you pick one of three bad options: write the same object once per type, give up the type and store any, or check every element when it comes back out. Generics are the fourth option. You write the object once, over a type T, and the compiler makes sure each use of it has one concrete T.

module bible/generics v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "compare" take Comparing, Order;

// Two type parameters; a successor with them swapped.
object Pair<K, V> {
    has key is K;
    has value is V;
    Pair(:key, :value);
    key() is K { key; }
    value() is V { value; }
    swapped() is Pair<V, K> { Pair(key: value, value: key); }
}

// An algorithm is an object too: the least of its values, for any T that
// orders itself.
object Least<T: Comparing<T>> {
    has first is T;
    has rest is @T;
    Least(first is T, rest is ...T) {
        self.first = first;
        self.rest = rest...;
    }
    value() is T {
        rest.reduce(first) -> best, item { if item.order(best) == Order.less { item; } else { best; }; };
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let pair = Pair(key: "answer", value: 42);
    let back = pair.swapped();
    out.writeln(pair.key() + " = " + pair.value().string());
    out.writeln(back.key().string() + " = " + back.value());
    out.writeln(Least(3, 9, 1, 4).value().string());
    out.writeln(Least("pear", "apple", "fig").value());
    out.writeln(Least(2.5, -0.5).value().string());
    0;
}

Output:

answer = 42
42 = answer
1
apple
-0.5
  • Pair<K, V> has two type parameters. swapped() returns a Pair<V, K>, a different specialization of the same declaration.
  • Least<T: Comparing<T>> is an algorithm written as an object. Its T must be able to order itself, and the compiler checks that before the constructor runs.
  • No call names a type. Pair(key: "answer", value: 42) is a Pair<string, int> and Least(3, 9, 1, 4) is a Least<int>: the compiler works out the arguments from the values.
  • Least(2.5, -0.5) is a third specialization, Least<float>. The type arguments distinguish these types.

This chapter covers what can be generic, inference, bounds, map-key parameters and specialization identity, then compares these language rules with Java, C#, Go, Rust, Haskell and OCaml.

17.1 Parameters on objects, roles and enums

Three kinds of declaration take type parameters: objects, roles and enums.

object Box<T> {
    has value is T;
    Box(:value);
    get() is T { value; }
}

role Echo<T> {
    echo(value is T) is T;
}

enum Slot<T> = (vacant, full(item is T));

The parameters follow the declaration's name in angle brackets. They are type names, so they are capitalised, and they must be unique and differ from the declaration's own name. A parameter is visible everywhere inside its declaration: in fields, constructors (full and shorthand), actions, successor actions and destroy of an object, in the signatures and the fake block of a role, in the payloads of an enum. Outside it the parameter does not exist; a caller sees Box<int>, never T.

A use of a generic type gives exactly as many arguments as the declaration has parameters, and a type without parameters takes none:

Generic type "Pair" expects 2 type argument(s), got 1
Type "Coin" is not generic and cannot accept type arguments

A parameter stands for one concrete type. It cannot take arguments of its own, so T<int> is not a type; Okkama has no higher-kinded parameters.

The enums Maybe<T> and Presence<T> of Chapter 7 are generic enums built into the compiler. A program declares its own the same way, as Slot<T> above. A case without a payload does not mention T, so where nothing else fixes the type it is written with its specialization: Slot<int>.vacant, like Maybe<Shape>.none.

No generic actions

The list leaves something out: an action cannot take type parameters of its own. There is no first<T>(items is @T) is T. This follows from the object model of Chapter 3. Okkama has no free functions and no static methods, so a generic function would need an object to live on, and that object would need its own T anyway. The language goes the other way and makes the algorithm the object. Least<T> in the example is what Java would write as static <T extends Comparable<T>> T least(T first, T... rest). It is a value that knows its inputs and computes its answer on request, the style that Elegant Objects recommends in place of static methods and utility classes [Bugayenko 2016].

Least(3, 9, 1, 4) constructs an object before value() reads it, so the algorithm pays for constructing that value. Inference has one home: the constructor call, with one set of error messages.

Where the idea comes from

Cardelli and Wegner's survey of polymorphism separates two kinds [Cardelli 1985]. Inclusion polymorphism is what roles give: one value is usable as several types, because it belongs to all of them. Parametric polymorphism is what this chapter is about: one piece of code works uniformly over a type that is supplied as a parameter. Both came into programming languages in the 1970s. CLU let a cluster, its abstract data type, take type parameters, and checked at compile time that the arguments offered the operations the cluster needed [Liskov 1977]. ML inferred polymorphic types for whole functions without any annotations [Milner 1978]. Object-oriented languages took parameters much later and with more compromises. Java added generics in version 5, in 2004, on top of a virtual machine that knew nothing about them [Bracha 1998], and C# added them in version 2.0, in 2005, together with a runtime that did [Kennedy 2001]. Go, which had shipped without generics for a decade, added them in version 1.18 in 2022 [Griesemer 2020; Scales 2022].

Okkama's generics are parametric polymorphism in CLU's sense, restricted to objects, roles and enums, with ML's idea that a programmer should rarely have to write type arguments, but without ML's global inference.

17.2 One T, one type

The whole model rests on one rule: within one specialization, T is one exact type. Every occurrence of T must resolve to the same type, and nothing is widened to make them agree.

module bible/exact v1.0.0;

import "compare" take Comparing, Order;

object Least<T: Comparing<T>> {
    has first is T;
    has rest is @T;
    Least(first is T, rest is ...T) {
        self.first = first;
        self.rest = rest...;
    }
}

main() is int {
    let least = Least(1, 2.0);
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

17-exact-rejected.ok:15:17: semantic error: Generic parameter "T" for object "Least" cannot be both int and float

1 is an int and 2.0 is a float. In Okkama these are different categories that never convert implicitly (Chapter 5), so Least(1, 2.0) has no T. The compiler does not look for a common supertype, does not invent a union int | float, and does not fall back to any. The program fails before anything runs, and the fix is an explicit conversion: Least(1.float(), 2.0). Version 0.4.2 applies the same rule to collection literals: [1, 2.0] is rejected unless an explicit @any is expected (Chapter 8).

Other languages answer the same question differently. Java's inference computes a least upper bound. For Arrays.asList(1, 2.0) it finds an intersection type of the form Number & Comparable<…>, a type that no programmer wrote and whose values can barely be used: Number has no arithmetic, so the list cannot be summed without casts [Gosling 2023]. Kotlin infers a similar intersection type. TypeScript infers the union (string | number)[] for [1, "two"]. Each answer compiles, and each pushes the problem to the place where the values are used.

Okkama keeps the problem where it was created. A type argument is evidence of what the values are, and an inferred T that no value has would be a guess. The rule also keeps every other part of the type system simple: once inference succeeds, T is an ordinary concrete type, and the body of Least<int> type-checks exactly as if it had been written for int.

17.3 Inference at construction

Box(value: 7) names a declaration, not a type. The specialization is worked out at the call, from two sources.

The arguments. Each constructor parameter whose type mentions a parameter gives one equation: value is T with the argument 7 gives T = int. The equations go into structure: a parameter items is @T with an @string argument gives T = string, a parameter %K:V with a %string:int gives two equations, a parameter Box<T> with a Box<float> argument gives T = float, and a variadic tail rest is ...T gives one equation per value. A shorthand constructor Box(:value) uses the field's type in the same way. If two equations disagree, the error names both answers:

Generic parameter "T" for object "Least" cannot be both int and float

The expected type. When the call stands where a type is already declared, in a typed binding, a field, an argument for a typed parameter, a result or return, that type is evidence too. This is what makes an empty collection usable:

module bible/evidence v1.0.0;

object Bucket<T> {
    has values is @T;
    Bucket(:values);
}

main() is int {
    let empty = Bucket(values: []);
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

17-evidence-rejected.ok:9:17: semantic error: Cannot infer generic parameter "T" for object "Bucket"

[] has no elements, so it says nothing about T, and without other evidence the compiler stops. A declared target fixes it: let empty is Bucket<int> = Bucket(values: []);. The declared type supplies evidence that is missing. It never overrides evidence that is present: in let wrong is Box<int> = Box(value: "x"); the argument and the target disagree, and that is an error, not a conversion.

The expected type reaches into nested constructions, but only through parameters it already fixes:

let x is Box<Empty<int>> = Box(item: Empty());

The target gives the outer T = Empty<int>. The inner Empty() stands where an Empty<int> is expected, so it gets its int from there. The compiler does not look ahead to later statements, does not try overloads to see which one type-checks, and does not search for a type that would make a program compile. Inference uses only what is visible at the call.

Roles as evidence

Roles take part in both directions. A role-typed target supplies the arguments of an object that implements the role:

module bible/identity v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

role Echo<T> {
    echo(value is T) is T;
}

object Loud does Echo<string> {
    Loud();
    echo(value is string) is string { value.upper() + "!"; }
}

object Same<T> does Echo<T> {
    Same();
    echo(value is T) is T { value; }
}

object Bucket<T> {
    has values is @T;
    Bucket(:values);
    size() is int { values.size(); }
    plus(value is T) is Bucket<T> { Bucket(values: values + [value]); }
}

enum Slot<T> = (vacant, full(item is T));

object Slots {
    Slots();
    total(slots is @Slot<int>) is int {
        slots.reduce(0) -> sum, slot { sum + match slot { case Slot.full(item) { item; } case Slot.vacant { 0; } }; };
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    // Same() has no argument to infer from: the target Echo<string> supplies T.
    let echoes is @Echo<string> = [Loud(), Same()];
    out.writeln(echoes.map() -> echo { echo.echo("hi"); }.join(" "));
    let numbers is Echo<int> = Same();
    out.writeln(numbers.echo(7).string());
    // An empty array is no evidence; the declared type is.
    let empty is Bucket<int> = Bucket(values: []);
    out.writeln(empty.plus(5).plus(6).size().string());
    let slots = [Slot.full(3), Slot<int>.vacant, Slot.full(4)];
    out.writeln(Slots().total(slots).string());
    0;
}

Output:

HI! hi
7
2
7

Same() has no arguments, so on its own it could not be specialized. In an array declared @Echo<string> each element is expected to be an Echo<string>, and Same<T> does Echo<T> matches that only with T = string. A builtin value can be evidence for a role parameter too: arrays are Iterating<T> and Sequencing<T>, so Sorted([5, 3, 8]) in Section 17.9 gets T = int from the array's elements.

When one equation gives a role and another gives an object that implements it, the role stays. A List<Json> that has a JsonBool prepended is still a List<Json>, not a List<JsonBool>. Inference never looks for a common role of two unrelated objects, however: if one argument is a Square and another a Circle, the program must say Shape somewhere.

Several constructors

An object may have several constructors (Chapter 12), and inference runs for each one that fits the call's shape. Fixed and shorthand constructors are tried before variadic ones, as in overload resolution. If two constructors fit and infer different specializations, the call is ambiguous and the compiler says so (Ambiguous construction of "Pair": constructors infer different generic arguments) instead of picking one.

Functions as evidence

An anonymous action may declare its result type, and that result is evidence for a generic parameter. This is how the standard library's SortedBy<T, K> learns its key type:

let quickest = SortedBy(origin: jobs, key: (job is Job) is int { job.hours(); });

The key's type (Job) is int meets the parameter key is (T) is K, giving T = Job and K = int. Before 0.4.1 an anonymous action could not declare its result, and the same call needed let quickest is SortedBy<Job, int> = … (#214).

No explicit specialization

There is no syntax to specialize at the call: Box<int>(value: 7) is an error (A type is not a value). The way to state a specialization is to declare the type of the place that receives the value. That keeps one way of doing it, and the type ends up on the binding, where a reader looks for it.

17.4 Bounds

A parameter may be required to implement a role:

role Comparing<T> {
    order(other is T) is Order;
}

object Least<T: Comparing<T>> { … }

Comparing is the standard library's three-way order (std/compare). T: Comparing<T> says that a T can be ordered against another T. The bound mentions the parameter it constrains. This is F-bounded polymorphism, named by Canning, Cook, Hill, Olthoff and Mitchell, who showed that ordinary bounded quantification cannot express "a type comparable with itself" and that a recursive bound can [Canning 1989]. Java's <T extends Comparable<T>> is the same idea, and its roots go back to CLU, one of the first languages built around parameterized abstract types, where a where clause required a type argument to provide the operations a module needed [Liskov 1977].

int, float, rat, byte, string and char implement Comparing of themselves, so Least accepts all of them. bool deliberately has no natural order:

module bible/bound v1.0.0;

import "compare" take Comparing, Order;

object Least<T: Comparing<T>> {
    has first is T;
    has rest is @T;
    Least(first is T, rest is ...T) {
        self.first = first;
        self.rest = rest...;
    }
}

main() is int {
    let least = Least(true, false);
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

17-bound-rejected.ok:15:17: semantic error: Generic parameter "T" for object "Least" has type bool, which does not satisfy Comparing<bool>

The bound is checked after inference has found T and before the constructor's body runs. It never takes part in inference: T: Comparing<T> does not tell the compiler what T is, and an object whose T cannot be inferred is not rescued by its bound. Nor does a bound convert anything. A T either implements the role or the program is rejected.

A role-typed argument satisfies a bound when the role narrows to it, that is, when it offers every action of the bound (Chapter 14). Given object Tagged<T: Named>, a value of a role Counted that has name() and count() satisfies T: Named. The specialization is then Tagged<Counted>, so get() hands back a Counted with count() still available, not a Named.

What bounds cannot do is as deliberate as what they can:

  • One bound per parameter. There is no T: Comparing<T> & Hashing. A parameter that needs two capabilities is better served by a role that composes them.
  • No category bounds. There is no T: number. Numbers in Okkama do not share a supertype, and arithmetic between categories needs explicit conversion. Generic arithmetic is written with the operator roles of Section 14.7, Adding<T, R> and its siblings, which an object implements per operand type.
  • No bounds on role parameters yet, no defaults, no variance annotations.

17.5 Parameters used as map keys

A map key must be a scalar, an enum without payloads, a string or a value object (Chapter 8). When a generic object uses its parameter as a key, as %T:V in a field, a signature or a body, or as the key of a map literal, every specialization has to respect that:

module bible/key v1.0.0;

// T is a map key here, so every specialization must be a key type.
object Tally<T> {
    has counts is %T:int;
    Tally() {
        let empty is %T:int = [:];
        counts = empty;
    }
    size() is int { counts.size(); }
}

main() is int {
    let words is Tally<string> = Tally();
    let rows is Tally<@int> = Tally();
    words.size() + rows.size();
}

The compiler answers:

17-key-rejected.ok:15:31: semantic error: Generic parameter "T" for object "Tally" is a map key: Map key type @int is not a scalar key type

Tally<string> is valid; Tally<@int> is rejected because arrays cannot be keys. In Wrap<U> { has inner is Tally<U>; }, U must satisfy the same key rule. Violating the key rule is never a request to compare keys by identity (#242).

17.6 A specialization is a type

Box<int> and Box<float> are different types, as different as Point and Money. A Box<float> cannot go where a Box<int> is expected, and that holds for fields, parameters, results, variadic tails, successors, typed bindings, catch clauses and imports. Role conformance is substituted too: Same<T> does Echo<T> makes Same<int> an Echo<int> and nothing else, so assigning it to an Echo<string> is rejected (Generic parameter "T" for object "Same" cannot be both string and int).

There is also no variance. Square implements Shape, but a Box<Square> is not a Box<Shape>:

Cannot initialize variable "shapes" of type Box<Shape> with Box<Square>

That is the safe answer for a type whose T appears in both directions, and Okkama does not ask the programmer to say which direction a parameter is used in. The common case still works because inference reads the target first: let direct is Box<Shape> = Box(value: Square(side: 3)); builds a Box<Shape> from the start, wrapping the square as a Shape.

Generic fakes

A role's fake block (Chapter 15) is written against the role's parameters, and it must conform symbolically. A fake whose echo takes int does not implement echo(value is T), even though Echo<int> is the only specialization the tests use. A fake has no constructor arguments to infer from, so its specialization comes from the target:

let echo is Echo<int> = Echo.fake();   // test mode only

Without a declared target the construction fails instead of guessing.

Reading the errors

Every generic error comes from one of a few checks, and its message says which:

Message What happened Usual fix
Generic parameter "T" for object "X" cannot be both A and B two equations disagree, or a target contradicts an argument convert one value explicitly, or correct the declared type
Cannot infer generic parameter "T" for object "X" no argument gives evidence (empty collections, no arguments) and no target is declared declare the type of the binding, field or parameter
… has type A, which does not satisfy R<A> the inferred type does not implement the bound implement the role, or wrap the value in an object that does
Generic parameter "T" for object "X" is a map key: … a key parameter got a type that cannot be a key use a scalar, an enum, a string or a value object
Ambiguous construction of "X": constructors infer different generic arguments two constructors fit with different specializations declare the target type
Generic type "X" expects N type argument(s), got M a written type has the wrong arity write every argument
A type is not a value an attempt to specialize at the call, Box<int>(…) move the type to the binding
The program requests a chain of more than 256 generic specializations … polymorphic recursion stop growing the type in the recursive call

17.7 A parameter or a role?

Roles (Chapter 14) and type parameters both let one piece of code work with many types, and a design often has to choose between them. Compare a total of areas written both ways:

// A role: one Totals object for any mix of shapes.
object Totals {
    has shapes is @Shape;
    Totals(:shapes);
    area() is int { shapes.reduce(0) -> sum, shape { sum + shape.area(); }; }
}

// A parameter: one specialization per element type.
object Total<T: Shape> {
    has items is @T;
    Total(:items);
    area() is int { items.reduce(0) -> sum, item { sum + item.area(); }; }
}

The role version accepts [Square(side: 2), Strip(width: 3)]. The parameter version accepts that array only as Total<Shape>, and otherwise needs every element to have the same type: Total(items: [Square(side: 2)]) is a Total<Square>. The difference shows when the object gives values back. A Total<Square> that offers largest() is T returns a Square, with all of its actions, while Totals can only return a Shape. A type parameter keeps the information about which type it holds, and a role deliberately forgets it.

So the rule of thumb is about what flows out. If the code only consumes values through the role's actions, a role-typed field is simpler and admits mixtures. If it hands values back, or builds new containers of them, or uses them as map keys, a parameter preserves their exact type for the caller.

17.8 A worked example: the best N

A leaderboard, a list of the most expensive orders, the three slowest requests: keeping the best N items of a stream is the same algorithm for any type that can be ordered. Here it is once, for every such type:

module bible/top v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "compare" take Comparing, Order;

// The best `size` items seen so far, largest first. Offering an item returns a
// new Top: the old one is unchanged.
object Top<T: Comparing<T>> {
    has size is int;
    has items is @T;
    Top(:size, :items);
    offered(item is T) is Top<T> {
        let larger = items.filter() -> kept { kept.order(item) != Order.less; };
        let smaller = items.filter() -> kept { kept.order(item) == Order.less; };
        Top(size: size, items: (larger + [item] + smaller).take(size));
    }
    items() is @T { items; }
}

// A domain object that orders itself: higher amount first, then by name.
object Bid does Comparing<Bid> {
    has bidder is string;
    has amount is int;
    Bid(:bidder, :amount);
    amount() is int { amount; }
    bidder() is string { bidder; }
    order(other is Bid) is Order {
        if amount != other.amount() { return amount.order(other.amount()); }
        other.bidder().order(bidder);
    }
    text() is string { bidder + ":" + amount.string(); }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    // No item yet, so the declared type supplies T.
    let scores is Top<int> = Top(size: 3, items: []);
    let best = [12, 40, 7, 33, 40, 18].reduce(scores) -> top, score { top.offered(score); };
    out.writeln(best.items().map() -> score { score.string(); }.join(" "));
    let words is Top<string> = Top(size: 2, items: []);
    out.writeln(["kiwi", "apple", "pear", "fig"].reduce(words) -> top, word { top.offered(word); }.items().join(" "));
    let bids is Top<Bid> = Top(size: 2, items: []);
    let won = [Bid(bidder: "ann", amount: 50), Bid(bidder: "bob", amount: 70), Bid(bidder: "cy", amount: 70)]
        .reduce(bids) -> top, bid { top.offered(bid); };
    out.writeln(won.items().map() -> bid { bid.text(); }.join(" "));
    0;
}

Output:

40 40 33
pear kiwi
bob:70 cy:70

The pieces of the chapter meet here.

  • The bound. Top<T: Comparing<T>> needs order() and nothing else, so it works for int, string and any domain object that implements Comparing of itself. Bid does, with its own policy: a higher amount wins and equal amounts go by name.
  • The target supplies T. An empty top has no items, so Top(size: 3, items: []) alone could not be specialized. Each start value is declared, let scores is Top<int> = …, and from there reduce carries the type: its accumulator is a Top<int>, and so is each offered(…).
  • Immutability. offered returns a new Top, so scores still holds the empty top after the loop. The successor-style value of Chapter 13 needs no special form here: the result type is the same specialization, Top<T>.
  • Three specializations. The program uses Top<int>, Top<string> and Top<Bid>. The comparison inside offered follows its element type: the builtin integer order in the first, the code-point order of strings in the second, and Bid.order in the third.

A role field could not replace the parameter here. Comparing<T> takes the type that an item is compared with, so a field has items is @Comparing<…> would have to name that type and the object would work for one type only. The parameter is what lets one declaration say "items that can be compared with each other".

17.9 Generics in the standard library

The standard library is the largest user of generics: 185 generic object declarations and 18 generic roles. Most of them fall into four groups.

  • Collection views and cursors. Taken<T>, Sliced<T>, Zipped<A, B>, Sorted<T: Comparing<T>>, SortedBy<T, K: Comparing<K>> and their cursors implement Iterating<T> and Sequencing<T>, so they chain with each other and with plain arrays.
  • Containers with behaviour. Cell<T> (Chapter 13), Atomic<T> and Channel<T> (Chapter 20).
  • Contracts. Comparing<T>, the operator roles Adding<T, R> and its siblings, Iterating<T>, Cursor<T>, List<T>, Set<T>.
  • Settlements of asynchronous steps (FormSettlement<T>, RobotsSettlement<T>), which hold the outcome of a step whatever its type.
module bible/library v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "collections/ordering" take Sorted, SortedBy;

object Job {
    has name is string;
    has hours is int;
    Job(:name, :hours);
    name() is string { name; }
    hours() is int { hours; }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    // Sorted<T: Comparing<T>>: T = int and T = string, two specializations.
    out.writeln(Sorted([5, 3, 8]).first().string() + " " + Sorted(["pear", "fig"]).first());
    // SortedBy<T, K: Comparing<K>>: K comes from the key's declared result.
    let jobs = [Job(name: "paint", hours: 6), Job(name: "wire", hours: 2), Job(name: "tile", hours: 4)];
    let quickest = SortedBy(origin: jobs, key: (job is Job) is int { job.hours(); });
    out.writeln(quickest.map() -> job { job.name(); }.join(" "));
    0;
}

Output:

3 fig
wire tile paint

The example uses two of them. Sorted is specialized twice, for int and for string, and each specialization gets its T from the array it receives. SortedBy gets T = Job from the array and K = int from the key's declared result. Every element type T has to implement Comparing<T>, and every key type K has to implement Comparing<K>, and the compiler checks both at the call.

17.10 Okkama among other languages

What can be generic Bounds Variance Type arguments
Java classes, interfaces, methods extends, several with & at the use site, wildcards inferred for methods, <>
C# classes, interfaces, methods, delegates where, several declared on interfaces and delegates inferred for methods
Go functions, types interfaces with type sets none inferred for functions
Rust functions, types, traits trait bounds, several inferred; matters for lifetimes inferred
Haskell functions, types, classes class constraints, several none (no subtyping) inferred (Hindley–Milner)
OCaml functions, types, modules (functors) through modules and signatures declared (+'a, -'a) inferred (Hindley–Milner)
Okkama objects, roles, enums one role, F-bounded allowed none inferred at construction, exact

Okkama sits at the conservative end on almost every column. It infers less than Haskell or OCaml, which find types for whole functions [Milner 1978]. It has fewer kinds of bound than C# or Rust, and no variance at all. What it gains is predictability. Every generic argument is decided at one kind of place, a constructor call, from the values in front of it. A reader can do the same inference by looking at the call, and an error message names the two types that disagree.

17.11 Limits

  • No generic actions. An algorithm generic in its inputs is written as a generic object (Section 17.1).
  • No variance. Box<Square> is not a Box<Shape>. Declare the target type at construction instead.
  • One bound, on objects only. No multiple bounds, no bounds on role parameters, no category bounds such as T: number, no default arguments, no higher-kinded parameters.
  • No call-site specialization. Box<int>(…) is not valid source; the specialization comes from the arguments or from a declared target.
  • Polymorphic recursion requiring unbounded specializations is rejected.
module bible/grow v1.0.0;

object Box<T> {
    has value is T;
    Box(:value);
    get() is T { value; }
}

object Grow<T> {
    has value is T;
    Grow(:value);
    deeper(depth is int) is int {
        if depth == 0 { return 0; }
        Grow(value: Box(value: value)).deeper(depth - 1) + 1;
    }
}

main() is int {
    Grow(value: 1).deeper(3);
}

The compiler answers:

17-grow-rejected.ok:12:5: semantic error: The program requests a chain of more than 256 generic specializations, each asking for the next: Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<…>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>.new#0 <- Grow<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box…>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>.deeper <- Grow<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box…>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>.deeper <- Grow<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box…>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>.deeper <- Grow<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box…>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>.deeper <- Grow<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Box…>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>.deeper <- …

17.12 What this design costs

Exact identity makes some programs longer. Mixed numbers need explicit conversions, empty collections need a declared type, and an algorithm over T becomes an object with a constructor. Polymorphic recursion that requires an unbounded succession of distinct specializations is rejected.

Generic code follows the ordinary object rules: Least<int> works with int, and a parameter preserves its exact type. Inference has one rule a reader can apply, and a failed inference names the types that disagree.

Chapter 18Anonymous actions and closures

Sometimes the piece of behaviour a caller wants to hand over is too small to deserve a name: a key to sort by, a check to apply, one step of a pipeline. Okkama lets an action be written where it is used, as a value, without a name. Such an anonymous action remembers the values it saw when it was created, so it can be returned, stored and called long after the code that made it has finished. That memory is what makes it a closure.

module bible/closures v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Apply {
    has input is int;
    Apply(:input);
    value(operation is (int) is int) is int { operation(input); }
}

object Pipeline {
    has steps is @(int) is int;
    Pipeline(:steps);
    run(value is int) is int { steps.reduce(value) -> current, step { step(current); }; }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let make_adder = (amount is int) is (int) is int {
        (value is int) is int { value + amount; };
    };
    let add_ten = make_adder(10);
    let double = (value is int) is int { value * 2; };
    out.writeln(add_ten(5).string() + " " + Apply(input: 21).value(double).string());
    out.writeln(Apply(input: 4).value(operation: (value is int) is int { value * value; }).string());
    let pipeline = Pipeline(steps: [add_ten, double, make_adder(-1)]);
    out.writeln(pipeline.run(1).string());
    0;
}

Output:

15 42
16
21
  • make_adder is an anonymous action that returns another one. The inner action uses amount, a parameter of the outer one, and keeps it: add_ten(5) is 15 after make_adder has returned.
  • Apply.value takes an action as a parameter, typed (int) is int, and calls it like any action.
  • An anonymous action can be passed by name, operation: (value is int) is int { … }, like any other argument.
  • Pipeline stores a list of actions of one type and applies them in order.

This chapter covers the syntax and types of anonymous actions, captures, equality, action values as data, resources, failure reports, history and comparisons with other languages.

18.1 Writing an anonymous action

An anonymous action uses the declaration syntax of a named action with the name left out:

() is int { 42; }
(value is int) is int { value * 2; }
(left is int, right is int) is int { left + right; }
(message is string) is void { log.write(message); }

Every parameter has a type, and the result is always declared, void included. Nothing is inferred from the body: the declaration is the whole contract. A list of parameter names followed by is, or an empty () followed by is, starts an anonymous action; ordinary parentheses still group expressions, so (value) and (a + b) mean what they always did.

The type of an anonymous action is its signature without the names:

() is int
(int) is int
(int, int) is string
((int) is int) is (int) is int     // takes an action, returns an action

Such types appear wherever types do: in fields, parameters, results, collections (@(int) is int) and type arguments.

An action value is called with parentheses and positional arguments, exactly as many as its type has parameters. A named call is rejected, because the names belong to the anonymous declaration and not to the type:

module bible/positional v1.0.0;

main() is int {
    let add = (left is int, right is int) is int { left + right; };
    add(left: 1, right: 2);
}

The compiler answers:

18-positional-rejected.ok:5:5: semantic error: Action values take positional arguments only

Not the blocks of map and for

The arrows in map and for belong to other constructs. Their blocks cannot be stored or returned. An anonymous action is a value with its own call boundary: next and last cannot leave a surrounding loop from inside it, even when it is created there:

module bible/escape v1.0.0;

main() is int {
    for 0..10 -> i {
        let check = () is void { last if i == 3; };
        check();
    }
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

18-escape-rejected.ok:5:34: semantic error: `last` used outside of a loop

A call of an action value is a boundary for control flow, as any action call is. A throw inside it travels out to the caller, and a defer inside it runs when that call ends.

18.2 What a closure remembers

When an anonymous action is evaluated, it captures the bindings it uses from the scope around it: locals, parameters, and self if it reads the receiver. It does not capture the scope itself.

module bible/capture v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Counter {
    has count is int;
    Counter(:count);
    count() is int { count; }
    bumped() is ^Counter { ^count = count + 1; }
    // A closure that reads a field keeps this receiver alive.
    reader() is () is int { () is int { count * 10; }; }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let counter = Counter(count: 1);
    let early = () is int { counter.count(); };
    counter = counter.bumped();
    let late = () is int { counter.count(); };
    out.writeln(early().string() + " " + late().string());
    let read = Counter(count: 4).reader();
    out.writeln(read().string());
    let ops is @(int) is int = [(x is int) is int { x + 1; }, (x is int) is int { x * 2; }];
    out.writeln(ops.reduce(5) -> value, op { op(value); }.string());
    0;
}

Output:

1 2
40
12

Figure 18.1. A capture is a snapshot: rebinding the name later changes nothing inside the closure.

The example shows the three rules.

  • A capture is a snapshot. early is created while counter holds a count of 1. counter = counter.bumped() then rebinds the local to a successor (Chapter 13), and late captures that one. Calling early later still sees the count it captured: rebinding a name outside the action does not reach into it.
  • Objects keep their identity. The snapshot holds the object, not a copy of it. Okkama objects are immutable, so a captured object always answers the same way, and nothing is lost by sharing it.
  • Reading a field captures the receiver. reader() returns an action that reads count. The action keeps its Counter alive after reader() returns, as a closure over self.

Only the names the body actually uses are captured. A large local next to a closure that never mentions it is not kept alive by the closure.

Values, not variables

In many languages a closure captures variables. A JavaScript closure in a loop over var i famously sees the last value of i, and Go before version 1.22 shared one loop variable among all the closures made in a loop [Go specification]. Kotlin and C# let a lambda assign to a captured local and the change is visible outside. Java forbids that: a captured local must be effectively final, never assigned after its declaration [Gosling 2023].

Okkama goes further than Java. Its locals are immutable to begin with, and a rebind (Chapter 13) is the only way a name gets a new value, so there is nothing for a closure to share but values. A closure is equivalent to a small immutable object that holds the captured values in fields and has one action. The equivalence is old: Landin introduced closures as a pair of a function and the environment it was created in [Landin 1964], and Scheme made them the basis of a whole language [Sussman 1975].

Rebinding a captured name inside the action is an error: Cannot rebind captured variable "counter" inside an anonymous action. Until 0.4.2 the compiler accepted it, and the rebind changed a copy that lived for one call (#321). The action's own parameters and locals, including one that shadows a captured name, stay rebindable; state that must outlive a call goes back to the caller as a successor.

Closures made in a loop

The difference shows in the classic test: one closure created in each pass of a loop.

module bible/closure_loop v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    // Each anonymous action is created in its own pass of the block and
    // keeps the value `n` had in that pass.
    let makers = [1, 2, 3].map() -> n { () is int { n * 10; }; };
    out.writeln(makers.map() -> make { make().string(); }.join(" "));
    0;
}

Output:

10 20 30

Each pass of the map block binds a fresh n, and each anonymous action captures the value of its own pass, so the three actions answer 10, 20 and 30. In JavaScript with var, the same three functions would all answer 30, because they share one variable that ends at the last value. Go behaved the same way for its loop variables until version 1.22 changed the rule after years of bugs [Go specification]. In Okkama there is no variable to share, so the question does not arise.

Captured successors

The result of a successor action (Chapter 13) must be used: a binding to it that can leave its scope unused is an error. The rule follows the successor into closures. A closure carries the obligation of each captured successor that its body uses on every normal path. Creating the closure, or binding it to a name, does not use the successor; calling the closure does, and returning it, passing it or storing it hands the obligation on with it:

module bible/closure_successor v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Counter {
    has count is int;
    Counter(:count);
    count() is int { count; }
    bumped() is ^Counter { ^count = count + 1; }
}

main() is int {
    let later = Counter(count: 1).bumped();
    let show = () is int { later.count(); };
    let alias = show;
    // Calling the closure uses the successor it captured.
    Stdout().writeln(alias().string());
    0;
}

Output:

2

alias and show are one closure, so one call through either name uses later. A closure that is never called, returned, passed or stored keeps the obligation, and the error names the successor and the action value that carries it:

module bible/closure_successor_rejected v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Counter {
    has count is int;
    Counter(:count);
    count() is int { count; }
    bumped() is ^Counter { ^count = count + 1; }
}

main() is int {
    let later = Counter(count: 1).bumped();
    let show = () is int { later.count(); };
    Stdout().writeln("made, never called");
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

18-successor-rejected.ok:14:9: semantic error: Successor action result must be used; "later" is carried by action value "show", which can leave scope without being called, returned, passed or stored

Two refinements keep the rule honest. A body that uses the successor on one branch only does not carry it, since a call might not use it; the successor must then be used elsewhere. And handing a closure on is a transfer, not a call: like a successor passed as an argument, it moves the responsibility without proving that the receiver ever calls it. Until 0.4.2 the compiler did not look inside closures at all, so even a called closure left its successor unused (#322). A bound action, later.count without the call, follows the same rule since 0.4.2: it carries its receiver's obligation until it is called or handed on, while a direct call later.count() uses the receiver at once (#324).

When the closure needs only what the successor knows, capturing that is still the simpler program: let count = later.count(); and then () is int { count; } holds a number, not an object with an obligation.

18.3 Types are exact

An action value has exactly the type it was declared with. A () is Square is not a () is Shape, even though every Square is a Shape:

module bible/exact v1.0.0;

role Shape { area() is int; }

object Square does Shape {
    has side is int;
    Square(:side);
    area() is int { side * side; }
}

main() is int {
    let make = () is Square { Square(side: 2); };
    let shapes is () is Shape = make;
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

18-exact-rejected.ok:13:33: semantic error: Cannot initialize variable "shapes" of type () is Shape with () is Square

This is the same rule as for generic types in Chapter 17: no variance, in either the parameters or the result. A caller that wants a () is Shape has to write one, () is Shape { Square(side: 2); }, and the wrap to the role happens inside.

Action types take part in everything else types do. Generic inference reads them (SortedBy learns K from the key's declared result, Section 17.3), overload resolution compares them exactly, and roles may declare actions that take or return them.

Two boundaries stay closed. An action value cannot become any, and it cannot cross the native ABI:

module bible/anyfn v1.0.0;

main() is int {
    let double = (x is int) is int { x * 2; };
    let boxed is any = double;
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

18-any-rejected.ok:5:24: semantic error: Cannot initialize variable "boxed" of type any with (int) is int

any is a box that may only be passed and stored (Chapter 4); a function in such a box could be neither called nor compared, and a native provider has no way to call back into Okkama code. The second rule may relax when natives get callbacks.

There is also no automatic conversion from an action to a role. A role with one action, such as a Comparing<T>, is not satisfied by a matching anonymous action; it needs an object that does it. Java's lambdas, which become instances of any functional interface with one abstract method, are the opposite choice.

Equality is identity

Two action values are equal only when they are the same value:

module bible/closure_identity v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Maker {
    Maker();
    adder(amount is int) is (int) is int { (value is int) is int { value + amount; }; }
}

main() is int {
    let maker = Maker();
    let one = maker.adder(1);
    let alias = one;
    let another_one = maker.adder(1);
    let literal = (value is int) is int { value + 1; };
    let twin = (value is int) is int { value + 1; };
    Stdout().writeln((one == alias).string() + " " + (one == another_one).string() + " " +
        (literal == twin).string() + " " + (Maker() == Maker()).string());
    0;
}

Output:

true false false true

one and alias are one closure under two names, so they are equal. another_one was made by the same action from the same argument, and twin has the same text as literal, but each is a closure of its own, and neither equals its look-alike. Objects are the opposite case: two Maker() are equal, because objects compare by type and fields (Chapter 12). An object that holds an action in a field compares that field by identity too: two objects holding the same closure are equal, two holding different but identical-looking closures are not.

Futures follow the same identity rule. Whether two functions return the same result for every argument is undecidable in general [Rice 1953]. Action values are not map keys: keys are scalars and value objects (Chapter 8).

18.4 Action values as data

Action types are ordinary types, so action values go where values go: into arrays, maps, fields, generic objects and Maybe, and in and out of other actions.

module bible/closure_table v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Rule {
    has accepts is (int) is bool;
    has name is string;
    Rule(:accepts, :name);
    check(value is int) is string { name + " " + accepts(value).string(); }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let operations is %string:(int, int) is int = [
        "+": (left is int, right is int) is int { left + right; },
        "*": (left is int, right is int) is int { left * right; }
    ];
    let times = operations["*"];
    out.writeln(times(6, 7).string() + " " + operations.keys().join(","));
    let minus = operations["-"] else (left is int, right is int) is int { left - right; };
    out.writeln(minus(10, 3).string());
    let limit = 10;
