    let small = Rule(accepts: (value is int) is bool { value < limit; }, name: "small");
    out.writeln(small.check(3) + ", " + small.check(30));
    0;
}

Output:

42 *,+
7
small true, small false
  • operations maps strings to actions of type (int, int) is int. The type is written %string:(int, int) is int, with the action type in place of the value type. Picking an action is an ordinary lookup, and a missing key takes the else branch like any map read (Chapter 8), here with a fallback action written in place. A table of actions is how dispatch by name is written without a chain of ifs.
  • Rule keeps a predicate in a field and calls the field like an action, accepts(value). The predicate was created in main and captured limit, so the rule carries that limit with it.

Generic objects take action types the same way. A let box is Box<(int) is int> = Box(item: …) holds one action, and a Maybe<(int) is int> holds one or none; chosen else (value is int) is int { value; } falls back to the identity action. Inference reads the declared signatures, as in Chapter 17.

An action can also take actions and return one:

module bible/closure_compose v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Compose {
    Compose();
    // An action that takes two actions and returns a third.
    then(first is (int) is int, second is (int) is int) is (int) is int {
        (value is int) is int { second(first(value)); };
    }
}

main() is int {
    let increment = (value is int) is int { value + 1; };
    let square = (value is int) is int { value * value; };
    let compose = Compose();
    let up_then_square = compose.then(increment, square);
    let square_then_up = compose.then(square, increment);
    Stdout().writeln(up_then_square(4).string() + " " + square_then_up(4).string());
    0;
}

Output:

25 17

then returns a closure over its two arguments. up_then_square(4) is (4 + 1)², 25, and square_then_up(4) is 4² + 1, 17. Haskell writes composition as one operator, .; in Okkama it is an action of an object with a full signature, ((int) is int, (int) is int) is (int) is int. That is longer, and it leaves nothing to infer.

18.5 Bound actions: an object's action as a value

An action of an object can be taken as a value without calling it. retail.of is a bound action: the action of together with the receiver retail, so calling it later uses that object's rate.

module bible/bound v1.0.0;

// An object's action taken as a value: `retail.of` without a call is a bound
// action. It goes wherever an action type is written, and it carries its
// receiver with it.

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Price {
    has rate is int;
    Price(:rate);
    of(units is int) is int { units * rate; }
}

object Report {
    has rule is (int) is int;
    Report(:rule);
    line(units is int) is string { units.string() + " -> " + rule(units).string(); }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let retail = Price(rate: 12);
    let wholesale = Price(rate: 9);
    let pick is (int) is int = retail.of;
    out.writeln(pick(3).string());
    let rules is %string:(int) is int = ["retail": retail.of, "wholesale": wholesale.of];
    out.writeln(Report(rule: rules["wholesale"] else retail.of).line(10));
    let all = [3, 5, 8].map() -> n { pick(n); };
    out.writeln(all.map() -> n { n.string(); }.join(" "));
    out.writeln((pick == retail.of).string());
    0;
}

Output:

36
10 -> 90
36 60 96
false
  • It goes where an action type is written. pick is declared (int) is int, the map's value type is (int) is int, and so is Report's field. A bound action fits any of them, because its signature is the action's signature without the receiver.
  • The type must be written before it can be called. Without the declared type on pick, the compiler refuses:
module bible/bound_rejected v1.0.0;

// A bound action needs a written action type before it can be called.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Price {
    has rate is int;
    Price(:rate);
    of(units is int) is int { units * rate; }
}

main() is int {
    let pick = Price(rate: 12).of;
    Stdout().writeln(pick(3).string());
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

18-bound-rejected.ok:14:22: semantic error: Bound action requires an exact action-type boundary before it can be called

The rule keeps the action's full signature visible at the point where the value is made. The same holds for every action value in Okkama (Section 18.3).

  • It carries its receiver. rules["wholesale"] computes with wholesale's rate, 9, though Report never sees a Price. The receiver is borrowed like any capture (Section 18.2), and an action whose receiver must be consumed carries that obligation too (Section 18.2, #322).
  • Equality is identity. pick == retail.of is false. Each .of makes a new value, and two action values are equal only when they are the same value (Section 18.3).
  • An async action binds the same way. endpoint.fetch of an async action is a value of type async (int) is string. Section 20.11 passes one to a retry policy.

Other languages bind methods too, and differ on the points above.

  • JavaScript detaches: const f = obj.method loses this, and calling f() reads undefined fields unless the code writes obj.method.bind(obj).
  • Python binds automatically: obj.method is a bound method object. Unlike Okkama, two bound methods of the same object and function compare equal with ==, though they are different objects.
  • Java and Kotlin write a method reference, retail::of, and need a target type, a functional interface or a function type, much like Okkama's written action type.
  • C# converts a method group to a delegate only where a delegate type is expected (Func<int, int> f = retail.Of;).

Okkama's rule is the Java and C# one: a bound action exists only where its type is written. Its receiver travels with it, as in Python.

18.6 Closures in the standard library

The library asks for behaviour in a few places, and it takes it as an action value. The most common is a sort key.

module bible/std_closures v1.0.0;

// Closures where the library asks for behaviour: a sort key written in place,
// a key that captures a local limit, and an object's action passed as the key.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "cell" take Cell;
import "collections/ordering" take SortedBy;
import "collections/iteration" take Iterating;

object Job {
    has name is string;
    has team is string;
    has hours is int;
    Job(:name, :team, :hours);
    name() is string { name; }
    team() is string { team; }
    hours() is int { hours; }
}

// A ranking of teams; unknown teams go last.
object Priorities {
    has rank is %string:int;
    Priorities(:rank);
    of(job is Job) is int { rank[job.team()] else 99; }
}

object Listing {
    Listing() {}
    // The names in walking order, gathered in a Cell (synchronous code).
    names(jobs is Iterating<Job>) is string {
        let shown = Cell("");
        for jobs -> job {
            shown.replace(shown.value() + " " + job.name());
        }
        shown.value();
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let list = Listing();
    let jobs = [
        Job(name: "deploy", team: "ops", hours: 2),
        Job(name: "refund", team: "billing", hours: 1),
        Job(name: "reindex", team: "search", hours: 5),
        Job(name: "backup", team: "ops", hours: 3)
    ];
    out.writeln("by hours:" + list.names(SortedBy(origin: jobs, key: (job is Job) is int { job.hours(); })));
    let limit = 2;
    let quick = SortedBy(origin: jobs, key: (job is Job) is int { if job.hours() <= limit { 0; } else { 1; } });
    out.writeln("quick first:" + list.names(quick));
    let priorities = Priorities(rank: ["billing": 1, "ops": 2]);
    out.writeln("by team:" + list.names(SortedBy(origin: jobs, key: priorities.of)));
    0;
}

Output:

by hours: refund deploy backup reindex
quick first: deploy refund reindex backup
by team: refund deploy backup reindex
  • A key written in place. SortedBy(origin: jobs, key: (job is Job) is int { job.hours(); }) sorts by hours. The key's type is written in the parameter, (T) is K, so the anonymous action needs no annotation beyond its own signature.
  • A key that captures. The quick key compares each job's hours with limit, a local of main, and puts the quick jobs first. The capture is a snapshot (Section 18.2): changing limit later would not change this sort. The sort is stable, so jobs with equal keys keep their input order: deploy before refund, reindex before backup.
  • A bound action as the key. priorities.of passes an object's action, and the parameter's written type is the boundary the bound action needs (Section 18.5). The ranking lives in an object with a name and a test, and the sort call stays one line.
  • A Cell gathers the names. Listing.names walks any Iterating<Job> and appends to a Cell, the mutable value of synchronous code. for and the six functional operations (map, filter, reduce, any, all, find) execute blocks in the current frame; those blocks may use a Cell.

An action that captures a Cell, a collection containing one, or another such local action is frame-bound. A bound action on a Cell, such as count.value, has the same restriction. It may be called synchronously, bound to a local name, or captured by another frame-bound action. Repeated local calls are allowed:

module bible/cell_local v1.0.0;
import "cell" take Cell;
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

main() is int {
    let count = Cell(0);
    let step = () is int {
        count.replace(count.value() + 1);
        count.value();
    };
    let nested = () is int { step(); };
    let read is () is int = count.value;
    Stdout().writeln(step().string());
    Stdout().writeln(nested().string());
    Stdout().writeln(read().string());
    0;
}

Output:

1
2
2

Every other use is rejected: returning it, passing it to any action (even a synchronous callback), storing it in a field, enum payload or collection, boxing it into any or a role, awaiting it, or spawning it. A synchronous forwarder could return or retain its callback, so it cannot receive one:

module bible/cell_escape v1.0.0;
import "cell" take Cell;

object Forwarder {
    Forwarder();
    forwarded(f is () is int) is () is int { f; }
}

main() is int {
    let count = Cell(0);
    let read = () is int { count.value(); };
    let escaped = Forwarder().forwarded(read);
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

18-cell-escape-rejected.ok:12:41: semantic error: An action that retains a Cell cannot be passed to an action: a cell stays in its synchronous frame; share state between tasks with Atomic

The Cell itself cannot be hidden in any, a role or a generic parameter. This includes inferred parameters, even those inferred from an action's signature. Cell<T> itself and builtin collections keep Cell types visible; ordinary synchronous Cell use remains valid. Object fields, enum payloads and cached once let values cannot hold a Cell. For state retained by an object or shared between tasks, use Atomic. Closures with ordinary immutable captures and Atomic captures keep their usual behavior.

The same shape recurs across the library: keys in SortedBy, mappings and conditions in the lazy views of collections/views, and the condition a test check such as Eventually polls. Where the behaviour needs state, a name or its own tests, the library takes a role instead, and Section 18.7 gives the rule for choosing.

18.7 Closures or objects

An anonymous action and a small object can do the same job. The pipeline of the first example could hold Step objects with an apply action instead of (int) is int values. Which one to write?

A named object costs a declaration and gives back a name, a place for documentation, the ability to implement roles, structural equality, and a destroy if it owns a resource. A closure costs nothing to declare and is right where it is used. The guidance that falls out of the language:

  • A closure for a parameter of behaviour. A sort key, a predicate, a transformation passed to one call. Its type says everything there is to say.
  • An object when the behaviour has a name in the domain. A discount policy, a retry strategy, a parser. It will be passed around, compared, tested with a fake (Chapter 15), or given a second action.
  • An object when there is state over time. A closure is a snapshot; an object can have successors.

Elegant Objects argues for objects everywhere [Bugayenko 2016], and Okkama mostly agrees: there are no free functions, so a closure is always created by some object's action and usually handed to another object. The anonymous action is the escape hatch for behaviour too small to name.

Closures also carry authority. An action that can write to a log, created where the log is in scope and handed to code that cannot see the log, gives exactly that ability and no other. This is the object-capability pattern of Miller's thesis, where a reference is the only way to an effect [Miller 2006]; in Okkama a closure is one more kind of reference.

Behaviour that waits needs an object

An anonymous action is always synchronous. It cannot be declared async (since 0.4.2 the parser says so at the async, #323), and an await inside it is rejected even when the closure is created inside an async action:

module bible/closure_await_rejected v1.0.0;

object Source {
    Source();
    async value() is int { 1; }
}

async main() is int {
    let source = Source();
    let read = () is int { await source.value(); };
    read();
}

The compiler answers:

18-await-rejected.ok:10:28: semantic error: await is available only inside an async action

The closure is an action of its own, and a synchronous one, so the await has no async action around it. Behaviour that has to wait is therefore passed as an object that does a role with an async action, and closures stay on the synchronous side:

module bible/closure_async v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

role Fetching {
    async fetch(id is int) is string;
}

object Table does Fetching {
    Table();
    async fetch(id is int) is string { "item " + id.string(); }
}

object Loader {
    has source is Fetching;
    has label is (string) is string;
    Loader(:source, :label);
    // The synchronous closure runs after the await, with what it captured.
    async load(id is int) is string { label(await source.fetch(id)); }
}

async main() is int {
    let prefix = "#";
    let loader = Loader(source: Table(), label: (text is string) is string { prefix + text; });
    Stdout().writeln(await loader.load(7));
    0;
}

Output:

#item 7

Loader takes both kinds. Its source is a Fetching, a role with an async fetch; its label is a plain (string) is string. In load the closure runs after the await, with the prefix it captured in main, and nothing it holds can have changed during the wait, because what it holds are values. This is where the snapshot rule pays off: a closure that is called across an await needs no thought about what other tasks did in the meantime.

The restriction keeps every suspension point in one kind of place: an await inside a named async action, whose declaration says that it waits (Chapter 20). A type such as (int) is int promises that calling the value does not suspend. Kotlin draws the same line in its types with suspend function types, and JavaScript with async functions, but both also allow anonymous functions that suspend; Okkama does not.

18.8 Resources and failure reports

Closures and resources

A closure capturing a resource carries its ownership (Chapter 11). Returning the closure moves the resource out of the creating scope; it is released when the scope that owns the closure ends. Capturing plain values does not create resources to release.

In a failure report

A failure raised inside an anonymous action is reported like any other (Chapter 10). Here main hands a checking closure to Runner.run, which calls it:

module bible/closure_report v1.0.0;

enum Bad is Error = (too_big(value is int));

object Runner {
    Runner();
    run(step is (int) is int) is int { step(3); }
}

main() is int {
    let check = (value is int) is int {
        if (value > 2) { throw Bad.too_big(value); }
        value;
    };
    Runner().run(check);
}
Bad: Bad.too_big(3)
  --> report.ok:12:26
   |
12 |         if (value > 2) { throw Bad.too_big(value); }
   |                          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
Stack trace (most recent call first):
  at lambda#0 (report.ok:12:26)
  at Runner.run (report.ok:7:40)
  at main (report.ok:15:5)

The report identifies the anonymous action as lambda#0 and points into its body. It shows where the failure occurred, not where the closure was created; the creating call may have returned long before.

18.9 Where closures came from

Closures are older than objects. Church's lambda calculus of 1936 already treated functions as values [Church 1936], and McCarthy built LISP on it in 1960 [McCarthy 1960]. LISP then met the question every language with function values has to answer: when a function uses a name it did not declare, which binding does it see, the one where it was created or the one where it is called? Early LISPs looked the name up where the function was called, and a function passed as an argument could see the wrong variable. This became known as the funarg problem. Moses argued in 1970 that it should be called the environment problem, because the cure is to give the function the environment it was created in [Moses 1970]. Landin had done exactly that in 1964: his SECD machine paired a function with that environment and called the pair a closure [Landin 1964]. Scheme made lexically scoped closures the basis of a whole language in 1975 [Sussman 1975].

Object-oriented languages took the idea in through blocks. Smalltalk-80 blocks are closures, and the library builds every control structure on them, conditionals and loops included [Goldberg 1983]. A ^ inside a block returns from the method that created the block, which is what lets a block act as the body of a loop. The mainstream came later: C# 2.0 added anonymous methods in 2005, and Java 8 added lambdas in 2014, typed by functional interfaces and limited to effectively final locals [Gosling 2023].

Okkama follows Landin and Scheme in what a closure is, a function together with what it saw, and departs from all of them in that what it saw is values only. It also keeps apart the two jobs Smalltalk gave to blocks. The blocks of for and map are control structures and are not values; anonymous actions are values and are not control structures, so a return inside one returns from that action, and next and last cannot reach an outer loop (Section 18.1). Since Okkama locals are never assigned, the later form of the funarg problem, which variable a closure shares with its creator, has no room to arise.

18.10 Okkama among other languages

Captures Assigning a captured name Typing
Java values of effectively final locals rejected functional interfaces, target-typed
Kotlin variables (boxed Ref when written) allowed, visible outside function types, with variance
C# variables (a shared display class) allowed, visible outside delegates, with variance
Go variables (per-iteration loop variables since 1.22) allowed, visible outside function types, exact
Rust by reference, by mutable reference, or by value (move) through FnMut, checked by the borrow checker Fn, FnMut, FnOnce traits
Haskell values (everything is immutable) not applicable inferred function types
OCaml values; ref cells are values too through a ref cell inferred function types
Okkama values of immutable locals, and self rejected (#321) declared, exact, no variance

Okkama sits with Haskell and OCaml on what is captured, a value and never a variable, and with Java on the declaration being explicit. It is stricter than all of them on types: an action value has exactly its declared signature, and nothing converts it to a role or to a wider function type.

18.11 Limits

  • No recursion by name. A let becomes visible only after its initializer, so an anonymous action cannot call itself through the let that holds it; the compiler reports an undefined action. The Book once promised otherwise, and 0.4.2 settled on the rule (#318). Recursion belongs to named actions, which get constant-stack self tail calls and the compiler's check for recursion that cannot end.
  • Equality by identity only, and an action value is never a map key.
  • Positional calls only, exactly the declared number of arguments; no variadic anonymous parameters, no defaults: (n is int = 1) is int { n; } is the syntax error "Anonymous action parameters cannot declare default values" (issue #958).
  • No currying or partial application. make_adder has to be written out.
  • No async anonymous actions. An action that awaits must be a named async action. It travels as a bound action of type async (…) is R (Section 18.5) or as an object that does a role.
  • No any, no native ABI, no conversion to a role.

18.12 What this design costs

Explicit signatures make short closures longer than in languages that infer them: (value is int) is int { value * 2; } where Kotlin writes { it * 2 }. Capturing values instead of variables rules out the closure that counts its own calls in a captured local; that state has to live in an object with successors, or in a Cell (Chapter 13). Exact function types without variance sometimes need a small wrapper action.

In return, a closure is predictable. What it captures is visible at the place it is written, nothing it holds can change behind its back, and its type is the line that declares it. A closure is a small immutable object that the language writes for you, and that keeps closures inside Okkama's object model instead of opening a second, functional one beside it.

Chapter 19Modules, imports, packages and blade

A program of any size is several files, and every language has to answer the same questions about them. What is the unit? How does one unit name another? What crosses the boundary between them, and what stays inside? Where is an imported file found, and how is a library from somebody else put next to the program? Okkama's answers are short. A file is a module. An import names another file by its path and lists what it takes. Only what a module declares itself crosses its boundary, and only if it is not hidden. Nothing runs because something was imported.

Here is a program made of three files. The first is a module that keeps an amount of money in cents:

module shop/money v1.0.0;

// An amount in cents. The rounding policy is the module's own business.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

const CURRENCY = "EUR";
const CENTS = 100;

hidden object Rounding {
    Rounding();
    half_up(cents is int, percent is int) is int { ((cents * percent + 50) / 100).int(); }
}

object Money {
    has cents is int;
    Money(:cents);
    plus(other is Money) is Money { Money(cents: cents + other.cents()); }
    percent(rate is int) is Money { Money(cents: Rounding().half_up(cents, rate)); }
    cents() is int { cents; }
    string() is string { (cents / CENTS).int().string() + "." + (cents % CENTS + CENTS).string().slice(1, 3) + " " + CURRENCY; }
}

// Never runs when the module is imported.
main() is int {
    Stdout().writeln("money: main");
    0;
}

The second keeps a basket of prices. It sits in the same directory and imports the first by its file name:

module shop/basket v1.0.0;

// Found beside this file: shop/money.ok, the same module the program imports.
import "money" take Money;

object Basket {
    has prices is @Money;
    Basket(:prices);
    added(price is Money) is Basket { Basket(prices: prices + [price]); }
    total() is Money { prices.reduce(Money(cents: 0)) -> sum, price { sum.plus(price); }; }
}

The program imports both:

module bible/shop v1.0.0;

// Three forms of import: names taken as bare bindings, a namespace, an alias.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "shop/money" take Money, CURRENCY;
import "shop/basket";
import "shop/money" as cash;

main() is int {
    let cart = basket.Basket(prices: [Money(cents: 1250)]).added(cash.Money(cents: 399));
    let total is Money = cart.total();
    Stdout().writeln(total.string());
    Stdout().writeln(total.percent(20).string() + " of VAT in " + CURRENCY);
    Stdout().writeln(cash.CENTS.string() + " cents to the " + cash.CURRENCY);
    0;
}

Output:

16.49 EUR
3.30 EUR of VAT in EUR
100 cents to the EUR
  • import "shop/money" take Money, CURRENCY; brings two names into the file as they are: Money(cents: 1250) and CURRENCY.
  • import "shop/basket"; brings no bare name. It makes a namespace named after the last component of the path, and basket.Basket(…) reaches the declaration through it.
  • import "shop/money" as cash; makes a namespace under a chosen name, and cash.Money and cash.CENTS are reached through it. The module was already imported by the first line; importing it again costs nothing and creates nothing twice.
  • The basket's Money and the program's Money are one type. basket.ok imports "money", which is found beside it, and that is the same file as the program's "shop/money". One file is one module however its path is spelled.
  • money.ok has a main() that prints money: main. The output does not contain it: an imported module's main() never runs.
  • Rounding is hidden. Money uses it, and nothing outside money.ok can name it.

This chapter covers what a module is, the three forms of import, where an import is found, what crosses a module's boundary and what does not, hidden declarations, module constants, packages and the blade tool, where these ideas came from, how they compare with other languages, and what the design costs.

19.1 A module is a file

Every Okkama source file begins with a module declaration:

module app v1.0.0;
module money/cash v1.0.0;
module money/cash;

The name is one or more lower-case identifiers separated by /. The version is optional; when present it is vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, and a module without one has major version 0. The declaration must be the first thing in the file, before the imports, and the imports must come before every other declaration. That order is fixed so that a reader learns what a file is and what it depends on from its first lines.

An import names a file, such as shop/money.ok; its declaration names the module and major version. These usually agree but need not. Type identity follows the declared module, major version and type name (19.4), not the path used to find the file.

What a version means

Only the major part of a version reaches the language. v1.4.2 and v1.5.0 of shop/money declare the same types: a program built against one can be rebuilt against the other, and every Money stays a Money. v2.0.0 declares new ones. shop/money#2::Money is not shop/money#1::Money, so code that passes a value of the old major where the new one is expected fails to compile, at the exact place where the two meet. That is the compiler's reading of Semantic Versioning [SemVer 2.0.0]: a major version is a promise broken on purpose, and the type system makes the breakage visible instead of letting it surface as a missing method at run time. The minor and patch parts are for people and for blade (19.7), which uses them to choose among releases.

A module's main() is the program's entry point when the module is the one being run, and it is nothing at all when the module is imported. There is no if __name__ == "__main__" test to write, because importing never runs anything: not main(), not a static initializer, not the top level of a file, because a file has no executable top level. The only things a module contains are declarations. That is the first and most important difference from scripting languages, where importing a module runs its code: an import in Okkama is a fact about names, and adding one cannot change what a program does.

Multi-file modules

A module can span several files. okkama run main.ok part.ok (or okkama build with several files) combines them into one declaration space, under three rules.

  • One name, one version. Every file declares the same module name and the same version, or every file no version; a mismatch is an error.
  • Imports stay with their file. Each file keeps its own imports: a name that part.ok takes is not visible in main.ok, even though their declarations are visible to each other. A file states its own dependencies and reads correctly on its own.
  • No order. The files are taken in name order, so the order they are given in changes nothing. A name declared in two of them is an error reported in both, and the combined module has at most one main().

There is no directory-as-module rule, as in Go: the files of a module are the files the command names, or the files blade.toml lists (19.7).

19.2 Three forms of import

An import line has one of three forms, or the last two combined.

Form What it brings into the file
import "shop/basket"; a namespace basket: basket.Basket(…), basket.Basket as a type
import "shop/money" as cash; a namespace cash instead of money
import "shop/money" take Money, CURRENCY; the bare names Money and CURRENCY, and no namespace
import "io/stdout" as out take Stdout; a namespace out that contains only Stdout

A namespace works in expressions and in types alike: basket.Basket(prices: …) constructs, and amount is shop.Money declares a parameter. Generic types are applied through it too: boxes.Box<int>.

There is no fourth form. Okkama has no wildcard import: no import "shop/money" take *, no Python from money import *, no Java import money.*, no Haskell or OCaml open. The reason is the reader. In an Okkama file every bare name is declared in that file or listed on an import line, so the origin of a name is always on the same page as its use. A wildcard moves that knowledge into another file, and changes its meaning whenever that other file gains a declaration. Two wildcard imports can make a name ambiguous that was not ambiguous yesterday, without a line of the importing file changing.

The cost of the rule is long take lists in files that use many declarations of one module. The usual answer is the namespace form: one import line, and cash.Money at each use.

One name, one source

A bare name is declared once in a file's scope. Taking the same name from two modules is an error that names both:

import "shop/money" take Money;
import "bank/money" take Money;
semantic error: Object "Money" is already declared by module "shop/money";
this import takes another from module "bank/money"

The same holds for a take against a declaration of the file itself, and for a namespace name bound twice. Namespaces are how two same-named declarations live in one file: import "shop/money" as shop; and import "bank/money" as bank; give shop.Money and bank.Money.

Importing the same module twice is not a collision. The second import shares the first one's module: nothing is loaded or registered twice, and a module reached through two different paths of the import graph, a diamond, is still one module.

Standard library paths

A declaration of the standard library can also be named in place, without an import, by a path starting with the reserved word std:

module bible/std_path v1.0.0;

// A standard-library declaration named in place: no import line.
main() is int {
    let out = std.io.stdout.Stdout();
    let order = std.compare.Order.less;
    out.writeln("order: " + std.runtime.debug.data_dump(order));
    0;
}

Output:

order: Order.less

The segments up to the first capitalized one are the module path (std.io.stdout.Stdout is Stdout from io/stdout); a path of lower-case segments only names a native action and must be called (std.runtime.debug.data_dump(order)). Such a path behaves exactly like a namespace import of that module made by the same file, and resolves only in the bundled standard library. It is meant for the one-off use. A file that writes std.io.stdout.Stdout() in five places is better off with an import line, so its dependencies are listed where a reader looks for them. Because the word is reserved, let std = 1; is an error:

semantic error: "std" is reserved for standard library paths (std.io.stdout.Stdout)

Naming a module

Because a plain import names its namespace after the last component of the path, a module's file name is read at every use: stdout.Stdout(), basket.Basket(…), path.Path("/tmp"). Three conventions follow from that, and the standard library keeps them.

  • Paths group by area, files name the thing. io/stdout, fs/path, fs/file, strings/parse, http/client. The directories say where to look, and the file name is the noun a namespace reads as.
  • One noun per module. A module named after what it holds reads well as a namespace (path.Path, json.Json). A module named utils or helpers reads as nothing, and gathers whatever has no better home.
  • take for the main noun, the namespace for the rest. A file that builds paths all day writes import "fs/path" take Path; and Path(…). A file that touches a module once writes the namespace, or a std. path, and leaves its bare names to its own declarations.

The doubled names that result (stdout.Stdout, basket.Basket) are the price of a namespace derived from the path. as shortens them where it matters: import "io/stdout" as out; and out.Stdout().

The module name in the declaration should match the path it is imported by. Nothing checks it, and a mismatch is legal: the declaration decides the types' identity, the path decides where the file is found. But a reader who sees import "shop/money" expects module shop/money, and a module that declares another name surprises everyone who greps for it.

19.3 Where an import is found

An import path is a source path, not a module name: "money" is money.ok, "foo/bar" is foo/bar.ok, and an explicit .ok is accepted as written. The file is looked up in four places, in order:

  1. the directory of the importing file;
  2. the root of the importing file's package, the nearest directory above it that holds a blade.toml (19.7), when there is one;
  3. the directories in OKKAMA_IMPORT_DIRS;
  4. the bundled standard library.

The directory the program is started from plays no part. A module tree behaves the same wherever it is run from, and two modules that import the same relative path from different directories load different files. This is why basket.ok can write import "money": it finds its sibling, whoever imports the basket and from wherever.

The lookup is local-first. A local json.ok shadows the standard library's json for the program's own imports, so a program can replace a library module without editing the files that import it. The standard library is protected in the other direction: its own imports resolve only inside the standard library, so a local file named io/stdout.ok cannot change what the library's modules see. A program that shadows a library module cannot also name it by a std. path. One program has one file for one module path.

The import graph is bounded: at most 1,024 nested imports from the root, 16,384 modules and 256 MiB of module sources. An import that crosses a bound is an error at that import. The bounds exist because compiling an untrusted tree must end, and no real program comes near them.

No cycles

Two modules that import each other are rejected:

module cycle/orders v1.0.0;

import "customers" take Customer;

object Order {
    has buyer is Customer;
    Order(:buyer);
}
module cycle/customers v1.0.0;

import "orders" take Order;

object Customer {
    has orders is @Order;
    Customer(:orders);
}
module bible/cycle v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "cycle/orders" take Order;

main() is int {
    Stdout().writeln("unreachable");
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

cycle/customers.ok:3:1: semantic error: Import cycle detected: cycle/orders -> customers -> orders

The diagnostic names the chain. Some languages allow cycles and pay for it in other ways. Python gives the second module a half-initialized first one, which fails at a distance with an attribute error. JavaScript modules hand out live bindings that are in a temporal dead zone until the cycle unwinds. Java allows cycles between classes and packages, though not between its newer modules. Go and OCaml forbid them, as Okkama does.

In a language whose modules contain only declarations, a cycle has no initialization problem to cause, so the rule is not forced by the implementation. It is a design rule. Two modules that need each other are one module split in two, or two modules missing a third. A cycle-free import graph is also a graph that can be read bottom-up, which is how a newcomer reads a code base.

Breaking a cycle with a contract module

Here the third module is the missing piece. An Order needs to know who buys, and a Customer needs to know what was bought, but neither needs the other's object: each needs a role. Those roles go into a module of their own, which imports nothing:

module trade/parties v1.0.0;

// The contracts both sides need: no objects, no imports.
role Buyer {
    name() is string;
}

role Purchase {
    total() is int;
}
module trade/orders v1.0.0;

import "parties" take Buyer, Purchase;

object Order does Purchase {
    has buyer is Buyer;
    has cents is int;
    Order(:buyer, :cents);
    total() is int { cents; }
    line() is string { buyer.name() + " pays " + cents.string(); }
}
module trade/customers v1.0.0;

import "parties" take Buyer, Purchase;

object Customer does Buyer {
    has label is string;
    has purchases is @Purchase;
    Customer(:label, :purchases);
    name() is string { label; }
    spent() is int { purchases.reduce(0) -> sum, purchase { sum + purchase.total(); }; }
}
module bible/contracts v1.0.0;

// orders and customers both import parties, and neither imports the other.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "trade/orders" take Order;
import "trade/customers" take Customer;

main() is int {
    let ada = Customer(label: "Ada", purchases: []);
    let first = Order(buyer: ada, cents: 1250);
    let second = Order(buyer: ada, cents: 399);
    let regular = Customer(label: "Ada", purchases: [first, second]);
    Stdout().writeln(first.line());
    Stdout().writeln(regular.name() + " spent " + regular.spent().string());
    0;
}

Output:

Ada pays 1250
Ada spent 1649

orders and customers both import parties, and neither imports the other. The graph is a V instead of a loop: parties at the bottom, the two object modules above it, the program on top.

The roles say exactly what each side uses of the other: a buyer's name, a purchase's total. That is less than the objects offer, and it is all the modules may rely on. A third kind of buyer, a company rather than a person, can join without touching orders. The cycle was a symptom: two modules that knew each other's objects instead of each other's contracts.

The standard library is layered the same way at its bottom.

  • compare declares Order and Comparing, imports nothing, and 83 of the library's modules import it.
  • collections/iteration declares Cursor and Iterating, also imports nothing, and 41 modules import it.

Figure 19.1. The layers of the standard library: two contract modules at the bottom import nothing.

A contract module is cheap: a few roles, no state, no imports. It turns a tangle into layers.

19.4 What crosses the boundary

A module exports what it declares itself, and nothing else. Its imports are its own business:

module bible/reexport v1.0.0;

// shop/basket imports Money, but does not own it: nothing is re-exported.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "shop/basket" take Basket, Money;

main() is int {
    Stdout().writeln(Basket(prices: [Money(cents: 1)]).total().string());
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

19-reexport-rejected.ok:5:35: semantic error: Import "shop/basket" has no declaration "Money"

shop/basket imports Money, and its Basket depends on it. But Money is not declared in basket.ok, so take Money from "shop/basket" finds nothing. The same holds for namespaces: basket.Money is not a name. There is no re-export, no Rust pub use, no JavaScript export * from, no OCaml include. A program that needs Money imports the module that declares it.

Selected declarations still bring everything they need to run. Basket works in the program although the program never imported Money through it: constructors, actions, defaults, lifecycle blocks and role fakes resolve names in the module that declares them, not in the module that calls them. That dependency closure is private. It makes the code run, and it puts no name in the importer's scope.

Two names, two types

Because a type's identity includes its module, two declarations with the same name in two modules are two types, even when they are written the same way:

module bank/money v2.0.0;

// The same name and the same field as shop/money, in another module.
object Money {
    has cents is int;
    Money(:cents);
    cents() is int { cents; }
}
module bible/identity v1.0.0;

// Two declarations named Money, from two modules: two types.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "shop/money" as shop;
import "bank/money" as bank;

object Till {
    Till();
    count(amount is shop.Money) is int { amount.cents(); }
}

main() is int {
    Stdout().writeln(Till().count(bank.Money(cents: 500)).string());
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

19-identity-rejected.ok:14:22: semantic error: No action "count" on object "Till" accepts (bank.Money)
Available: count(amount is shop.Money)

bank.Money has a field cents and an action cents(), like shop.Money, and the call is still rejected: Okkama types are nominal (Chapter 4), and the name a type is nominal over is module#major::Name. The same is true of two major versions of one module: shop/money#1::Money and shop/money#2::Money would be different types, which is what a major version is for.

The diagnostic names the two types apart. A type whose name another declaration of the program also has is written the way the file of the diagnostic can name it: bank.Money through the namespace its reader wrote, Money when that is the Money in scope, otherwise Money from "bank/money", and the same inside composite types (@bank.Money, Box<shop.Money>). A call that fits no candidate then lists the candidates it had, up to four, so the line under the error shows which Money the action wanted. Every other name stays short: in a program whose type names are all different, nothing changes. Until 0.5.3 the module was left out of every message, and this one read "Money does not accept Money" (issue #338).

This is information hiding in Parnas's sense [Parnas 1972]: a module is the unit of a design decision, and what it exposes is a promise. A re-export makes a module promise what it does not own. When the owner changes, every module that re-exported the name changes its promise without changing a line. Okkama keeps each promise in the module that can keep it.

19.5 Hidden declarations

Everything a module declares is public unless it says otherwise. hidden before object, role, enum or const keeps a declaration inside its module:

module bible/hidden v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "shop/money" take Rounding;

main() is int {
    Stdout().writeln(Rounding().half_up(1000, 15).string());
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

19-hidden-rejected.ok:4:26: semantic error: Import "shop/money" cannot take hidden declaration "Rounding"

Rounding is visible in every file of shop/money, in its tests and its fakes, and in every body defined in the module. Outside, take Rounding is rejected, and a namespace does not reveal it either (Type "money.Rounding" is hidden in module "shop/money").

Hiding is enforced at the boundary, not only at the import line. The rules:

  • Values leave only as public types. A value of a hidden type crosses only under a public one: a role it does, Error, or any. A role never converts back (Chapter 14), so outside code holds only the view.
  • Public signatures cannot name hidden types. Parameters and results of public actions, constructor parameters, role signatures, enum payloads, generic arguments and bounds, and cap fields are all public. Any of them that names a hidden type is an error at the declaration. Hidden actions, fields and bodies may use hidden types freely.
  • A public object cannot do a hidden role. Its does list is part of its public contract. A hidden object may do public and hidden roles, which is how an implementation is hidden behind a contract: a public role, a hidden object that does it, and a public action that returns the role.
  • A hidden error enum stays out of reach. It can be thrown out of the module, but it can then be caught only as Error, and okkama lint reports such throws from public actions (hidden-error).

A contract and a hidden implementation

The rules support one pattern above all: a public role, a hidden object that does it, and a public entry that hands out the role.

module billing/payments v1.0.0;

// The contract is public; the implementation is not.
role Payment {
    id() is string;
    amount() is int;
    authorized() is Payment;
    state() is string;
}

hidden enum Stage = (created, authorized);

hidden object CardPayment does Payment {
    has key is string;
    has cents is int;
    has stage is Stage = Stage.created;
    CardPayment(:key, :cents);
    CardPayment(:key, :cents, :stage);
    id() is string { key; }
    amount() is int { cents; }
    authorized() is Payment { CardPayment(key: key, cents: cents, stage: Stage.authorized); }
    state() is string {
        match stage {
            case Stage.created { "created"; }
            case Stage.authorized { "authorized"; }
        };
    }
}

object Payments {
    Payments();
    open(id is string, cents is int) is Payment { CardPayment(key: id, cents: cents); }
}
module bible/payments v1.0.0;

// Callers hold a Payment; CardPayment and its stages stay in the module.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "billing/payments" take Payments, Payment;

object Receipt {
    Receipt();
    line(payment is Payment) is string { payment.id() + " " + payment.amount().string() + " " + payment.state(); }
}

main() is int {
    let opened = Payments().open("p-1", 1250);
    let done is Payment = opened.authorized();
    Stdout().writeln(Receipt().line(opened));
    Stdout().writeln(Receipt().line(done));
    0;
}

Output:

p-1 1250 created
p-1 1250 authorized

The program sees four things: Payments, Payment, and the four actions of the role. It does not see CardPayment, its constructor, its fields or the Stage enum. authorized() returns a new Payment, and the old one stays created, as every value does (Chapter 13).

Everything the module hides it can change without telling anyone:

  • split CardPayment into one object per stage;
  • add a Stage.refunded;
  • keep the amount as a rat;
  • store the state in a map.

None of these changes reaches a caller, because a caller cannot have named what changed. The compiler enforces the boundary from both sides. If open were declared to return CardPayment, the declaration itself would be an error, because a public action cannot name a hidden type. If the program wrote take CardPayment, the import would be. The module's public surface is exactly the role and the factory, and it cannot grow by accident.

This is the shape Chapter 14 recommends for roles in general, enforced at the scale of a module. A role names what callers may rely on; hidden makes sure they cannot rely on anything else.

hidden is a contextual keyword: has hidden is int is still a field named hidden. The same word before an action keeps that action inside its object (§12.7): in both places it means not part of the public contract.

Okkama's default is the opposite of Go's capitalization rule, Rust's private-by-default and Java's package-private. Those languages make the writer opt in to exposure. Okkama makes the writer opt out, on the grounds that most declarations of a module are its reason to exist, and a hidden marks the few that are not. Whether that is the right default is a question of style. A module of twenty declarations with three helpers reads better with three hiddens than with seventeen pubs. A module with one public entry and twenty internals reads worse.

19.6 Module constants

A module can name values the compiler computes (issue #153):

module bible/constants v1.0.0;

// Computed by the compiler, in any order, with the program's own arithmetic.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

const MB = 1024 * KB;
const KB = 1024;
const LIMITS = ["upload": 10 * MB, "header": 64 * KB];
const SIZES is @int = [KB, MB, 1024 * MB];
const HALF = 1 / 2;
const HUGE = 4294967296 * 4294967296 * 4294967296;
const NAME = "okkama-" + LANG;
const LANG = "en";
hidden const SALT = "x";

main() is int {
    Stdout().writeln(NAME + " " + LIMITS["upload"].string() + " " + SIZES.size().string());
    Stdout().writeln(HALF.string() + " " + HUGE.string());
    0;
}

Output:

okkama-en 10485760 3
1/2 79228162514264337593543950336

const NAME = value; is made of literals, payload-free enum cases, rat(n, d), scalar casts, operators, other constants, and arrays and maps of such values. The constants of a module may be declared in any order (MB uses KB, declared after it). The computation has the semantics of the running program, not of a separate constant language: 1 / 2 is the rat 1/2, and 2⁹⁶ is an exact integer that would overflow any machine word. A failing computation (1 % 0) and a cycle between constants are compile errors, and so is anything that would run code:

module bible/const_call v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

const WIDTH = "okkama".length();

main() is int {
    Stdout().writeln(WIDTH.string());
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

19-const-call-rejected.ok:5:15: semantic error: Constant "WIDTH" cannot be computed by the compiler: it calls an action or a constructor; a constant is made of literals, operators and other constants

A constant is public like an object: take LANG or settings.LANG reaches it, and hidden const keeps it in its module. Repeated uses of an array or map constant do not copy the whole collection.

Constants are not a way to share objects. There is no module-level let, no static field and no singleton: an expensive object such as a compiled regular expression or a database connection is built once where the program starts, in main(), and passed to the objects that need it. Its lifetime and its users stay visible in the code, and a test can pass another one. That is the same rule Chapter 12 states for objects: what an object needs, it gets through its constructor.

19.7 Packages and blade

blade is Okkama's package tool. Through 0.5.1 it was the youngest part of the toolchain, a working core with large gaps; 0.5.3 rebuilt it around three decisions this section explains: a package is an ordinary git repository, the version a project gets is the lowest one that satisfies everyone, and nothing blade does may lose work a programmer did by hand. Nothing in this section is run as an example, because installing a package runs git, and the book's examples run in a cage without processes.

A project

A directory that holds a blade.toml is a package root. A file belongs to the package of the nearest such directory above it, and a project is a package that is not installed inside another project. blade new demo creates one:

[module]
name = "demo"
version = "1.0.0"

[build]
entry = "src/main.ok"
output = "target/demo.spb"

[run]
args = []
env = {}

[dependencies]
module demo;
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

main() is int {

    Stdout().writeln("hello from okkama");
    0;
}

The module declares no version. In a package the version lives in one place, and a module file that declares one is an error at the version. The package's files import one another as in 19.3: beside the importing file, then from the package root. blade build compiles the project as [build] says; blade run builds when a source, blade.toml or blade.lock is newer than the output, then runs it as [run] says, and the program's exit status is blade's.

A package is a repository

A package is a git repository with its modules in src/:

json/
  src/json.ok           module json;
  src/json/parser.ok    module json/parser;
  blade.toml            only if json has dependencies of its own
  LICENSE, examples/, tests/ …

Its name is the key a project declares it under, and its version is its vX.Y.Z tag. Neither has to be written inside the package: a repository that has never heard of blade, but keeps Okkama modules in src/, is already a package. A blade.toml is needed only to declare dependencies of its own; a [module] in it is optional, and when present its name and version must agree with the key and the tag, which catches a release made from the wrong commit. A package without blade.toml is installed with a generated one, the same bytes every time, so that the compiler knows its files belong to the package and not to the project.

Blade checks only src/**/*.ok, and refuses a package, naming it and its tag, whose modules do not parse, declare a version, are named outside <name> and <name>/…, or declare native actions (natives come from the runtime, never from a package). Everything else in the repository, examples and tests included, is copied as it is and never executed, and symbolic links are refused anywhere. Installing a package therefore runs none of its code: the first line of the package's that executes is one the project calls.

blade add NAME GIT [MIN] declares a dependency and installs it:

blade add json https://example.org/okkama/json 1.4.0

writes

[dependencies]
json = { git = "https://example.org/okkama/json", version = "1.4.0" }

Without MIN the minimum is the repository's newest tag, so a new dependency starts current and the manifest says which version that was. A local directory is declared by hand, tools = { path = "../tools" }, and its version is the one in its blade.toml, since a directory has no tags.

Dependencies land in pkg/<name>/ of the project root, and the project imports them by that path, src/ included:

import "pkg/json/src/json/parser" take Parser;

An import path that starts with pkg/ resolves against the project root only. It must name a dependency declared in the [dependencies] of the importing file's own package. Transitive dependencies are not importable: if web depends on json, the project cannot import "pkg/json/…" until it declares json itself. This is 19.4's no-re-export rule at the scale of packages. What a program uses, it lists.

The lowest version that satisfies everyone

A requirement is a minimum. version = "1.4.0" means 1.4.0 or any later 1.x; below 1.0 the minor is the breaking part, so "0.3.1" means 0.3.1 or a later 0.3.x. The version a project gets is the lowest one that meets every minimum anyone in the project states for that package, and this is the whole rule. It is Go's minimal version selection [Cox 2018], and it has three consequences that the other common rule, "the highest version that satisfies all requirements", does not have.

Minimal version selection has three consequences. A release upstream changes nothing until a manifest raises a minimum. Every selected version is explicitly required by some manifest. Only dependencies reachable through the selected versions are installed; dependencies unique to a version not selected cannot cause an error.

The price is the one Go pays. An upgrade is a decision somebody makes: blade add json URL 1.5.0 raises the minimum, and blade update json resolves json again while every other package keeps its locked version unless the new one forces it up. And one version of each package per project is still the rule, so two majors of one package are an error that shows how each was reached:

no single major of "json":
  app → http 2.1.0 → json ≥ 1.2.0
  app → next 1.0.0 → json ≥ 2.0.0

One version per package matches the nominal identity of 19.4. Every module of the program sees the same json module, so a Json value made by one dependency is the Json type another dependency expects. The diamond across majors is the cost: two dependencies that need different majors of one package cannot both be installed, although the language could tell their types apart. npm makes the opposite choice and installs a copy per dependent, so a program can hold two incompatible Money types without knowing it; Cargo allows several semver-incompatible versions of one crate in a build and unifies compatible ones.

The lock and sync

blade.lock records each installed package: version, source, the git commit the tag pointed at, and a SHA-256 of its files. Under minimum version selection the lock is not what makes a build reproducible, the manifests already do that; it makes it verifiable and offline. blade sync installs exactly what the lock records, and is how a fresh clone gets its dependencies:

  • a package already in pkg/ with its locked checksum stays as it is, so a project that commits pkg/ syncs with no network and no git;
  • any other is fetched by its locked commit, not by its tag, so a tag deleted or moved upstream changes nothing; its files must have the locked checksum, and a commit that is gone is an error that names it;
  • what the lock does not have leaves pkg/.

A sync never picks a version. When the lock does not match the manifests, it changes nothing and says which command does:

blade.lock does not match blade.toml:
  json: blade.toml wants ≥ 1.5.0, blade.lock has 1.4.2 — run `blade update json`
  util: no longer required — run `blade update`

blade build and blade run never touch the network either: a dependency that is not installed points to blade sync. The only commands that fetch new versions are the ones that say so, add and update, and even they stop when a tag now points at a different commit than the lock remembers, until blade update NAME accepts the new state. A moved tag is how a supply chain is attacked, and blade will not follow one silently.

Work done by hand is never lost

Programmers patch dependencies: a print in a parser to see what it gets, a fix that has not been released yet. A package manager that reinstalls over such a change destroys work without asking, and the next run of the program behaves as if the fix had never been made. Blade records what it installed in pkg/.blade-installed and compares before it touches anything:

  • a package whose files differ from the record (a changed file, an added one, a removed one) stops any command that would replace or remove it, blade sync included, before anything changes:

    pkg/json has local changes (src/parser.ok differs from blade.lock);
move them away or delete pkg/json, then run the command again

  • an entry of pkg/ that blade did not install (pkg/notes) is never deleted: every install stops and names it.

There is no --force. Deleting pkg/json is how one accepts a reinstall, and that is a decision the programmer makes with the file in front of them. A pulled blade.lock with new versions is not a local change: the record tells an old version from an edited one, so blade sync installs the new versions. The files an operating system leaves in folders it shows, Finder's .DS_Store and Windows' Thumbs.db, are neither: they stay and change nothing.

Installation is all or nothing. The packages that change are assembled in pkg.blade-new/ and moved into pkg/ only when every one was fetched and checked; an interrupted blade is finished or undone by the next one, and packages that do not change keep their files untouched.

What blade does not do yet

  • No registry. Packages come from git URLs and paths, and there is no index, search or blade publish.
  • No workspaces. Several packages developed together each have their own pkg/.
  • Diamonds across majors fail, as above.
  • Shallow tooling around the lock. No blade tree or blade why.
  • No build profiles or features, and no conditional dependencies.

These are the ordinary gaps of a young ecosystem. The design decisions are the ones described above: a version in one place, packages as plain repositories whose code does not run at install, imports by explicit pkg/ paths, one version per package, the lowest version that satisfies everyone, and no command that overwrites what a programmer wrote.

19.8 A program and its dependencies

Imports are resolved before execution, following the lookup rules of 19.3. A missing file or name, a hidden declaration, a cycle or a crossed bound rejects the program before it starts. A valid program has found every module it will use.

19.9 Where modules came from

The word module in its modern sense comes from David Parnas's 1972 paper on decomposition [Parnas 1972]. Parnas compared two ways of splitting the same program. The first gave a module to each step of the processing. The second gave a module to each design decision likely to change, and hid that decision behind an interface. The second survived changes that broke the first. Everything since is a mechanism for that idea: a boundary, a list of what crosses it, and a promise that the rest may change.

Niklaus Wirth's Modula-2 [Wirth 1982] gave the mechanism the shape most languages still use. Its definition module stated what a module exports, and a separate implementation module kept the rest. Its import lists, FROM InOut IMPORT WriteString, WriteLn;, named exactly what a client took, much like Okkama's take. Standard ML went further [MacQueen 1984]: modules (structures) are checked against interfaces (signatures) and can be parameterized by other modules (functors). OCaml inherited that, and its open and include are the wildcard import and the re-export Okkama leaves out.

The languages most programmers use took simpler paths. Java organized classes into packages with a directory each, added import p.*, and in Java 9 added modules on top of packages [Gosling 2023]. Python and JavaScript made a module an object built by running a file, which is why importing runs code and cycles produce half-built modules. Go made a directory a package, exported names by capitalization, and forbade cycles. Rust made a module tree inside each crate, with private-by-default items and pub use re-exports.

Okkama's module system is closest to Modula-2's import lists and Go's discipline: a file of declarations, explicit lists of what is taken, no cycles, no effects on import. It differs from both in two places: names are public unless hidden, and identity includes the module and its major version.

19.10 Okkama among other languages

Unit Default visibility Wildcard import Re-export Import runs code Import cycles Versions per program
Okkama file (or listed files) public; hidden no no no rejected one per package
Go directory capitalized names import . (discouraged) no (aliases only) init() rejected one per major
Rust module in a crate private; pub use m::* pub use no allowed in a crate several per crate
Java class in a package; modules package-private import p.* no (modules: requires transitive) static initializers allowed one on the class path
Python file public; _ by convention from m import * any imported name the whole file allowed, half-built one per environment
JavaScript file private; export import * as (namespace only) export * from the whole file allowed, live bindings duplicates in node_modules
OCaml file plus signature per signature open M include M top-level effects rejected one per build

Two columns separate Okkama from most of the list: imports that run no code, and boundaries that pass nothing on. Both come from the same principle as the rest of the language. An import line is a statement about names that a reader can trust without opening the imported file.

19.11 Limits

  • No re-export. A library that wants to present one front module for many internal ones must wrap them: declare objects that delegate, or roles that its internals implement. There is no pub use.
  • No conditional or dynamic import. Which modules a program uses is fixed when it is compiled; a plug-in system is built from roles and values passed in, not from loading files at run time.
  • The version lives in two places. Outside a package, in the module line; inside one, never in a module: in blade.toml for a project or a local package, in the vX.Y.Z tag for a package from git. A module moved into a package must lose its version, and a module taken out of one must gain it.
  • Multi-file modules are listed, not discovered. A module's files are the ones the command line or blade.toml names; a forgotten file is a missing declaration, not a smaller module.
  • A shadowed library module cannot be named with std.. One module path, one file, per program.
  • blade's ecosystem is young. No registry, no workspaces, no two majors of one package in one project (19.7).

19.12 What this design costs

Every rule in this chapter removes an option that other languages offer, and each removal has a price.

No wildcard imports means long import lines. A file that uses fifteen declarations of one module either lists fifteen names or writes a prefix fifteen times. Okkama accepts the length: the alternative is a file whose names have no visible origin. No re-export means libraries cannot build a front module that renames their internals. They must wrap, which is more code and one more call. No cycles means that two modules that grew together must be pulled apart before they can be imported, sometimes at an inconvenient moment. Identity by module and major version means that two libraries which each declare Money cannot pass their values to each other. They must convert, explicitly, at the boundary between them.

What the rules buy is the same thing four times over: a reader who can trust an import line. It says exactly which names a file uses and where they come from. It runs nothing, so a file can be imported to read its declarations. It brings nothing the imported file does not own, so a change in a third file cannot add a name to it. And a type it brings is the type the imported file declares, not another type with the same name. Chapter 1 called that the razor applied to software: no entity that does not have to exist, and no name whose origin is not in front of the reader.

Chapter 20Async, futures and structured concurrency

A program waits. It waits for a file, a socket, a database, a timer, another part of itself. While one part waits, another could work, and every language of the last twenty years has had to say how. Okkama's answer has four parts. An async action returns a Future<T> instead of a T. await waits for a future inside another async action, and nowhere else. spawn starts work that runs beside the code that started it. And one cooperative scheduler runs one task at a time, so the code between two awaits of a task is never interleaved with anybody else's.

Here is the smallest async program worth reading:

module bible/lazy v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Oven {
    has name is string;

    Oven(name is string) {
        self.name = name;
    }

    async baked() is string {
        Stdout().writeln("baking " + name);
        name + " bread";
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let pending = Oven("rye").baked();
    Stdout().writeln("ordered; done: " + pending.done().string());
    let first = await pending;
    let second = await pending;
    Stdout().writeln(first + ", " + second + "; done: " + pending.done().string());
    0;
}

Output:

ordered; done: false
baking rye
rye bread, rye bread; done: true
  • Oven("rye").baked() does not bake. The call returns a future, and the first line of output shows that nothing has run yet: done: false, and no baking rye.
  • The first await pending starts the body, which prints baking rye and produces "rye bread".
  • The second await pending does not bake again. A future runs its body at most once and keeps the outcome; every later await reads it.
  • async main() is what makes await legal in main. A program whose main is synchronous can create futures but cannot wait for them.

20.1 A future is a value that is not computed yet

An action declared async and is T is checked as producing a T. Calling it produces a Future<T>:

Oven("rye").baked()          : Future<string>
await Oven("rye").baked()    : string

A future has exactly three public actions, and none of them reads the value:

  • done() is true once the future has settled: with a value, with a failure, or cancelled with its cleanup finished;
  • cancel() asks the future to stop (Section 20.5);
  • cancelled() is true once cancellation has finished.

The only way to get the value is await. There is no result(), no value(), no get() that blocks. That is deliberate: a call that blocks the thread until a value is there would stop the one scheduler, and with it every other task of the program.

The rules around await are few:

  • There is no implicit await. A Future<int> is not an int, and passing one where the other is expected is a type error.
  • await is legal only inside an async action, async main included. Awaiting in a synchronous action is a compile error, and so is awaiting something that is not a future.
  • A failure thrown by the body is kept like a value and thrown again at every await, where an ordinary try/catch takes it.
  • Locals survive suspension. The body resumes at the operand it was waiting for, without evaluating earlier operands or statements again.
  • await is a unary operator: (await reply.item()).string() needs the parentheses, and await load() + 1 means (await load()) + 1.
  • An async action declared is void produces a future without a value. It is awaited for its effect, as a statement, never as an expression.

The call is lazy. That choice decides more than it seems to. A lazy future that nobody awaits costs one object and runs no code, so returning one from an action is free, and an action can build several and decide later which to await. A future that starts when it is created would already be running by then, and the caller would own a task it may not want. spawn is the explicit way to start one now (Section 20.4).

20.2 Where futures came from

The future is older than most languages that have one. Baker and Hewitt named it in 1977, in work on actor systems, as a value that stands for a computation still running; their paper is about collecting the futures that nobody will ever read [Jr. 1977]. Halstead's Multilisp made it a language construct in 1985: (future e) starts evaluating e in parallel and returns a placeholder at once, and any strict use of the placeholder waits for the value [Jr. 1985]. That future is eager and implicit: a program does not say where it waits.

Liskov and Shrira's promises (1988) moved the idea to distributed calls and made it typed: a call returns a promise, the caller continues, and claiming the promise later yields the result or the exception the call raised [Liskov 1988]. The two halves Okkama keeps are already there: the outcome includes failures, and it is collected explicitly.

The async/await pair came from F#. Its asynchronous workflows (2007, described in [Syme 2011]) let a programmer write a sequential-looking body that waits at each let!, and an F# Async<T> is a recipe: it runs only when started, and it can be started more than once. C# 5 (2012) took the syntax with a different value: its Task<T> is already running when the call returns. JavaScript's promises (2015) and async functions (2017) are eager in the same way. Rust's futures (2019) went back to lazy values that do nothing until polled.

Okkama sits between them. Its future is lazy like F#'s and Rust's: a call starts nothing. But it runs at most once and keeps its outcome, like C#'s and JavaScript's: awaiting it twice does not run it twice. A future in Okkama is a single computation that has not started yet, not a recipe for many.

The price of async/await in every language that has it is what Nystrom called the colour of a function [Nystrom 2015]: an async function can be called from anywhere, but its result can be awaited only from another async function, so asynchrony spreads up the call graph. Okkama pays it in full, and on purpose. An action that can suspend says so in its signature, because a suspension point is where other tasks run (Section 20.3), and a reader who cannot see where that happens cannot reason about the code.

20.3 One scheduler, one task at a time

A run has one scheduler. async main drives it until the root future settles; a synchronous main does not drive it at all. Async does not create threads, and it does not make CPU-bound work faster: two tasks that compute take turns on one core. What async gives is that a task waiting for something does not hold up the others.

Scheduling is cooperative. One task runs at a time, until it suspends at an await of a future that has not settled, or until it ends. Then the scheduler runs the next ready task. A task becomes ready when something it waits for happens: a future it awaits completes, an Event it waits on is set, a channel hands it a value, a permit it asked for is returned, or it is cancelled. Ready tasks run in the order they were woken.

The rule that matters most is what waking does not do. It does not run the woken task. The task that called set() or cancel() keeps running until it suspends, and only then does the woken task get its turn:

module bible/wake v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "async/event" take Event;

object Waiter {
    has ready is Event;
    has started is Event;
    Waiter(:ready, :started);
    async run() is int {
        started.set();
        await ready.wait();
        Stdout().writeln("waiter: woke");
        1;
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let ready = Event();
    let started = Event();
    let waiter = spawn Waiter(ready: ready, started: started).run();
    await started.wait();
    Stdout().writeln("main: before set");
    ready.set();
    Stdout().writeln("main: after set");
    await waiter;
    0;
}

Output:

main: before set
main: after set
waiter: woke

main: after set comes before waiter: woke. So the code of a task between two suspension points is never interleaved with another task's code. A task can read some state, decide, and write the result without a lock, as long as it does not await in between. Every await is a point where the world may have changed; nothing else is.

This is the guarantee asyncio, JavaScript, Trio and Kotlin's coroutines give, and it is what makes cooperative concurrency easier to reason about than threads.

Two kinds of start stay immediate. spawn runs the new task at once, until its first suspension, before the statement after spawn. The first await of a cold future runs its body at once too; the awaiting task is suspended anyway. And awaiting a future that has already settled does not suspend at all: it returns the kept outcome, and no other task runs in between.

None of this is a thread-safety guarantee. Two tasks that each read, await and then write can still lose an update, because the await between the read and the write lets the other task in. Cooperative scheduling tells a reader where interleaving can happen; it does not make it impossible.

Where the rule came from

Cooperative multitasking is older than async. Classic Mac OS ran its applications this way from MultiFinder in 1987 to Mac OS 9, and 16-bit Windows did the same: a program kept the processor until it called back into the system, so one program stuck in a loop froze the machine. Okkama accepts that cost inside one run and not across programs. A task that computes without awaiting holds up every other task of its run, and nothing preempts it (Section 20.15). Erlang went the other way: its processes are preempted, so a process that keeps computing does not starve the rest. It does not need the guarantee above, because its processes share no memory. Go started cooperative and made goroutines asynchronously preemptible in Go 1.14, in 2020, so that "loops without function calls no longer potentially deadlock the scheduler" [Authors 2020].

The narrower rule, that waking never runs the woken code inside the waker, has its own history in JavaScript. Promises/A+ requires that a promise's callbacks "must not be called until the execution context stack contains only platform code" [Promises/A+], that is, never inside the call that settled the promise. The reason was a class of bugs that Isaac Schlueter called releasing Zalgo [Schlueter 2013]. An API that calls its callback sometimes at once and sometimes later runs the code after the call in two different orders, and only one of them gets tested. His advice was to pick one timing and keep it.

20.4 spawn: work that runs beside its starter

spawn takes a call of an object's action and starts it now. Its result is the same Future<T> the call would have returned, so await collects it later; there is no second type for a running task, and no Future<Future<T>>. What spawn starts depends on the action:

  • An async action becomes a task of the current run. It shares the scheduler with its starter and may hold objects, futures, channel endpoints and other values that only make sense inside one run. It gives concurrency, not parallelism: it runs when the others wait.
  • A synchronous action runs in a separate worker process, in parallel with the program. Receiver and arguments are evaluated in the parent, left to right, and copied to the worker; only transferable values cross: int, float, string, char, byte, bool, and arrays and maps of them. Objects, futures, closures and native handles cannot. The worker's result or failure comes back into the future.
async main() is int {
    let left is Future<int> = spawn Worker(seed: 7).calculate(input: 20);
    let right is Future<int> = spawn Worker(seed: 9).calculate(input: 6);
    (await left) + (await right);
}

Both workers compute at the same time, before either future is awaited. The form is narrow on purpose: only spawn Receiver(…).action(…) or a bound action value is a spawn target, not a block or an arbitrary expression, so what crosses the process boundary is always a receiver and arguments that the compiler has checked.

(This chapter's examples do not start worker processes; they run in a sandbox that forbids it. The program above is the specification's.)

A spawned task must be accounted for. When async main returns, the scheduler cancels every spawned task that has not finished and waits for its cleanup. A spawned task that failed and that nobody awaited makes the whole run fail, with that task's failure: an error is not lost because nobody was listening.

20.5 Structured await and cancellation

cancel() asks a future to stop. Cancellation is cooperative: it is delivered at the task's suspension point, unwinds the task like a failure (its defers and destroys run), and the task's awaits then throw the built-in Cancelled. A future that never started is simply marked cancelled; its body never runs.

Figure 20.1. Structured await: cancelling a task cancels the future it awaits, and the task resumes only after that future has settled.

What happens to the future a cancelled task was waiting for? Okkama's answer is that await is structured (issue #147). Cancelling a task cancels the future it awaits, if that future is its own: one its await started, a task it spawned, or an asynchronous operation it requested. And the cancelled task does not finish until that future has settled, cleanup included. Only then does its own await throw Cancelled and its own cleanup run:

module bible/cancel v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "async/event" take Event;

object Delivery {
    has loaded is Event;
    has road is Event;

    Delivery(:loaded, :road);

    async run() is string {
        defer Stdout().writeln("delivery: van returned to the depot");
        loaded.set();
        await road.wait();
        "delivered";
    }
}

object Order {
    has delivery is Delivery;
