    Order(:delivery);

    async run() is string {
        defer Stdout().writeln("order: closed");
        await delivery.run();
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let loaded = Event();
    let road = Event();
    let order = spawn Order(delivery: Delivery(loaded: loaded, road: road)).run();
    await loaded.wait();
    order.cancel();
    Stdout().writeln("customer: cancel");
    let outcome = try {
        await order;
    }
    catch e is Cancelled {
        "cancelled";
    };
    Stdout().writeln("outcome: " + outcome + "; cancelled: " + order.cancelled().string());
    0;
}

Output:

customer: cancel
delivery: van returned to the depot
order: closed
outcome: cancelled; cancelled: true
  • order.cancel() returns at once. It does not run the delivery's cleanup; that happens when main suspends at await order.
  • The delivery is cancelled because the order was waiting for it, and only the order. Its defer runs first: the van returns before the order closes.
  • await order throws Cancelled only after both have finished, and cancelled() is then true.

A future that another task also awaits is not cancelled with one of its waiters: the cancelled task only stops waiting for it, and the others still get its outcome.

When the await has already finished

There is a moment between two states that the rule above does not cover. A task's awaited future settles; the task becomes ready to resume; before its turn comes, someone cancels it. Is the task still "waiting at a suspension point"?

The cancellation rule is:

  • An await is finished once its future has settled. A cancellation that arrives after that does not undo it; the task runs on with the value or the failure it was given.
  • The cancellation stays requested, and the task's next await raises Cancelled before it starts anything.

The rule is the one that keeps information: a value that arrived is not discarded, a failure that happened is not hidden behind Cancelled, and a task that is cancelled still stops at its next suspension. A sibling of an AllFutures that failed in the same turn appears among the secondary failures, in input order.

A related rule settles what a stream of completions does after it is cancelled (issue #548). Cancelling a pending completion() request cancels the stream's unfinished inputs, waits for their cleanup and fails with the cancellation; every later request fails the same way, with Cancelled rather than NoFutures, because the stream was cancelled, not exhausted.

The rule makes a common case need nothing at all. A task that awaits one child needs no group, no supervisor and no "settle" object in a defer: cancelling the task reaches the child and waits for it. Groups exist for real fan-out, where one task owns several children at once (Section 20.7).

This is structured concurrency in Smith's sense [Smith 2018]: no child outlives the scope that is waiting for it. Smith's Trio makes the scope explicit, as a nursery block that every task must be started in. Kotlin (2018) made every coroutine a child of a scope, so that a scope does not finish before its children and cancelling it cancels them [Elizarov 2018]. Okkama gets the same property from the await itself, without a scope object: the thing a task is waiting for is its child for as long as it waits. What it does not get is the nursery's guarantee for work that nobody awaits. A spawned task that its starter forgets runs on until async main returns and the scheduler cancels it.

Where structured concurrency came from

Smith's argument starts from Dijkstra's letter about goto [Dijkstra 1968]. A goto lets control leave a block and never come back, so a reader cannot treat the block as a unit: whatever it was supposed to finish may still be going on elsewhere. Structured programming replaced it with constructs that have one entry and one exit. A function that starts a thread or a goroutine and returns does what goto did, Smith says: the work it started outlives the call, and no caller can know when it ends or where its errors go. A nursery puts concurrency back into the shape of a block.

The idea is older than the name. Erlang [Armstrong 2003] linked processes so that a crash travels along the links, and supervisors restart what they started, so that a tree of processes fails and recovers as one. That tree is built and torn down at run time, by convention and library; the language does not stop a process from outliving its parent.

After Trio the idea went into the mainstream quickly. Kotlin made every coroutine the child of a CoroutineScope in 2018 [Elizarov 2018]. Swift shipped task groups and async let with structured child tasks in 2021 [Evolution 2021]. Python 3.11 (2022) added asyncio.TaskGroup. Java 21 (2023) previewed StructuredTaskScope [OpenJDK 2023]. All of them give the scope an object or a block. Okkama gives it the await: a task that waits for a future it started owns it while it waits, which covers the common case of one child without any extra construct, and leaves the objects of Section 20.7 for the cases with many.

20.6 Channels and the state owner

Okkama has no mutable fields. The one value tasks can share and replace is an Atomic (Section 20.8), a single cell replaced whole; a counter, a cache or a repository that several tasks update is not written to by all of them. They send each other values. async/channel provides Channel<T>, a bounded FIFO of values of one type, and two capabilities over it: Sending<T>, which can only send, and Receiving<T>, which can only receive.

Figure 20.2. The state owner: tasks send commands through a channel to the one task that holds the state.

A component with state is one task that owns the state as a local binding and changes it by rebinding that binding to a successor. Everybody else talks to it through a channel:

module bible/ledger v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "async/channel" take Channel, Sending, Receiving;

object Balance {
    has amount is int;

    Balance(:amount);

    amount() is int {
        amount;
    }

    deposited(sum is int) is ^Balance {
        ^amount = amount + sum;
    }
}

enum Command = (deposit(sum is int), report(reply is Sending<int>), stop);

object Ledger {
    has inbox is Receiving<Command>;

    Ledger(:inbox);

    async run() is int {
        let balance = Balance(amount: 0);
        let served = 0;
        loop {
            let command = await inbox.item();
            match command {
                case Command.deposit(sum) {
                    balance = balance.deposited(sum);
                }
                case Command.report(reply) {
                    await reply.send(balance.amount());
                }
                case Command.stop {
                    last;
                }
            }
        }
        balance.amount();
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let channel is Channel<Command> = Channel(capacity: 4);
    let ledger = spawn Ledger(inbox: channel.receiving()).run();
    let teller = channel.sending();
    await teller.send(Command.deposit(30));
    await teller.send(Command.deposit(12));
    let replies is Channel<int> = Channel(capacity: 1);
    await teller.send(Command.report(replies.sending()));
    Stdout().writeln("balance: " + (await replies.receiving().item()).string());
    await teller.send(Command.stop);
    Stdout().writeln("final: " + (await ledger).string());
    0;
}

Output:

balance: 42
final: 42
  • The ledger's balance is a local of run(). Nobody else can reach it, so nobody else can change it, and the commands that change it are handled one at a time, in the order they arrived.
  • balance = balance.deposited(sum) rebinds the local to the successor that deposited returned. Balance itself never changes.
  • A command that needs an answer carries its own reply channel of capacity 1. Every request has its own, so concurrent answers cannot reach the wrong client.
  • The teller holds only a Sending<Command>. It can ask; it cannot read the ledger's inbox, close the reply channels of others or touch the balance.

This is the actor pattern of Erlang [Armstrong 2003] built from ordinary parts: a task, a channel and a match over commands, with no new syntax. What Erlang's mailboxes do not have, and Okkama's channels do, is a bound. A channel of capacity 4 holds four values; the fifth send suspends until the owner takes one, so a fast producer cannot bury a slow owner under messages. Capacity 0 is a rendezvous: a send finishes only when a receiver takes the value.

The rest of a channel's contract is short:

  • values, blocked senders and waiting receivers are served in FIFO order, and each value is received exactly once;
  • either endpoint may close() the channel, any number of times; after it, sends throw ChannelClosed, values already buffered can still be received, and then item() throws ChannelClosed too;
  • dropping an endpoint does not close the channel, and neither does the failure of a task that used it. The owner closes it, usually in a defer;
  • cancelling a task blocked in send or item() ends its wait, and the next value goes to the next waiter.

There is no try_send, no try_receive, no closed(): a task that wants to know whether it can proceed waits, and the scheduler runs somebody else meanwhile.

Several channels at once: SelectedReceiving

A task that serves more than one source waits on all of them and takes whichever message comes first. SelectedReceiving does that over receivers of one element type:

module bible/select v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "async/channel" take Channel, Sending, SelectedReceiving, SelectedItem, ChannelClosed;

// Two sources of one kind of message: orders from the shop, orders by phone.
object Source {
    has output is Sending<string>;
    has prefix is string;
    has count is int;
    Source(output is Sending<string>, prefix is string, count is int) {
        self.output = output; self.prefix = prefix; self.count = count;
    }
    async run() is void {
        defer output.close();
        for 1..=count -> n { await output.send(prefix + " " + n.string()); }
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let shop is Channel<string> = Channel(capacity: 1);
    let phone is Channel<string> = Channel(capacity: 1);
    let a = spawn Source(output: shop.sending(), prefix: "shop", count: 3).run();
    let b = spawn Source(output: phone.sending(), prefix: "phone", count: 2).run();
    let names = ["shop", "phone"];
    let orders is SelectedReceiving<string> =
        SelectedReceiving(receivers: [shop.receiving(), phone.receiving()]);
    loop {
        let got = try { Maybe.some(await orders.item()); }
                  catch e is ChannelClosed { Maybe<SelectedItem<string>>.none; };
        match got {
            case Maybe.some(item) { out.writeln(names[item.source()] + ": " + item.value()); }
            case Maybe.none { last; }
        }
    }
    await a;
    await b;
    out.writeln("both sources closed");
    0;
}

Output:

shop: shop 1
phone: phone 1
shop: shop 2
phone: phone 2
shop: shop 3
both sources closed
  • One message per item(). await orders.item() commits to exactly one receive and answers a SelectedItem: source() is the position of the winning receiver in the array, value() the message.
  • Fair by rotation. When several sources are ready, the first in the array wins the first tie, and the next tie starts from the source after the previous winner. Neither source starves the other, and the order of the output above is the same on every run.
  • Closed means exhausted. A closed channel's buffered messages are still delivered. item() throws ChannelClosed only when every source is closed and empty, which is how the loop above ends.
  • Mistakes are typed errors. An empty array of receivers is EmptyChannelSelection, the same channel twice is DuplicateChannelReceiver, and a second item() while one is pending is ConcurrentChannelSelection.
  • Cancellation withdraws every alternative. A task cancelled while it waits takes nothing from any channel; a receive that already committed is delivered. Within and Before (Section 20.7) put a deadline on item().

This is Go's select and CSP's guarded choice [Hoare 1978] as an object: the choice has a name, a type and an error vocabulary, and it composes with the deadlines the next section introduces.

20.7 Fan-out, races and deadlines

Structured await covers a task that waits for one thing. When a task starts several and waits for all of them, or for the first, it needs an object that owns them all. async/collect and async/timeout provide them:

module bible/fanout v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "async/event" take Event;
import "async/collect" take AllFutures;
import "async/timeout" take Within, TimedOut;
import "time/clock" take SystemClock;
import "time/duration" take Duration, DurationUnit;
import "collections/sequence" take Sequencing;

object Supplier {
    has name is string;
    has price is int;

    Supplier(:name, :price);

    async quote() is int {
        price;
    }
}

object Courier {
    has never is Event;

    Courier(:never);

    async eta() is int {
        defer Stdout().writeln("courier: request withdrawn");
        await never.wait();
        0;
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let quotes is @Future<int> = [
        Supplier(name: "mill", price: 40).quote(),
        Supplier(name: "farm", price: 35).quote(),
        Supplier(name: "port", price: 52).quote(),
    ];
    let all is AllFutures<int> = AllFutures(origins: quotes);
    let prices is Sequencing<int> = await all.results();
    Stdout().writeln("quotes: " + prices.size().string());
    let bounded is Within<int> = Within(
        origin: Courier(never: Event()).eta(),
        limit: Duration(value: 20.rat(), unit: DurationUnit.millisecond),
        clock: SystemClock(),
    );
    let eta = try {
        await bounded.outcome();
    }
    catch e is TimedOut {
        -1;
    };
    Stdout().writeln("eta: " + eta.string());
    0;
}

Output:

quotes: 3
courier: request withdrawn
eta: -1
  • AllFutures(origins: quotes).results() starts all three quotes and waits for all of them. The results come back in the order of the inputs, not the order of completion. If one fails, the others are cancelled and their cleanup awaited before the failure is thrown.
  • Within(origin:, limit:, clock:).outcome() gives the courier 20 milliseconds. When time wins, the courier's request is cancelled and its cleanup runs (courier: request withdrawn) before TimedOut is thrown. Before is the same with a deadline computed once and shared by several operations.

The other collectors and the two owners of a changing set of children follow.

The first to finish: Raced and FirstSuccessful

module bible/race v1.0.0;

// Raced takes the first outcome to settle and cancels the rest;
// FirstSuccessful passes over failures to the first success, and throws the
// first failure when every origin fails.
import "async/collect" take Raced, FirstSuccessful, NoFutures;
import "async/event" take Event;
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Broken is Error = (broken, again);

object Waiter {
    has event is Event;
    Waiter(:event);
    async value(v is int) is int {
        defer Stdout().writeln("waiter " + v.string() + " ends");
        await event.wait();
        v;
    }
}

object Source {
    Source();
    async value(label is string, v is int) is int {
        Stdout().writeln(label);
        v;
    }
    async broken(which is int) is int {
        Stdout().writeln("broken " + which.string());
        if which == 1 { throw Broken.broken; } else { throw Broken.again; }
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let never = Event();
    let race is @Future<int> = [Waiter(event: never).value(1), Source().value("fast", 2)];
    out.writeln("winner " + (await Raced(origins: race).winner()).string());
    let mixed is @Future<int> = [Source().broken(1), Source().value("ok", 3)];
    out.writeln("first success " + (await FirstSuccessful(origins: mixed).outcome()).string());
    let failing is @Future<int> = [Source().broken(1), Source().broken(2)];
    out.writeln(try { (await FirstSuccessful(origins: failing).outcome()).string(); }
        catch Broken.broken { "first failure: broken"; } catch Broken.again { "first failure: again"; });
    let nothing is @Future<int> = [];
    out.writeln(try { (await Raced(origins: nothing).winner()).string(); } catch e is NoFutures { "no futures"; });
    0;
}

Output:

fast
waiter 1 ends
winner 2
broken 1
ok
first success 3
broken 1
broken 2
first failure: broken
no futures
  • Raced(origins:).winner() starts every origin and returns the first outcome to settle, a success or a failure. The waiter that never wakes is cancelled, and its defer runs (waiter 1 ends) before winner 2 is printed: the race is over only when no origin is still running.
  • FirstSuccessful(origins:).outcome() passes over failures while a success is still possible. When every origin fails, the first failure is thrown, and the later ones travel with it as secondary failures (Section 20.13).
  • With no origins at all, both throw NoFutures. AllFutures of nothing is an empty result instead, since all of nothing has succeeded.

In the order they finish: FutureCompletions

module bible/completions v1.0.0;

// FutureCompletions hands the futures back in the order they finish, not
// the order they were given.
import "async/collect" take FutureCompletions, NoFutures;
import "async/event" take Event;
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Gate {
    has event is Event;
    Gate(:event);
    async named(name is string) is string {
        await event.wait();
        name;
    }
}

object Now {
    Now();
    async named(name is string) is string { name; }
}

async main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let first = Event();
    let second = Event();
    let futures is @Future<string> = [Gate(event: second).named("slow"), Now().named("quick"),
        Gate(event: first).named("middle")];
    let completions is FutureCompletions<string> = FutureCompletions(origins: futures);
    out.writeln("remaining " + completions.remaining_count().string());
    first.set();
    out.writeln(await (await completions.completion()));
    out.writeln(await (await completions.completion()));
    second.set();
    out.writeln(await (await completions.completion()));
    out.writeln("remaining " + completions.remaining_count().string());
    out.writeln(try { await (await completions.completion()); } catch e is NoFutures { "none left"; });
    0;
}

Output:

remaining 3
quick
middle
slow
remaining 0
none left

FutureCompletions(origins:) hands back the futures in the order they settle, not the order they were given. Each completion() gives the next one, already settled, so awaiting it costs nothing. remaining_count() says how many have not been handed out. After the last one, completion() throws NoFutures. This is the shape of a crawler that handles each page as it arrives, or a server that answers whichever backend replies first and keeps the rest.

A changing set of children: FutureGroup

The collectors take their origins at once. A task that discovers its work while it runs (a connection per client, a request per link found) needs an owner it can add to:

module bible/group v1.0.0;

// A FutureGroup owns a changing set of children: `start` registers and starts
// one (the same future twice is one child), `wait` seals the group and waits
// for every child, and a child started after that is refused.
import "async/scope" take FutureGroup, FinishedFutureGroup;
import "async/event" take Event;
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Worker {
    has id is int;
    has gate is Event;
    Worker(:id, :gate);
    async run() is int {
        await gate.wait();
        Stdout().writeln("worker " + id.string());
        id;
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let gate = Event();
    let group is FutureGroup<int> = FutureGroup();
    let first = Worker(id: 1, gate: gate).run();
    group.start(first);
    group.start(Worker(id: 2, gate: gate).run());
    group.start(first);
    out.writeln("active " + group.active().string());
    gate.set();
    await group.wait();
    out.writeln("active " + group.active().string() + ", first gave " + (await first).string());
    let late = try { group.start(Worker(id: 3, gate: gate).run()); "started"; } catch e is FinishedFutureGroup { "refused"; };
    out.writeln("late start " + late);
    0;
}

Output:

active 2
worker 1
worker 2
active 0, first gave 1
late start refused
  • start(f) registers a future and starts it. The same future registered twice is one child, so active() counts two.
  • wait() seals the group and waits for every child. A child's failure is observed there: the first in registration order is thrown, and the others travel with it.
  • After wait() or cancel(), the group is finished, and start throws FinishedFutureGroup. A group cannot quietly grow after its owner stopped waiting for it.

A body with its children: FutureScope

A FutureGroup passed around can be waited for by anyone, or by no one. FutureScope ties the group to one body:

module bible/scope v1.0.0;

// A FutureScope runs one body with a group it may start children in; the
// scope's outcome is the body's result once every child has finished. A
// body that fails cancels the children it started and waits for them.
import "async/scope" take FutureScope, Supervising;
import "async/event" take Event;
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Refused is Error = (refused);

object Child {
    has name is string;
    has gate is Event;
    Child(:name, :gate);
    async run() is int {
        defer Stdout().writeln(name + " done");
        await gate.wait();
        1;
    }
}

object Batch {
    has gate is Event;
    Batch(:gate);
    async run(children is Supervising<int>) is string {
        children.start(Child(name: "a", gate: gate).run());
        children.start(Child(name: "b", gate: gate).run());
        gate.set();
        "batch";
    }
    async fail(children is Supervising<int>) is string {
        children.start(Child(name: "c", gate: gate).run());
        throw Refused.refused;
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let scope is FutureScope<int, string> = FutureScope(action: Batch(gate: Event()).run);
    out.writeln("outcome " + await scope.outcome());
    let failing is FutureScope<int, string> = FutureScope(action: Batch(gate: Event()).fail);
    out.writeln(try { await failing.outcome(); } catch e is Refused { "refused"; });
    0;
}

Output:

a done
b done
outcome batch
c done
refused

The body receives a Supervising<int>, a role that can start children, count them and cancel them, but cannot wait for the group. Waiting is what ends a group, and the scope keeps that for itself. The scope's outcome() is the body's result once every child has finished (a done, b done, then outcome batch). When the body fails, the scope cancels the children it started, waits for their cleanup (c done), and then throws the body's failure. A scope owns children of one result type; children of another type get a nested scope. The Trio and Kotlin nurseries of Section 20.5 have the same shape. Okkama's version names the capability the body gets (Supervising), so the body cannot finish the scope it runs in.

Each of these objects follows the rule of Section 20.5: a child it cancels is waited for, so when its results(), winner(), outcome() or wait() returns or throws, no child it started is still running. The deadline uses a monotonic clock that the program passes in (SystemClock() here, a manual clock in a test); a civil Instant is not accepted as a deadline, so a change of the wall clock cannot fire or hold back a timeout.

20.8 Waiting for each other: events, locks, semaphores, barriers

Channels carry values. The other modules of async/ coordinate tasks without carrying anything:

  • Event (async/event) is a one-way latch. wait() suspends until somebody calls set(); after that, every wait() returns at once. Event(true) starts set. The examples of this chapter use events to hand control from one task to another at a point the reader can see.
  • Lock (async/lock) gives one task at a time a LockGuard; close() on the guard releases it.
  • Semaphore (async/semaphore) hands out up to n Permits; a task that asks for one more waits until a permit is closed.
  • Barrier (async/barrier) releases a group of tasks together, once the last of them has arrived.
  • Atomic<T> (async/atomic) is a cell with value(), replace() and compare_and_replace(). It is the one place in the standard library where a value can be changed in place, and it exists for coordination, not for application state: a counter of active tasks, a flag that a loop polls.
  • Cancellation (async/cancellation) is a token that long synchronous loops check between steps, because cancellation reaches a task only at a suspension point and a loop that never suspends would never see it.

A lock holds across a suspension:

module bible/lock v1.0.0;

// A Lock gives one task at a time a guard; a second task asking for it waits
// until the first closes its guard, even across a suspension.
import "async/lock" take Lock;
import "async/event" take Event;
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object User {
    has name is string;
    has device is Lock;
    has gate is Event;
    User(:name, :device, :gate);
    async run() is void {
        let guard = await device.guard();
        defer guard.close();
        Stdout().writeln(name + " enters");
        await gate.wait();
        Stdout().writeln(name + " leaves");
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let device = Lock();
    let gate = Event();
    let a = spawn User(name: "a", device: device, gate: gate).run();
    let b = spawn User(name: "b", device: device, gate: gate).run();
    Stdout().writeln("locked " + device.locked().string());
    gate.set();
    await a;
    await b;
    Stdout().writeln("locked " + device.locked().string());
    0;
}

Output:

a enters
locked true
a leaves
b enters
b leaves
locked false

b asks for the guard while a holds it, and waits. a's defer closes the guard when a leaves, and only then does b enter. The guard must be closed explicitly: it is not a resource with a destroy, and a guard left open keeps the lock held after its task has ended. defer guard.close() right after taking it is the idiom, and the same holds for a semaphore's permit.

A semaphore admits up to n at once:

module bible/semaphore v1.0.0;

// A Semaphore hands out at most n permits: the third task waits until one
// of the first two closes its permit.
import "async/semaphore" take Semaphore;
import "async/event" take Event;
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Job {
    has name is string;
    has slots is Semaphore;
    has gate is Event;
    Job(:name, :slots, :gate);
    async run() is void {
        let permit = await slots.permit();
        defer permit.close();
        Stdout().writeln(name + " runs, free " + slots.permits().string());
        await gate.wait();
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let slots = Semaphore(permits: 2);
    let gate = Event();
    let a = spawn Job(name: "a", slots: slots, gate: gate).run();
    let b = spawn Job(name: "b", slots: slots, gate: gate).run();
    let c = spawn Job(name: "c", slots: slots, gate: gate).run();
    Stdout().writeln("waiting, free " + slots.permits().string());
    gate.set();
    await a;
    await b;
    await c;
    Stdout().writeln("done, free " + slots.permits().string());
    0;
}

Output:

a runs, free 1
b runs, free 0
waiting, free 0
c runs, free 1
done, free 2

The third job waits for a permit until the gate opens and the first job's defer closes its own. permits() counts what is free.

A barrier releases its parties together:

module bible/barrier v1.0.0;

// A Barrier releases its parties together once the last has arrived; each
// arrival gets its index, and the last one is parties - 1.
import "async/barrier" take Barrier;
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Party {
    has name is string;
    has phase is Barrier;
    Party(:name, :phase);
    async step() is void {
        Stdout().writeln(name + " arrives");
        let arrival = await phase.wait();
        Stdout().writeln(name + " goes" + (if arrival == 2 { " last"; } else { ""; }));
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let phase = Barrier(parties: 3);
    let a = spawn Party(name: "a", phase: phase).step();
    let b = spawn Party(name: "b", phase: phase).step();
    let c = spawn Party(name: "c", phase: phase).step();
    await a;
    await b;
    await c;
    0;
}

Output:

a arrives
b arrives
c arrives
c goes last
a goes
b goes

Each wait() returns the arrival's index, and the last arrival gets parties - 1. The last one does not suspend, so it goes first, and the others follow in the order they arrived. After a release the barrier starts a new generation, ready for the next phase.

A cancellation request reaches code that checks it:

module bible/cancellation v1.0.0;

// A Cancellation is a request that cooperating code checks: a synchronous
// loop between its steps (check throws Cancelled once it is requested), a
// task by awaiting it. Holders of the Cancelling role can observe the
// request but not issue it.
import "async/cancellation" take Cancellation, Cancelling;
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Monitor {
    has cancelling is Cancelling;
    Monitor(:cancelling);
    async run() is void {
        await cancelling.wait();
        Stdout().writeln("monitor: cancellation requested");
    }
}

object Worker {
    has cancelling is Cancelling;
    Worker(:cancelling);
    process(records is @string, stop is Cancellation) is int {
        let done = (0..records.size()).reduce(0) -> count, index {
            cancelling.check();
            Stdout().writeln("processed " + records.item(index));
            if records.item(index) == "stop" { stop.cancel(); }
            count + 1;
        };
        done;
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let cancellation = Cancellation();
    let monitor = spawn Monitor(cancelling: cancellation.cancelling()).run();
    let worker = Worker(cancelling: cancellation.cancelling());
    let outcome = try { worker.process(["a", "b", "stop", "c"], cancellation).string(); }
        catch e is Cancelled { "cancelled"; };
    Stdout().writeln("worker: " + outcome);
    await monitor;
    0;
}

Output:

processed a
processed b
processed stop
worker: cancelled
monitor: cancellation requested

check() throws the builtin Cancelled once the request is made. Here the record stop makes it, so the next step's check throws and c is never processed. The monitor waits with wait() and wakes when the request is made. Both hold the restricted Cancelling role, which can observe a request but not make one. Only the holder of the Cancellation decides.

All of them are cooperative: a task waiting on any of them is suspended, and the scheduler runs others. Waking a waiter follows the rule of Section 20.3: set(), close() on a guard or a permit, or the last arrival at a barrier makes the waiters ready; they run after the current task suspends, in the order they started waiting.

A lock in Okkama protects less than a lock in Java. The only shared mutable memory is an Atomic, replaced whole in one step, so a lock serializes sections of work, for example two tasks that must not talk to the same device at once. When the work is "update the shared state", the state owner of Section 20.6 is the better tool: it needs no lock because nobody but the owner can reach the state.

20.9 Resources across suspension

A resource held by a task must be released when the task ends, however it ends: by returning, by failing, or by being cancelled. Chapter 11 described defer and destroy for synchronous code. Both work unchanged across await: the scope that registered them is still the scope when the task resumes, and unwinding a cancelled task runs them like any other unwinding.

Some cleanup has to wait itself: return a connection to a pool, flush a buffer to a socket, tell a server that a session ends. An async destroy block is allowed to await, and the scope that owns the object awaits it when it closes (issue #154):

module bible/lease v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "async/event" take Event;

object Lease {
    has returned is Event;

    Lease(:returned);

    async destroy {
        await returned.wait();
        Stdout().writeln("lease: returned to the pool");
    }
}

object Job {
    has started is Event;
    has returned is Event;

    Job(:started, :returned);

    async run() is int {
        let lease = Lease(returned: returned);
        started.set();
        await Event().wait();
        1;
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let started = Event();
    let returned = Event();
    let job = spawn Job(started: started, returned: returned).run();
    await started.wait();
    job.cancel();
    Stdout().writeln("main: cancel requested; done: " + job.done().string());
    returned.set();
    let outcome = try {
        await job;
    }
    catch e is Cancelled {
        -1;
    };
    Stdout().writeln("main: job " + outcome.string());
    0;
}

Output:

main: cancel requested; done: false
lease: returned to the pool
main: job -1
  • job.cancel() returns before any cleanup has run: done is still false.
  • The job is cancelled at its await. Its scope closes, and the lease's async destroy runs. It waits for returned, which main sets.
  • The cleanup is shielded: cancellation does not interrupt it. The job's future settles only after the lease has been returned, so await job throws Cancelled after lease: returned to the pool, never before.

An async destroy can only belong to an object owned by an async scope. A synchronous action cannot await, so it cannot own an object whose cleanup suspends: Lease has an async destroy; own it in an async action. The rule keeps "every cleanup has run" true at the end of every scope.

What a future keeps, and for how long

A future holds the values it was given in two ways. A value it takes, such as a fresh object passed straight into an async action, belongs to the task: the body owns it and destroys it when the body ends. A value it borrows, a binding or a parameter of whoever created the future, stays with its owner. The future only reads it, so the owner must not destroy it while the future can still run.

Two rules keep that true without anyone writing cleanup by hand:

module bible/keeps v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "async/scope" take FutureGroup;
import "async/event" take Event;

object Lamp {
    has name is string;

    Lamp(:name);

    label() is string { name; }

    destroy { Stdout().writeln("off: " + name); }
}

object Reader {
    Reader();

    async read(lamp is Lamp) is int { lamp.label().length(); }

    async later(lamp is Lamp, gate is Event) is int {
        await gate.wait();
        Stdout().writeln("reads " + lamp.label());
        1;
    }
}

object Desk {
    Desk();

    // The returned future borrows `lamp`: the lamp stays with the caller.
    start(lamp is Lamp) is Future<int> { Reader().read(lamp); }

    // A child started in the caller's group keeps what it borrows.
    async lend(group is FutureGroup<int>, gate is Event) is void {
        let lamp = Lamp(name: "lent");
        let child = Reader().later(lamp, gate);
        group.start(child);
        Stdout().writeln("lend ends");
    }
}

async main() is int {
    {
        let desk = Lamp(name: "desk");
        let reading = Desk().start(desk);
        Stdout().writeln("read " + (await reading).string());
    }
    let gate = Event();
    let group is FutureGroup<int> = FutureGroup();
    await Desk().lend(group, gate);
    gate.set();
    await group.wait();
    Stdout().writeln("main ends");
    0;
}

Output:

read 4
off: desk
lend ends
reads lent
main ends
off: lent
  • Desk.start(lamp) returns a future that borrows its parameter. The lamp goes back to the caller beside the future, and the caller's scope destroys it when it closes, after the future has been awaited (off: desk follows read 4). A function can return such a future further in the same way: what it borrows travels with it to whoever receives it.
  • Desk.lend starts a child in its caller's group and returns while the child still waits on the gate. The child outlives lend's scope, so everything of lend the child can still use goes with it: lent is not destroyed when lend ends. It is destroyed when the program ends, after main ends, by the same owner that settles every task left running at the end.

The second rule has a price. What a running child borrows is kept until the program ends, not until the child finishes, because two children can borrow the same value. A server that starts one detached child per request and lets each borrow a large value keeps all of them alive. Wait for the children (await group.wait(), a FutureScope) when that matters.

The rule does not depend on where the child is bound or whose value it reads (issue #882). A child created in the same expression that starts it, group.start(Reader().later(lamp, gate)), leaves its starter at that moment, so the starter keeps what the child borrows. A child bound in an inner block, { let child = Reader().later(lamp, gate); group.start(child); }, can borrow lamp from the action around the block: when that action ends, the child is still running, and lamp waits for the end of the program as well. Every owner the child borrows from keeps the value, not only the one it leaves.

20.10 Streams: for await

A source that produces values one at a time, each after a wait, is consumed with for await. The source is anything with an async next() that returns Maybe<T>: Maybe.some(value) is the next item, Maybe.none the end.

module bible/stream v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "async/channel" take Channel, Sending;

object Reader {
    has output is Sending<string>;

    Reader(:output);

    async run() is int {
        defer output.close();
        for ["flour", "water", "salt"] -> line {
            await output.send(line);
        }
        3;
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let channel is Channel<string> = Channel(capacity: 1);
    let reader = spawn Reader(output: channel.sending()).run();
    for await channel.receiving() -> line {
        Stdout().writeln("line: " + line);
    }
    Stdout().writeln("lines sent: " + (await reader).string());
    0;
}

Output:

line: flour
line: water
line: salt
lines sent: 3

Each iteration awaits one next(); there is no prefetch, so the loop asks for a value only when the body is ready for it. last leaves the loop without asking again, next goes to the next item, and failures and cancellation unwind as in an ordinary loop. The loop does not close its source: here the reader closes the channel when it has sent everything, and that close is what next() turns into Maybe.none.

A channel's receiving end is such a source since 0.5.5 (issue #199): its next() gives Maybe.none once the channel is closed and drained. Before that, a program wrapped the receiver in a small object of its own with that one action, and any object with an async next() of that shape still works the same way.

What in the standard library is async

About a hundred std modules have async actions, and they are where a program waits for the world:

  • networks: net/tcp, net/udp, net/unix, net/tls, net/dns, and net/tcp_racing, which races connection attempts to several addresses;
  • HTTP: the client and the server, about fifty modules under http/;
  • databases: db/connection, db/pool, db/transaction, db/query, SQLite and PostgreSQL. Rows come one at a time through for await;
  • processes and terminals: os/process and the capture of commands and pipelines, terminal/session, terminal/prompt;
  • the rest: fs/watch (changes to files), logging/queue and logging/syslog, mail (SMTP), and time/clock for waiting on time.

Reading and writing ordinary files, JSON, text and everything that only computes are synchronous: they do not wait for anything another task could use the time for. The standard library is due to be rewritten (planned for 0.7.0), and which of its operations suspend is one of the things the rewrite will decide again; the language rules of this chapter do not depend on it.

20.11 Async in roles, generics and tests

Being async is part of an action's signature, and roles keep it. A role that declares async load(key is string) is string is implemented only by an async action of the same shape; a synchronous load does not do the role:

module bible/shape v1.0.0;

role Store {
    async load(key is string) is string;
}

object Memory does Store {
    Memory();

    load(key is string) is string {
        key;
    }
}

main() is int { 0; }

The compiler answers:

20-shape-rejected.ok:7:8: semantic error: Action "load" on object "Memory" must match async shape for role "Store"

The rule goes both ways. A caller of a role's async action always gets a future, whoever implements it, so the caller's code does not change when a cache in memory replaces a database; and an implementation cannot quietly block the scheduler by answering synchronously where the role promised to wait.

Future<T> is an ordinary generic type, invariant like every Okkama generic: a Future<Money> is not a Future<Amount> even if Money does Amount (Chapter 17). Channel<T>, Sending<T> and Receiving<T> are the same, and a reply channel in a command carries its own T.

A role's fake (Chapter 15) may have async actions too, and tests may be async:

module bible/store v1.0.0;

role Store {
    async load(key is string) is string;

    fake {
        has prefix is string = "fake:";

        async load(key is string) is string {
            prefix + key;
        }
    }
}

object Greeter {
    has store is Store;

    Greeter(:store);

    async greeting(user is string) is string {
        "hello, " + (await store.load(user));
    }
}

async test "a greeting reads the store" {
    let greeter = Greeter(store: Store.fake());
    test.is(await greeter.greeting("ann"), "hello, fake:ann");
}

async test "two greetings run side by side" {
    let store = Store.fake();
    let first = spawn Greeter(store: store).greeting("ann");
    let second = spawn Greeter(store: store).greeting("bob");
    test.is((await first) + " / " + (await second), "hello, fake:ann / hello, fake:bob");
}

Output:

=== RUN   a greeting reads the store
--- PASS: a greeting reads the store
=== RUN   two greetings run side by side
--- PASS: two greetings run side by side
PASS

The second test spawns two greeters and awaits both. spawn needs a call of the form Receiver(…).action(…) (or a typed bound action value): the receiver is built in the spawn itself, so what the task runs on is never a local that the spawning code still uses. An async test runs on the same scheduler as async main; when it ends, its spawned tasks are cancelled and drained, and a failure nobody awaited fails the test.

Async actions as values

A bound async action is a value of type async (T, …) is R. A policy that should not know what it repeats takes one:

module bible/retry v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Busy is Error = (at(attempt is int));

object Endpoint {
    has failures is int;

    Endpoint(:failures);

    async fetch(attempt is int) is string {
        Stdout().writeln("fetch: attempt " + attempt.string());
        if attempt <= failures {
            throw Busy.at(attempt);
        }
        "200 OK";
    }
}

object Retry {
    has attempts is int;

    Retry(:attempts);

    async run(work is async (int) is string, attempt is int) is string {
        try {
            await work(attempt);
        }
        catch e is Busy {
            if attempt == attempts {
                throw e;
            }
            await self.run(work, attempt + 1);
        };
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let patient = Retry(attempts: 3);
    let body = await patient.run(Endpoint(failures: 2).fetch, 1);
    Stdout().writeln("main: " + body);
    let outcome = try {
        await patient.run(Endpoint(failures: 5).fetch, 1);
    }
    catch e is Busy {
        "gave up";
    };
    Stdout().writeln("main: " + outcome);
    0;
}

Output:

fetch: attempt 1
fetch: attempt 2
fetch: attempt 3
main: 200 OK
fetch: attempt 1
fetch: attempt 2
fetch: attempt 3
main: gave up

Retry.run calls work(attempt) and gets a future, as from any async call. It awaits the future inside try and, on Busy, runs again with the next attempt number until the attempts run out; then it rethrows the last failure, which main catches. Endpoint(failures: 2).fetch is the action bound to its object, so whatever the work needs between attempts lives in that object's fields. The attempt number is an argument because the endpoint is immutable and has nowhere to count. One Retry value serves both endpoints.

Anonymous actions cannot be async:

module bible/closure v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

async main() is int {
    let base = 41;
    let work is async () is int = async () is int { base + 1; };
    Stdout().writeln((await work()).string());
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

20-async-closure-rejected.ok:7:35: syntax error at "async": Anonymous actions cannot be async; declare a named async action instead.
  |
7 |     let work is async () is int = async () is int { base + 1; };
  |                                   ^^^^^

The compiler names the way out: a named async action. A small object with one async action takes the place of an async closure, and its fields are what the closure would have captured, written down where a reader sees them. A synchronous anonymous action may still be passed to async code and called there; only its body cannot suspend.

Time in tests

Code that waits for time is the hardest to test: a test that really waits 30 seconds is slow, and one that waits less is flaky. testing/time gives a test a ManualClock, which Within, Before and every other user of the Timing role accept in place of the system clock. Its time moves only when the test calls advance:

module bible/deadline v1.0.0;

import "async/event" take Event;
import "async/timeout" take Within, TimedOut;
import "time/clock" take Instant;
import "time/duration" take Duration, DurationUnit;
import "testing/time" take ManualClock;

object Courier {
    has never is Event;

    Courier(:never);

    async eta() is int {
        await never.wait();
        0;
    }
}

object Dispatch {
    has clock is ManualClock;

    Dispatch(:clock);

    async eta() is int {
        let bounded is Within<int> = Within(
            origin: Courier(never: Event()).eta(),
            limit: Duration(30.rat(), DurationUnit.second),
            clock: clock,
        );
        try {
            await bounded.outcome();
        }
        catch e is TimedOut {
            -1;
        }
    }
}

async test "a courier that never answers times out after thirty seconds" {
    let clock = ManualClock(Instant(Duration(0.rat(), DurationUnit.second)));
    defer clock.close();
    let eta = spawn Dispatch(clock: clock).eta();
    test.is(clock.pending(), 1);
    clock.advance(Duration(29.rat(), DurationUnit.second));
    test.ok(!eta.done());
    clock.advance(Duration(1.rat(), DurationUnit.second));
    test.is(await eta, -1);
}

Output:

=== RUN   a courier that never answers times out after thirty seconds
--- PASS: a courier that never answers times out after thirty seconds
PASS
  • spawn runs Dispatch.eta() until it suspends, waiting on the clock; clock.pending() is 1.
  • After 29 seconds of manual time nothing has fired, and the task is still waiting.
  • The thirtieth second fires the deadline. The courier is cancelled, and await eta returns −1 without a second of real time passing.

The test is deterministic twice over: the clock moves only when told, and the scheduler runs tasks in an order fixed by the rules of Section 20.3. A test of concurrent code in Okkama does not need retries, sleeps or timeouts of its own.

20.12 Worked examples: a pool and a pipeline

The pieces of this chapter fit together in a pool that lends a limited number of connections to whoever asks. Four jobs share a pool of two:

module bible/pool v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "async/event" take Event;
import "async/semaphore" take Semaphore, Permit;
import "async/collect" take AllFutures;
import "collections/sequence" take Sequencing;

object Connection {
    has permit is Permit;
    has job is int;

    Connection(:permit, :job);

    destroy {
        permit.close();
        Stdout().writeln("job " + job.string() + ": connection returned");
    }
}

object Pool {
    has slots is Semaphore;

    Pool(size is int) {
        slots = Semaphore(size);
    }

    async connection(job is int) is Connection {
        Connection(permit: await slots.permit(), job: job);
    }
}

object Job {
    has pool is Pool;
    has go is Event;
    has id is int;

    Job(:pool, :go, :id);

    async run() is int {
        let connection = await pool.connection(id);
        Stdout().writeln("job " + id.string() + ": connected");
        await go.wait();
        id * 10;
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let pool = Pool(2);
    let go = Event();
    let jobs is @Future<int> = [1, 2, 3, 4].map() -> id { spawn Job(pool: pool, go: go, id: id).run(); };
    Stdout().writeln("main: four jobs started");
    go.set();
    let all is AllFutures<int> = AllFutures(origins: jobs);
    let results is Sequencing<int> = await all.results();
    Stdout().writeln("main: " + results.size().string() + " results");
    0;
}

Output:

job 1: connected
job 2: connected
main: four jobs started
job 1: connection returned
job 2: connection returned
job 3: connected
job 3: connection returned
job 4: connected
job 4: connection returned
main: 4 results

The output follows from the rules of Section 20.3, step by step:

  • spawn runs each job at once, until it suspends. Jobs 1 and 2 get a permit without waiting, print connected and suspend at go.wait(). Jobs 3 and 4 find no permit left and suspend in permit(), in that order.
  • main prints its line, sets go and suspends at await all.results(). Setting go made jobs 1 and 2 ready; it ran neither.
  • Job 1 resumes, returns 10 and ends. Its scope closes, so the connection's destroy runs: the permit goes back, and job 3, the first waiting for the semaphore, becomes ready behind job 2. Job 2 does the same and wakes job 4.
  • Job 3 resumes inside permit(), connects, and its go.wait() returns at once because go is already set, so it ends without suspending. Then job 4.

Nothing in the program says "job 3 after job 2". The order comes from three rules: a wake makes a task ready but does not run it, ready tasks run in the order they were woken, and waiters of a semaphore are served first come, first served. The pool itself is a dozen lines, and no line of it handles concurrency: the Semaphore bounds the connections, destroy returns them on every path out of a job, cancellation included, and AllFutures makes main wait for all four.

A pipeline with backpressure

The second classic shape is a pipeline: stages connected by channels, each a task that reads from one channel and writes to the next.

module bible/pipeline v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "async/channel" take Channel, Sending, Receiving, ChannelClosed;

object Source {
    has output is Sending<int>;

    Source(:output);

    async run() is int {
        defer output.close();
        for 1..=5 -> n {
            await output.send(n);
            Stdout().writeln("source: sent " + n.string());
        }
        5;
    }
}

object Square {
    has input is Receiving<int>;
    has output is Sending<int>;

    Square(:input, :output);

    async run() is int {
        defer output.close();
        loop {
            let n = try {
                await input.item();
            }
            catch e is ChannelClosed {
                last;
            };
            await output.send(n * n);
        }
        0;
    }
}

object Total {
    has input is Receiving<int>;

    Total(:input);

    async sum(acc is int) is int {
        let n = try {
            await input.item();
        }
        catch e is ChannelClosed {
            return acc;
        };
        Stdout().writeln("total: got " + n.string());
        await self.sum(acc + n);
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let numbers is Channel<int> = Channel(capacity: 1);
    let squares is Channel<int> = Channel(capacity: 1);
    let source = spawn Source(output: numbers.sending()).run();
    let square = spawn Square(input: numbers.receiving(), output: squares.sending()).run();
    let total = await Total(input: squares.receiving()).sum(0);
    await source;
    await square;
    Stdout().writeln("sum of squares: " + total.string());
    0;
}

Output:

source: sent 1
total: got 1
total: got 4
source: sent 2
source: sent 3
source: sent 4
source: sent 5
total: got 9
total: got 16
total: got 25
sum of squares: 55
  • Each stage closes its output in a defer, so the end of the input travels down the pipeline: the source finishes and closes numbers, Square sees ChannelClosed, leaves its loop and closes squares, and Total returns its sum.
  • The channels hold one value each. The source can be at most a value or two ahead of the consumer; when Total is slow, send suspends the stages behind it. That is backpressure, and it needs no code: the bound of the channel is the policy.
  • The interleaving of source: sent and total: got looks irregular, but it is fixed by the rules of Section 20.3, so it is the same on every run.

Neither shape needs a lock, a shared variable or a callback. Tasks own their state, channels move values between them, and the scheduler decides only the order, deterministically.

20.13 Failures across tasks

A failure inside a task belongs to the task's future. It is kept there, like a value, and thrown at every await of that future, where an ordinary try/catch takes it. A failure that nobody awaits is not dropped:

module bible/lost v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Refused is Error = (because(reason is string));

object Payment {
    Payment();

    async charge() is int {
        throw Refused.because("card expired");
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let payment = spawn Payment().charge();
    Stdout().writeln("main: done, without awaiting the payment");
    0;
}

Output:

main: done, without awaiting the payment
exit 1

main finishes normally, but the run exits with status 1 and prints the payment's failure on stderr: Refused: Refused.because("card expired"). When async main returns, the scheduler cancels the spawned tasks still running, waits for their cleanup, and then looks for a spawned task that failed and was never awaited. The first one found in spawn order fails the run. A failure cancelled away is not one of them: Cancelled is what the scheduler asked for.

The rule is the asynchronous form of the one in Chapter 10: a failure is either handled or reported, never lost on the way. A program that really does not care whether a background task failed says so where it starts it, with a try around the body of the task.

When nothing can run

A task that waits for an event only another waiting task can set waits forever. The scheduler notices when that has happened to the whole program: no task is ready, and no pending timer, socket operation or process worker could wake one.

module bible/stuck v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "async/event" take Event;

object Clerk {
    has mine is Event;
    has theirs is Event;

    Clerk(:mine, :theirs);

    async sign(name is string) is int {
        Stdout().writeln(name + ": waiting for the other signature");
        await theirs.wait();
        mine.set();
        1;
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let a = Event();
    let b = Event();
    let first = spawn Clerk(mine: a, theirs: b).sign("buyer");
    let second = spawn Clerk(mine: b, theirs: a).sign("seller");
    let signed = await first + await second;
    Stdout().writeln("signed: " + signed.string());
    0;
}

Output:

buyer: waiting for the other signature
seller: waiting for the other signature
exit 1

Both clerks print their line and wait; main waits for the first of them. No task is ready and no pending operation can wake one, so the run ends with status 1 and, on stderr, RuntimeError: async main cannot complete: no task can make progress. The lines already printed stay printed.

The check is exact, not a guess. It never fires because something took long: a task that waits for a timer an hour away is not stuck, and other tasks can run while it waits. It is also global. Two tasks that wait for each other while a third keeps a timer or a socket alive are not reported until nothing else is pending, so a server that listens forever never trips it, and a deadlock inside it shows up as requests that never complete, as in any other language.

Go's runtime makes the same global check and stops with fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock! [scheduler]. Node.js exits with code 13 when a top-level await never settles [documentation]. Python's asyncio.run and Rust's Tokio have no such check: the event loop waits for an event that cannot come, and the process hangs.

20.14 Okkama among other languages

Okkama C# JavaScript Python asyncio Rust Kotlin Go
A call starts the work no (lazy) yes yes no (coroutine) no (lazy) async {}: yes go: yes
Outcome kept, awaitable again yes yes yes Task: yes no Deferred: yes —
Wait only in async code yes yes yes yes yes suspend only no colour
Runs between suspension points without interleaving yes no (thread pool) yes yes depends on executor depends on dispatcher no
Cancelling a waiter cancels what it waits for yes (#147) no no yes dropping a future yes (scope) no
Children outlive their scope spawned only yes yes without TaskGroup yes (spawn) no yes
Parallelism process workers threads workers processes, threads threads threads threads
Lost failure fails the run unobserved-task event unhandledrejection; Node.js exits "never retrieved" log #[must_use] warning cancels the scope a panic ends the program

Two columns stand out. JavaScript and asyncio make the same promise as Okkama about interleaving, and pay the same price, a colour on every function that waits. Go makes no promise and pays no colour: any function can block, any goroutine can run at any moment, and shared state needs locks or channels by convention. Okkama chose the coloured side because it already makes effects visible elsewhere (successors, ^ fields, try), and a suspension point is an effect: the place where the rest of the program may change things.

20.15 Limits

  • Detached work. A spawned task that its starter neither awaits nor cancels runs until async main returns. Nothing ties it to the scope that spawned it; only FutureGroup and FutureScope do that, explicitly.
  • No cancellation in synchronous code. Cancellation is delivered at a suspension point. A long synchronous loop sees it only if it checks a Cancellation token.
  • Parts of std are still synchronous. Since 0.5.5 a server reads rooted files off the program's thread (issue #121), a child process's pipes are asynchronous (issue #196), and CSV streams are walked with for await (issue #204). Since 0.6.2 the I/O decorators have asynchronous forms such as LimitedAsyncReading (issue #131), several channels are waited on with SelectedReceiving (issue #509), and nine cleanup guards of the HTTP and TCP modules are async destroy objects (issue #329). Other modules still read and write synchronously.

20.16 What this design costs

Laziness costs an explicit spawn wherever work should start now, and a reader has to know that Oven("rye").baked() alone does nothing. Colour costs async signatures all the way up from the first action that waits, and an async main. The single scheduler costs parallelism inside one process: the only way to use two cores is a worker process, which copies its arguments and its result and cannot share objects. Structured await costs a waiting caller the time the child takes to clean up when it is cancelled.

A suspended task holds a few hundred bytes; ten thousand waiting tasks are cheap. The values those tasks retain still count: a task holding a large collection keeps that collection alive while it waits.

What they buy is a program in which every point where other code can run is written down as await, in which no child that a task waits for outlives it, in which a failure cannot disappear, and in which the scheduling rules determine the order of output.

Chapter 21Processes, natives and capabilities

Everything the earlier chapters built computes. An object holds values, an action derives new ones, a future waits for a result that another part of the program will produce. None of it reaches outside the program. The world outside — files, sockets, clocks, other processes, the terminal — is reached in one way only: through a native, a function supplied by the host and the program declares. This chapter is about that boundary: how a native is declared and answered, what a program holds when it holds a file or a socket, how authority over the host is passed around as an ordinary value, how work moves into another process, and what an embedder can deny.

21.1 One door to the host

An Okkama program cannot open a file by itself. io/stdout, fs/file, net/tcp, time/clock and the rest of the library that touches the host are written in Okkama, and each of them ends, a few calls down, in a declaration such as this one from runtime/time:

native monotonic_clock() is int;

A native declaration has a signature and no body. Calling it requests the provider registered for that module and name. The runtime/* modules are where the standard library declares natives; the layers above them are ordinary Okkama that can be read, tested and faked.

Any module may declare a native. Declaring one does not create it:

module bible/unregistered v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

// A native declared outside the runtime's modules: nothing answers it.
native object Vault;
native vault_open(name is string) is Vault;

main() is int {
    Stdout().writeln("before the call");
    let vault = vault_open("settings");
    Stdout().writeln("after the call");
    0;
}

Output:

before the call
exit 1

The program compiles and starts. before the call is printed; the call fails with RuntimeError: Native symbol "bible/unregistered@1::vault_open/1" is not registered, and the run ends with status 1. A native's name is its module, the module's major version, its own name and its arity, and only a provider registered under exactly that name answers it. A program cannot reach the host by inventing a declaration: the set of doors is the set the host provides (Section 21.6).

The rule has a cost that the next sections pay off. Every effect a program can have outside itself has a name in runtime/*, so the list of what a program might do is short and fixed: it is the list of natives its imports reach. That list is what the native groups of Section 21.6 restrict.

21.2 What a native may take and return

The native ABI is deliberately narrow. The natives of the standard library take and return int, float, bool, string, arrays and maps of such values (@byte, @string, %string:int) and native objects; a few diagnostic ones take any. No native takes or returns an action value, so none can call back into Okkama. A native declaration has no body, no defaults and no variadic parameters. What crosses is data, copied or encoded; what comes back is data or a handle.

A native may be async. runtime/network declares thirteen of them, among them DNS lookups and socket reads and writes:

native async dns_addresses(host is string, port is int) is @@string;
native async udp_receive(origin is SocketState, limit is int) is @byte;

A call returns a future like any async action. The host operation starts without blocking the scheduler, other tasks run meanwhile, and the future settles when the host reports (Chapter 20). The program never sees the host's threads or callbacks.

This is narrower than most foreign-function interfaces, on purpose. A C library called through an FFI can keep a pointer into the caller's memory, call a function it was given at any later time, or run on a thread the caller does not know about. None of that is possible here: when a native returns, or its future settles, it holds nothing of the program's.

21.3 Native objects: handles

A file, a socket, a timer or a database connection is represented in the program by a native object:

native object FileHandle;
native open(path is @byte, flags is int, mode is int) is FileHandle;
native close(handle is FileHandle) is bool;

A native object is a type with no fields, no actions and no constructor. Only its provider can make one. The program can store it, pass it and give it back to the natives of the same module, and nothing else: it cannot be compared, used as a map key, put into any, printed or taken apart. What stands behind it — a file descriptor, a socket, a TLS session — never becomes a value the program can see.

Closing a handle is idempotent, and using a closed handle fails safely:

module bible/handle v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "encoding/utf" take Utf8Encoded;
import "runtime/fs" take open, write, close, path_encode;

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    // write 2 | create 4 | truncate 8, mode 0644
    let handle = open(path_encode("21-handle.txt"), 14, 420);
    out.writeln("wrote " + write(handle, Utf8Encoded("hello\n").bytes()).string() + " bytes");
    out.writeln("closed: " + close(handle).string());
    out.writeln("closed again: " + close(handle).string());
    let late = try {
        write(handle, Utf8Encoded("late\n").bytes()).string();
    }
    catch failure is NativeFailure {
        failure.code();
    };
    out.writeln("write after close: " + late);
    0;
}

Output:

wrote 6 bytes
closed: true
closed again: true
write after close: already_closed
  • close returns true both times. Closing is idempotent, and the resource behind the handle is released exactly once.
  • Writing through the closed handle does not reach a reused descriptor or crash: it fails with a NativeFailure whose code is already_closed, which an ordinary catch takes.
  • If the program forgot close, the runtime would close every remaining handle when the run ends, however it ends, at the end of the run.

Programs rarely hold handles directly. std wraps each in an object with a destroy (Chapter 11), so files and connections close when their owner’s scope ends; the handle is a private field.

21.4 Authority is a value

A program run from the command line has the authority of the user who ran it: it may read any file that user may read. Okkama does not change that (Section 21.7). What std does is make the authority visible. Wherever a library could act on an ambient, process-wide notion — the current directory, the environment, the standard streams — it asks instead for an object that names what it may use:

module bible/directory v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "fs/directory" take DirectoryLocating, Directory;
import "fs/path" take Path;

// A report writer is given the directory it may write into; it has no way
// to name any other.
object Reports {
    has home is DirectoryLocating;

    Reports(:home);

    location(name is string) is string {
        home.path().string() + "/" + name + ".txt";
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let nightly = Reports(home: Directory(path: Path("/srv/app/reports")));
    let scratch = Reports(home: Directory(path: Path("/tmp/run-42")));
    out.writeln(nightly.location("sales"));
    out.writeln(scratch.location("sales"));
    0;
}

Output:

/srv/app/reports/sales.txt
/tmp/run-42/sales.txt

Figure 21.1. Authority is a value: the program reaches the host only through the objects it was given, and the embedder decides which native groups exist.

Reports is given a DirectoryLocating, a role with one action, path(), and builds its file names inside that directory. It has no way to name another one: there is no chdir in std, no global "current directory" that some other code could change behind its back, and WorkingDirectory(), the process's own directory, is just one more object that does the role and has to be passed like any other. Two Reports with two directories are two writers with two different authorities, side by side in one program.

FileRoot takes the same idea down to the operating system. It opens its directory once, as a descriptor, and resolves every later path relative to it, segment by segment, so a name like ../../etc/passwd or a symbolic link planted by another process cannot lead outside: "coordinates never become joined ambient paths", as its module says. The children it returns hold descriptors of their own and stay valid after the root is closed.

This is the object-capability discipline, named by Mark Miller in his work on the E language [Miller 2006] and older than it: Dennis and Van Horn described capabilities as unforgeable references that carry the right to use what they designate [Dennis 1966]. In a capability system a function can affect only what it was given, so reading its parameters tells you what it can do. Okkama's std follows the discipline where it costs nothing and the language keeps it honest — objects cannot be forged, fields are private, roles cannot be downcast (Chapter 14) — but it is a discipline of the library, not a guarantee of the language: a program may still import runtime/fs and open a path by name, as the example of Section 21.3 did.

21.4.1 The environment and the clock

The same discipline covers the two other things a program usually reaches for without asking: its environment variables and the time.

Environment is a snapshot, not a window. Environment() reads the process environment exactly once, when it is constructed, and from then on the object answers from its own copy; nothing another part of the program does to the process can change what it says. Environment(values: …) makes one that never looked at the process at all. addition(name, value) and difference(name) return new snapshots and leave the receiver as it was, which is how a child process gets an environment of its own (Section 21.5) without the parent's changing. A variable is read like a json value (#134): text(name) gives it as a string and throws MissingEnvironmentVariable when it is not set, int, boolean and list read it typed (list splits PATH-like values at the platform's separator), and maybe(name).text() else "stranger" reads an optional one in one line. A variable that is missing and one that is empty are different answers: membership asks the first question, text the second. A name with = or NUL in it is refused before any snapshot can hold it.

Time comes through a role. Timing has three actions — the wall-clock instant(), the monotonic_instant() that only moves forward, and an async wait — and SystemClock is the object that does it with the host's clocks. Code that measures or waits asks for a Timing; a test gives it the ManualClock of Chapter 20, which advances only when the test says so, and a program can write its own:

module bible/authority v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "os/environment" take Environment;
import "time/clock" take Timing, Instant, MonotonicInstant;
import "time/duration" take Duration, DurationUnit;

// A clock that always reads the same instant: what a test or a replay
// hands to code that asks for the time.
object FixedClock does Timing {
    has at is Instant;

    FixedClock(:at);

    instant() is Instant { at; }

    monotonic_instant() is MonotonicInstant {
        MonotonicInstant(origin: at.unix_duration());
    }

    async wait(duration is Duration) is void {}
}

// What a greeting may read arrives as values: it has no other way to reach
// the process environment or the system clock.
object Greeting {
    has environment is Environment;
    has clock is Timing;

    Greeting(:environment, :clock);

    text() is string {
        let name = environment.maybe("USER").text() else "stranger";
        "hello, " + name + ", at " + clock.instant().unix_duration()::Span::seconds.string() + " s";
    }
}

main() is int {
    let noon = Instant(origin: Duration(value: 43200.rat(), unit: DurationUnit.second));
    let clock = FixedClock(at: noon);
    Stdout().writeln(Greeting(environment: Environment(values: ["USER": "ada"]), clock: clock).text());
    Stdout().writeln(Greeting(environment: Environment(values: [:]), clock: clock).text());
    0;
}

Output:

hello, ada, at 43200 s
hello, stranger, at 43200 s

Greeting can read exactly two things outside itself, and both are its fields. Run it twice with two snapshots and one fixed clock, and it prints two lines that do not depend on who runs it or when. That is the practical payoff of authority as a value: the parameters of an object are a complete list of what it can observe, so a test needs no mocking framework and a replay needs no patched system calls.

The clock keeps one more promise. A monotonic instant carries the domain of the clock that made it, and subtracting or comparing instants of two domains throws IncompatibleClock instead of returning a number that means nothing: a reading of the manual clock and a reading of the system clock are not on one line, and std will not pretend they are. An instant made directly, as FixedClock makes its own, belongs to the explicit domain.

As with directories, this is the library's discipline, and std does not yet keep it everywhere. Environment() and SystemClock() can be constructed anywhere, and some of std's own modules still do so where they should ask: the HTTP client and its sessions, TLS, async/timeout and the cookie jar make their own SystemClock(), and os/command reads Environment() to pass it on. A test of such code cannot hand it a manual clock. Making every module take its clock and its environment as values is one of the principles of the standard library's review after 0.5.3 (issue #352).

21.5 Running other programs

A program that runs another one describes it first, as a value:

let status is Commanding = Command(
    program: Path("/usr/bin/git"),
    arguments: ["status", "--short"],
    environment: environment,
    directory: repository,
);

Command (os/command) holds the program, the exact arguments, the environment and the directory, and nothing reads the process's own state behind its back. No shell is involved at any point: each argument reaches the child as one string, so a file name with a space, a quote or a semicolon is a file name and not a second command. Path("git") without a directory asks the runtime to look the program up in the PATH of the command's own environment. A program that does want to inherit says so with InheritedCommand, which reads the process environment and working directory when it runs and only then.

Process (os/process) owns the child of a command: its standard streams, signal, and async exit(), which waits for the child without blocking the other tasks. Constructing a Process does not start it; its first operation does, exactly once. close() is idempotent: it stops and reaps a running child and discards what was left unread. A process handle still open when the run ends is closed by the runtime like any other (Section 21.3), so no child outlives the program by accident.

The common case needs neither object spelled out. Run (os/run, issue #197) runs a program found on PATH with this process's environment and directory, and gives back what it printed:

let branch = await Run("git", ["rev-parse", "--abbrev-ref", "HEAD"]).text();
let finished = await Run("make", ["test"]).completion();   // any exit code

text() and bytes() want exit code 0. Any other end is CommandFailed.exited(code, errors), carrying what the program wrote to standard error, so a tool that failed cannot pass for one that printed nothing. Each stream is kept up to 1 MiB; more is CaptureLimitExceeded, not a silent cut. Run inherits the way InheritedCommand does, and its documentation says so; code that must not hand the process's environment to a child builds a Command and captures it with CommandCapture, which also sets the input, the directory and the limit.

A child that has to be talked to rather than waited for is driven through Process.streams() (issue #196). Its input does AsyncWriting and Closing; its outputs do AsyncReading, with lines() for for await. A slow child then holds up only the task that talks to it:

let child = Process(command: InheritedCommand(program: Path("sort")));
await child.streams().input().write("pear\napple\n");
child.streams().input().close();
for await child.streams().output().lines() -> line {
    Stdout().writeln(line);    // apple, then pear
}

The design leaves out what the shell gives for free and what most process APIs inherit by default: globbing, word splitting, redirection syntax, an implicit environment. Each of them is a way for data to become code or for one part of a program to act with another part's settings. A command built from values carries exactly what it was given.

21.5.1 Process workers

Section 20.4 introduced process workers: spawn of a synchronous action runs it in another process, in parallel with the program. The process boundary determines what it can receive and return.

The worker runs the same program. It runs one action instead of main, with the parent’s environment and working directory. It receives a receiver and arguments but no objects, open handles or tasks from the parent.

Only values cross. The receiver's fields and the arguments are encoded in the parent and decoded in the child: int, float, string, char, byte, bool, and arrays and maps of them. An object cannot cross, because an object is an identity (Chapter 12), and an identity does not survive a copy into another address space; a future, a closure or a native handle is the same kind of thing, and a spawn given one fails at once with spawn cannot transfer …, before any process starts. A worker that needs a file gets the path, not the open File. It opens the file itself, with the authority it was started with.

A failure comes back as text. If the action fails, its failure is written into the reply as a description, and await of the future raises a runtime failure with that text. The failure's object stays in the worker. catch e is ParseError in the parent does not match a ParseError thrown in a worker. This is the same rule seen from the other side: the error object is an identity too. A worker that should report several kinds of outcome returns them as data, an enum of results, which does cross.

Cancellation kills the worker. Unlike an async task, a synchronous worker has no suspension points for cooperative cancellation. Cancelling its future kills it; the future settles as Cancelled only after the worker has ended. A worker cancelled before starting is never started. Its defers and destroys do not run. If cleanup matters, pass it a deadline and let it finish cooperatively instead.

Output is passed on whole. What the action prints reaches the parent's standard output and error when the worker reports back, before its result, so the output of one worker is never interleaved with another's line by line. A killed worker reports nothing, and its output is dropped with it.

The narrowness is deliberate, and other languages show what the wider designs cost. Python's multiprocessing pickles arbitrary objects across the boundary, which makes an object in the child a look-alike of one in the parent: equal-looking, separately mutable, and silently out of date.
