This is the decide-then-do shape of Section 25.5, and for a command-line tool it pays off at once: the part that has logic can be tested by comparing values, and the part that does input and output has no logic left to test.

The program a user runs is three lines on top of the module:

main() is int {
    Shell().printed(Tool().outcome(ProcessArguments().strings(), Disk()));
}

main returns the exit status, and the runtime hands it to the operating system. The example below runs the same tool twice from inside a program, with fixed arguments over a small file, tally/sample.txt, so that its output can be checked:

module bible/tally_run v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout, Stderr;
import "tally/tool" take Tool, Disk, Outcome;

// The shell: run the tool, print what it decided, return its status.
object Shell {
    Shell();

    printed(outcome is Outcome) is int {
        for outcome.out() -> line { Stdout().writeln(line); }
        for outcome.err() -> line { Stderr().writeln(line); }
        outcome.code();
    }
}

main() is int {
    let tool = Tool();
    let shell = Shell();
    let first = shell.printed(tool.outcome(["--top", "2", "tally/sample.txt"], Disk()));
    Stdout().writeln("exit " + first.string());
    let second = shell.printed(tool.outcome(["-i", "-n", "2", "tally/sample.txt"], Disk()));
    Stdout().writeln("exit " + second.string());
    0;
}

Output:

2 lines, 12 words, 8 distinct
3 the
2 on
exit 0
2 lines, 12 words, 7 distinct
4 the
2 on
exit 0
  • The first run lists the two most frequent words. "the" and "The" count as different words.
  • The second run adds -i, short for --ignore-case, and -n 2, the short form of --top. The distinct count drops from 8 to 7 and "the" reaches 4.
  • Shell.printed sends out to Stdout and err to Stderr in order, and returns the code. A real program returns that code from main.

The split between Tool and Shell also decides where a future change goes. Coloured output for a terminal, a --json flag or a progress line on the standard error are changes to how decisions are printed, and they stay in the shell. Counting differently is a change to the decisions, and it stays in Tally.

23.5 Failures at the edge

A tool meets three kinds of failure, and they deserve three different answers.

A wrong command line is the user's mistake, made a moment ago and easy to fix. cli/command reports it as CliFailure.detailed(index, token, message). tally adds one refusal of its own for a negative --top, as a case of its own TallyError enum (Chapter 10). Both are answered on the standard error with the reason and a hint, Try 'tally --help'., and exit status 2. No trace is shown: the user needs to know what to type, not where the program was.

A failure of the work, here a file that does not exist or cannot be read, is answered with the file system's own description and exit status 1. fs/file has already turned the host's error into a case of FileError (Section 10.11), so the tool never sees an operating-system code and behaves the same on every platform.

A bug in the program is not caught at all. An index out of range, a broken invariant or an UndeclaredCliName ends the run with the language's failure report, and the exit status says the run failed. This is the argument of Section 10.4 applied to a tool. A catch broad enough to turn bugs into a friendly "something went wrong" would hide the one report that lets someone fix the program.

The try in Tool.outcome therefore names exactly the failures the tool can answer, CliFailure, TallyError and FileError, and nothing else. Each catch produces an Outcome, so the error paths are values too and are tested the same way as the happy path.

23.6 Testing a tool without a terminal

A command-line tool is often tested last and worst, by running it in a shell and looking at the output, because its inputs and outputs are the process's own. tally needs none of that. Its arguments are a parameter, its sources are a role, and its output is a value. A test gives all three:

module bible/tally_tests v1.0.0;

import "fs/error" take FileError;
import "tally/tool" take Tool, Sources;

// Prepared text instead of the disk and the terminal.
object Given does Sources {
    has files is %string:@string;
    has typed is @string;

    Given(:files, :typed);

    file(path is string) is @string {
        confirm files.has(path) else throw FileError.not_found(path);
        files[path];
    }

    input() is @string { typed; }
}

test "files are read in order and counted together" {
    let sources = Given(files: ["a": ["red blue"], "b": ["blue"]], typed: []);
    let outcome = Tool().outcome(["a", "b"], sources);
    test.is(outcome.code(), 0);
    test.is(outcome.out(), ["2 lines, 3 words, 2 distinct", "2 blue", "1 red"]);
}

test "no file means the standard input" {
    let sources = Given(files: [:], typed: ["one two", "two"]);
    let outcome = Tool().outcome(["-n", "1"], sources);
    test.is(outcome.out(), ["2 lines, 3 words, 2 distinct", "2 two"]);
}

test "a missing file is an error with status 1" {
    let outcome = Tool().outcome(["nowhere"], Given(files: [:], typed: []));
    test.is(outcome.code(), 1);
    test.is(outcome.err(), ["tally: FileError.not_found(\"nowhere\")"]);
    test.is(outcome.out(), []);
}

test "a bad argument is a usage error with status 2" {
    let outcome = Tool().outcome(["--top", "many"], Given(files: [:], typed: []));
    test.is(outcome.code(), 2);
    test.is(outcome.err().size(), 2);
}

test "help goes to the standard output with status 0" {
    let outcome = Tool().outcome(["--help"], Given(files: [:], typed: []));
    test.is(outcome.code(), 0);
    test.is(outcome.out().first().starts_with("Usage:"), true);
}

Output:

=== RUN   files are read in order and counted together
--- PASS: files are read in order and counted together
=== RUN   no file means the standard input
--- PASS: no file means the standard input
=== RUN   a missing file is an error with status 1
--- PASS: a missing file is an error with status 1
=== RUN   a bad argument is a usage error with status 2
--- PASS: a bad argument is a usage error with status 2
=== RUN   help goes to the standard output with status 0
--- PASS: help goes to the standard output with status 0
PASS
  • Given implements Sources with a map of file names to lines and a list of lines for the standard input. A missing name throws the same FileError.not_found the disk would throw, so the error path is real.
  • Each test calls Tool().outcome with an argument list and compares the Outcome: the status, the output lines and the message lines. The tests read like a specification of the command line: what happens with two files, with none, with a missing one, with a bad value and with --help.
  • Nothing is mocked inside the tool. Tally and WordCount are covered through the tool's own behaviour, and they could be tested directly as values if they grew more complex.

Code that reads the process's arguments itself, instead of taking them as a parameter, can still be tested: ProcessArguments(arguments: …) builds the same object from a prepared list. Taking arguments as a parameter is simpler, and is the shape this chapter recommends.

23.7 Input: whole or streamed

Disk reads a file whole, file.text().lines(), and reads the standard input whole too, through Utf8Input(origin: Stdin()).content(). For a tool that counts, this is the simple and honest choice: the result needs every line anyway, and the counts are much smaller than the text. Two properties of the standard library make it safe:

  • Decoding is strict. A file or an input that is not valid UTF-8 is refused with the position of the first bad byte. A tool that should read anything can ask for Stdin(decoding: InputDecoding.lenient), which replaces bad bytes with U+FFFD, and say so in its help.
  • Resources close on every path. The file is closed by defer whether lines() succeeds or throws, and Utf8Input is closed the same way (Chapter 11).

A tool that filters rather than counts, printing each line as it arrives the way grep does, should stream instead. for Stdin() -> line { … } reads one line at a time in batches, and for file.text() -> line { … } does the same for a file. Streaming changes the shape of the tool more than its code: the decisions can no longer be collected into one Outcome at the end. The core then becomes a value that takes one line and returns the lines to print for it, and the shell prints them as it goes. The decide-then-do split survives, at the granularity of a line.

module bible/filter v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

// A filter decides one line at a time. It keeps what the end of the run
// needs (here the number of matches) and returns what to print now.
object Matcher {
    has needle is string;
    has fold is bool = false;
    has matched is int = 0;

    Matcher(:needle, :fold);

    hit(line is string) is bool {
        if fold { line.lower().contains(needle.lower()); } else { line.contains(needle); }
    }

    // The lines to print for this input line.
    shown(line is string) is @string {
        if self.hit(line) { [line]; } else { []; }
    }

    // The matcher after this line.
    after(line is string) is ^Matcher {
        ^matched = if self.hit(line) { matched + 1; } else { matched; };
    }

    // As grep: 0 when something matched, 1 when nothing did.
    status() is int {
        if matched > 0 { 0; } else { 1; }
    }
}

// The shell: in a real tool the lines come from `for Stdin() -> line`.
object Filter {
    has input is @string;

    Filter(:input);

    run(matcher is Matcher) is int {
        let out = Stdout();
        let current = matcher;
        for input -> line {
            for current.shown(line) -> printed { out.writeln(printed); }
            current = current.after(line);
        }
        current.status();
    }
}

main() is int {
    let filter = Filter(input: ["Error: disk full", "ok", "error: retry", "ok"]);
    let first = filter.run(Matcher(needle: "error"));
    Stdout().writeln("status " + first.string());
    let second = filter.run(Matcher(needle: "error", fold: true));
    Stdout().writeln("status " + second.string());
    let third = filter.run(Matcher(needle: "panic"));
    Stdout().writeln("status " + third.string());
    0;
}

Output:

error: retry
status 0
Error: disk full
error: retry
status 0
status 1
  • Matcher is the core. shown(line) says what to print for one line and after(line) returns the matcher for the next one, with the count of matches so far. It keeps only what the end of the run needs, never the text.
  • Filter.run is the shell. It walks the lines, prints what shown returns and rebinds current to its successor. In a real tool the loop is for Stdin() -> line, and nothing else changes.
  • status() follows grep's convention: 0 when something matched, 1 when nothing did. A tool's exit status is part of its contract, and scripts test it (if tally-filter error log; then …), so the convention is chosen once and documented in the help.

cli/arguments sets its own limits. By default it reads at most 4,096 arguments and 1 MiB of them, and refuses more with ArgumentLimitExceeded instead of growing without bound. A tool that is meant to take huge argument lists, for example from xargs, can set other limits through the constructor that takes them.

23.8 Output for people and for programs

A tool's output has two readers. A person at a terminal wants alignment, emphasis and perhaps colour. A program reading a pipe wants a stable, parseable format and no escape codes. The Command Line Interface Guidelines recommend detecting which one is there, and offering --json when the output is likely to be consumed by another program [Prasad 2020].

The decision belongs at the edge, made once, from facts the program is given:

module bible/tally_output v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "os/environment" take Environment;
import "terminal/capability" take DetectedTerminalCapabilities, ColorPolicy, TerminalColorDepth;
import "terminal/style" take TextStyle, StyledText, DefaultColor, TextAttribute;
import "json" take Json, JsonField;

// What the tool found, rendered for people or for programs.
object Report {
    has lines is int;
    has words is int;
    has top is @string;

    Report(:lines, :words, :top);

    text(depth is TerminalColorDepth) is @string {
        let bold = TextStyle(foreground: DefaultColor(), background: DefaultColor(), attributes: [TextAttribute.bold]);
        let header = lines.string() + " lines, " + words.string() + " words";
        [StyledText(origin: header, style: bold).rendered(depth)] + top;
    }

    json() is string {
        let words_json = top.map() -> word { Json(word); };
        Json(JsonField("lines", lines), JsonField("words", words), JsonField("top", Json(items: words_json))).string();
    }
}

// Colours are decided once, from the facts a real run reads: whether the
// output is a terminal, the environment (NO_COLOR, TERM) and a policy.
object Display {
    has depth is TerminalColorDepth;

    Display(terminal is bool, environment is Environment) {
        let detected = DetectedTerminalCapabilities(
            input: false,
            output: terminal,
            native_depth: TerminalColorDepth.basic,
            columns: 80,
            rows: 24,
            environment: environment,
            policy: ColorPolicy.automatic,
        );
        depth = detected.capabilities()::Support::colors;
    }

    depth() is TerminalColorDepth { depth; }

    named() is string {
        match depth {
            case TerminalColorDepth.disabled { "no colour"; }
            case TerminalColorDepth.basic { "8 colours"; }
            case TerminalColorDepth.indexed { "256 colours"; }
            case TerminalColorDepth.true_color { "true colour"; }
        };
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let report = Report(lines: 2, words: 12, top: ["the", "on"]);
    let piped = Display(terminal: false, environment: Environment(values: [:]));
    let muted = Display(terminal: true, environment: Environment(values: ["NO_COLOR": "1"]));
    let shown = Display(terminal: true, environment: Environment(values: ["TERM": "xterm"]));
    for [piped, muted, shown] -> display {
        let first = report.text(display.depth()).first().replace("\u{1b}", "ESC");
        out.writeln(display.named() + ": " + first);
    }
    out.writeln(report.json());
    0;
}

Output:

no colour: 2 lines, 12 words
no colour: 2 lines, 12 words
8 colours: ESC[1;39;49m2 lines, 12 wordsESC[0m
{"lines":2,"words":12,"top":["the","on"]}
  • DetectedTerminalCapabilities decides the colour depth from whether the output is a terminal, the environment (NO_COLOR, TERM) and a policy (automatic, never, always). A pipe and NO_COLOR=1 both give no colour. A terminal gives what it supports.
  • The report is rendered for a depth, so the same Report gives plain text, coloured text or JSON. The counting code never sees any of this.
  • The facts are passed in. In a real run they come from the terminal session and Environment(). In the example they are fixed, which is why the example can check what each case prints.

The JSON form is built with the json module's Json and JsonField, not by concatenating strings, so quoting and escaping are always right. A field added later does not break readers that ignore it, which is the usual reason to prefer an object over an array at the top level.

23.9 Changing files safely

A tool that only reads cannot damage anything. A tool that rewrites files — a formatter, a migration, a bulk rename — can, and its users expect two things from it: a way to see what it would do before it does it, and an original that survives if the run is interrupted halfway.

Both follow from the decide-then-do shape. The change is a value first, and writing it is a separate step:

module bible/tidy v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "fs/path" take Path;
import "fs/file" take File, FileMode;
import "fs/entry" take FileEntry;
import "fs/directory" take Directory;
import "fs/temp" take TemporaryDirectory;

// What tidying one file would do: a value, decided before anything is written.
object Change {
    has path is Path;
    has before is @string;
    has after is @string;

    Change(:path, :before, :after);

    // How many lines differ.
    edits() is int {
        (0..before.size()).filter() -> index { before[index] != after[index]; }.size();
    }

    path() is Path { path; }
    after() is @string { after; }
}

object Tidy {
    Tidy();

    // The decision: trailing spaces removed from every line.
    planned(path is Path) is Change {
        let file = File(path: path);
        defer file.close();
        let before = file.text().lines();
        Change(path: path, before: before, after: before.map() -> line { line.trim_end(); });
    }

    // Doing it safely: write a sibling file, then move it over the original
    // in one step. A failure before the move leaves the original whole.
    applied(change is Change) is void {
        let sibling = Path(change.path().string() + ".tidy");
        let file = File(path: sibling, mode: FileMode.writing);
        for change.after() -> line { file.text().writeln(line); }
        file.close();
        FileEntry(sibling).move(destination: change.path(), overwrite: true);
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let scratch = TemporaryDirectory(parent: Directory(Path(".")), prefix: "tidy-");
    defer scratch.close();
    let notes = scratch.path().child("notes.txt");
    let seed = File(path: notes, mode: FileMode.writing);
    seed.text().writeln("buy milk   ");
    seed.text().writeln("call Ada");
    seed.text().writeln("fix the gate  ");
    seed.close();

    let tidy = Tidy();
    let change = tidy.planned(notes);
    out.writeln("--dry-run: would change " + change.edits().string() + " of 3 lines");
    tidy.applied(change);
    out.writeln("after: " + tidy.planned(notes).edits().string() + " lines to change");
    0;
}

Output:

--dry-run: would change 2 of 3 lines
after: 0 lines to change
  • Tidy.planned reads a file and returns a Change that holds the lines before and after. Nothing is written. --dry-run is simply "print the plan and stop", and costs no extra code in the core.
  • Tidy.applied writes the new text to a sibling file and then moves it over the original with FileEntry.move(destination:, overwrite: true), which replaces the destination in one step. If the run fails while writing, the original is untouched and only the sibling is left behind. A tool that must never leave even that writes through TemporaryFile in the same directory, which removes itself on close.
  • The example works inside a TemporaryDirectory made in the current directory, and defer scratch.close() removes it with everything in it, so the run leaves nothing behind.

File(path: path).text().replace(text) does all of this in one call: it writes a temporary file beside the original, synchronizes it, renames it over the original and synchronizes the directory, so after a crash or a power cut the file is the whole old text or the whole new one (#122).

A rewrite of many files should also stop cleanly when the user presses Ctrl-C. Without help a signal ends the process at once, between two files or in the middle of one, and no defer runs. An Interruption from os/signal takes SIGINT and SIGTERM instead, and the loop decides where stopping is safe:

let interruption = Interruption();
for files -> file {
    interruption.check();      // throws Interrupted between two files
    Tidy(file).applied();
}

interruption.status() is then the conventional exit status, 130 after Ctrl-C, and a second Ctrl-C during the cleanup ends the process at once (#638).

23.10 Configuration and the environment

tally has two options and no configuration, and many tools should stay that way. When a tool does grow settings, the Command Line Interface Guidelines give the usual order of precedence: flags override environment variables, which override a configuration file, which overrides the built-in defaults [Prasad 2020]. Two parts of the language help to keep that order honest.

The first is that the environment is a value, not a global (Section 21.4). A tool takes an environment snapshot in main and passes it, or the one setting it needs, to the code that uses it. Nothing deep in the program reads a variable behind its caller's back, and a test passes a prepared environment the same way tally's tests pass prepared sources.

module bible/tally_settings v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "os/environment" take Environment;
import "cli/command" take CliCommand, Option;

// The order of precedence: a flag, then the environment, then the default.
// The environment is a value given to the object, never read behind its back.
object TopSetting {
    has command is CliCommand;
    has environment is Environment;

    TopSetting(:environment) {
        command = CliCommand(name: "tally", options: [Option(name: "top", short: "n", value: "N")]);
    }

    top(arguments is @string) is int {
        let call = command.invocation(arguments);
        call.int("top") else (environment.maybe("TALLY_TOP").int() else 3);
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let plain = TopSetting(environment: Environment(values: [:]));
    let configured = TopSetting(environment: Environment(values: ["TALLY_TOP": "10"]));
    out.writeln("default: " + plain.top([]).string());
    out.writeln("environment: " + configured.top([]).string());
    out.writeln("flag: " + configured.top(["-n", "2"]).string());
    0;
}

Output:

default: 3
environment: 10
flag: 2
  • Environment(values: …) is a snapshot that contains exactly the given variables and nothing of the process, so each case in the example is isolated. A real program passes Environment(), read once in main.
  • The precedence is one expression: call.int("top") else (environment.maybe("TALLY_TOP").int() else 3). Each else is the next layer down, and the order can be read off the line.
  • A malformed value is not silently skipped. --top many is a CliFailure, and TALLY_TOP=many is an InvalidEnvironmentValue naming the variable. A layer that is present but wrong is an error, not a reason to fall through to the next layer.

The second is Invocation.settings(), which returns every value read from the command line keyed by SettingKey. A configuration file read through the config modules gives settings with the same keys, so the order of precedence becomes a sequence of layers, each laid over the one before. An option declared with an explicit key is stored under that key, which lets --top on the command line and top = 5 in a file mean the same setting.

23.11 Growing: subcommands

Tools grow by verbs. git has commit and log, cargo has build and test, and a tool that started with one job often gains a second. In cli/command a subcommand is a CliCommand listed in its parent's commands. Each declares only the options it takes, and the root can declare options shared by all of them. Reading the arguments selects one command, and call.command() returns the declared object, so the program compares objects rather than strings:

module bible/tally_commands v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "cli/command" take CliCommand, Option, Flag, CliFailure;

// Two subcommands under one root. Each declares only what it takes.
object Commands {
    has count is CliCommand;
    has top is CliCommand;
    has root is CliCommand;

    Commands() {
        let counting = CliCommand(name: "count", summary: "Count lines and words");
        let ranking = CliCommand(
            name: "top",
            summary: "List the most frequent words",
            options: [Option(name: "n", value: "N", help: "How many words")],
        );
        count = counting;
        top = ranking;
        root = CliCommand(
            name: "tally",
            flags: [Flag(name: "help", short: "h", help: "Show this help")],
            commands: [counting, ranking],
        );
    }

    // What the arguments select, as text the example can print.
    selected(arguments is @string) is string {
        try {
            let call = root.invocation(arguments);
            if call.command() == top {
                "top, n = " + (call.int("n") else 3).string();
            } else if call.command() == count {
                "count";
            } else {
                "root only, path " + call.path().join(" ");
            }
        }
        catch e is CliFailure {
            "refused: " + e.text();
        };
    }
}

main() is int {
    let commands = Commands();
    let out = Stdout();
    out.writeln(commands.selected(["count"]));
    out.writeln(commands.selected(["top", "--n", "5"]));
    out.writeln(commands.selected(["top"]));
    out.writeln(commands.selected([]));
    out.writeln(commands.selected(["sort"]));
    0;
}

Output:

count
top, n = 5
top, n = 3
refused: CliFailure.detailed(0, "", "child command required")
refused: CliFailure.detailed(0, "sort", "unknown child command")
  • top --n 5 selects top and reads its own option. top alone takes the default with else.
  • A root with subcommands is a branch. It expects one of its children, so an empty command line and an unknown verb are both a CliFailure naming the argument, which the tool answers with status 2 as in Section 23.5.
  • call.path() gives the names from the root to the selected command, for messages such as tally top: …. The usage text of a subcommand comes from its own declaration, so tally top --help can show only what top takes.

The objects in Commands are the same values the program later compares against. A subcommand is renamed in one place, and a typo in a comparison is a compile error, not a branch that is never taken.

23.12 Shipping it

A tool is used through its help text more than through its documentation. tally --help prints command.usage(program: "tally"): the summary, the usage line, and the options, flags and operands with their help, wrapped to 80 columns or to the width given. Because it is generated from the declaration, adding an option to CliCommand adds it to the help. command.completion(program: "tally", shell: CompletionShell.zsh) gives a completion script for the shell, and a tool often offers it as a hidden subcommand that users run once and save.

During development a tool runs from source, with its arguments after the file: okkama run tally.ok --top 5 notes.txt. To ship it, okkama build tally.ok -o tally.spb compiles it into a bytecode file that okkama exec runs without recompiling (Chapter 19 covers modules, packages and their versions). The program is the same either way. Its behaviour does not depend on how it was started.

23.13 What the design costs

The tool in this chapter is longer than the shortest program that would print the same counts. A twenty-line script with a loop over the arguments, a mutable map and print calls would do the job for its author. The difference is in what the extra lines buy:

  • The command line is declared once. Parsing, help and completion follow from it, and the usage text cannot drift away from the parser.
  • Every outcome is a value. The error paths are tested as easily as the normal one, and a change to output formatting cannot change what is counted.
  • Failures are sorted by kind. A user mistake gets a hint and status 2, a failed file gets status 1, and a bug keeps its report.
  • The outside world enters through one role. Tests need no terminal, no files and no process.

Two costs remain. Reading whole files holds the text in memory, which is the right trade for a counter and the wrong one for a filter (Section 23.7). And the successor style rebuilds a Tally for every line. For text in the megabytes this is fast enough. For gigabytes, a tool would count in larger steps or stream and keep only the counts, still without mutating anything it shares.

Chapter 24Building a web service

A command-line tool runs once and exits. A web service starts and keeps answering, many requests at a time, until someone stops it. This chapter builds a small one: a JSON API for notes, with the four operations most services begin with, list, read, create and delete:

GET    /api/notes        a page of notes: {"items": […], "next": "…"}
POST   /api/notes        create one from {"title": "…"}; 201 and its location
GET    /api/notes/:id    one note, or 404
DELETE /api/notes/:id    remove it; 204, or 404

The previous chapter's habits carry over: decide in values, keep the outside world behind a role, test without the real thing. What is new is concurrency. Requests overlap, so state shared between them needs an owner (Section 25.9), and every endpoint is an async action (Chapter 20). The chapter builds the service over memory first, then puts PostgreSQL behind the same role without touching a line of the API.

24.1 What a service is made of

HTTP is a protocol of messages. A request carries a method, a target, header fields and perhaps a body; a response carries a status, header fields and perhaps a body [RFC 9110]. A service is a function from requests to responses that keeps some state between them. The standard library's web modules give that function a shape with four parts, each of them a value:

  • A route table (web/routing) says which method and path reach which endpoint. It is declared, like cli/command's commands in Chapter 23, and it is checked when it is built: two routes with the same shape are refused, a known path with the wrong method answers 405 with Allow, and HEAD follows GET.
  • An endpoint is any bound action of type async (WebRequest) is Responding. A controller object keeps its dependencies in its fields and offers one action per operation.
  • A request (web/request) gives the route parameters, the query, the header fields and a body read under a byte limit, each typed.
  • A reply (web/reply) is a value that knows how to become a response: JsonReply, CreatedReply, NoContentReply, TextReply and others, each with the defaults of its kind.

The server itself (web/app) binds the table to an address and serves it. It is the only part that touches the network, and the tests in this chapter never start it.

24.2 The service

The notes service is one module. Its parts are shown together, then taken one at a time.

module notes/api v1.0.0;

// A small JSON API for notes: list, show, create, remove.
import "async/atomic" take Atomic;
import "json" take Json, JsonField;
import "http/message" take Responding;
import "web/request" take WebRequest;
import "http/status" take Status;
import "web/reply" take JsonReply, CreatedReply, NoContentReply;
import "web/exception" take Exception, ProblemReply;
import "web/routing" take WebRoutes, Scope, Resource, Get, Post, Delete, ExceptionScope;

object Note {
    has id is int;
    has title is string;

    Note(:id, :title);

    id() is int { id; }
    title() is string { title; }

    json() is Json {
        Json(JsonField("id", id), JsonField("title", title));
    }
}

// What a store refuses. The store knows the rule; the service knows the status.
enum StoreRefusal is Error = (duplicate(title is string));

// Where notes live. The API sees a role; memory and a database are two doers.
role NoteStore {
    // Up to count notes with identifiers above id, in identifier order.
    async after(id is int, count is int) is @Note;
    async find(id is int) is Maybe<Note>;
    // A new note; StoreRefusal.duplicate if the title is taken.
    async added(title is string) is Note;
    async removed(id is int) is bool;
}

// Everything the store holds, as one value: replaced whole, never edited.
object Shelf {
    has upcoming is int = 1;
    has notes is %int:Note = [:];

    Shelf(:upcoming, :notes);

    upcoming() is int { upcoming; }
    notes() is %int:Note { notes; }
}

object MemoryStore does NoteStore {
    has shelf is Atomic<Shelf>;

    MemoryStore() {
        shelf = Atomic(Shelf());
    }

    async after(id is int, count is int) is @Note {
        shelf.value().notes().values().filter() -> note { note.id() > id; }.take(count);
    }

    async find(id is int) is Maybe<Note> {
        let notes = shelf.value().notes();
        if notes.has(id) { Maybe.some(notes[id]); } else { Maybe.none; }
    }

    // Read, decide, publish only if nobody published in between.
    async added(title is string) is Note {
        loop {
            let current = shelf.value();
            let taken = current.notes().values().filter() -> note { note.title() == title; };
            confirm taken.size() == 0 else throw StoreRefusal.duplicate(title);
            let note = Note(id: current.upcoming(), title: title);
            let revised = Shelf(upcoming: current.upcoming() + 1, notes: current.notes() + [note.id(): note]);
            if shelf.compare_and_replace(expected: current, revised: revised) {
                last note;
            }
        };
    }

    async removed(id is int) is bool {
        loop {
            let current = shelf.value();
            if !current.notes().has(id) {
                last false;
            }
            let revised = Shelf(upcoming: current.upcoming(), notes: current.notes() - [id: current.notes()[id]]);
            if shelf.compare_and_replace(expected: current, revised: revised) {
                last true;
            }
        };
    }
}

object NotesApi {
    has store is NoteStore;

    NotesApi(:store);

    // One page: ?after=<id>&limit=<n>, and where the next page starts.
    async list(request is WebRequest) is Responding {
        let after = request.query().maybe("after").int() else 0;
        let limit = request.query().maybe("limit").int() else 20;
        confirm limit >= 1 && limit <= 100 else throw Exception.status(400, "limit must be from 1 to 100");
        let found = await store.after(after, limit + 1);
        let shown = found.take(limit);
        let items = JsonField("items", Json(items: shown.map() -> note { note.json(); }));
        if found.size() > limit {
            let onward = "/api/notes?after=" + shown[limit - 1].id().string() + "&limit=" + limit.string();
            JsonReply(value: Json(items, JsonField("next", onward)));
        } else {
            JsonReply(value: Json(items));
        }
    }

    async show(request is WebRequest) is Responding {
        let id = request.path().int("id");
        match await store.find(id) {
            case Maybe.some(note) { JsonReply(value: note.json()); }
            case Maybe.none { throw Exception.status(404, "no note " + id.string()); }
        };
    }

    async add(request is WebRequest) is Responding {
        let body = await request.json(4096);
        let title = body.text("title").trim();
        confirm !title.empty() else throw Exception.status(422, "title is empty");
        let note = await store.added(title);
        CreatedReply(location: "/api/notes/" + note.id().string(), value: note.json());
    }

    async remove(request is WebRequest) is Responding {
        let id = request.path().int("id");
        confirm await store.removed(id) else throw Exception.status(404, "no note " + id.string());
        NoContentReply();
    }
}

// Turns the store's refusals into statuses; any other error passes outwards.
object StoreRefusals does ExceptionScope {
    StoreRefusals();

    async scoped(request is WebRequest, endpoint is async (WebRequest) is Responding) is Responding {
        let reply is Responding = try {
            await endpoint(request);
        }
        catch StoreRefusal.duplicate(title) {
            ProblemReply(status: Status.conflict, detail: "a note titled '" + title + "' exists");
        };
        reply;
    }
}

// The route table: one place that says which URL reaches which action.
object NotesService {
    has api is NotesApi;

    NotesService(:api);

    routes() is WebRoutes {
        WebRoutes(
            Scope("/api", StoreRefusals(),
                Resource("/notes", Get(api.list), Post(api.add)),
                Resource("/notes/:id", Get(api.show), Delete(api.remove)),
            ),
        );
    }
}
  • Note is a value with an identifier and a title, and knows its JSON form.
  • NoteStore is the role for storage. The API depends on the role, so memory today and a database tomorrow are two implementations of one contract (Section 25.5). Its actions are async, because a database answers later; Section 24.9 shows that doer.
  • StoreRefusal is what a store may refuse: a title that is already taken. The store knows the rule; it does not know HTTP.
  • MemoryStore keeps every note in one Shelf value inside an Atomic. Section 24.8 explains why it is built that way.
  • NotesApi is the controller. Each endpoint reads what it needs from the request, asks the store, and returns a reply.
  • StoreRefusals is an exception scope: it turns the store's refusals into statuses (Section 24.6).
  • NotesService.routes() is the route table: one place that says which URL reaches which action. Scope("/api", …) writes the prefix once, and Resource writes a path once for several methods.

24.3 Endpoints

An endpoint reads the request through typed accessors. request.path().int("id") reads the :id of the pattern as an int; a value that is not a number is answered 400 by the framework before the endpoint continues, so /api/notes/seven never reaches the store. The query and the header fields read the same way. A parameter that may be absent is read with maybe, which gives a Maybe (Chapter 7), so a default is one else: request.query().maybe("limit").int() else 20. Absent means the default; present but malformed, ?limit=many, is still a 400. The endpoint never sees a string where it asked for a number.

The body is read with a limit: await request.json(4096) accepts at most 4096 bytes, requires a JSON media type and parses the document at once. A body that is too large is a 413, a body of the wrong type a 415, a syntax error a 400, and a member that is missing or of the wrong kind, read later from the returned RequestJson, a 422 that names the JSON pointer. None of these needs a line in the endpoint. Reading without a limit is not offered: a service that accepts any body accepts a body larger than its memory.

Replies are values. JsonReply(value:) is 200 with application/json; CreatedReply(location:, value:) is 201 with a Location field and the new resource; NoContentReply() is 204 with no body at all. Each takes only what differs from its defaults, so an endpoint states its outcome and not the framing. A reply cannot be inconsistent: TextReply(text: "", status: Status.no_content) is refused with InvalidReply, because a 204 cannot carry a body, even an empty one. NoContentReply is the way to say "nothing".

An endpoint ends with one reply or one thrown error, and nothing in between writes to the network. add is typical: read the body, check the title, ask the store, answer 201. It has no status codes for the body's own failures, no header handling and no serialisation code, because each of those belongs to a value that already knows it.

24.4 Lists come in pages

A list endpoint that returns every note works on the first day and fails on a later one, when a client asks for a hundred thousand notes and the service builds the whole answer in memory. A list in an API is therefore a page: some items, and a way to ask for the ones after them.

There are two common ways to say "the ones after them". An offset page asks for "items 40 to 59": ?offset=40&limit=20. It is easy to write and has two faults. A note created or deleted before position 40 while the client reads shifts every later item by one, so the client sees one note twice or misses one. And a database answers an offset by reading and throwing away the first forty rows, so the fortieth page costs forty times the first. A keyset page, also called a cursor page, asks for "items after the last one I saw": ?after=40&limit=20, where 40 is the identifier of the previous page's last note. Creations and deletions elsewhere in the list do not move it, and a database answers it from the index on the key, so every page costs the same.

NotesApi.list is a keyset page:

  • after and limit come from the query, with defaults 0 and 20. A limit outside 1..100 is a 400; a service sets its own upper bound, because a client that may ask for any number of items may ask for all of them.
  • The endpoint asks the store for limit + 1 notes. If it gets more than limit, there is a next page, and the extra note is not shown; this costs one item and saves a second query that would count.
  • The answer is {"items": […]}, plus "next": "/api/notes?after=2&limit=2" when there is a next page. The client follows the link it was given and never builds one. When next is absent, the list is over.

The order is the store's, and it must be stable. MemoryStore.after filters and takes from notes().values(), which is in identifier order because a map keeps its keys sorted (Section 8.3): iteration order never depends on hashing or on the order of insertion, so two calls with the same after see the same sequence. A store over a database writes the same contract as ORDER BY id.

The cursor here is the identifier itself, which is fine for a list ordered by identifier. A list ordered by something else, a date or a title, needs a cursor that carries every key of the order, and services usually make it opaque (an encoded token) so that clients cannot build one by hand. The endpoint changes; the shape, items plus a link, does not.

24.5 Failures become statuses

A service has the same three kinds of failure as a tool (Section 23.5), and HTTP gives each a place.

The client's mistakes are 4xx statuses. An endpoint states its own with throw Exception.status(404, "no note 9"), and confirm … else throw turns a precondition into one (confirm await store.removed(id) else throw …). The framework answers a thrown Exception with a problem-details body, RFC 9457's standard JSON form for errors [RFC 9457]:

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"type":"about:blank","title":"Not Found","status":404,"detail":"no note 9"}

Clients get one shape for every error, and the detail goes to them, so it must never carry internal diagnostics.

Translated failures of the layers below are the subject of the next section: the store refuses in its own terms, and an exception scope turns the refusal into a status.

Bugs are not caught. Any other error reaches the server, which answers 500 without a body. The client learns that the request failed and nothing about why, which is both the safe answer and the honest one. A failure of the database itself, a lost connection or a timeout, takes the same path: it is not the client's mistake, and nothing the client could change would fix it.

24.6 Exception scopes

The store refuses a duplicate title with StoreRefusal.duplicate(title), an error of its own. It could have thrown Exception.status(409, …) directly, and it would have been wrong to: a store that speaks HTTP cannot be used by a command-line import tool, and every other caller would have to know that 409 means "taken". The refusal belongs to the store; the status belongs to the service.

The translation is an object that does ExceptionScope. Its one action, scoped, receives the request and the endpoint, runs the endpoint, and answers what it throws:

object StoreRefusals does ExceptionScope {
    StoreRefusals();

    async scoped(request is WebRequest, endpoint is async (WebRequest) is Responding) is Responding {
        let reply is Responding = try {
            await endpoint(request);
        }
        catch StoreRefusal.duplicate(title) {
            ProblemReply(status: Status.conflict, detail: "a note titled '" + title + "' exists");
        };
        reply;
    }
}

The table gives it a place: Scope("/api", StoreRefusals(), …) puts it around every route of the scope. A scope can sit on the whole table, on a Scope or on a Resource, at the level where its errors can occur, and the rules are the ones of Section 10.12's boundary:

  • It catches what it knows. StoreRefusals names one case of one enum. Every other error passes outwards unchanged, to the next scope or to the framework.
  • Outer before inner. Exception scopes and arounds run outer before inner, and within one level in the order they are written. An error thrown by the endpoint meets the innermost scope first.
  • The framework is last. After every scope has had its chance, the framework answers a thrown Exception with its problem reply, and lets anything else reach the server's 500.

A scope answers with a reply, ProblemReply(status:, detail:) here, which gives the same RFC 9457 body as a thrown Exception. It could also throw Exception.status(409, …) and let the framework answer; the reply is more direct, and it lets a scope add header fields, a Retry-After for a quota for example.

The test that checks it is a client's test: post the same title twice and read a 409 with the problem's detail. When Section 24.9 replaces the store, the refusal comes from a database constraint instead of a scan, and this scope and this test stay as they are.

24.7 Code around endpoints

Some concerns belong to every request rather than to one endpoint: an access log, authentication, a maintenance switch, headers that every reply carries. web/routing puts them in the table with Around, at the level they apply to: the whole table, a Scope, or a Resource. An around is any object that does Surrounding: it receives the request and the rest of the chain as inner, and may call it, work with its reply, or answer by itself.

The standard library brings AccessLog, BearerAuth and Cors. The example below makes reading public and changing guarded, and adds its own around:

module bible/notes_guarded v1.0.0;

import "async/atomic" take Atomic;
import "json" take Json, JsonField;
import "http/body" take JsonBody;
import "http/header" take Headers, Header;
import "http/message" take Responding;
import "http/status" take Status;
import "web/request" take WebRequest;
import "web/exception" take ProblemReply;
import "web/routing" take WebRoutes, Scope, Resource, Get, Post, Delete, Around, Surrounding;
import "web/around" take BearerAuth;
import "web/testing" take WebTestClient;
import "notes/api" take NotesApi, MemoryStore;

// An around that may answer by itself: while the switch is on, every request
// gets 503 and no endpoint runs.
object Maintenance does Surrounding {
    has on is Atomic<bool>;

    Maintenance(:on);

    async around(request is WebRequest, inner is async (WebRequest) is Responding) is Responding {
        if on.value() {
            ProblemReply(status: Status.service_unavailable, detail: "down for maintenance");
        } else {
            await inner(request);
        }
    }
}

// Reading is public; changing needs the token.
object Guarded {
    has api is NotesApi;
    has switch is Atomic<bool>;

    Guarded(:api, :switch);

    routes() is WebRoutes {
        WebRoutes(
            Around(Maintenance(on: switch)),
            Scope("/api",
                Resource("/notes", Get(api.list)),
                Resource("/notes/:id", Get(api.show)),
                Scope("/notes", Around(BearerAuth(token: "s3cret")),
                    Post(path: "", endpoint: api.add),
                    Delete(path: "/:id", endpoint: api.remove),
                ),
            ),
        );
    }
}

object Setup {
    has switch is Atomic<bool>;

    Setup() {
        switch = Atomic(false);
    }

    client() is WebTestClient {
        WebTestClient(Guarded(api: NotesApi(store: MemoryStore()), switch: switch).routes());
    }

    switch() is Atomic<bool> { switch; }
}

object Token {
    Token();

    headers() is Headers {
        Headers(Header(name: "Authorization", value: "Bearer s3cret"));
    }
}

async test "reading needs no token" {
    test.is((await Setup().client().get("/api/notes"))::Head::code, 200);
}

async test "changing without the token is a 401" {
    let reply = await Setup().client().post("/api/notes", JsonBody(Json(JsonField("title", "x"))));
    test.is(reply::Head::code, 401);
}

async test "changing with the token works" {
    let body = JsonBody(Json(JsonField("title", "tea")));
    let reply = await Setup().client().post(target: "/api/notes", body: body, headers: Token().headers());
    test.is(reply::Head::code, 201);
}

async test "maintenance answers before any endpoint" {
    let setup = Setup();
    let client = setup.client();
    setup.switch().replace(true);
    test.is((await client.get("/api/notes"))::Head::code, 503);
    setup.switch().replace(false);
    test.is((await client.get("/api/notes"))::Head::code, 200);
}

Output:

=== RUN   reading needs no token
--- PASS: reading needs no token
=== RUN   changing without the token is a 401
--- PASS: changing without the token is a 401
=== RUN   changing with the token works
--- PASS: changing with the token works
=== RUN   maintenance answers before any endpoint
--- PASS: maintenance answers before any endpoint
PASS
  • Around(BearerAuth(token: …)) sits on the inner Scope("/notes", …) that holds only POST and DELETE, so the GET routes beside it are untouched. A request without Authorization: Bearer s3cret gets 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer; the token is compared in constant time.
  • Maintenance is the application's own around. While its switch is on it answers 503 itself and never calls inner, so no endpoint runs. The switch is an Atomic<bool>: an operator can flip it from another task, and every request sees one consistent value.
  • Arounds run outer before inner, in the order they are written, so maintenance is decided before authentication, and authentication before the endpoint.

An around and an exception scope look alike and differ in what they see. An around sees every request and every reply, including the problem reply of an Exception thrown further in; an exception scope sees only the errors that an endpoint throws, and only the ones it names. Logging and authentication are arounds; translating a layer's errors is a scope.

An around is where cross-cutting code goes, and only there. An endpoint that checks a token itself, or writes its own log line, is the "same defer around every use" smell of Section 25.7 in HTTP form.

24.8 State shared between requests

Requests are served concurrently, so the store is shared by every task that serves a request. Okkama does not let objects change in place, and a Cell cannot cross into async code (Section 25.9). That leaves two shapes: an owner task that receives messages, or an Atomic, one value that tasks share and replace whole.

MemoryStore uses an Atomic, and keeps everything it owns in one value, Shelf: the next identifier and the map of notes. Adding a note reads the shelf, checks that the title is free, builds a new shelf with the note added, and publishes it with compare_and_replace(expected:, revised:), which succeeds only if no other task published since the read. If one did, the loop reads again and decides again. Deleting works the same way. Each operation is one atomic publication of a complete, consistent value, so a reader never sees a note without its identifier counted, and two concurrent creations never get the same identifier.

The check and the publication are one decision. If added checked the title against one shelf and published against another, two requests with the same title could both pass the check. Because the check is inside the loop, a retry checks again against the shelf it will publish over, and the rule "titles are unique" holds for every value that is ever published.

When does the retry actually happen? Section 20.3 says that the code of a task between two suspension points is never interleaved with another task's. MemoryStore.added is async but never awaits, so two requests cannot interleave inside it, and today its loop always succeeds the first time. The loop is there for the version that waits: a store that asks a spam filter about the title between reading the shelf and publishing has a suspension point in the middle, other requests run there, and compare_and_replace is what notices that the shelf moved. The loop costs one comparison when it succeeds, and it keeps the store correct under a change that nobody will remember to review for concurrency.

The owner-task shape of Section 25.9 suits stores that do slow work in order, such as appending to a file. A store that already lives elsewhere, a database, needs neither: it is a role whose implementation sends queries, and the database is the owner.

24.9 A database behind the role

NoteStore was written for this moment. A store over PostgreSQL is another doer of the same role, in a module of its own:

module notes/postgres v1.0.0;

// The same NoteStore over PostgreSQL, with this table:
//
//     CREATE TABLE notes (id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, title text NOT NULL UNIQUE);
import "db/pool" take DbPool;
import "db/error" take DbFailure;
import "db/value" take DbInteger, DbText;
import "db/row" take Row;
import "api" take Note, NoteStore, StoreRefusal;

object PostgresStore does NoteStore {
    has pool is DbPool;

    PostgresStore(:pool);

    async after(id is int, count is int) is @Note {
        let db = await pool.connection();
        defer db.close();
        let rows = await db.query("SELECT id, title FROM notes WHERE id > $1 ORDER BY id LIMIT $2",
            DbInteger(id), DbInteger(count)).all(count);
        rows.map() -> row { self.note(row); };
    }

    async find(id is int) is Maybe<Note> {
        let db = await pool.connection();
        defer db.close();
        match await db.query("SELECT id, title FROM notes WHERE id = $1", DbInteger(id)).maybe() {
            case Maybe.some(row) { Maybe.some(self.note(row)); }
            case Maybe.none { Maybe.none; }
        };
    }

    // The UNIQUE constraint decides, and SQLSTATE 23505 says it refused.
    async added(title is string) is Note {
        let db = await pool.connection();
        defer db.close();
        let row = try {
            await db.query("INSERT INTO notes (title) VALUES ($1) RETURNING id, title", DbText(title)).one();
        }
        catch DbFailure.detailed(kind, operation, code, message) {
            if code == "23505" {
                throw StoreRefusal.duplicate(title);
            }
            throw;
        };
        self.note(row);
    }

    async removed(id is int) is bool {
        let db = await pool.connection();
        defer db.close();
        match await db.query("DELETE FROM notes WHERE id = $1 RETURNING id", DbInteger(id)).maybe() {
            case Maybe.some(row) { true; }
            case Maybe.none { false; }
        };
    }

    hidden note(row is Row) is Note {
        Note(id: row.int("id"), title: row.text("title"));
    }
}
  • It holds a pool, not a connection. DbPool (db/pool) hands out connections and takes them back. Each action takes one, and defer db.close() returns it to the pool on every way out, a failure included (Chapter 11). Requests run concurrently, and one connection runs one statement at a time, so a store that held one connection would make every request wait for the others.
  • Parameters are never SQL text. $1 and $2 are PostgreSQL's placeholders, and the values travel separately, as DbInteger(id) and DbText(title). A title such as '); DROP TABLE notes; -- is a strange note and nothing more.
  • The database decides uniqueness. The table declares title UNIQUE, and an insert of a taken title fails with SQLSTATE 23505, which the driver reports as DbFailure.detailed with that code. added catches it, throws the role's StoreRefusal.duplicate, and rethrows every other failure with a bare throw; (Section 10.6). There is no read-then-write, and no race between two servers: the constraint is checked where the data lives.
  • Pages come from the index. WHERE id > $1 ORDER BY id LIMIT $2 is the keyset page of Section 24.4 in SQL. With the primary key's index, the thousandth page costs what the first does. .all(count) reads at most the rows it asked for.
  • Each read takes only what it needs. .maybe() is at most one row, .one() exactly one, .all(max_rows) a bounded list (db/row). removed asks for the deleted row back, RETURNING id, so "was there a note" is the presence of a row and not a count to compare.

What did not change is the point. NotesApi, StoreRefusals, the route table and every test of Section 24.10 are the same code. The duplicate title is still a 409, because StoreRefusals translates the role's refusal, whichever doer raised it. The role's actions became async once, when the role was written, and the memory store pays little for it: an action that never awaits runs its body to the end the first time it is awaited (Section 20.3).

Wiring is a different main (Section 24.11), and it is the only place that names PostgreSQL:

let pool = DbPool(
    origin: PostgresConnector(PostgresDatabase(url: "postgresql://notes@127.0.0.1:5432/notes")),
    options: PoolOptions(minimum: 0, maximum: 8, idle_timeout: Duration(minutes: 5),
        lifetime: Duration(minutes: 30), acquisition_timeout: Duration(seconds: 5)),
    clock: SystemClock(),
);
defer pool.close();
let service = NotesService(api: NotesApi(store: PostgresStore(pool: pool)));

Building the pool opens nothing; the first connection is made when the first request needs one. PoolOptions bounds the pool, at most eight connections here, replaced after five idle minutes or thirty in service, and a request that cannot get a connection within five seconds fails with TimedOut, which reaches the client as a 500, not as a hang.

The tests of this chapter run over MemoryStore, in the book's sandbox, with no database. They check the HTTP contract, which is the same for both stores. What they cannot check is that the SQL is right: that RETURNING names the columns note reads, that the constraint has the code the store expects. That belongs to a second run of the same tests with Fresh building a PostgresStore over a disposable database, in CI, where a database is part of the environment. One suite, two stores: the role is the contract, and both doers are tested against it.

24.10 Testing without a network

web/testing gives WebTestClient, which calls a route table the way a real HTTP client calls a server, without a socket. A request goes through the routes, their arounds and exception scopes, and comes back as the same ClientResponse a real client reads:

module bible/notes_tests v1.0.0;

import "json" take Json, JsonField;
import "http/body" take JsonBody;
import "async/collect" take AllFutures;
import "web/testing" take WebTestClient;
import "notes/api" take NotesService, NotesApi, MemoryStore;

object Fresh {
    Fresh();

    client() is WebTestClient {
        WebTestClient(NotesService(api: NotesApi(store: MemoryStore())).routes());
    }
}

async test "a created note can be listed and read" {
    let client = Fresh().client();
    let created = await client.post("/api/notes", JsonBody(Json(JsonField("title", "buy tea"))));
    test.is(created::Head::code, 201);
    let page = await client.get("/api/notes/1");
    test.is(page::Head::code, 200);
    test.is((await page.json()).text("title"), "buy tea");
    let all = await client.get("/api/notes");
    test.is((await all.json()).get("items").size(), 1);
}

async test "a missing note is a 404 problem" {
    let page = await Fresh().client().get("/api/notes/9");
    test.is(page::Head::code, 404);
    test.is((await page.json()).text("detail"), "no note 9");
}

async test "an empty title is refused with 422" {
    let reply = await Fresh().client().post("/api/notes", JsonBody(Json(JsonField("title", "  "))));
    test.is(reply::Head::code, 422);
}

async test "a removed note is gone" {
    let client = Fresh().client();
    await client.post("/api/notes", JsonBody(Json(JsonField("title", "call Ada"))));
    test.is((await client.delete("/api/notes/1"))::Head::code, 204);
    test.is((await client.get("/api/notes/1"))::Head::code, 404);
    test.is((await client.delete("/api/notes/1"))::Head::code, 404);
}

async test "a non-number id is a 400" {
    test.is((await Fresh().client().get("/api/notes/seven"))::Head::code, 400);
}

async test "a page links to the next one until the end" {
    let client = Fresh().client();
    for ["tea", "milk", "bread", "eggs", "salt"] -> title {
        await client.post("/api/notes", JsonBody(Json(JsonField("title", title))));
    }
    let first = await (await client.get("/api/notes?limit=2")).json();
    test.is(first.get("items").size(), 2);
    test.is(first.text("next"), "/api/notes?after=2&limit=2");
    let second = await (await client.get(first.text("next"))).json();
    test.is(second.get("items").at(0).text("title"), "bread");
    let third = await (await client.get(second.text("next"))).json();
    test.is(third.get("items").size(), 1);
    test.is(third.has("next"), false);
}

async test "a limit out of range is a 400" {
    test.is((await Fresh().client().get("/api/notes?limit=0"))::Head::code, 400);
    test.is((await Fresh().client().get("/api/notes?limit=many"))::Head::code, 400);
}

async test "a taken title is a 409 problem" {
    let client = Fresh().client();
    await client.post("/api/notes", JsonBody(Json(JsonField("title", "buy tea"))));
    let again = await client.post("/api/notes", JsonBody(Json(JsonField("title", "buy tea"))));
    test.is(again::Head::code, 409);
    test.is((await again.json()).text("detail"), "a note titled 'buy tea' exists");
}

// One client creating one note, as a task of its own.
object Poster {
    has client is WebTestClient;
    has title is string;

    Poster(:client, :title);

    async run() is int {
        let reply = await client.post("/api/notes", JsonBody(Json(JsonField("title", title))));
        reply::Head::code;
    }
}

async test "concurrent creations all land, each with its own id" {
    let client = Fresh().client();
    let posting is @Future<int> = [
        spawn Poster(client: client, title: "one").run(),
        spawn Poster(client: client, title: "two").run(),
        spawn Poster(client: client, title: "three").run(),
        spawn Poster(client: client, title: "four").run(),
    ];
    await AllFutures(origins: posting).results();
    let page = await (await client.get("/api/notes")).json();
    let ids = page.get("items").items().map() -> item { item.int("id"); };
    test.is(ids, [1, 2, 3, 4]);
}

Output:

=== RUN   a created note can be listed and read
--- PASS: a created note can be listed and read
=== RUN   a missing note is a 404 problem
--- PASS: a missing note is a 404 problem
=== RUN   an empty title is refused with 422
--- PASS: an empty title is refused with 422
=== RUN   a removed note is gone
--- PASS: a removed note is gone
=== RUN   a non-number id is a 400
--- PASS: a non-number id is a 400
=== RUN   a page links to the next one until the end
--- PASS: a page links to the next one until the end
=== RUN   a limit out of range is a 400
--- PASS: a limit out of range is a 400
=== RUN   a taken title is a 409 problem
--- PASS: a taken title is a 409 problem
=== RUN   concurrent creations all land, each with its own id
--- PASS: concurrent creations all land, each with its own id
PASS
  • Fresh().client() builds the whole service over an empty MemoryStore, so every test starts from nothing and tests cannot see each other's notes.
  • The tests check what a client sees: statuses (::Head::code), JSON bodies and the problem detail. They exercise the framework's own answers too, the 400 for a non-number identifier or limit and the 404 for a missing note.
  • The paging test follows next exactly as a client would, from the first page to the last, and checks that the last page has no link. It never builds a URL of its own after the first.
  • Tests are async test, because endpoints are async actions.
  • Nothing here listens on a port, so the tests run in parallel with others, in the book's sandbox, and in CI without a network.

The last test is about concurrency. Poster is one client creating one note, and spawn Poster(…).run() starts it as a task of the current run (Section 20.4); four of them run concurrently against one service, and AllFutures(origins:).results() waits for all four. The test then reads the list and expects identifiers 1 to 4. A lost update would show here: notes are keyed by identifier, so two creations that got the same one would leave three notes, not four.

As Section 24.8 explained, this store cannot lose an update today, because nothing interleaves inside added. The test is still worth its lines. It states the property that clients rely on, four creations make four notes, in the terms they see it, and it keeps stating it when someone adds an await to added. A test of concurrency that passes on correct code and would fail on a plausible wrong change is the kind worth keeping; one that only passes is not.

24.11 Running it

The program that serves the API for real is short:

async main() is int {
    let service = NotesService(api: NotesApi(store: MemoryStore()));
    await WebApplication(service.routes()).listen(address: "127.0.0.1", port: 8000);
    0;
}

With PostgreSQL, main builds the pool and the store of Section 24.9 instead of MemoryStore(), and keeps everything else.

listen serves until the process receives SIGTERM or SIGINT. Then the server stops accepting connections, gives the requests in flight ten seconds to finish, closes, and listen returns, so main can finish its own cleanup: the defer pool.close() of the database version runs after the last request has finished with its connection. A second signal ends the process at once. A deployment that stops a service with SIGTERM therefore gets a graceful shutdown without any code in the service.

The address is an IP literal; web/app does no name resolution. The port, the address, the database URL and other settings come in the same layers as a tool's (Section 23.10): a flag, then the environment, then a default, read in main and passed down. A database password does not belong in a URL that a log might print: PostgresDatabase(url:, password:) takes it separately, as SecretBytes. HTTPS takes a TLS identity, listen(address:, port:, tls:), and then offers HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1 to clients.

24.12 What the design costs

The service is longer than a script that would answer the same four requests with a mutable dictionary and a handler per URL. What the extra length buys:

  • Every request is checked before it reaches the endpoint: the route, the method, the path and query parameters, the media type and the body size. An endpoint starts with values that already make sense.
  • Errors have one shape (RFC 9457) and the right status. A layer's refusals are translated in one place, and bugs are not dressed up as client mistakes.
  • Lists are bounded. No request can make the service build an answer of every note, and pages stay correct while the list changes.
  • Shared state cannot be torn. The store publishes whole values through an Atomic, the one thing tasks can share and replace, and an Atomic is replaced whole, never in part.
  • Storage is replaceable. The database arrived as a new doer of the role, and the API, the routes and the tests did not change.
  • The service is tested as its clients see it, without a network and without a running server.

The memory store pays for it with a copy of the shelf on every change, and with a scan of every title on every creation. For a store of a few thousand notes both are invisible; for millions, the store belongs in a database behind the same role, where the index does the scan and there is no copy. The async endpoints and the async role cost a little per request compared to synchronous ones; Chapter 20 explains what that buys.

Chapter 25Patterns and anti-patterns

Every language comes with a second grammar that no parser checks: the shapes experienced programmers reach for when a problem has a familiar outline. Some of those shapes exist because the language makes the direct solution awkward; some exist because the direct solution is wrong and the shape is how people learned to avoid it. This chapter collects the shapes Okkama programs take, the ones it makes unnecessary, and the ones it forbids. Most of them have appeared already, one chapter at a time; here they are put side by side, with the reasons that connect them.

25.1 What a pattern is, and what a language does to it

The word comes from architecture. Christopher Alexander and his colleagues described a pattern as a problem that occurs over and over in an environment, together with the core of a solution that can be used a million times without being done the same way twice, and they wrote 253 of them, from the shape of a region down to the height of a window sill [Alexander 1977]. The idea crossed into software in 1994, when Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides catalogued 23 patterns of object-oriented design: Strategy, Decorator, Observer, Builder, Singleton and the rest [Gamma 1994]. The book gave a generation of programmers a shared vocabulary.

It also gave critics a target. Two years later Peter Norvig showed that 16 of the 23 patterns become invisible or much simpler in a language with first-class functions, dynamic types and macros: a Strategy is a function, a Command is a closure, a Visitor is a generic function [Norvig 1996]. His point was not that the patterns were wrong but that a pattern is often the shadow of a missing feature. Where the language has the feature, the pattern disappears into it.

The opposite shadow has a name too. Andrew Koenig called an antipattern a solution that looks like a pattern but makes things worse [Koenig 1995], and Brown and his co-authors built a catalogue of them, from the Blob to Lava Flow [Brown 1998]. An antipattern is a pattern a language allows and should not.

Okkama sits at a particular point between the two. It removes several features whose absence creates patterns elsewhere: there is no inheritance, no null, no mutable field, no global state, no getter syntax. And it adds rules that turn some well-known antipatterns into compile errors. The result is a language in which a handful of shapes are not patterns at all but the only way to write the program, and in which the remaining judgement is narrower than in Java or Kotlin, though not absent.

25.2 Behaviour by composition, not by flags

A common way to make an object do several related things is to give it switches. A label that can be prefixed and framed gets a prefix field and a framed flag, and its one action reads them on every call. Adding a third option means touching the constructor, the fields and every branch of the action; combining options means testing every combination of flags.

Okkama has no inheritance to tempt a programmer into a subclass per option, so the alternative the language offers is the one Elegant Objects argues for: one small object per behaviour, each holding the object it decorates, all doing the same role [Bugayenko 2016]. Chapter 14 showed the technique on prices; here it is applied to the flags it replaces.

module bible/flags v1.0.0;

// Anti-pattern: one object that reads its flags on every call. Pattern: one
// small object per behaviour, composed through a role.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object FlagLabel {
    has text is string;
    has prefix is string;
    has framed is bool;
    FlagLabel(:text, :prefix, :framed);
    shown() is string {
        let body = prefix + text;
        if framed { "[" + body + "]"; } else { body; }
    }
}

role Label {
    shown() is string;
}

object Plain does Label {
    has text is string;
    Plain(:text);
    shown() is string { text; }
}

object Prefixed does Label {
    has origin is Label;
    has prefix is string;
    Prefixed(:origin, :prefix);
    shown() is string { prefix + origin.shown(); }
}

object Framed does Label {
    has origin is Label;
    Framed(:origin);
    shown() is string { "[" + origin.shown() + "]"; }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    out.writeln(FlagLabel(text: "draft", prefix: "! ", framed: true).shown());
    let inner is Label = Framed(origin: Prefixed(origin: Plain(text: "draft"), prefix: "! "));
    let outer is Label = Prefixed(origin: Framed(origin: Plain(text: "draft")), prefix: "! ");
    out.writeln(inner.shown());
    out.writeln(outer.shown());
    0;
}

Output:

[! draft]
[! draft]
! [draft]

The program prints:

[! draft]
[! draft]
! [draft]

The first line comes from FlagLabel, whose one action decides everything. The second and third come from compositions of three objects that each do one thing, and they differ only in the order of composition. That order is a decision FlagLabel cannot express without another flag: it hard-codes "prefix inside the frame". With decorators, both orders are available, and a new behaviour, a Truncated or an Upper, is a new object of a few lines that no existing object has to know about.

The decorators pay for this freedom with one indirection per layer and with more declarations than the flag version. For a label with two options the flag version is shorter, and nothing in the language forbids it. The rule of thumb that Okkama code follows is about change, not about size: as soon as an option interacts with another, or a second caller wants a different combination, the flags become a small interpreter of their own, and the composition is the cheaper program to keep.

Composite: a container that does its parts' role

The same idea covers trees. When a container does the role of the things it holds, a caller cannot tell one item from a bundle of them, and a bundle of bundles needs no special case. Gamma and his co-authors called this Composite [Gamma 1994]; in Okkama it is a role, a leaf object and a container object whose field is an array of the role.

module bible/composite v1.0.0;

// Composite: the leaf and the container do the same role, so a bundle of
// bundles is priced the same way as one item.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "cell" take Cell;

role Priced {
    total() is int;
    label() is string;
}

object Item does Priced {
    has name is string;
    has price is int;
    Item(:name, :price);
    total() is int { price; }
    label() is string { name; }
}

object Bundle does Priced {
    has name is string;
    has parts is @Priced;
    has percent is int = 0;
    Bundle(:name, :parts);
    Bundle(:name, :parts, :percent);

    total() is int {
        let sum = Cell(0);
        for parts -> part {
            sum.replace(sum.value() + part.total());
        }
        let full = sum.value();
        full - (full * percent / 100).int();
    }

    label() is string { name + " of " + parts.size().string(); }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let tea is Priced = Item(name: "tea", price: 300);
    let cups is Priced = Bundle(name: "cups", parts: [Item(name: "cup", price: 150), Item(name: "cup", price: 150)]);
    let gift is Priced = Bundle(name: "gift", parts: [tea, cups], percent: 10);
    for [tea, cups, gift] -> priced {
        out.writeln(priced.label() + ": " + priced.total().string());
    }
    0;
}

Output:

tea: 300
cups of 2: 300
gift of 2: 540

Bundle sums its parts with a Cell inside one synchronous action, which is exactly the local use cells are for, and applies its own discount on top. The gift contains an item and a bundle and prices both the same way. Two constructors give the discount a default without a flag that every bundle must pass.

Strategy: a role, or an action value

Strategy, a behaviour the caller chooses, has two forms in Okkama, and the choice between them is the same each time. A behaviour that has a name, is used in several places or is replaced in tests is a role with objects that do it. A question asked once, by one caller, is an action value passed to the call (Chapter 18).

module bible/strategy v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Player {
    has name is string;
    has score is int;
    has seconds is int;

    Player(:name, :score, :seconds);

    name() is string { name; }
    score() is int { score; }
    seconds() is int { seconds; }
}

// A named policy that several places use, and that tests replace, is a role.
role Ranking {
    better(a is Player, b is Player) is bool;
}

object ByScore does Ranking {
    ByScore();

    better(a is Player, b is Player) is bool {
        a.score() > b.score();
    }
}

object Board {
    has players is @Player;
    has ranking is Ranking;

    Board(:players, :ranking);

    leader() is string {
        players.reduce(players.first()) -> best, player {
            if ranking.better(player, best) { player; } else { best; }
        }.name();
    }

    // A one-off question, asked once by one caller, takes an action value.
    first(where is (Player) is bool) is string {
        let found = players.filter() -> player { where(player); };
        if found.size() > 0 { found.first().name(); } else { "nobody"; }
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let board = Board(
        players: [
            Player(name: "ada", score: 90, seconds: 41),
            Player(name: "alan", score: 95, seconds: 58),
            Player(name: "grace", score: 95, seconds: 37),
        ],
        ranking: ByScore(),
    );
    out.writeln("leader: " + board.leader());
    out.writeln("under 40 s: " + board.first((player is Player) is bool { player.seconds() < 40; }));
    out.writeln("over 100: " + board.first((player is Player) is bool { player.score() > 100; }));
    0;
}

Output:

leader: alan
under 40 s: grace
over 100: nobody
  • Ranking is a policy of the board. The board keeps it, every leader query uses it, and a test can give the board another Ranking. ByScore keeps the earlier player on a tie, because better is strict.
  • first asks one question, with a condition the caller writes in place. A role for "under 40 seconds" would be a declaration used once.
  • When the same anonymous action appears at a second call site, it has become a policy and wants a name: a role, or at least an object that holds the action.

25.3 Change as a value: successor pipelines

Builders, setters and mutable "state" objects exist in other languages because an object there can change in place. In Okkama it cannot. A field is bound once, by the constructor; an action that changes state is declared is ^Type, stages new field values with ^field = …, and returns a new object, the successor (Chapter 13). The old object stays as it was.

This one rule turns several patterns into ordinary code. A builder is a chain of successor calls. An undo stack is a list of earlier values. A snapshot before a risky step is a variable that is not touched. The next example takes an order through four stages and keeps all of them.

module bible/pipeline v1.0.0;

// Pattern: each change of state is a successor, so every stage of a
// pipeline is a value that can be kept, compared and reused.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum OrderError is Error = (closed, empty);

object Order {
    has lines is int = 0;
    has total is int = 0;
    has percent is int = 0;
    has open is bool = true;
    Order();

    added(price is int) is ^Order {
        confirm open else throw OrderError.closed;
        ^lines = lines + 1;
        ^total = total + price;
    }

    discounted(by is int) is ^Order {
        confirm open else throw OrderError.closed;
        ^percent = by;
    }

    closed() is ^Order {
        confirm lines > 0 else throw OrderError.empty;
        ^open = false;
    }

    due() is int { total - (total * percent / 100).int(); }

    summary() is string {
        lines.string() + " lines, due " + self.due().string() + (if open { ", open"; } else { ", closed"; });
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
