    let empty = Order();
    let basket = empty.added(300).added(200);
    let offer = basket.discounted(10);
    let paid = offer.closed();
    for [empty, basket, offer, paid] -> stage {
        out.writeln(stage.summary());
    }
    let late = try { paid.added(50).summary(); } catch e is OrderError { e.text(); };
    out.writeln(late);
    0;
}

Output:

0 lines, due 0, open
2 lines, due 500, open
2 lines, due 450, open
2 lines, due 450, closed
OrderError.closed

Each stage is a value. empty, basket, offer and paid can be printed, compared, stored in a collection or passed to another task, and none of them can be changed by a later step. The rule that a closed order accepts nothing more is checked where the change is asked for, by confirm in the successor, and the refusal is a typed error rather than a silent no-op.

Two details of the example are deliberate. The successor stages only the fields it changes; the others carry over from the original. And the object calls its own query through self.due(): inside an object, its actions are reached through self, its fields by name.

The antipattern this replaces is the object with a "current state" that every action updates, where the order of calls matters and nothing records it. Okkama refuses it at the level of the language: assigning a field after construction is a compile error, with a diagnostic that names the alternative:

Field "count" cannot be assigned after construction: objects are immutable; return a successor instead (`is ^Counter` and `^count = …`)

What the language does not refuse is a value that changes over time inside one piece of synchronous code, such as a running total in a loop. For that it has Cell, a box with value() and replace() (Chapter 13). A cell is a local tool: it cannot be a field of an object, so it cannot become the hidden mutable state of one.

Field "reading" cannot hold a Cell: a cell stays in synchronous code; state an object shares with tasks is an Atomic

Builder: options are named arguments

Bloch recommends a builder for a constructor with many parameters, most of them optional [Bloch 2018]. A positional constructor with a dozen arguments is unreadable where it is called, and one constructor per combination of options multiplies. Named arguments with defaults remove both problems, and the builder with them.

module bible/options v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum BadFetch is Error = (timeout(seconds is int), retries(count is int));

// Every option has a name and a default; a call names only what differs.
object Fetch {
    has url is string;
    has timeout is int = 30;
    has retries is int = 0;
    has redirects is bool = true;

    Fetch(:url, :timeout, :retries, :redirects) {
        confirm timeout > 0 else throw BadFetch.timeout(timeout);
        confirm retries >= 0 else throw BadFetch.retries(retries);
    }

    shown() is string {
        let follow = if redirects { "follows redirects" } else { "stays put" };
        url + ": " + timeout.string() + " s, " + retries.string() + " retries, " + follow;
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    out.writeln(Fetch(url: "/status").shown());
    out.writeln(Fetch(url: "/report", retries: 3).shown());
    out.writeln(Fetch(redirects: false, url: "/login", timeout: 5).shown());
    let refused = try {
        Fetch(url: "/slow", timeout: 0).shown();
    }
    catch e is BadFetch {
        "refused: " + e.text();
    };
    out.writeln(refused);
    0;
}

Output:

/status: 30 s, 0 retries, follows redirects
/report: 30 s, 3 retries, follows redirects
/login: 5 s, 0 retries, stays put
refused: BadFetch.timeout(0)
  • Every option is a field with a default. A call names the ones that differ, in any order, and the rest keep their defaults (Section 12.4).
  • The constructor body checks the combination once. A Fetch that exists is valid, which a builder guarantees only if its build() repeats the checks.
  • When options are gathered in several steps, say from a file and then from the command line, the successor chain of this section does the gathering: each step returns an object with one more decision made.

Typestate: when an invalid step should not compile

A successor chain checks at run time that a step is allowed. When a protocol has a few well-known states, the check can move into the types. Each state becomes a role that exposes only the actions valid in it, and each transition returns the role of the next state. A created payment offers authorize; an authorized one offers capture; a captured one offers refund; and calling refund on a created payment does not type-check, because the role Created has no such action. The pattern is old: Strom and Yemini called it typestate in 1986 [Strom 1986]. In Okkama it needs nothing beyond roles and ordinary actions.

module bible/typestate v1.0.0;

// Typestate: one role per state of a payment. A role offers only the steps
// valid in its state, and each step returns the role of the next state.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

role Created {
    id() is string;
    authorized() is Authorized;
}

role Authorized {
    id() is string;
    captured(amount is int) is Captured;
}

role Captured {
    id() is string;
    amount() is int;
    refunded() is Refunded;
}

role Refunded {
    id() is string;
}

object NewPayment does Created {
    has number is string;
    NewPayment(:number);
    id() is string { number; }
    authorized() is Authorized { AuthorizedPayment(number: number); }
}

object AuthorizedPayment does Authorized {
    has number is string;
    AuthorizedPayment(:number);
    id() is string { number; }
    captured(amount is int) is Captured { CapturedPayment(number: number, total: amount); }
}

object CapturedPayment does Captured {
    has number is string;
    has total is int;
    CapturedPayment(:number, :total);
    id() is string { number; }
    amount() is int { total; }
    refunded() is Refunded { RefundedPayment(number: number); }
}

object RefundedPayment does Refunded {
    has number is string;
    RefundedPayment(:number);
    id() is string { number; }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let created is Created = NewPayment(number: "p-17");
    let captured = created.authorized().captured(250);
    out.writeln(captured.id() + " captured " + captured.amount().string());
    let refunded = captured.refunded();
    out.writeln(refunded.id() + " refunded");
    0;
}

Output:

p-17 captured 250
p-17 refunded

Figure 25.1. Typestate: each state is a role, and a step the state does not offer does not compile.

Each object does exactly one role, and a variable typed by the role sees only the steps of that state. The guarantee holds even when the object itself has more actions than its role exposes. In the next program NewPayment does have a refunded action, but a value typed Created cannot reach it:

module bible/typestate_rejected v1.0.0;

role Created {
    id() is string;
}

object NewPayment does Created {
    has number is string;
    NewPayment(:number);
    id() is string { number; }
    refunded() is string { "refunded " + number; }
}

main() is int {
    let created is Created = NewPayment(number: "p-17");
    created.refunded();
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

25-typestate-rejected.ok:16:13: semantic error: Role "Created" has no action "refunded"

Typestate costs one role and one object per state, and transitions that build new objects rather than successors, because the next state is a different type. It is worth it where a wrong step is expensive: payments, connections, documents that move through approval. Where the states are many and the transitions few, a successor with confirm checks (Section 25.3's Order) is the lighter tool.

Memento: the past is a list of values

Undo is a pattern in most languages because keeping the past takes work: the state must be copied before it changes, or every change must know how to reverse itself [Gamma 1994]. In Okkama a successor leaves the earlier value as it was, and nothing can change it later. Keeping the past means keeping the earlier values.

module bible/undo v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Undo is Error = (nothing);

object Draft {
    has text is string;

    Draft(:text);

    typed(more is string) is ^Draft {
        ^text = text + more;
    }

    text() is string {
        text;
    }
}

// The past is a list of earlier values. Nothing is copied to keep it:
// a value that cannot change is its own snapshot.
object Editor {
    has draft is Draft;
    has past is @Draft;

    Editor(:draft, :past);

    typed(more is string) is ^Editor {
        ^draft = draft.typed(more);
        ^past = past + [draft];
    }

    undone() is ^Editor {
        confirm past.size() > 0 else throw Undo.nothing;
        ^draft = past.last();
        ^past = past.take(past.size() - 1);
    }

    text() is string {
        draft.text() + " (" + past.size().string() + " back)";
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let editor = Editor(draft: Draft(text: ""), past: []);
    editor = editor.typed("Dear Ada");
    editor = editor.typed(", thanks");
    out.writeln(editor.text());
    editor = editor.undone();
    out.writeln(editor.text());
    editor = editor.typed(", welcome");
    out.writeln(editor.text());
    editor = editor.undone();
    editor = editor.undone();
    let refused = try { editor.undone().text(); } catch e is Undo { "refused: " + e.text(); };
    out.writeln(refused);
    0;
}

Output:

Dear Ada, thanks (2 back)
Dear Ada (1 back)
Dear Ada, welcome (2 back)
refused: Undo.nothing
  • typed makes a new Draft and keeps the old one in past. Nothing has to be copied: a value that cannot change is its own snapshot.
  • undone takes the last kept draft back and drops it from the list. With nothing to undo it refuses by name, instead of returning the editor unchanged.
  • Redo has the same shape mirrored: a second list for the drafts that undo dropped, emptied by the next typed.

25.4 Refusals have names

A function that cannot do what was asked has three classic ways to say so: a special value (-1, "", null), an untyped exception carrying a message, or a typed failure the caller can match. Okkama keeps only the third. There is no null to return, an object cannot be an error, and a failure that carries information is a case of an Error enum (Chapter 10):

Object "Failure" cannot do Error: errors are enums, declare `enum Failure is Error = (...)`

The pattern built on this rule has three parts. A module names all its refusals in one enum, with the data that explains each in its payload. Every precondition is checked at the boundary, where the bad input arrives, with confirm … else throw. And a caller catches only the refusals it can answer, letting everything else go up.

module bible/refusals v1.0.0;

// Pattern: the module names its refusals in one Error enum and checks them
// with confirm at the boundary; a caller catches only what it can answer.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Refusal is Error = (non_positive(amount is int), insufficient(balance is int, amount is int));

object Account {
    has balance is int;
    Account(:balance);

    withdrawn(amount is int) is ^Account {
        confirm amount > 0 else throw Refusal.non_positive(amount);
        confirm amount <= balance else throw Refusal.insufficient(balance, amount);
        ^balance = balance - amount;
    }

    shown() is string { "balance " + balance.string(); }
}

object Teller {
    has account is Account;
    Teller(:account);

    answer(amount is int) is string {
        let reply = try { account.withdrawn(amount).shown(); } catch e is Refusal { "refused: " + e.text(); };
        reply;
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let teller = Teller(account: Account(balance: 100));
    for [30, 0, 150] -> amount {
        out.writeln(amount.string() + " -> " + teller.answer(amount));
    }
    0;
}

Output:

30 -> balance 70
0 -> refused: Refusal.non_positive(0)
150 -> refused: Refusal.insufficient(100, 150)

The teller turns refusals into a reply because replying is its job. A Program failure such as a broken invariant, or a refusal from some other module, passes through the catch untouched, because the clause names Refusal and nothing else. A catch can also name a single case and bind its payload, catch Refusal.insufficient(balance, amount) { … }, which is how a caller answers one refusal and leaves the rest to someone else.

Two antipatterns are on the other side of this rule. One is the catch-all: catching every failure to keep a loop running, which also catches the failures that mean the program is broken. Okkama makes it hard: a typed catch names a type, and panics and program failures are not typed throws at all, so they cannot be caught as one (Chapter 10). The other is the refusal that is not a refusal: an action that returns a default when it cannot do its work. When absence is a legitimate answer, the language has a type for it (Section 25.8); when it is not, the action should refuse.

At the scale of a module, the same rule makes refusals change their names at the boundary. A layer catches the refusals of the layer below that it understands and refuses in its own terms, so its callers never name the layer below and do not change when it is replaced (Section 10.12).

25.5 Every dependency is a role, every role has a fake

Objects in Okkama reach the outside world through the objects they are given: there is no global state and no static field (Chapter 22). An object that sends mail holds a mailer; an object that reads time holds a clock. When the held object's type is a role rather than a concrete object, the dependency can be replaced, and the replacement for tests comes with the role itself: every role may declare a fake, a test-only implementation that the compiler keeps out of production code (Chapter 15).

module bible/signup v1.0.0;

// Pattern: every dependency is a role, every role ships a fake, and the
// fake records what happened in its own fields, through successors.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

role Mailer {
    sent(to is string) is ^Mailer;
    count() is int;

    fake {
        has total is int = 0;
        has latest is string = "";
        sent(to is string) is ^Mailer {
            ^total = total + 1;
            ^latest = to;
        }
        count() is int { total; }
    }
}

object PrintedMailer does Mailer {
    has total is int = 0;
    PrintedMailer();
    sent(to is string) is ^PrintedMailer {
        Stdout().writeln("mail to " + to);
        ^total = total + 1;
    }
    count() is int { total; }
}

object Signup {
    has mailer is Mailer;
    has members is int = 0;
    Signup(:mailer);

    joined(name is string) is ^Signup {
        ^members = members + 1;
        ^mailer = mailer.sent(name);
    }

    mails() is int { mailer.count(); }
}

test "every member gets one welcome mail" {
    let signup = Signup(mailer: Mailer.fake()).joined("ada").joined("grace");
    test.is(signup.mails(), 2);
}

test "the first signup is untouched by its successors" {
    let first = Signup(mailer: Mailer.fake());
    let later = first.joined("ada");
    test.is(first.mails(), 0);
    test.is(later.mails(), 1);
}

main() is int {
    let signup = Signup(mailer: PrintedMailer()).joined("ada");
    Stdout().writeln(signup.mails().string() + " mail sent");
    0;
}

Output:

=== RUN   every member gets one welcome mail
--- PASS: every member gets one welcome mail
=== RUN   the first signup is untouched by its successors
--- PASS: the first signup is untouched by its successors
PASS

The fake records what happened in its own fields, through successors, the same way production objects do. A test does not configure expectations the way a mock framework would; it uses the fake and then asks it what it saw. This is the distinction Martin Fowler drew between state verification with stubs and behaviour verification with mocks [Fowler 2007], and the one Meszaros's catalogue of test doubles calls a fake object: a working implementation, simpler than the real one [Meszaros 2007]. Because the fake lives next to the role, every implementation of the role and every test of its users agree on what the role means.

The example shows one more consequence of successors. Sending mail is a state change of the mailer, so sent returns a successor, and Signup stages it: ^mailer = mailer.sent(name). A production mailer that only prints still returns a successor of its own type, ^PrintedMailer; the compiler insists on that, and its diagnostic says how:

Successor action "sent" on object "PrintedMailer" must return ^PrintedMailer; declare ^Mailer in a role signature and implement it as ^PrintedMailer

The antipattern this replaces is the hidden collaborator: an object that creates its own database connection, reads the clock directly or writes to a global logger, and so can be tested only by replacing the world around it. In Okkama such an object can still be written, by constructing SystemClock() or Stdout() itself, but nothing global can be patched in a test to undo it. So the habit, and the standard library's rule (Section 22.6), is to take the clock and the destination as values.

Decide, then do

A role and its fake make a dependency replaceable. One step further takes the dependency out of the logic altogether: the logic decides and returns its decisions as values, and a thin outer layer carries them out. Gary Bernhardt called this shape a functional core in an imperative shell [Bernhardt 2012]. Immutable objects and enums with payloads make it the natural shape in Okkama.

module bible/decide v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

// What the core decided. Nothing has happened yet.
enum Effect = (
    charge(customer is string, cents is int),
    reorder(item is string, count is int),
    receipt(customer is string, text is string)
);

object Line {
    has item is string;
    has count is int;
    has price is int;
    has stock is int;

    Line(:item, :count, :price, :stock);

    cost() is int {
        count * price;
    }

    missing() is int {
        if stock < count { count - stock; } else { 0; }
    }

    item() is string {
        item;
    }
}

// The core decides and returns its decisions as values. It writes nothing,
// sends nothing and reads no clock.
object Checkout {
    has customer is string;
    has lines is @Line;

    Checkout(:customer, :lines);

    effects() is @Effect {
        let total = lines.reduce(0) -> sum, line { sum + line.cost(); };
        let short = lines.filter() -> line { line.missing() > 0; };
        let reorders = short.map() -> line { Effect.reorder(line.item(), line.missing()); };
        [Effect.charge(customer, total)] + reorders + [Effect.receipt(customer, "paid " + total.string())];
    }
}

// The shell performs decisions and makes none.
object Shell {
    has out is Stdout;

    Shell(:out);

    performed(effect is Effect) is void {
        match effect {
            case Effect.charge(customer, cents) {
                out.writeln("charge " + customer + " " + cents.string());
            }
            case Effect.reorder(item, count) {
                out.writeln("reorder " + count.string() + " x " + item);
            }
            case Effect.receipt(customer, text) {
                out.writeln("mail " + customer + ": " + text);
            }
        }
    }
}

main() is int {
    let checkout = Checkout(customer: "ada", lines: [
        Line(item: "tea", count: 2, price: 450, stock: 10),
        Line(item: "cups", count: 6, price: 120, stock: 4),
    ]);
    let effects = checkout.effects();
    let charged = effects.first() == Effect.charge("ada", 1620);
    Stdout().writeln(effects.size().string() + " effects, charge first: " + charged.string());
    let shell = Shell(out: Stdout());
    for effects -> effect {
        shell.performed(effect);
    }
    0;
}

Output:

3 effects, charge first: true
charge ada 1620
reorder 2 x cups
mail ada: paid 1620
  • Checkout.effects() reads only its own fields. It writes nothing, sends nothing and reads no clock, so the same order always gives the same decisions.
  • The decisions are an enum. The shell's match covers every case, and a new kind of effect makes the compiler point at the shell.
  • A test of the core compares values, as main does with the first effect. It needs no fake, because the core has no dependency to replace, and the shell has almost no logic left to test.

The same shape answers Observer in a language where objects do not change. An action does not notify listeners; it returns what happened, and its caller passes that on. Where the listeners are tasks, the values travel over a channel to their owner (Section 25.9).

25.6 A table of cases

Some actions have one rule and many inputs that matter. A tariff is the usual example: the price changes at fixed weights, and every change is a place where an off-by-one hides. One test per weight repeats the same three lines ten times, and the repetition hides the one thing that differs between them. The pattern turns the cases into data: a table with one row per case, and one loop that checks every row. Go programmers know it as table-driven tests [Go Wiki]. The idea is older: Ward Cunningham's Fit let customers write business rules as tables of examples that ran as tests [Mugridge 2005].

module bible/postage v1.0.0;

// Pattern: a table of cases. Each row is a value; one loop checks them all,
// and the row's input travels with its answer, so a failure names the row.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Postage = (
    letter(cents is int),
    parcel(cents is int),
    refused(reason is string)
);

object Tariff {
    Tariff();

    priced(grams is int) is Postage {
        if grams <= 0 { Postage.refused("no weight"); }
        else if grams <= 20 { Postage.letter(85); }
        else if grams <= 100 { Postage.letter(150); }
        else if grams <= 500 { Postage.parcel(450); }
        else if grams <= 2000 { Postage.parcel(900); }
        else { Postage.refused("over 2 kg"); }
    }
}

// What a test compares: the weight and the postage, together.
object Priced {
    has grams is int;
    has postage is Postage;
    Priced(:grams, :postage);
}

// One row of the table.
object Case {
    has grams is int;
    has expected is Postage;
    Case(:grams, :expected);

    wanted() is Priced { Priced(grams: grams, postage: expected); }
    got(tariff is Tariff) is Priced { Priced(grams: grams, postage: tariff.priced(grams)); }
}

test "postage at every boundary" {
    let cases = [
        Case(grams: 0, expected: Postage.refused("no weight")),
        Case(grams: 1, expected: Postage.letter(85)),
        Case(grams: 20, expected: Postage.letter(85)),
        Case(grams: 21, expected: Postage.letter(150)),
        Case(grams: 100, expected: Postage.letter(150)),
        Case(grams: 101, expected: Postage.parcel(450)),
        Case(grams: 500, expected: Postage.parcel(450)),
        Case(grams: 501, expected: Postage.parcel(900)),
        Case(grams: 2000, expected: Postage.parcel(900)),
        Case(grams: 2001, expected: Postage.refused("over 2 kg"))
    ];
    let tariff = Tariff();
    for cases -> row {
        test.is(row.got(tariff), row.wanted());
    }
}

main() is int {
    match Tariff().priced(250) {
        case Postage.letter(cents) { Stdout().writeln("letter, " + cents.string() + " cents"); }
        case Postage.parcel(cents) { Stdout().writeln("parcel, " + cents.string() + " cents"); }
        case Postage.refused(reason) { Stdout().writeln("refused: " + reason); }
    }
    0;
}

Output:

=== RUN   postage at every boundary
--- PASS: postage at every boundary
PASS
  • A row is an object with named fields, so the table reads as a table: Case(grams: 20, expected: Postage.letter(85)). The named arguments are the column headings, repeated on every line where a reader needs them.
  • The expected column holds values of the domain, here an enum with payloads, not strings that describe them. test.is compares them structurally (Section 15.2), so a refusal's reason and a parcel's price are both checked.
  • One run reports every wrong row. A failed assertion does not stop the test, so the loop goes on after the first mismatch. In Go the same choice falls to the author, who must call t.Errorf rather than t.Fatalf.
  • The row brings its input along with its answer. got and wanted both return a Priced, which holds the weight with the postage, and so the report names the row.

That last point is the one that is easy to skip. Suppose the row offered its two fields and the loop compared only the postage: test.is(tariff.priced(row.grams()), row.expected()). Then two wrong rows report this way:

--- FAIL: postage at every boundary
    expected Postage.parcel(450), got Postage.parcel(900)
    expected Postage.refused("too heavy"), got Postage.refused("over 2 kg")

Two rows of the table expect Postage.parcel(450), and the report does not say which of them failed. With the weight carried along, it does:

--- FAIL: postage at every boundary
    expected Priced(grams: 501, postage: Postage.parcel(450)), got Priced(grams: 501, postage: Postage.parcel(900))
    expected Priced(grams: 2001, postage: Postage.refused("too heavy")), got Priced(grams: 2001, postage: Postage.refused("over 2 kg"))

The rows are chosen at the edges. Each tier is checked at its first and its last weight (20 and 21, 100 and 101, 500 and 501), and the table also holds one row on each side outside the range: 0 and 2001. This is boundary value analysis, which Myers described as one of the most useful ways to choose test cases, and also one of the easiest to do badly [Myers 1979]. A table makes the edges visible. An edge without a row is a missing line, and a reviewer can see that it is missing.

A table and a property (Section 15.6) answer different questions. The table holds the cases someone chose for a reason, and the reason is usually an edge. A property generates the cases nobody thought of, and checks a rule that holds for all of them: here, that the price never falls as the weight grows. A tariff deserves both.

The report needs one more word. A table is one test, and a row gets a name of its own only when it runs inside test.case(name) { … }, as in Go's t.Run and JUnit's parameterized tests [JUnit User Guide]. Then the report lists every row as postage/50 g, and okkama run -t --filter "postage/50 g" runs that row alone (Section 15.9). Without test.case, the whole table is one line when it passes, and a row names itself only when it fails, through the input it carries.

25.7 Resources belong to scopes

A resource is an object with a destroy block. The scope that owns it destroys it when the scope ends, whatever way it ends, in reverse order of creation, after the scope's defer blocks have run (Chapter 11). The pattern that follows is simple to state: open a resource where it is needed, bind it with let in the narrowest block that uses it, and put its cleanup in destroy, not in an action a caller must remember to call.

The antipatterns it replaces are familiar from languages with explicit cleanup: the close() that is skipped on an early return, the dispose() called twice, the object that is "opened" in a second step after construction and is unusable in between. In Okkama none of them is necessary. An object that needs a resource takes it in its constructor and is complete when the constructor returns; the end of its scope is the only cleanup point; and a result returned from an action carries its resources to the caller's scope, so the caller owns what it was given (Chapter 11).

module bible/section v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Bad is Error = (row(value is int));

// The pair "begin" / "end" belongs to an object, not to every caller:
// the end is written when the section's scope ends, however it ends.
object Section {
    has name is string;

    Section(:name) {
        Stdout().writeln("begin " + name);
    }

    destroy {
        Stdout().writeln("end " + name);
    }
}

object Importer {
    Importer();

    imported(rows is @int) is int {
        let section = Section(name: "import");
        for rows -> row {
            let step = Section(name: "row " + row.string());
            confirm row >= 0 else throw Bad.row(row);
        }
        rows.size();
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    out.writeln("imported " + Importer().imported([1, 2]).string());
    let outcome = try {
        Importer().imported([3, -1, 4]).string();
    }
    catch e is Bad {
        "refused: " + e.text();
    };
    out.writeln(outcome);
    0;
}

Output:

begin import
begin row 1
end row 1
begin row 2
end row 2
end import
imported 2
begin import
begin row 3
end row 3
begin row -1
end row -1
end import
refused: Bad.row(-1)
  • Section writes begin in its constructor and end in its destroy. A caller writes one let and has nothing to remember.
  • Each pass of the loop is a scope: one row's section ends before the next row's begins.
  • The refusal of row −1 leaves both scopes. Both ends are written, the innermost first, before the caller handles the refusal. Row 4 is never reached.

defer covers the cases that are actions rather than objects: restoring a setting, writing a final line to a log, releasing something the program did not create. It runs at the end of the scope, reads the bindings as they are then, and runs before the scope's resources are destroyed. A rule of thumb from code review: if the same defer appears around every use of an object, the object wants a destroy.

25.8 Absence is a type

Okkama has no null. A value that may be missing has the type Maybe<T>, and the type system makes the caller decide what absence means: a fallback with else or a match (Chapter 7). The pattern is to put absence in the signature of the action that can produce it, and nowhere else. A lookup that can fail to find returns Maybe; a lookup that must find refuses with a typed error.

The same pattern works for a whole program: decide absence at the edge, where data comes in, and let the objects inside hold values that are there.

module bible/edge v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Missing is Error = (setting(name is string));

// What a settings file gave: any key may be missing.
object RawSettings {
    has values is %string:string;

    RawSettings(:values);

    setting(name is string) is Maybe<string> {
        if values.has(name) { Maybe.some(values[name]); } else { Maybe.none; }
    }

    required(name is string) is string {
        confirm values.has(name) else throw Missing.setting(name);
        values[name];
    }
}

// What the program runs with: absence was decided once, at the edge.
object Settings {
    has host is string;
    has user is string;

    Settings(raw is RawSettings) {
        host = raw.setting("host") else "localhost";
        user = raw.required("user");
    }

    address() is string {
        user + "@" + host;
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let full = Settings(RawSettings(values: ["host": "db.local", "user": "ada"]));
    out.writeln(full.address());
    let partial = Settings(RawSettings(values: ["user": "grace"]));
    out.writeln(partial.address());
    let refused = try {
        Settings(RawSettings(values: ["host": "db.local"])).address();
    }
    catch e is Missing {
        "refused: " + e.text();
    };
    out.writeln(refused);
    0;
}

Output:

ada@db.local
grace@localhost
refused: Missing.setting("user")
  • RawSettings is the edge. It answers with Maybe where a key may be missing, and refuses with a typed error where the program cannot go on without one.
  • Settings makes both decisions once, in its constructor: a missing host falls back to localhost, a missing user is refused. Its fields are plain strings, and nothing that reads them checks for absence again.
  • A refused construction produces no object. There is no half-built Settings with an empty user to pass on.

The antipatterns on the other side are the sentinel value and the "empty object": -1 for "not found", "" for "no name", an object whose every field is a default. They survive in Okkama only if a programmer writes them, since the language provides no null to tempt anyone and an explicit type for the honest answer. When a value is optional for a while and then becomes required, the change is visible in the types, and the compiler finds every caller that has to decide.

25.9 Shared state has one owner

Asynchronous code needs state that more than one task can see. Okkama's answer is structural: state shared between tasks lives in one task, the owner, and others talk to it through channels (Chapter 20). A ledger that several workers update is one object in one task, receiving messages; the workers hold the sending end of a channel, not the ledger. For the few values that really are shared, such as a counter or a flag, Atomic gives a small set of operations that are safe across tasks. The ledger of Section 20.6 is the pattern in full: an enum of commands, one task that owns the balance and serves them in a loop, and replies sent back over a channel the caller provides. The next example has several writers instead of one.

module bible/owner v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
import "async/channel" take Channel, Sending, Receiving;
import "async/collect" take AllFutures;
import "collections/sequence" take Sequencing;

// State that several tasks update lives in one task, its owner. The others
// hold only the sending end of the owner's inbox.
enum Visit = (page(path is string), summary(reply is Sending<string>), stop);

object Tally {
    has total is int;
    has home is int;

    Tally(:total, :home);

    counted(path is string) is ^Tally {
        ^total = total + 1;
        ^home = if path == "/" { home + 1; } else { home; };
    }

    summary() is string {
        total.string() + " pages, " + home.string() + " home";
    }

    total() is int {
        total;
    }
}

object Visits {
    has inbox is Receiving<Visit>;

    Visits(:inbox);

    async run() is int {
        let tally = Tally(total: 0, home: 0);
        loop {
            let visit = await inbox.item();
            match visit {
                case Visit.page(path) {
                    tally = tally.counted(path);
                }
                case Visit.summary(reply) {
                    await reply.send(tally.summary());
                }
                case Visit.stop {
                    last;
                }
            }
        }
        tally.total();
    }
}

object Reader {
    has paths is @string;
    has out is Sending<Visit>;

    Reader(:paths, :out);

    async read() is int {
        for paths -> path {
            await out.send(Visit.page(path));
        }
        paths.size();
    }
}

async main() is int {
    let inbox is Channel<Visit> = Channel(capacity: 4);
    let owner = spawn Visits(inbox: inbox.receiving()).run();
    let readers is @Future<int> = [
        spawn Reader(paths: ["/", "/news", "/"], out: inbox.sending()).read(),
        spawn Reader(paths: ["/about", "/"], out: inbox.sending()).read(),
    ];
    let all is AllFutures<int> = AllFutures(origins: readers);
    let sent is Sequencing<int> = await all.results();
    let replies is Channel<string> = Channel(capacity: 1);
    let desk = inbox.sending();
    await desk.send(Visit.summary(replies.sending()));
    Stdout().writeln("summary: " + (await replies.receiving().item()));
    await desk.send(Visit.stop);
    Stdout().writeln("owner: " + (await owner).string() + " pages from " + sent.size().string() + " readers");
    0;
}

Output:

summary: 5 pages, 3 home
owner: 5 pages from 2 readers
  • The count lives in Tally, a local of Visits.run(). The readers cannot reach it. Each holds a Sending<Visit> and nothing else.
  • The owner changes its state by successor, tally = tally.counted(path), one message at a time. Two readers never update the count at once, because only one task updates it.
  • A question is a message too. summary carries the channel for the answer, so the reply goes to whoever asked, and the state never leaves its owner.

This replaces the most expensive antipattern of concurrent programming, the object shared by many threads and guarded by locks taken in the right order by convention. In Okkama a Cell cannot cross into an async context and an object cannot hold one, so mutable state that tasks share is either inside its owner or in an Atomic, by construction.

module bible/shared_rejected v1.0.0;

import "cell" take Cell;

// A visit counter that tasks would share and mutate in place.
object Hits {
    has count is Cell<int>;

    Hits(:count);
}

main() is int {
    let hits = Hits(count: Cell(0));
    0;
}

The compiler answers:

25-shared-rejected.ok:7:9: semantic error: Field "count" cannot hold a Cell: a cell stays in synchronous code; state an object shares with tasks is an Atomic

The diagnostic names the way out: state an object shares with tasks is an Atomic. State that is more than a counter or a flag goes to an owner.

The structured rules of Chapter 20 add the second half of the pattern: cancelling a task cancels what it waits for, and when async main returns, the tasks still running are cancelled and their cleanup is awaited before the run ends. Work that runs "in the background, somewhere", outliving the program that started it, is not a shape the language provides.

25.10 Anti-patterns the compiler refuses

Several shapes that code review catches in other languages are diagnostics in Okkama. The table collects the ones the earlier chapters showed, with the compiler's words.

Anti-pattern Diagnostic
Setter, mutable field Field "count" cannot be assigned after construction: objects are immutable; return a successor instead
Staging outside a successor `^field = value` is allowed only in successor actions
Getter for raw state Field "cents" of object "Cash" is private; call an action instead
Hidden mutable box in an object Field "reading" cannot hold a Cell: a cell stays in synchronous code; state an object shares with tasks is an Atomic
Using an object before it exists Cannot call actions on self before construction completes
Error as an object with a message Object "Failure" cannot do Error: errors are enums, declare enum Failure is Error = (...)``
Downcast from a role to a concrete object Cannot initialize variable "customer" of type Customer with Presentation
Rebinding a value that has no successors Cannot rebind variable "n": type "int" has no successor actions
Treating "present or absent" as optional with a fallback Optional fallback requires Maybe<T>; fold Presence explicitly
Discarding a successor must-use: a successor that is not used is an error (Chapter 13)

Each line closes a door that an elegant-objects code review would otherwise have to watch [Bugayenko 2016; Bugayenko 2017]. The language cannot tell good design from bad, but it can make some bad designs impossible to write, and Okkama spends its rules there.

25.11 Anti-patterns the compiler allows

The rest is judgement. These are the shapes that compile and still make a program worse, and the reasons Okkama code avoids them.

  • The flag object. Section 25.2: an object whose actions branch on its own fields to choose a behaviour. Decorators through a role replace it once the options interact.
  • The data bag. An object that is a list of fields and one action per field returning it. Fields are private, so the getters must be written by hand, and writing them is the warning. An object should answer questions about what it is for, not hand out its parts: invoice.total(), not invoice.lines() added up by the caller.
  • The matryoshka. Objects nested several layers deep only to reach a value, Report(Section(Table(Rows(Source(...))))), where each layer adds no behaviour. The standard library's review rejected exactly this shape (Chapter 22): one object that knows how to answer, with its parts as named arguments, reads better and runs faster.
  • The god object. One object that holds every dependency of a program and offers an action for every operation. Composition through roles splits it naturally: an object for each responsibility, wired together in main.
  • Stringly typed protocols. Messages, states or commands encoded as strings and compared with ==. An enum names the cases, carries their data, and makes match exhaustive (Chapter 16).
  • Catching to continue. A catch for a broad type around a loop body, so that a failure becomes a skipped iteration. If an iteration may refuse, the refusal has a name and the loop catches that name.
  • The cell as a field substitute. A Cell threaded through many actions to simulate a mutable object. A successor chain says the same thing with values that can be inspected afterwards.
  • Spawn and forget. Starting tasks whose results nobody awaits. Structured concurrency limits the damage, since tasks still running when async main returns are cancelled and their cleanup is awaited, but a task nobody awaits is a task whose result nobody checks.

None of these is forbidden, and some are the right answer in small programs. They are listed because each of them was found in real Okkama code, and each was replaced, in the standard library review or in the examples of this book, by one of the patterns above.

25.12 A refactoring, step by step

The anti-patterns of the previous section rarely come alone. The next program has three of them: a status that is a string, an urgency that is a flag, and a ticket that hands out its fields so that the caller can decide what to print.

module bible/before v1.0.0;

// Before: the status is a string, urgency is a flag, and the object hands
// out its parts so that the caller can decide everything.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

object Ticket {
    has title is string;
    has status is string;
    has urgent is bool;
    Ticket(:title, :status, :urgent);
    title() is string { title; }
    status() is string { status; }
    urgent() is bool { urgent; }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let tickets = [
        Ticket(title: "printer", status: "open", urgent: true),
        Ticket(title: "coffee", status: "closed", urgent: false),
        Ticket(title: "wifi", status: "open", urgent: false)
    ];
    for tickets -> ticket {
        if ticket.status() == "open" {
            let mark = if ticket.urgent() { "!"; } else { " "; };
            out.writeln(mark + " " + ticket.title());
        }
    }
    0;
}

Output:

! printer
  wifi

It works, and it is the kind of code the rules of the language do not prevent. The refactoring takes it apart one smell at a time, without changing what it prints.

  1. The string becomes an enum. status == "open" compiles for any string, including "opne". enum Status = (open, closed) names the two states, and a match over it is exhaustive: a third state added later is a compile error at every place that has to decide about it (Chapter 16).
  2. The getters become a question. The caller wanted one thing from each ticket: its line in the queue, if it has one. So the ticket answers that, line() is Maybe<string>, and title(), status() and urgent() disappear. Absence is in the type: a closed ticket has no line.
  3. The flag becomes a decorator. Urgency changes how a line looks, so it is an object that holds a ticket and marks its line, doing the same role Queued. A ticket that stops being urgent is the ticket without the wrapper; no field has to be reset.
module bible/after v1.0.0;

// After: the status is an enum, urgency is a decorator, and each ticket
// answers the one question the caller has: how it shows in the queue.
import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Status = (open, closed);

role Queued {
    line() is Maybe<string>;
}

object Ticket does Queued {
    has title is string;
    has status is Status;
    Ticket(:title, :status);
    line() is Maybe<string> {
        match status {
            case Status.open { Maybe.some("  " + title); }
            case Status.closed { Maybe.none; }
        }
    }
}

object Urgent does Queued {
    has origin is Queued;
    Urgent(:origin);
    line() is Maybe<string> {
        match origin.line() { case Maybe.some(text): Maybe.some("!" + text.slice(1, text.length())); case Maybe.none: Maybe.none; };
    }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let queue is @Queued = [
        Urgent(origin: Ticket(title: "printer", status: Status.open)),
        Ticket(title: "coffee", status: Status.closed),
        Ticket(title: "wifi", status: Status.open)
    ];
    for queue -> ticket {
        match ticket.line() {
            case Maybe.some(text) { out.writeln(text); }
            case Maybe.none { }
        }
    }
    0;
}

Output:

! printer
  wifi

The output is the same, and the second program is longer. What it buys is the place where each decision lives. The meaning of "open" is in the enum; the line of a ticket is in the ticket; the mark of urgency is in Urgent; main only prints. A new kind of mark, a new state or a different queue format is a change in one object, and the compiler finds every place a new state has to be handled.

25.13 The classic catalogue, read in Okkama

The 23 patterns of Gamma and his co-authors are a useful checklist of what a language makes easy, hard or unnecessary [Gamma 1994]. The table goes through the ones that change most.

Pattern In Okkama
Strategy A role and the objects that do it; an anonymous action for a one-off (Section 25.2)
Decorator A role, implemented by objects that hold another implementation (Section 25.2)
Composite A role done by both the leaf and the container, which holds a collection of the role
Builder A chain of successors, or a constructor with named and defaulted fields (Section 25.3)
Prototype Unneeded: objects are immutable, so sharing one is copying it
Singleton Not expressible: no global state and no static fields; one instance made in main and passed down
Factory method Several constructors, one per form (Chapter 12), or an action that returns a role
Template method No inheritance; a decorator, or an object that takes the varying step as a role
Observer Events returned as values (Section 25.5); a channel to an owning task, or an event that waiters await (Chapter 20)
Memento Unneeded as a mechanism: earlier values stay valid, and undo is a list of them (Section 25.3)
Iterator for over collections, ranges and async streams (for await)
State Typestate: a role per state, each transition returns the next state's role (Section 25.3); successors on one object (Section 14.5)
Command An enum case per command, with a match that interprets it; or an action value
Visitor match over an enum; across roles, the expression problem stands (Chapter 16)
Null object Unneeded as a workaround: absence is Maybe; still useful as a real "do nothing" implementation of a role

Norvig's observation holds in Okkama too, in its own way. Patterns that exist to work around mutable shared state, such as Prototype and the defensive copies of Builder, disappear because the state cannot be mutated. Patterns that exist to work around inheritance, Template Method first among them, are replaced by composition because there is no inheritance to work around. And Singleton, a pattern for global state, has no expression at all.

25.14 What the patterns cost

The patterns of this chapter trade size for change. A decorator chain has more declarations than a flag object; a role and its fake are more text than a concrete dependency; a successor allocates a new object where a setter would write one word; a typestate needs a role per state. For a short script these costs are real, and an Okkama programmer who writes a fifty-line tool with two flags and one concrete dependency is not wrong.

The costs pay back as a program grows and as it is changed by people who did not write it. Values that cannot change can be shared without fear and reasoned about locally; dependencies that are roles can be replaced in a test without a framework; refusals that are names can be handled exactly; resources that belong to scopes are released on every path. The rules that make some antipatterns into compile errors also make some useful shapes impossible: there is no way to cache a value inside an object after construction other than once let (Chapter 13), no way to share a mutable counter between objects other than an Atomic or an owning task, and no way to write the small mutable helper object other languages reach for. Those limits are deliberate, and Chapter 27 discusses the ones that are not.

Chapter 26Okkama Among Languages

The earlier chapters compared Okkama with other languages one construct at a time: numbers in Chapter 5, types in Chapter 4, collections in Chapter 8, roles in Chapter 14, tests in Chapter 15. This chapter turns the comparison around. It takes six languages that a reader of this book is likely to know, Java, Kotlin, Go, Rust, Haskell and OCaml, and asks of each the same questions the manifesto answered for Okkama (Chapter 3). Six more, Python, Swift, Erlang, Clojure, C# and TypeScript, follow in shorter sections, because readers come to Okkama from them as well.

A comparison of languages is easy to make unfair. Each of these languages was designed for a purpose, by people who weighed the same trade-offs and chose differently, and each has decades of programs behind it that Okkama does not. The aim here is not a ranking. It is to show where Okkama's choices sit among choices that working languages have made, so that a reader who knows one of them can see what is familiar, what is different, and what is missing.

26.1 The rules side by side

Java Kotlin Go Rust Haskell OCaml Okkama
Absence null in every reference type [Gosling 2023] nullable types T?, checked [Kotlin specification] nil for pointers, interfaces, maps, slices [Go specification] Option [Klabnik 2023] Maybe [Haskell 2010] option [OCaml Manual] Maybe (Chapter 7)
Change mutable fields; immutable records val/var; copy on data classes [Kotlin documentation] mutable immutable bindings, mut immutable; IORef, ST immutable bindings; mutable fields and ref successors; Cell in synchronous code (Chapter 13)
Implementation inheritance classes, single classes, final unless open [Kotlin documentation] none; embedding none none classes, rarely used none (Chapter 2)
Contracts interfaces, with default methods interfaces interfaces, structural traits type classes module signatures roles, nominal, no bodies (Chapter 14)
Showing state getters; record accessors [Bierman 2021] properties exported fields and methods pub fields, methods record fields, export lists record fields, abstract types caps the object grants (Section 12.8)
Failures checked and unchecked exceptions unchecked exceptions [Kotlin documentation] error values, panic Result, panic Maybe, Either; exceptions in IO exceptions, result typed errors and panics (Chapter 10)
Resource release try-with-resources use [Kotlin standard library] defer Drop bracket [Haskell base library] Fun.protect [OCaml Manual] destroy, defer (Chapter 11)
Integers fixed width, wrap fixed width, wrap fixed width, wrap panic in debug builds, wrap in release Int bounded, Integer unbounded fixed width, wrap [OCaml Manual] unbounded (Chapter 5)
Concurrency threads; virtual threads [JEP 444]; structured concurrency in preview [OpenJDK 2023] coroutines, structured [Kotlin documentation] goroutines and channels threads; async with library runtimes green threads, STM domains [OCaml Manual] and libraries structured async, process workers (Chapter 20)

Read across a row and Okkama is rarely alone. Rust, Haskell and OCaml share its answer to absence; Go, Rust and Haskell share its refusal of implementation inheritance; Haskell's Integer, the type its integer literals default to, is unbounded like Okkama's int. Read down a column and the picture changes: no other language in the table gives all of Okkama's answers at once, and that is the design's one new idea (Section 1.10).

26.2 Java

Java is the language Okkama argues with most, because Elegant Objects, the discipline Okkama turns into rules, was written for Java programmers (Section 2.7). Almost every Okkama rule is something a Java team can adopt by convention: final fields, no setters, no null, composition instead of extends, small interfaces with fakes. What Java cannot give is the guarantee. A convention holds as long as every reviewer catches every exception to it; in Okkama the compiler does.

Java answers some of the same problems with newer features. Records are immutable carriers of data [Gosling 2023], close to what Section 27.4 calls a shorthand for data objects. Virtual threads make blocking code cheap [JEP 444], and structured concurrency, still a preview in Java 21, gives tasks a parent scope that waits for them [OpenJDK 2023]. Java keeps null, checked exceptions and class inheritance, and for a language with Java's installed base, removing them is not an option. Okkama had no installed base, which is the only reason it could start where Java's best practice ends.

26.3 Kotlin

Kotlin took Java's runtime and changed its defaults: classes are final unless declared open [Kotlin documentation], nullability is part of a type and checked by the compiler [Kotlin specification], data classes come with copy [Kotlin documentation], and all exceptions are unchecked [Kotlin documentation]. Its coroutines are structured: a coroutine belongs to a scope that does not complete until its children do [Kotlin documentation], which is the model of Chapter 20.

The difference from Okkama is one of degree. Kotlin makes the safer choice the easier one, and keeps the other within reach: var, open, !! and platform types from Java are all available when a programmer wants them. Okkama removes the other choice. A Kotlin team can write Okkama-style code; an Okkama program cannot be written any other way.

26.4 Go

Go and Okkama agree on more than their surfaces suggest. Neither has classes or inheritance, both treat errors as values that a function hands back rather than throws past its caller, both release resources with defer [Go specification], and both keep the language small. The disagreements are just as basic. Go's interfaces are structural, satisfied by any type with the right methods; Okkama's roles are declared (Section 14.2). Go's values are mutable and its nil reaches pointers, interfaces, maps and slices. And Go's go statement starts a goroutine that nothing waits for, the unstructured concurrency that Chapter 20 argues against.

Go chose simplicity of the language and left discipline to the programmer and to tools such as linters. Okkama chose simplicity of the program: a smaller set of things that can go wrong, bought with a stricter language.

26.5 Rust

Rust is the closest relative in purpose. It has no null, no inheritance, values immutable unless declared mut, errors as Result, and resources released by Drop when their owner goes out of scope [Klabnik 2023]. Its traits are nominal contracts, like roles, though they may carry default methods. Where Rust differs is in what it asks of the programmer to get there. Ownership and borrowing are checked at compile time and written in the program: lifetimes, & and &mut, moves. The reward is memory safety without a garbage collector and control over every allocation.

Okkama makes a different trade. Its memory is managed automatically, and deterministic destruction is reserved for resources (Section 11.1), so most programs never mention ownership, and a resource is released by the scope that made it without annotations. Rust also overflows: integer arithmetic panics in debug builds and wraps in release builds [Klabnik 2023], where Okkama's integers grow (Chapter 5). A program that needs Rust's control of memory should be written in Rust.

26.6 Haskell

Haskell is the purest language in the table: values never change, effects are confined to types such as IO, absence is Maybe, and contracts are type classes [Haskell 2010]. Much of Okkama's vocabulary comes from this line, through ML: enums with payloads and match (Chapter 16), Maybe, roles that resemble type classes with declared instances (Section 14.10).

Two differences matter. Haskell infers types across a whole program, while Okkama infers only inside bodies and asks for every declaration to be annotated (Section 4.5). And Haskell is lazy by default: an expression is evaluated when its value is needed, which makes some programs elegant and the cost and the order of evaluation harder to see. Okkama is strict, and its order of evaluation is fixed and written down (Section 9.7). Haskell's purity is enforced by types; Okkama's immutability is enforced by the absence of assignment, and its effects are ordinary calls on objects that carry the authority for them (Chapter 21).

26.7 OCaml

OCaml is ML with objects and an industrial track record. Bindings are immutable, absence is option, failures are exceptions or result, and modules with signatures and functors are its main tool for abstraction [OCaml Manual]. It also has a class system with inheritance, which most OCaml code does not use, and mutable record fields and references when a program wants them. Its integers have a fixed width and wrap on overflow [OCaml Manual]. Since OCaml 5, domains run in parallel on several cores [OCaml Manual].

OCaml shows that an expression-oriented, immutable-by-default language with algebraic data types can be fast and practical. It keeps the escape hatches, mutable fields and classes, that Okkama removed, and it has the recursive variants and nested patterns that Okkama does not have yet (Section 27.2).

26.8 Python

Python is the language most readers have written something in, and its design statement says, among other things, that practicality beats purity [Peters 2004]. Some of Okkama's answers are Python's too. Its int has been one unbounded type since PEP 237 [PEP 237], exact fractions are a standard module (fractions.Fraction) [Python fractions] where Okkama has the built-in rat, and with releases a resource when a block ends [Rossum 2005], the idea behind defer and destroy. Since Python 3.11 asyncio.TaskGroup awaits every task created in it when its block exits [Python asyncio], which is the structured await of Chapter 20 as a library object.

The differences are in where the rules live. Types are optional annotations [Rossum 2014], checked by tools outside the interpreter; a program whose annotations are wrong still runs. None can stand where any value is expected, objects are mutable unless a class takes care, and a class may inherit from several others. A call works on any object with the right methods, the structural typing that Section 14.2 contrasts with roles. Exceptions are unchecked, and a bare except Exception catches errors and bugs alike, where Okkama separates the two channels (Chapter 10). A float holds infinities and NaN (Section 5.5).

Python trades guarantees for the speed of writing a first version, and it makes that trade on purpose. A Python program that follows Okkama's rules by convention, with frozen dataclasses, no None in signatures and annotations checked in continuous integration, is close to an Okkama program in shape. What it lacks is the guarantee that a module someone else wrote follows the same conventions.

26.9 Swift

Swift, introduced by Apple in 2014, is the industrial language closest to Okkama in its defaults [The Swift Programming Language]. Values of struct and enum types are copied, not shared; let declares a constant; absence is an optional T? that the compiler checks; enumerations carry associated values and are taken apart by switch with exhaustiveness checking. Integer arithmetic traps on overflow by default, and wrapping needs explicit operators such as &+. Structured concurrency, async let and task groups, is part of the language [Evolution 2021].

Swift keeps both worlds, as Kotlin does. Beside value types it has classes with single inheritance and shared, mutable instances. Its protocols are nominal contracts like roles, but a protocol extension can give them default implementations, the inheritance of behaviour that Okkama declined (Section 1.9, #146). Memory is managed by reference counting, so a class instance's deinit runs as soon as the last strong reference goes: memory and resources are released by one mechanism, where Okkama collects memory and gives deterministic release only to objects with destroy (Chapter 11). A function that can fail is marked throws, and each call marks try; an Okkama signature does not say that an action can fail (Section 10.19).

26.10 Erlang

Erlang was built at Ericsson for telephone switches that must not stop [Armstrong 2003]. Its data is immutable, a variable is bound once, integers are unbounded, and functions take their arguments apart by pattern matching. Its unit of concurrency is the process: an isolated, cheap thread with its own heap that shares nothing and communicates only by messages [Erlang Reference Manual]. Its unit of failure handling is the process too. Instead of handling every error where it occurs, a process that meets one is allowed to crash, and a supervisor that is linked to it restarts it in a known state.

Okkama shares the first half of this design: immutable values, no shared mutable state between tasks, and the state-owner pattern of Section 20.6, in which one task owns a piece of state and others send it requests over a channel, which is how an Erlang process holds state. It differs in the second half. Okkama's tasks run in one program and are structured: a failure travels to the task that awaits, as a typed value it can handle, and nothing restarts automatically. Isolation by memory is what process workers give (Chapter 21), at the price of a separate program. Erlang is also dynamically typed, with static checking left to optional tools.

26.11 Clojure

Clojure is a Lisp for the JVM, which Rich Hickey released in 2007 after two years of work on his own time [Hickey 2020]. Of all the languages in this chapter, it has thought hardest about the question Okkama answers with successors: what changes when "nothing changes". Its answer separates values from identities.

  • A value never changes. Its vectors, maps and sets are persistent: an "update" returns a new collection that shares most of its structure with the old one, through Bagwell's hash array mapped tries [Bagwell 2001; Clojure Reference].
  • An identity is a reference, such as an atom, a ref or an agent, that holds one value after another. Each one has its own rule for how the next value replaces the current one.

Okkama keeps the first half and drops the second. Its values are immutable, and its maps and arrays share structure in the same way (Chapter 8). A successor is Clojure's assoc with a name and a type. Okkama has no general reference type for identity, though. State that really changes lives in a task that owns it (Section 20.6), or in Atomic and Cell, which are ordinary library objects. Clojure makes the reference the central idea, and Okkama makes it a rare tool.

The differences come from typing and from Lisp.

  • Clojure is dynamically typed. Its data is "just maps" with keyword keys. Okkama data is named objects whose fields the compiler knows.
  • nil is everywhere in Clojure. A missing key yields nil, and much of the core library is written to accept it. Okkama spells absence out as Maybe and else (Chapter 7).
  • Clojure's protocols are open. extend-protocol makes a type that already exists, String for example, satisfy a new protocol after the fact. Okkama's roles are declared by the object itself, and it has no retroactive conformance (Section 14.2).
  • Resources are closed by with-open. It is a macro around try and finally, and only code that remembers to use it gets the release. Okkama ties release to the owner's scope (Chapter 11).

26.12 C#

C# appeared in 2002 as Microsoft's answer to Java, and it has absorbed more of the ideas in this book than any other mainstream language [C# documentation]. Each of them arrived as an addition, never as a default:

  • generics, iterators and nullable value types in 2005;
  • LINQ, with lazy queries over sequences, in 2007;
  • async and await in 2012;
  • nullable reference types, switch expressions, using declarations and default interface members in 2019;
  • records with value equality and with expressions in 2020 [C# language reference];
  • union types and closed hierarchies in November 2026.

Several of these look like Okkama. A record's with expression, order with { Status = Paid }, is a successor: a new value with one field changed. A using declaration disposes a resource when its scope ends, as Okkama's destroy does. A switch expression over a closed hierarchy is a match over a variant. The async model that C# introduced spread to JavaScript, Python and Rust (Section 20.2).

The difference is the direction of the defaults.

  • Mutability is the default. A record is immutable, but a class is mutable unless written otherwise.
  • null stays. Nullable reference types produce warnings, and a ! silences them (Section 7.12).
  • Release is opt-in. A resource is disposed only where its user wrote using. Forgetting it leaves the object to a finalizer, if the object has one.
  • Behaviour is inherited. Classes inherit implementations, and since 2019 interfaces can carry default ones.
  • A task starts at once. An async method begins as soon as it is called, while an Okkama future waits for its first await (Section 20.1).

C# shows how far a language can travel toward these ideas while keeping every program that was written before. Okkama shows the language that results when nothing has to be kept.

26.13 TypeScript

TypeScript adds static types to JavaScript, which it compiles to, and the types are erased in the output. Its type system is structural by design: "type compatibility in TypeScript is based on structural subtyping", and a value fits an interface if it has the members, whatever it was declared to be [TypeScript Handbook]. That is the opposite of Okkama's roles, which an object must claim by name (Section 14.2). The choice suits a language that has to describe JavaScript written without any types.

On absence, TypeScript went where Okkama did. Under strictNullChecks, null and undefined are types of their own. A string cannot hold them, and a union string | undefined must be narrowed before use [TypeScript Handbook]. Unions of object types with a literal tag, the "discriminated unions", are checked by the same narrowing, which gives TypeScript something close to Okkama's variants without a separate kind of declaration.

The language is deliberately unsound. The handbook says so itself: the type system "allows certain operations that can't be known at compile-time to be safe" [TypeScript Handbook]. any turns checking off. Function parameters were compared bivariantly until a strict flag was added, and casts are never checked at run time, because the types no longer exist then. TypeScript's types describe a program they cannot fully constrain. Okkama's types are the program's own rules, and its run time keeps them: a value has one concrete type, and a role reference cannot be cast down to the object behind it (Section 14.3).

26.14 A port, step by step

The rules are easiest to compare on one small class. Here is a bank account in Java, written the way a Java course would write it:

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class Account {
    private final String owner;
    private long cents;

    public Account(String owner, long cents) {
        if (cents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative balance");
        this.owner = owner;
        this.cents = cents;
    }

    public void withdraw(long amount) {
        if (amount > cents) throw new IllegalStateException("overdrawn: " + cents + " < " + amount);
        cents -= amount;
    }

    public String shown() { return owner + " " + cents; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, Account> accounts = new HashMap<>();
        accounts.put("ada", new Account("ada", 1000));
        Account ada = accounts.get("ada");
        ada.withdraw(300);
        System.out.println(ada.shown());
        Account bob = accounts.get("bob");
        System.out.println(bob == null ? "no bob" : bob.shown());
        try {
            ada.withdraw(5000);
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("refused: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        System.out.println("in the map: " + accounts.get("ada").shown());
    }
}

Run with Java 26, it prints:

ada 700
no bob
refused: overdrawn: 700 < 5000
in the map: ada 700

The same program in Okkama:

module app v1.0.0;

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;

enum Refused is Error = (negative, overdrawn(balance is int, wanted is int));

object Account {
    has owner is string;
    has cents is int;
    Account(:owner, :cents) {
        confirm cents >= 0 else throw Refused.negative;
    }
    withdrawn(amount is int) is ^Account {
        confirm amount <= cents else throw Refused.overdrawn(cents, amount);
        ^cents = cents - amount;
    }
    shown() is string { owner + " " + cents.string(); }
}

main() is int {
    let out = Stdout();
    let accounts = ["ada": Account(owner: "ada", cents: 1000)];
    let ada = accounts["ada"].withdrawn(300);
    out.writeln(ada.shown());
    out.writeln(if accounts.has("bob") { accounts["bob"].shown(); } else { "no bob"; });
    let refused = try { ada.withdrawn(5000).shown(); }
        catch Refused.overdrawn(balance, wanted) {
            "refused: overdrawn: " + balance.string() + " < " + wanted.string();
        };
    out.writeln(refused);
    // The map still holds the account it was given; the new state is a new value.
    out.writeln("in the map: " + accounts["ada"].shown());
    let updated = accounts + ["ada": ada];
    out.writeln("in the updated map: " + updated["ada"].shown());
    0;
}

Output:

ada 700
no bob
refused: overdrawn: 700 < 5000
in the map: ada 1000
in the updated map: ada 700

Each change in the port is a decision that the Java version left implicit.

  • The balance is no longer a mutable field. withdraw becomes withdrawn, a successor (Chapter 13). The Java map shows the changed balance, ada 700, because the map and ada share one mutable object. The Okkama map still holds the account it was given, ada 1000, and the new state reaches the map only when the program puts it there: accounts + ["ada": ada]. A port has to decide, at every mutation, who should see the change.
  • The missing key is no longer null. accounts.get("bob") returns null, and the code must remember to check it. In Okkama a missing key is a failure unless the lookup says what to do: here accounts.has, or accounts["bob"] else …, or a Maybe (Chapter 7).
  • The exceptions become a vocabulary. IllegalArgumentException and IllegalStateException say that something is wrong; the enum Refused says what: negative and overdrawn(balance, wanted). The caller catches the case it handles and reads its payload instead of parsing a message (Chapter 10).
  • The constructor keeps its check. Java's if … throw becomes confirm … else throw, and in neither language can an account exist with a negative balance.

What the port did not need: getters (shown() is the one question the program asks; a caller that needed a few facts would get a cap, Section 12.8), a final keyword (every field is final), and a check that owner is not null (a string cannot be absent). The port is about as long as the original; it says more about what can happen.

26.15 What the comparison shows

Three things stand out.

  • Okkama's rules are not new. Each comes from a language in this table or from the literature behind it. What is new is that all of them hold at once, in one language, by rule rather than by convention.
  • The other languages keep exits. Kotlin's var, Rust's unsafe [Klabnik 2023], OCaml's mutable fields, Java's null: each language with a safer default also keeps the less safe choice for the programs that need it. Okkama has fewer exits: Cell for synchronous code, Atomic for state shared between tasks, and natives for the host. A program that needs another one is a program Okkama does not serve well, and Chapter 27 lists where that shows.
  • Maturity is the largest difference. Every language in the table has libraries, tools, books and production systems built over years or decades. Okkama has a conformance suite, a standard library being rewritten, and this book. A comparison of designs is only half of a comparison of languages.

Chapter 27Weaknesses, Open Problems and the Road Ahead

Every chapter of this book ends by counting what its design costs and what does not work yet. This chapter gathers those counts in one place and sorts them by kind, because the kinds call for different answers:

  • what was missing and has since been added, which shows how the razor's gaps are closed;
  • what the language intends to have and does not have yet;
  • what the standard library and the tools still lack;
  • open questions, where both answers have a case and none is decided;
  • costs accepted on purpose, which are not on any road to change.

Each item appears in one group only. Items with an issue are cited by its number, so a reader can check the state after November 2026, when this chapter was written; items without one point to the section that argues them.

27.1 Closed while this book was written

Chapter 1 admitted that some removals were made before their replacements were complete, and that the standard library audit of November 2026 had asked for the operations a smaller design needs. Most of those requests were answered within days, in 0.4.1 and 0.4.2:

Issue What was missing What the language has now
#210 searching, trimming and case in strings builtins (Section 6.4)
#211 searching and reshaping arrays contains, index_of, reversed, take, drop (Section 8.1)
#231 turning a char into a number or a string, and back code(), char(n), string() (Section 6.7)
#145, #151 appending to arrays, updating maps + and - on collections (Section 8.5)
#150 searches that stop at the first decisive element any, all, find (Section 8.2)
#149 default parameter values trailing parameters with defaults (Section 13.2)
#152 a mutable value for synchronous code Cell (Section 13.11)
#153 named compile-time values const (Section 19.6)
#154 releasing a resource that must wait async destroy (Section 11.8)
#147 cancelling the future a task awaits structured await (Section 20.5)
#214 result types on anonymous actions (n is int) is int { … } (Section 4.5)
#215 operators on library number types operator roles (Section 14.7)
#216 asserting that a block throws test.throws (Section 15.2)
#233 a silent requirement of ordering() the diagnostic names the import (Section 8.1)
#256–#258 diagnostics for while, += and break; else if; postfix return Section 9.11

Two requests were declined, with reasons that are part of the design: default bodies in roles (#146, Section 1.9) and chainable actions for roles (#213), where the owner's answer was that lazy views keep composition explicit. The table is the razor's procedure in action: a missing operation is added as an operation, not by bringing back the entity whose removal made it necessary.

What writing this book found

A book whose examples must run is a test suite that reads the language the way its users will. Writing this one turned up three gaps that no test had caught, each where an example did something ordinary.

  • Fractions handed out text (#743, closed). Measuring how far exact fractions grow (Section 5.11) showed that rat.numerator() and rat.denominator() returned their parts as text. The choice was made when int had a fixed width and kept after int became unbounded. They return int since 0.6.0.
  • A successor's future could be dropped (#754, fixed). The Book says that an async successor's obligation moves into its future, which must be awaited or handed on (Section 13.14). The checker rejected a dropped call but accepted a future bound to a name and never awaited. Since 0.6.0 the check is complete; making it complete raised one question for the owner, and the answer is that cancel() discharges the obligation.
  • A failed test could not say why (#756, fixed). When test.is compared two objects that differ, the report printed their heap identities, Duration@52e44f14340, instead of their values (Section 15.8). Since 0.6.0 it prints Duration(origin: 2).

The first changed what programs see, and the second settled a question the rule had left open; both took the owner's decision. All three are places where the implementation had fallen behind what the rules already said, which is the kind of gap a book of running examples is good at finding.

27.2 Missing from the language

Three open issues describe what the language plans to have and lacks. All three are about enums and patterns, and together they are the largest difference between Okkama's enums and the algebraic data types of ML, Rust or Haskell (Section 16.7).

  • Recursive variants (#287). A case cannot carry a value of its own enum, so a tree or an expression type cannot be declared directly. Today such a structure is an object graph built from roles, or an array of nodes that refer to each other by index.
  • Nested patterns (#288). case Pair.both(Maybe.some(x), y) is rejected; the inner value is taken apart by a second match in the body.
  • Variants as map keys (#289). A payload-free enum can key a map; a variant cannot, even when its payloads could.

The first two are the ones that matter for programs. Interpreters, parsers and compilers are the classic programs written with recursive types and nested patterns, and in Okkama they are written today with more objects and more matches than in the languages Okkama compares itself with.

27.3 The library and the tools

The standard library was written quickly, before several builtins existed, and it is to be rewritten in the style Chapter 22 describes. Most of its open items wait for that rewrite.

  • Closed in 0.6.2. Five items this section used to list are done: the library calls the string builtins instead of its old workarounds (#260), LocalizedCase gives Turkish, Azeri and Lithuanian case (#261), the I/O decorators have asynchronous forms (#131), nine cleanup guards are async destroy objects (#329), and okkama run -t has report formats, seeds, workers and deadlines (#339).
  • Absence is not reported uniformly. Some modules return a Maybe, some throw a typed error for a missing value, some take a fallback (Section 7.14). The json module's reading style is the reference the library is being aligned with.
  • The test runner. TAP is not one of its report formats, and a per-test deadline needs --workers: a test in the runner's own process cannot be stopped from outside (Section 15.11).
  • A set that has been added to cannot be walked (Section 8.11). addition and difference return the role Set<T>, which cannot also promise Iterating<T> until roles compose. Either role composition or an addition that returns the concrete set closes it.
  • Packages (Section 19.11). blade has no registry and no workspaces, and a program cannot depend on two major versions of one package.
  • Authority below the native groups (Section 21.8). A host can deny a group of natives, but not one call; finer, per-object capabilities for the library are future work.

27.4 Open questions

These are designs that have been considered and not decided. Each has a case on both sides, and the razor does not settle it by itself: it asks what work the new entity would do that nothing present can.
